In hepatocellular carcinoma, differential nucleosome analysis revealed cancer-associated chromatin remodeling involving regulatory pathways, transcription factor motifs, and candidate genes. Importantly, tissue-derived nucleosome signatures were detectable in cfDNA, enabling classification among three cancer types (AUROC = 0.877) and colorectal cancer detection (AUROC = 0.930), with an AUROC of 0.773 in an independent validation cohort. We also developed OncoNucAtlas, a publicly accessible database facilitating exploration of these nucleosome landscapes. Conclusions: Our study cancer-associated nucleosome organization as a complementary source of epigenomic information and demonstrates the potential of tissue-derived nucleosome signatures for cfDNA-based cancer detection. The pan-cancer atlas provides a resource for investigating tumor heterogeneity and developing noninvasive cancer detection approaches.
affiliations: Soochow University (corresponding author)

papers.title: PlasmoRhythm: A comprehensive database for malaria-associated rhythmic transcripts, proteins, and metabolites
papers.abstract: Abstract: Motivation: The malaria transmission cycle is temporally organized across three interacting biological systems: the parasite, vertebrate host, and mosquito vector. Rhythms in parasite development, host physiology, and vector behavior govern infection dynamics, transmission, and the efficacy of stage-specific antimalarial interventions. However, the molecular architecture connecting these rhythms remains difficult to interrogate because time-resolved omics datasets are distributed across species, experimental paradigms, and analytical frameworks, with no unified resource for comparative analysis. Results: We developed PlasmoRhythm, a curated database integrating 67 transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets from 15 studies, encompassing 1,126 sampling events across Plasmodium species, mammalian hosts, and Anopheles vectors. Harmonized metadata and rhythmicity outputs from JTK_CYCLE, ARSER, Lomb-Scargle, and the meta2d function support interactive cross-study interrogation of molecular profiles. Dedicated modules enable the exploration of rhythmic virulence factors and antimalarial drug interactors, providing a unified framework for hypothesis generation across the malaria transmission cycle. Availability: PlasmoRhythm is freely accessible at https://project.iith.ac.in/cgntlab/PlasmoRhythm/.
affiliations: Department of Biotechnology, Indian Institute of Technology Hyderabad, Kandi, Sangareddy, Telangana, India (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pathological musculoskeletal characterisation of a new model of spontaneous OA in CD1 mice.
papers.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a whole joint disease involving pathological changes in cartilage, synovium, ligaments, menisci and periarticular muscle. This study provides a comprehensive musculoskeletal characterisation of spontaneous OA in male CD1 mice to evaluate their suitability as a model of naturally occurring disease. Knee joints from 3-4 and 6-8 month old mice were analysed histologically, OARSI scoring and immunohistochemistry for markers of chondrogenesis and endochondral ossification. Quadriceps and gastrocnemius muscles were examined for fibre cross sectional area. CD1 mice displayed mild OA at 3-4 months, progressing to moderate to severe disease by 6-8 months. Cartilage loss, synovial hyperplasia and fibrosis increased across compartments. Anterior cruciate and collateral ligaments, and medial meniscus exhibited marked pathological remodelling, including proteoglycan rich rounded cell regions and evidence of endochondral ossification with increased COL2, SOX9, RUNX2 and ASPN expression. Gastrocnemius muscle showed significant atrophy at 6-8 months, correlating with OA severity, whereas quadriceps atrophy was not significant. These findings establish CD1 mice as a robust spontaneous OA model that recapitulates the multi-tissue complexity of human disease. Because CD1 mice are globally available, cost-effective, genetically diverse and frequently, this model offers a practical and translationally relevant platform for investigating whole-joint organ mechanisms of OA progression and for evaluating therapies aimed at modifying disease across the entire joint.
affiliations: University of Liverpool (corresponding author)

papers.title: DNA-Encoded Library-Guided Discovery of a First-in-Class Molecular Glue of the NOS1AP-SCRIB Complex in Alzheimer's Disease Patient-Derived Neurons
papers.abstract: NOS1AP is an adaptor for neuronal nitric oxide synthase that engages several partner proteins and is implicated in Alzheimer's disease. Efforts to drug NOS1AP have sought to disrupt these; we instead report pharmacological stabilization of one interaction. Affinity selection of a 1.4-billion-member DNA-encoded library identified a benzimidazole-5-carboxamide chemotype, optimized by fragment-directed SAR to NOSTRA with submicromolar NOS1AP binding affinity. Of six interactions, NOSTRA enhanced only SCRIB binding, with a cooperativity factor of 30, predominantly through a 14-fold slowing of dissociation; native mass spectrometry resolved a NOS1AP:NOSTRA:SCRIB ternary complex. In healthy human iPSC-derived cortical neurons, NOSTRA engaged the endogenous complex and activated Rac1 without cytotoxicity; in Alzheimer's patient-derived neurons, it lowered the A{beta}42/A{beta}40 ratio and p-tau217, reduced neurofilament light and improved network activity. With an in vitro ADME profile consistent with CNS exposure, NOSTRA is the first molecular glue for a NOS1AP complex, establishing interaction stabilization as a viable NOS1AP pharmacology.
affiliations: Columbia University Irving Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Beyond Better Models: Barriers and a Path Forward in Generalisable TCR Antigen Specificity Prediction
papers.abstract: T cells are at the centre of adaptive immunity, protecting the organism against infection and cancer. T cell receptors (TCRs), expressed on the surface of T cells, enable the recognition of target cells through interactions with peptides presented by major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) molecules. Reliable, large-scale mapping of TCRs to their cognate pMHCs remains a holy grail of modern systems immunology, with far-reaching implications for cancer immunotherapy, vaccine development, and the understanding and treatment of autoimmune diseases. While exhaustive experimental mapping remains intractable due to the enormous combinatorial sequence space of TCRs and pMHCs, computational approaches offer a promising alternative. Consequently, we have witnessed increasingly sophisticated computational models of TCR antigen specificity, from small neural networks to deep generative models and large protein language models. However, several independent benchmarks have shown that these models, despite their size and sophistication, largely fail to generalise to TCRs or pMHCs not present in the data available during model development. Here, we investigate possible reasons for this and suggest a path forward to generalisable TCR:pMHC prediction. First, our analysis of the largest public repositories of TCR:pMHC data reveals significant biases towards a small number of antigens and MHC molecules, sparse sampling of TCR sequence space per pMHC, as well as inconsistencies and inaccuracies in data collation. Second, we show the importance of carefully setting up model evaluation to measure discrimination based on antigen specificity instead of confounding factors present in the evaluation data. Finally, we highlight the need for and propose how best to match the evaluation metric with the specific downstream application of the predictions. Our investigation suggests that we, as a community, need more representative and better curated data, and a robust set of metrics and benchmarks to guide future model development towards generalisable TCR:pMHC specificity prediction.
affiliations: The University of Oxford (corresponding author)

papers.title: CAPO: Compute-Aware Automated Protein-Model Optimization
papers.abstract: Protein models such as Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM), AlphaFold and Boltz have transformed computational protein science, yet a pretrained model rarely transfers to a particular laboratory's assay without adaptation to its data and experimental setting, and that adaptation is technically demanding and spends real compute budget. Existing agentic systems can automate model training, yet typically treat fine-tuning as a reliable tool call: feasibility and cost are estimated rather than measured, and infeasibility is discovered only after compute has been spent. We formulate protein-model adaptation as a gated decision problem: given a task, raw data and a compute budget c_max, a system should decide whether and how to adapt a model before committing expensive computation. We introduce CAPO (Compute-Aware Automated Protein-Model Optimization), a multi-agent system built around one rule: gate before you train. CAPO measures feasibility on the target accelerator, projects cost against the available budget, runs a canary inside the actual training loop and maintains an auditable artifact trail; critically, it can decline an unaffordable adaptation and select a cheaper alternative. We evaluate CAPO, without system changes, on three protein-modeling tasks: (i) SARS-CoV-2 host-range prediction, (ii) hit-to-lead affinity ranking and (iii) temporal variant-effect reclassification. On host range, CAPO partially fine-tuned an 8-million-parameter ESM-2 model to a species-averaged MCC of 0.826, compared with 0.743 for a hand-designed expert transformer; it matched a general coding agent while using 57.4% less GPU time and reduced failed training trials from four to zero. For hit-to-lead affinity ranking, CAPO rejected Boltz-2 fine-tuning and instead trained an assay-calibrated lightweight head over frozen representations, improving ranking on 11 of 15 held-out targets in 1.68 GPU-hours. On temporally held-out ClinVar variants, rank-4 low-rank adaptation of ESM-2 reached an MCC of 0.478, compared with 0.252 for a one-hot baseline and 0.000 for the frozen zero-shot score. These results come from single runs, without a gate ablation and with one generalist-agent comparison. Within those limits, they show that measured admission control can make protein-model adaptation not only automated but selective: deciding what to compute, what not to compute and why.
affiliations: Botnar Institute of Immune Engineering (corresponding author)

papers.title: Comparison of the performance of sporophytes derived from narrow and wide genetic crosses between strains of the cultivated kelp Saccharina latissima
papers.abstract: Seaweed mariculture allows sustainable production of large quantities of biomass for multiple downstream applications but the genotypes cultivated by this industry need to be improved to increase efficiency and cost-effectiveness. It is important that the genetic improvement of cultivated strains does not lead to the introduction of foreign genetic material into wild seaweed populations, which are already under threat from global heating. To circumvent this problem, efforts are being made to develop breeding approaches based on the use of locally-resourced genetic material. The aim of this study was to evaluate the potential effectiveness of this 'local' breeding strategy compared to a classical breeding approach based on wide genetic crosses. Analyses of growth rates and cell wall composition of F1 hybrids derived from either intra- or inter-population crosses between Saccharina latissima strains from two localities, southern Brittany, France and the Faroe Islands, did not identify any clear advantage of inter- compared to intra-population crosses. Breeding based on locally-resourced strains would therefore appear to be a valid approach for current strain selection programs. The study also established a large collection of gametophyte strains from multiple sites for future breeding programs and showed that these strains retained the capacity to become fertile after more than ten years in culture.
affiliations: Sorbonne University, CNRS, Integrative Biology of Marine Models Laboratory, Station Biologique de Roscoff, Roscoff, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: FluOpti: an open-source system for programmable whole-plate optogenetics and multi-fluorescence imaging
papers.abstract: Bacteria are able to self-organize into complex spatial communities, such as colonies, biofilms and swarms. Probing cells and gene networks with dynamic stimuli while preserving their spatial organization is therefore essential for understanding how bacterial communities organize across spatial and temporal scales. Optogenetics offers a powerful approach for such a task given the precise control of stimulus delivery without the perturbations normally associated with the addition of liquid inducers. However, most optogenetics devices have been developed to work with liquid cell cultures or to deliver a spatial pattern without the concurrent recording of gene responses and colony growth. Here, we describe FluOpti, an open source, low-cost device for controlling gene expression, through programmable light inputs, and recording multi-fluorescence responses and colony growth across whole petri dishes. White light LEDs are used for brightfield imaging while green and red LEDs are used as optogenetic inputs to activate and inactivate target genes via the CcaS/R two component system in E. coli. Low cost blue and orange acrylic are used as excitation and emission filters for fluorescence imaging, respectively. We developed custom software to analyze colony growth and optogenetic responses from 72-hour time-lapse experiments. A mathematical model was developed to predict gene expression levels in response to green-to-red light ratio stimuli. We use FluOpti to reveal a spatially structured response to optogenetic stimuli, with gene activation rates differing in cells located at the center and edge of colonies. to validate its use at a whole petri dish scale, FluOpti was used to depict how Voronoi territories can act as predictors of colony size, in congruence with previous studies. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of the device for studying gene networks at multiple spatio-temporal scales, from individual colonies to the whole petri dish. Performing optogenetics studies in whole petri dishes while preserving spatial arrangements could offer valuable insights into the spatial biology of gene networks in microbial populations.
affiliations: ANID - Millennium Science Initiative Program - Millennium Institute for Integrative Biology (iBio), Institute for Biological and Medical Engineering, Schools o (corresponding author)

papers.title: Determinants of cysteine coverage by chemoproteomics
papers.abstract: Covalent chemoproteomics has become a powerful route to expanding the druggable proteome, enabling proteome-wide screening of compounds that covalently modify nucleophilic residues, most commonly cysteine. Yet typical experiments detect only 5-18% of the ~250,000 cysteines encoded by the human proteome, and the determinants of this limited coverage remain poorlydefined. Here we combine cysteine featurisation, explainable machine learning (ML) and robust statistical filtering to establish what governs cysteine detectability in iodoacetamide- desthiobiotin (IA-DTB) chemoproteomics. Using a scalable feature-generation pipeline, we computed physicochemical and structural properties for cysteines and the corresponding tryptic peptides and trained models that predict detectability with high accuracy. Shapley analysis identifies protein abundance and intrinsic peptide properties governing LC-MS behaviour as the dominant determinants, whereas cysteine structural descriptors contribute comparatively little, indicating that detection is constrained downstream of probe reactivity. We further introduce a distance-based statistical filter that improves reproducibility across replicates, and show that cell line selection, subcellular fractionation and alternative electrophiles together expand coverage by >30%. More broadly, this work moves optimisation of chemoproteomics workflows from empirical trial-and-error towards rational, data-driven design.
affiliations: Crick-GSK Biomedical LinkLabs, GSK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Relation-Aware Graph-Hypergraph Networks for Antibody Sequence-Structure Co-Design
papers.abstract: Motivation: The design of antibody complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) is pivotal for therapeutic development, yet remains challenged by the complexity of the antibody-antigen interface. Existing methods, which largely rely on pairwise relationships, struggle to capture intrinsic multi-body interactions and global structural constraints. Results: We propose the Relation-Aware Graph-Hypergraph Network (RA-GHN), a framework that unifies graph-based pairwise modeling with biophysical hypergraphs to capture high-order cooperative effects. Its heterogeneous hypergraph uses epitope-paratope interaction patches, spatial structural clusters, and high-degree hub structures. A dual-pathway architecture integrates a Relation-Aware Equivariant Graph Network with an Equivariant Hypergraph Encoder while preserving SE(3)-equivariance. We also introduce the Structure-Sequence Decoupling Index, which balances structural reliability with sequence novelty. Experiments show that RA-GHN outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across standard benchmarks and affinity optimization tasks.
affiliations: Macao Polytechnic University (corresponding author)

papers.title: DIMPLE: A Tree-Guided Divide-and-Conquer Framework for ILS-Aware Phylogenetic Network Inference on Large-Scale Data
papers.abstract: Inferring evolutionary histories of species provides a foundation for comparative genomics and evolutionary analyses. Extensive evidence of reticulate evolution motivates the inference of phylogenetic networks, which represent relationships that species trees cannot capture. However, accurate reconstruction of large phylogenetic networks remains a major challenge because of the vast space of possible network topologies. Here, we propose DIMPLE, a divide-and-conquer framework for phylogenetic network inference without an explicit restriction on network level. DIMPLE uses a tree-of-blobs (TOB), which represents the tree-like relationships between regions of potential reticulation while leaving relationships within those regions unresolved. Within each unresolved region, DIMPLE partitions the set of taxa into pairwise-disjoint subsets, each containing at most a user-specified number of taxa. Multiple division runs are allowed, and subsets from different runs may overlap. DIMPLE infers a subnetwork on each subset, merges the subnetworks within each region, and uses the TOB to assemble the resulting networks into a network on the full taxon set. Experiments with true inputs demonstrate accurate merging, with improved reticulation recovery over existing methods on higher-level networks. With estimated inputs, DIMPLE achieves competitive topological accuracy and more consistently recovers hybrid ancestry than competing methods across varying levels of network complexity. Its computational requirements support analyses of hundreds of taxa. Applications to fern and gymnosperm datasets recover documented hybridization and previously reported phylogenetic conflict.
affiliations: Rice Univeristy (corresponding author)

papers.title: DeepD enables efficient genome modeling and controllable long-context sequence generation across domains of life
papers.abstract: Genome foundation models hold great potential for advancing biological research, but modeling diverse complex genomes and generating controllable genome-scale sequences remain challenging. We present DeepD, a phylogeny-informed sparse mixture-of-experts model operating at single-nucleotide resolution over a 1-million-token context while reducing active computation. Pretrained on unselected whole-genome sequences across all domains of life, DeepD learns genic and intergenic sequence features and supports broad sequence-to-function prediction across species. DeepD performs well in human protein fitness and disease variants effect prediction, such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, with particular strength in regulatory regions, such as promoter and transcription-factor binding sites. Expert routing captures exon-intron boundaries, transposable elements, and distal cis-regulatory elements. DeepD also generates experimentally validated core promoters with specified transcriptional strengths. Finally, the Context-Anchor-Body strategy enables generation of complete yeast chromosome sequences and megabase-scale Arabidopsis segments, preserving gene structure and order while introducing variations within natural ranges. Together, DeepD is an efficient genome foundation model that unifies accurate sequence-to-function prediction with controllable genome-scale generation, advancing predictive and generative design of complex genomes.
affiliations: China Agricultural University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Enhanced DNA Scanning and Target Specificity via Motif Sequestration
papers.abstract: Sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins must efficiently locate their target sequences within large, structurally heterogeneous genomes while avoiding nonproductive off-target interactions. Here, we show that an autoinhibitory conformational state of the site-specific recombinase Cre lowers nonspecific DNA-binding affinity to promote one-dimensional DNA scanning while suppressing off-target assembly of recombinogenic complexes. Recent studies indicate that the C-terminal segment of Cre transiently adopts a sequestered conformation that occludes the catalytic domain's DNA-binding surface. Using NMR spectroscopy, single-molecule fluorescence microscopy, and optical trapping, we investigated how this conformational equilibrium regulates target search. NMR measurements reveal that the sequestered state predominates in the absence of DNA and persists at noncognate sites, whereas binding to cognate loxP sequences relieves autoinhibition. Single-molecule tracking demonstrates that full-length Cre undergoes processive one-dimensional diffusion and transitions to stable binding upon cognate-site recognition, whereas C-terminal truncation impairs scanning efficiency by arresting diffusion. These findings demonstrate how transient motif sequestration coordinates target search with site-specific complex assembly, suggesting a general mechanism by which DNA-modifying enzymes balance search efficiency and target specificity.
affiliations: The Ohio State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Carbendazim Disrupts Cellular Homeostasis and Proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans: A Global Proteomic Approach
papers.abstract: The extensive use of the broad-spectrum fungicide carbendazim (CBZ) has raised increasing environmental concerns due to its persistence and toxicity, leading to regulatory restrictions in several countries. Despite its widespread occurrence, the molecular mechanisms underlying CBZ toxicity in non-target organisms remain poorly understood. Here, we employed quantitative proteomics to characterize the systemic molecular response of Caenorhabditis elegans following exposure to a sublethal concentration of CBZ (0.01 mg.mL-1) from the L1 larval stage to day 1 of adulthood. A total of 273 differentially abundant proteins were identified in the N2 strain. Functional enrichment analysis revealed coordinated alterations in biological processes associated with protein synthesis, proteostasis, mitochondrial function, energy and lipid metabolism, intracellular trafficking, chromatin organization, and redox homeostasis, indicating extensive cellular reprogramming in response to CBZ exposure. Protein-protein interaction network analysis further identified ribosomal proteins and translation-associated factors as the principal hub proteins, suggesting that disruption of the translational machinery represents a central molecular event underlying CBZ toxicity. Collectively, these findings show that CBZ's biological effects extend beyond its established role as a microtubule-disrupting fungicide, affecting multiple interconnected cellular pathways involved in maintaining homeostasis. This study provides the first comprehensive proteomic characterization of CBZ toxicity in C. elegans, offering new mechanistic insights into its mode of action and highlighting the utility of integrative proteomics for assessing the impact of environmental contaminants on non-target organisms.
affiliations: Federal University of Pampa (corresponding author)

papers.title: Gut microbially produced phenolic acids have differential and sex-dependent effects on host metabolic health
papers.abstract: Gut microbiota-derived metabolites are increasingly recognized as important regulators of host metabolism, but the specific functions of individual metabolites remain poorly understood. We therefore investigated the metabolic effects of two structurally related, phenylalanine-derived microbial metabolites phenylacetic acid (PAA) and phenylpropionic acid (PPA) in a mouse model of diet-induced obesity. Although clinical studies have linked PAA and its downstream product phenylacetylglutamine to metabolic disease, PAA did not alter body mass or adiposity in this model. Instead, it improved glucose tolerance selectively in male mice and markedly remodeled lipid metabolism in both sexes, reducing circulating triglycerides and acylcarnitines and activating hepatic PPAR--associated transcriptional programs associated with fatty acid {omega}-hydroxylation and peroxisomal lipid metabolism. Despite this extensive metabolic remodeling, PAA did not worsen hepatic steatosis, fibrosis, or markers of liver injury. By contrast, PPA had minimal effects on hepatic metabolic pathways but produced pronounced sex-dependent physiological responses, increasing adiposity in female mice and improving glucose tolerance in male mice. These findings show that structurally related microbial metabolites can have distinct, sex-dependent metabolic effects and highlight the need to define the actions of individual microbiome-derived metabolites when developing targeted therapies for metabolic disease.
affiliations: Cleveland Clinic Research (corresponding author)

papers.title: CXCL9-Dependent Immune Networks of Spontaneous Tertiary Lymphoid Structures in a Murine Subcutaneous Tumor Model
papers.abstract: Recent discoveries have identified human tumor tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) as organized clusters of innate and adaptive immune cells and stromal cells. Cancer-associated TLS can promote tumor clearance and enhance responses to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) immunotherapy. However, the absence of TLS in conventional mouse tumor models, particularly subcutaneous transplant models, limits experimental manipulation and study of TLS development. By tuning tumor antigen expression, we have generated a subcutaneous tumor model that naturally forms TLS within the immune-hot, vasculature-rich peritumoral adipose tissue. These TLS were identified as clusters of B and T cells in close proximity to high endothelial venules. TLS organization was underpinned by spatially compartmentalized chemokine expression, with CCL21 produced in the T cell zone of perivascular TLS and CXCL13 present in the B cell region. Single cell transcriptomic sequencing showed that the immune composition in the TLS forming peritumoral tissue resembled human cancer TLS signatures. Upon anti-PD-L1 ICB treatment, TLS underwent expansion, which was associated with increased interferon responses in macrophages and coincided with tumor clearance. We further identified the interferon-inducible chemokine CXCL9 as a key regulator of the TLS microenvironment. CXCL9-expressing macrophages populated TLS, interacting with B cells following ICB treatment. CXCL9 deficiency reduced B cell recruitment to peritumoral tissue and TLS formation. Further T and B cell receptor sequencing indicated a CXCL9-dependent promotion of antigen-specific responses within the tumor and TLS niche. Combined, these findings establish a tractable subcutaneous model of naturally arising tumor TLS and define the cellular and molecular networks that regulate their formation and function. This provides a platform to dissect how TLS develop and test strategies that promote TLS formation to enhance cancer therapy.
affiliations: Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research (corresponding author)

papers.title: IL-2 and CD40L can establish and sustain a human B cell-mediated immune regulatory network
papers.abstract: B cells can control inflammation, but the factors governing B cell-mediated immune regulatory network remain unclear. We report that IL-2/CD40L enable class-switched memory (CSM) B cells to acquire an immunosuppressive phenotype characterized by the expression of surface TIGIT as well as multiple other inhibitory receptors (PD-1, LAG-3, GITR, CD39, and CTLA-4) and soluble molecules (IL-10, granzyme B, and IL-35). TIGIT+ CSM B cells expressing functional CCR9 exhibit significant defects in total immunoglobulin secretion, while preserving IgA2 secretion. Furthermore, IL-2/CD40L-induced ex vivo-generated TIGIT+ CSM B cells suppress human T cell-mediated inflammation in a xenogeneic mouse model of acute graft-versus-host disease, while promoting IL-10-producing regulatory T cell (Treg) response. These findings identify IL-2/CD40L as key drivers of a B cell-mediated immune regulatory network, especially by generating TIGIT+ CSM B cells that can further promote Treg response. This study supports the development of TIGIT+ B cell-based therapy models for inflammatory diseases.
affiliations: Mayo clinic (corresponding author)

papers.title: A CAR T cell-amplified suppressive B cell circuit in AML
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is constrained by a hostile bone marrow niche. Here we identify atypical memory B cells (Batyp) as a suppressive population within this microenvironment. Across single cell and flow cytometry cohorts, Batyp were expanded in AML, and their molecular and phenotypic profiles resembled those of atypical B cells associated with chronic inflammatory conditions. Batyp were polarized within the AML microenvironment, and this was amplified by CAR T cell-AML interactions. Mechanistically, polarization was dependent on Toll-like receptor, interferon and CD70-CD27 signaling. Batyp suppressed T cell and CAR T cell responses via PD-1- and TGF-beta signaling, and were enriched in non-responding patients with AML and myeloma. CD180-directed CAR T cells, targeting an antigen shared by Batyp and AML blasts, resisted suppression in vitro and cleared disease in B cell-humanized xenografts while sparing hematopoietic stem cells, with B cell engagement further enhancing their expansion. CAR T cells thus reinforce their own suppressive niche through Batyp polarization, a constraint that can be relieved by dual blast- and B cell-targeting strategies.
affiliations: Department of Medicine III, LMU University Hospital, LMU Medizin, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitaet Muenchen, Munich, Germany; Institute of Clinical Pharmacology, (corresponding author)

papers.title: Sustained antigenic engagement programs multidimensional CTL states with distinct cytotoxic capacities
papers.abstract: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) eliminate infected or malignant cells through repeated target-cell encounters, yet how they sustain cytotoxic activity during extended antigenic stimulation remains poorly understood. In particular, it remains unclear whether preserved population-level killing reflects maintenance of a uniform effector phenotype or diversification into functionally distinct CTL populations. Here, we combined live-cell imaging, high-dimensional cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, phenotypic trajectory analysis, population sorting, and rechallenge killing assays to define how human clonal CTLs remodel during sustained antigenic engagement. Prior antigen encounter altered the kinetics and pattern of target-cell membrane permeabilization but did not compromise overall subsequent killing upon rechallenge. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling after prolonged engagement revealed broad remodeling of antigen-experienced CTLs and heterogeneous cytotoxic transcriptional programs. Time-resolved scRNA-seq further showed that these functional dimensions remodeled with distinct kinetics, with rapid induction of activation- and cytotoxicity-associated programs, later remodeling of vesicular-trafficking programs, and progressive reduction of adhesion/ contact interaction -associated programs. High-dimensional cytometry showed that this temporal remodeling was accompanied by progressive redistribution of CTLs across a multidimensional protein-expression landscape defined by distinct combinations of cytotoxic, vesicular/degranulation, activation, cytokine, adhesion, and regulatory features. Phenotypic trajectory analysis organized this protein landscape along a temporal remodeling axis, with early lytic-granule-rich profiles giving way to multiple late-engaged phenotypes with distinct combinations of functional protein features. Surface-marker-defined late CTL populations displayed distinct killing capacities upon rechallenge, demonstrating that preserved population-level cytotoxicity can coexist with substantial functional heterogeneity. Finally, CAR T cells exposed to CD19+ targets retained cytotoxic activity upon rechallenge and acquired multidimensional phenotypic features that partially overlapped with the remodeling framework identified in clonal CTLs. Reanalysis of longitudinal patient-derived CAR T-cell transcriptomes further showed that related functional programs were dynamically organized after infusion, with the features distinguishing responder and non-responder tisa-cel samples changing between the infusion product and day 7. Together, these findings indicate that sustained CTL killing is accompanied by progressive multidimensional remodeling and diversification rather than maintenance of a fixed effector phenotype. Our findings support a model in which population-level cytotoxic activity can be maintained while the CTLs composing that population progressively diversify into functionally distinct states during sustained antigenic engagement.
affiliations: National Institute of Health and Medical Research (INSERM) UMR1037, Cancer research center of Toulouse (CRCT), Toulouse, FR (corresponding author)

papers.title: Alternative splicing use ratio is not conserved between human and mouse immune cells
papers.abstract: Most human genes have mouse orthologs. However, orthology at the level of exons and alternative splicing events is not well defined, and the use of alternative splicing events in immune cell types has not been compared between human and mouse. We mapped exons and alternative splicing events between human and mouse. Based on this mapping, the use ratio of orthologous alternative splicing events was compared between human and mouse immune cell types and fibroblasts. Out of the 1,823 human-mouse orthologous alternative splicing events that are expressed in the five tested immune cell types, most (62-67%) showed a significant difference in use ratio between human and mouse, and less than third (21-25%) retained the same ratio. Our results reveal both conserved and divergent alternative splicing usage ratio, and highlight the dynamic evolution of alternative splicing regulation across human and mouse immune cell types. By integrating exon orthology with observed splicing patterns, our analysis provides a functional framework for studying mammalian splicing ratio evolution beyond static transcript annotations.
affiliations: Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (corresponding author)

papers.title: Stage-specific checkpoint signalling by ATM, ATR and DNA-PK safeguards oocyte genome integrity
papers.abstract: In somatic cells, DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are potentially catastrophic lesions that activate phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase-related kinase (PIKK) signalling to promote DNA repair or eliminate damaged cells. During meiosis, however, DSBs are deliberately generated as essential intermediates in homologous recombination, raising the question of how DNA damage signalling distinguishes programmed recombination from genome instability. To define how PIKK signalling is adapted to these distinct contexts, we resolved the function of the three PIKKs ATM, ATR and DNA-PK in physiological meiotic recombination and the response to postnatal DNA damage in mouse oocytes. Following postnatal irradiation, ATM functions as the dominant response kinase, with ATR and DNA-PK acting redundantly to eliminate damaged oocytes. In contrast, meiotic surveillance is mediated by ATR, with ATR removal rescuing oocyte loss in response to asynapsis and, independently, to persistent meiotic DSBs. Our findings demonstrate that DNA damage signalling is developmentally reconfigured during oogenesis and highlight distinct pathways of oocyte elimination that may ultimately inform strategies to maintain the ovarian reserve in mammals.
affiliations: The Francis Crick Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: cBAF drives AR-V7 expression through regulation of transcriptional termination in castration-resistant prostate cancer
papers.abstract: The androgen receptor splice variant AR-V7 drives resistance to androgen receptor-targeted therapies in castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), but the mechanisms governing its expression remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the canonical BAF (cBAF) chromatin remodeling complex as a selective regulator of AR-V7 expression. Pharmacologic and genetic disruption of cBAF reduced AR-V7 levels, suppressed AR-V7-dependent transcriptional programs, and impaired CRPC cell proliferation. Mechanistically, cBAF binds an intronic regulatory element downstream of AR cryptic exon 3, where it maintains chromatin accessibility, enhancer activity, and promoter-enhancer looping. cBAF loss decreases recruitment of transcription termination machinery, reduces RNA polymerase II Thr4 phosphorylation, and promotes transcriptional readthrough beyond the AR-V7 polyadenylation site. POINT-seq revealed that cBAF-dependent transcriptional termination is required for AR-V7 biogenesis and regulates termination at a subset of genes genome-wide. Together, these findings uncover a role for cBAF in chromatin-mediated control of transcriptional termination and establish this mechanism as a critical determinant of AR-V7 expression.
affiliations: Purdue University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Thille, a chromosome-level type B avocado genome, and the structural and allelic variation at candidate flowering-type loci
papers.abstract: Avocado (Persea americana Mill.) is heterodichogamous: each flower opens first as female and then as male, and cultivars fall into two complementary flowering types, A and B, determined by the transcription factor SDMYB, whose dominant allele confers type A. Avocado genomes have so far come from type A cultivars. Here we report a chromosome-level genome of Thille, a type B cultivar used in breeding. From 72.2 Gb of PacBio HiFi reads (81x coverage) and Omni-C data, the assembly places 859.8 Mb, 96% of the expected 896 Mb genome, in 12 chromosomes with an NG50 of 84.5 Mb, a consensus quality of QV 69.95, and 97.3% complete BUSCO genes; repeats occupy 64.0% of the assembly, and 35,386 protein-coding genes were predicted. We compared Thille with the type A cultivars Hass and Puebla, a predominantly Guatemalan hybrid, and with a West Indian (WI) accession, a Lowland botanical group variety of unreported flowering type. The assemblies differ by large rearrangements, including an 18.8 Mb inversion on chromosome 12 specific to Hass. Using phased reads and haplotype assemblies, we reconstructed the alleles of candidate flowering genes from a type A versus type B Fst scan. Both WI haplotypes carry the recessive SDMYB allele found in Thille; based on this study and the previous study of SDMYB, we predict the WI accession to be type B. Six genes, including SDMYB, carry an allele shared by all three type A cultivars and absent from Thille and WI. The genome and HiFi reads are available under BioProject PRJNA1142556.
affiliations: Department of Computer Science, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA, 95616; Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of California, La (corresponding author)

papers.title: RiboBridge couples RNA backbone generation to sequence design through a learned interaction topology
papers.abstract: Designing ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecules with prescribed structures and functions is central to RNA engineering. Backbone-first approaches generate three-dimensional geometry before assigning a nucleotide sequence, yet leave open how that geometry should be represented for downstream sequence design. Here we introduce RiboBridge, which infers a probabilistic residue-pair state from backbone geometry, recycles binary pair probabilities through a second pass and transfers binary and typed signals as soft attention biases for sequence decoding. On 550 generated backbones, pair-type decoding achieved joint refolding validity of 0.451 versus 0.335 for an architecture-matched topology-free decoder. On a matched 110-backbone intervention cohort, replacing aligned pair states with exact-length donors matched on pair-state statistics reduced joint validity from 0.464 to 0.214, showing backbone alignment matters. Pair-confidence ranking enriched the joint-validity rate from 0.451 overall to 0.596 among the top 248 before external refolding, with the same ranking signal transferring to independently generated RFDpoly and RNA-FrameFlow backbones. On 53 experimentally determined backbones, pair-coupled decoding improved secondary-structure agreement relative to residue-wise argmax. These results support a learned relational interface between sequence-free backbone generation and sequence design.
affiliations: School of Engineering, Westlake University, Hangzhou, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: Metalink: Joint taxonomic and functional profiling of metagenomes and metatranscriptomes across resolution scales
papers.abstract: Metagenomic and metatranscriptomic analyses remain largely fragmented: taxonomic and functional profiling are performed separately, often at a single resolution (reads, contigs, or MAGs) yielding separate species or function lists rather than mechanistic insights. Here, we developed Metalink, a tool that unifies taxonomic and functional profiling into coupled outputs across all three resolution levels. Metalink is built on three innovations. First, we constructed a Last Common Function-based functional Hierarchy (LCFH) from ~424 million proteins, organizing KEGG Orthologs into a tree structure that enables LCA-like functional assignment. Second, a unified framework integrates the taxonomy of Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB), the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV), and NCBI for consistent classification across reads, contigs, and MAGs. Third, a multi-level integration strategy with overlap-based deduplication balances accuracy and completeness. At the read level, Metalink exceeds both HUMAnN3 and eggNOG-Mapper in functional assignment accuracy while running ~30-fold faster and 1,000-fold faster, respectively; at the contig level, its functional profiles remain highly consistent with eggNOG-Mapper. Multi-level integration further improves taxonomic resolution over single-level analyses and outperforms leading taxonomic profilers on the CAMI II benchmarks. Metalink's joint outputs move the analysis of metagenomes and metatranscriptomes from cataloging species and functions toward mechanistic inference of species-function-environment triadic associations. By enabling these integrated analyses across resolution scales, Metalink provides a general framework for linking community composition to its functional potential across diverse ecosystems.
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Distance-AF Multimer: A Multi-Step Approach for Protein Complex Structure Modeling with User-Defined Distance Constraints
papers.abstract: The three-dimensional structure of proteins provides essential insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying their function. Many biological activities are mediated through protein interactions, making accurate structural determination of protein complexes important. Despite significant advances in computational protein structure prediction, there are still many cases where protein complexes are not correctly assembled. In particular, there are cases where experimental data, such as distances between residue pairs in interacting proteins are available, yet existing prediction methods fail to produce models consistent with these data. Here, we present Distance-AF Multimer, a method that guides and refines AlphaFold-Multimer docking predictions using user-provided residue pair distance information. This approach extends our previously successful data-guided single-protein modeling method, Distance-AF. Distance-AF Multimer operates in a two-step process, starting from multiple initial conformations and iteratively refining them to satisfy the provided distance constraints. We evaluated Distance-AF Multimer on protein-complex benchmarks spanning different chain counts and docking errors, demonstrating competitive or superior performance compared to other existing deep-learning-based structure prediction methods. In addition to dimer cases, we also demonstrated the potential of Distance-AF Multimer for large-scale protein assemblies containing multiple chains, including those with more than 5 chains.
affiliations: Purdue University (corresponding author)

papers.title: An integrated database of ion channels
papers.abstract: Ion channels play critical roles in a wide range of physiological processes, including the propagation of nerve impulses, insulin secretion and regulation of heart rate. Alterations in ion-channels function or expression can contribute to the development of various diseases, including cancers, genetic disorders, and infectious diseases. Ion channels represent the second-largest class of membrane proteins considered potential targets for therapeutic intervention. However, a comprehensive data resource integrating information on human ion channels and their associations with diseases has been limited. Therefore, the Integrated Database of Ion Channels (IDIC) was developed, comprising information on 493 human ion channels. The database contains a broad range of ion-channel annotations, including gene and protein information, structural details, protein signature sequences, protein domains, nuclear localization signals, and signal peptides. It also provides cross-references to several established biological resources, including the Human Genome Organization Gene Nomenclature Committee (HGNC), National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene, Vertebrate Genome Annotation (VEGA), Ensembl, and the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Furthermore, IDIC incorporates genomic variations identified in various tumors and disease associations involving ion channels, which have been systematically curated from published literature. Through concise search methods and user-friendly browsing functionalities, IDIC serves as an integrated resource for exploring human ion channels and investigating their structural, functional, genetic, and disease-related characteristics. Thus, the database can facilitate a better understanding of ion channels and their potential involvement in diverse human diseases.
affiliations: Institute of Bioinformatics, Bangalore (corresponding author)

papers.title: Hierarchical distribution matching enables comprehensive characterization of common and condition-specific cell niches in spatial omics data
papers.abstract: Deciphering cell niches in complex tissues is essential for understanding tissue structure and disease. Recent advances in spatial omics have enabled subcellular resolution and accurate cell identity mapping. However, robust delineation of cell niches and disease-associated spatial patterns remains difficult. We introduce Harmonics, a novel computational framework that systematically identifies both common and condition-specific cell niches from spatial omics data through hierarchical distribution matching. Harmonics also includes a suite of downstream modules that facilitate comprehensive niche characterization. We demonstrate its scalability, accuracy and generalizability across datasets spanning diverse species, tissues, diseases, spatial modalities, and technological platforms. For condition-agnostic datasets, Harmonics outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and robustness, and further demonstrates the capability to resolve niche structures at finer granularity. Across diverse diseases including pulmonary fibrosis, triple-negative breast cancer, and colorectal cancer, Harmonics enables precise identification of condition-specific niches and reveals disease-associated dynamics, subtype-specific spatial patterns, and structured immune architectures. We envision Harmonics as a practical and versatile tool for spatial niche analysis that can be applied across a wide range of biological contexts and seamlessly integrated with existing spatial omics workflows.
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Latent-Factor Stability Is Not Sufficient: Evaluating SABLE-MO in Simulated and Cancer Multi-Omics Data
papers.abstract: Reproducibility is often used to assess latent factors learned from multi-omics data. Yet factors that recur across model refits may not reflect the shared biological structure of interest. We investigated this issue using SABLE-MO, a shared/private representation-learning framework with a sep-arate factor-retention procedure. We evaluated the method in simulations with known latent structure. The original retention rule produced no false biological shared-factor acceptance across 800 independent-null datasets, but accepted at least one false factor in 70 of 200 correlated-private datasets (35%). Following an exploratory analysis of this failure, we increased the lower-decile aligned-correlation threshold from 0.40 to 0.60 and tested it on a new, independently seeded simulation bank. False acceptance decreased from 33% to 19%, while recovery of true shared factors changed only slightly (94.375% to 94.0%). Exact modality-support attribution reached 67.5%, below its prespecified criterion. We also analyzed matched RNA expression, DNA methylation, and copy- number data from TARGET osteosarcoma (78 patients), TCGA-SARC (250), and TCGA-KIRC (304). Outcome-blind model selec- tion favored a simpler shared/private representation in TARGET.In both TCGA cohorts, the more complex representation improved cross-view retrieval and missing-view reconstruction relative to the simpler model, but worsened ordinary reconstruction. These external comparisons were performed before factor retention. Our results show that factor reproducibility, representation quality,and biological interpretation require separate assessment. Stricter retention reduced errors in a specific simulated setting but did not eliminate them
affiliations: Lakehead University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Free-Energy and Molecular Dynamics Analysis of Ser195 and Thr195 Rotameric States in Thrombin
papers.abstract: Ser195 is highly conserved as the catalytic nucleophile in trypsin like serine proteases, yet the molecular basis for the strong preference for serine over the chemically similar threonine residue remains unclear. Here, we used well tempered metadynamics and microsecond long molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to characterize the conformational energetics of S195 and T195 in thrombin. Well tempered metadynamics revealed distinct rotameric free energy landscapes in both the apo and the ligand bound systems. In the apo state, S195 preferentially occupied a lower angle rotameric state, while T195 exhibited two low energy states with similar free energies. Unbiased simulations further showed greater conformational heterogeneity and increased higher angle sampling for T195. Evaluation of the His57 to residue 195 hydrogen bond further revealed that S195 maintained close hydrogen bond distances across both rotameric regions, whereas T195 exhibited longer and more variable His57 to hydroxyl distances with reduced distance based occupancy. Analysis of the local environment showed that the additional T195 methyl group was associated with redistributed protein contacts. Additional rotamer conditioned analyses demonstrated differences in local packing within corresponding conformational states. Furthermore, solvent accessibility and water contact analyses revealed that the effects of the substitution on the catalytic side chain environment depend on rotameric conformation. Together, these findings demonstrate that two complementary simulation approaches converge on similar conformational preferences and suggest that the S195T substitution alters the rotameric free energy landscape in association with changes in catalytic geometry, local packing, and solvation. These results provide insight into the evolutionary preference for serine over threonine at the catalytic position of thrombin.
affiliations: University of Arkansas (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pleiotropy links host axes of defense against a pathogen
papers.abstract: Organisms face ubiquitous threats from pathogens, and in response hosts have evolved a cascade of defenses to avoid, resist, or tolerate infection. While these stepwise defenses may act independently, they can be pleiotropically linked via shared molecular mechanisms, regulation, and crosstalk. Here, we tested the extent to which pleiotropy shapes multiple axes of defense using knockouts of 16 single genes involved in innate immunity of Caenorhabditis elegans against the opportunistic bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Host genotype had variable effects on components of host defense. Traits such as infection-induced mortality and body size varied frequently across host genotypes, while behavioral avoidance, bacterial uptake, and susceptibility to bacterial colonization varied less frequently. Broadly, pleiotropy between defenses was common, driving patterns of variation that linked several traits together. However, important components of defense like mortality, avoidance, and susceptibility to colonization were more independent from one another. Our results show that pleiotropy between defenses can be common, highlighting the importance of moving beyond single phenotypes to understand multiple dimensions of host-pathogen interactions.
affiliations: University of British Columbia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Protein Crowding Buffers Membrane Fluidity
papers.abstract: Like cholesterol, protein crowding has been shown to alter the temperature dependence of lateral diffusion in biomembranes, eventually eliminating the distinct liquid-gel phase transition. Here, we resolve the molecular origin of this protein effect with coarse-grained and all-atom simulations of protein-crowded phosphatidylcholine bilayers, which give access to lipid structure and dynamics on both sides of the transition temperature. Unlike cholesterol, which is known to induce a continuous liquid ordered phase by having opposite effects on the two phases, we find that membrane proteins decrease lipid order at all temperatures studied. The disordering is stronger at low temperatures, so that once the proteins cover roughly half of the membrane area the low- and high-temperature phases become alike and the transition is lost. Our results suggest that in addition to local cholesterol concentration, local protein concentration may also help dictate membrane fluidity and especially its response to temperature change.
affiliations: Tampere University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Distinct activation mechanisms underlie ligand efficacy at a GPCR
papers.abstract: Ligands that bind to the same G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) can produce widely different levels of signaling. These differences in efficacy are central to pharmacology, yet how a receptor sequence determines signaling level remains incompletely understood. Here we develop a deep mutational pharmacology approach to measure how each residue in the -opioid receptor (OR) shapes responses to 15 opioids, yielding ~400,000 measurements of variant effects on signaling and expression, including full concentration-response series for three agonists. Mutational effects on potency are strongest near the orthosteric pocket, whereas effects on efficacy extend through the transmembrane core and intracellular face. Ligands share many functional determinants, but sensitivity to mutation differs with efficacy. As efficacy decreases, the residues required for signaling shift from the binding pocket towards the intracellular face; partial agonists therefore depend on residues that are dispensable for full agonists. Mutations can broadly increase receptor responses, allowing antagonists such as naloxone to produce signaling comparable to a full agonist and increasing the efficacy of partial agonist ligands. Combined mutations can also reorder the relative efficacies of ligands, showing that sequence changes reshape pharmacological differences rather than simply increasing or decreasing all responses together. These findings support a model in which ligands of different efficacy activate the receptor through distinct allosteric mechanisms which are determined by residues distributed across the receptor. Mapping these contributions across diverse ligands with deep mutational pharmacology provides a way to understand how one receptor converts molecular recognition into a range of signaling outputs.
affiliations: University of California, San Francisco (corresponding author)

papers.title: Piezophilic activity dominates the Puerto Rico Trench deep subseafloor biosphere
papers.abstract: Hydrostatic pressure defines the deep ocean, yet its role in structuring microbial activity across the subseafloor biosphere remains poorly understood. Here, we assessed pressure effects on anabolic activity in sediment communities across margin-proximal, bathyal, abyssal, and hadal settings of the Puerto Rico Trench (493-8,385 m water depth). Community-level responses to pressure reversed with burial, revealing an unrecognized shift toward piezophily in communities down to 20 meters below seafloor (mbsf). Atmospheric pressure yielded higher proportions of active cells in surficial sediments, whereas in situ pressure yielded higher proportions in the subseafloor. Pressure also structured active-community composition; in trench-axis sediments down to 8.35 mbsf, JS1/Atribacterota populations within widespread hadal lineages exhibited a physiological response to in situ pressure, indicative of subseafloor piezophily. These findings suggest that hydrostatic pressure acts as an ecological filter after burial, favoring piezophilic traits that may support microbial persistence in the deep subseafloor biosphere.
affiliations: Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego (corresponding author)

papers.title: Modelling Plant Cortical Microtubules: Curvature Sensing from Bending Energy
papers.abstract: Within plant cells, the self-organization of cortical microtubules (MTs) into ordered arrays is an important process for directional growth. There is growing evidence that cortical MTs respond to cell shape and/or mechanical stresses in the cell wall, requiring in silico models on complicated surfaces to provide a complete understanding. Most models assume that MTs are directionally persistent, following geodesics of the surface. This ignores the expected tendency of these elastic filaments to minimize curvature. Our recent model incorporated minimization of MT curvature in cylindrical cells and found curvature to be significant in biasing the array organization. Here, we generalize to a larger class of surfaces, studying individual microtubule shapes to provide insights into the role of geometric cues and highlight differences with previous models that use the geodesic assumption. We first show that geodesic models, including current models with finite persistence lengths, exhibit an invariance across certain geometries, leading to biophysically counterintuitive results. Incorporating curvature minimization, we show the difficulties imposed by high-curvature cell edges, elucidating potential new roles of proteins in helping microtubules traverse edges. Lastly, we show that geometries with competing curvature cues result in diverse curves previously not considered. These results provide geometric intuition for how various cell geometries affect individual cortical microtubules, helping us to better understand the processes required for the establishment of microtubule arrays in broad contexts such as: bundles spanning adjacent cell faces in prism-like root and leaf epidermis cells, protruding geometries of trichome cells, and rounded surfaces such as confined protoplasts.
affiliations: The University of British Columbia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chromosome-level genome and caste transcriptomes for Africa's most widespread social wasp (Belonogaster juncea) reveal unexpected genomic diversity
papers.abstract: Belonogaster is an African genus of primitively eusocial wasps. They are widespread and conspicuous across sub-Saharan Africa and yet are among the least studied groups of social wasps. Here, we present the first high-quality, chromosome-level genome assembly for a representative of this genus, Belonogaster juncea, complemented by an RNA-seq analysis of brain transcription among individuals representing reproductive and non-reproductive castes. The assembled genome spans 315.8 Mb with a scaffold N50 of 7.91 Mb. The annotation contained 15,159 protein-coding genes and 20,046 isoforms, with Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs (BUSCO) completeness of 98.0% for the genome and 97.8% for the annotation. Using this new assembly, we show that the B. juncea genome differs notably from other social wasp genomes: a single satellite repeat makes up a fifth of its chromosome-scale sequence, it has the highest putative chromosome number in a sequenced wasp genome to date, and it shows high levels of syntenic breaks. We find caste neuro-transcription differences between queens and workers, revealing 573 differentially expressed genes (341 worker biased, 232 queen biased), with significant overlap in caste-specific genes when compared to Polistes dominula and Liostenogaster flavolineata. This genomic resource provides a foundation for understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying primitive eusociality and social evolution in wasps, and opens up new research opportunities for a genus of little-studied insects from the Global South.
affiliations: University College London (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mapping the sequence preference of the generalist class II lanthipeptide synthetase ProcM by mRNA display
papers.abstract: The biosynthetic machineries of ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) are often substrate tolerant. A remarkable example is the class II lanthipeptide synthetase ProcM, which naturally functions as a generalist enzyme that has not evolved to use a specific substrate during its evolutionary history. Although ProcM has been studied extensively, the sequence features associated with productive modification remain underexplored. In this study, we use the ultrahigh-throughput mRNA display technique to map the sequence compatibility of ProcM across a focused library. This approach expands the landscape of ProcM reactivity beyond native substrates and individually characterized variants. Machine learning (ML) analysis revealed that the dataset contains sequence patterns associated with ProcM reactivity, with models achieving a balanced accuracy of 0.73. This moderate predictive performance contrasts with the near-perfect accuracy reported for specialized enzymes. This suggests that predicting substrate compatibility for generalist enzymes is more challenging due to uneven representation of reactive and nonreactive sequences and limitations of the available data.. Our results provide a high-throughput view of ProcM reactivity and highlight differences with previous high-throughput studies on substrate selectivity of RiPP modification enzymes. Future studies will need to assess whether these differences are common when comparing generalist with specialist enzymes.
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (corresponding author)

papers.title: Generative steering to adapt proteins beyond native biological contexts
papers.abstract: Proteins evolved for native biological contexts often fail when deployed in new cellular environments or therapeutic settings. We present ProVADA, a test-time framework that steers a pretrained protein generator toward externally defined properties while preserving functional constraints. Its Mixture-Adaptation Directed Annealing sampler combines coordinated mutations, population selection, and annealing to navigate rugged objective landscapes. Experimentally, ProVADA converted secreted human renin into an active, drug-inhibitable cytosolic protease and extensively deimmunized two murine single-chain antibody fragments to reduce HLA visibility while retaining antigen recognition. ESCAPE-seq measurements confirmed substantial depletion of HLA-I binder peptides across alleles. Deimmunized FMC63 variants retained CAR-T-cell killing and showed fewer binders than a tested humanized comparator. Together, these results demonstrate that broad sequence redesign can adapt functional proteins to non-native biological contexts.
affiliations: Stanford University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Generative modeling of spatially resolved perturbation responses with CONCERT
papers.abstract: Spatial perturbation transcriptomics measures gene expression responses to genetic or chemical perturbations in intact tissue. Each response depends on the intrinsic state of a cell and on its niche, the neighboring cells through which perturbation effects propagate. Here we present CONCERT a niche-aware Gaussian process variational autoencoder that embeds each perturbation with the niche of the receiving cell and learns a spatial kernel for each perturbation, whose lengthscale sets how far the effect extends in tissue. We evaluate CONCERT in within-niche prediction, for held-out cells in the niche where a perturbation was measured, and in cross-slide prediction, for a slide from which the perturbation was withheld during training. On a SPAC-seq screen of hundreds of knockouts at single-cell resolution and on Perturb-map lung tumors at spot resolution, CONCERT predicts response magnitude and gene ranking more accurately than counterfactual models trained on dissociated cells, spatial perturbation models and spatial nearest neighbor aggregation. In dextran sodium sulfate colitis, where each mouse is sampled once, CONCERT reconstructs spatial gene expression at unmeasured time points, enabling longitudinal comparison that separates changes over time from differences between mice. The predictions recover the nonmonotonic course of injury, which peaks at day 9 and resolves by day 21. In ischemic stroke, CONCERT predicts responses to lesions of different sizes and locations, in single sections and across serial sections in three dimensions, and reproduces the expression patterns of the lesion core and perilesional tissue. Across lung tumor, colon and brain tissue, CONCERT predicts niche-aware counterfactual responses at locations where a perturbation was not measured and reconstructs missing spatial data.
affiliations: Harvard University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Rigidity-Aware Geometric Pretraining for Protein Design and Conformational Ensembles
papers.abstract: Generative models have recently advanced de novo protein design by learning the statistical regularities of natural structures. However, current approaches face three key limitations: (1) Existing methods cannot jointly learn protein geometry and design tasks, where pretraining can be a solution; (2) Current pretraining methods mostly rely on local, non-rigid atomic representations for property prediction downstream tasks, limiting global geometric understanding for protein generation tasks; and (3) Existing approaches have yet to effectively model the rich dynamic and conformational information of protein structures. To overcome these issues, we introduce RigidSSL (Rigidity-Aware Self-Supervised Learning}, a geometric pretraining framework that front-loads geometry learning prior to generative finetuning. Phase I (RigidSSL-Perturb) learns geometric priors from 432K structures from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database with simulated perturbations. Phase II (RigidSSL-MD) refines these representations on 1.3K molecular dynamics trajectories to capture physically realistic transitions. Underpinning both phases is a bi-directional, rigidity-aware flow matching objective that jointly optimizes translational and rotational dynamics to maximize mutual information between conformations. Empirically, RigidSSL variants improve designability by up to 43% while enhancing novelty and diversity in unconditional generation. Furthermore, RigidSSL-Perturb improves the success rate by 5.8% in zero-shot motif scaffolding and RigidSSL-MD captures more biophysically realistic conformational ensembles in G protein-coupled receptor modeling. The code is available at: https://github.com/ZhanghanNi/RigidSSL.git.
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (corresponding author)

papers.title: Identifying and targeting abnormal mitochondrial localization associated with psychosis
papers.abstract: Therapeutics working by novel mechanisms are needed for patients with psychiatric conditions. Cell-based assays to identify candidates that reverse observed abnormalities, even if in subsets of patients, could accelerate the process. Here, we imaged peripheral cells (skin fibroblasts) of 168 individuals, stained for DNA, actin, and mitochondria. We found mitochondria tend to be farther from the cell border for patients who experience psychosis (including subsets of individuals with bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and schizoaffective disorder), a phenotype not seen in patients diagnosed with major depression. Because the phenotype could be identified by a single metric, we could query existing databases of cells stained for their mitochondria and treated with various chemical or genetic perturbations. We identified compounds and genes both negatively and positively affecting the psychosis-associated phenotype, including some known to impact psychiatric conditions. Developing therapeutics with novel mechanisms is a complex multi-step challenge. This cell-based assay holds promise for virtual and physical screening to identify candidates for treating psychiatric conditions.
affiliations: Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Imaging Platform, Cambridge, MA, US (corresponding author)

papers.title: Antibody-drug conjugate combination therapy targeting LGR5 and MET with different payloads enhances efficacy in preclinical colorectal cancer models
papers.abstract: Leucine-rich repeat-containing G protein-coupled receptor 5 (LGR5) is a marker of cancer stem-like cells frequently upregulated in colorectal cancer (CRC) with lower expression in normal tissues, making it a favorable target for antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs). ADCs combine antibody specificity with potent cytotoxic payloads to enhance efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity. LGR5-targeting ADCs incorporating different payloads demonstrate strong initial tumor inhibition, yet tumors eventually recur due in part to LGR5 downregulation, necessitating more effective strategies to prevent relapse. We show treatment with chemotherapies or an LGR5-targeting ADC coupled to a topoisomerase 1 inhibitor payload (8E11-CPT2) reduces LGR5 levels and increases MET receptor expression and/or activation in CRC cells, supporting a therapeutic approach to target LGR5 and MET simultaneously. Accordingly, we engineered a MET-targeting ADC (ABT-700-SG3199) via site-specific conjugation of the anti-MET antibody telisotuzumab (ABT-700) with the DNA-crosslinking pyrrolobenzodiazepine (PBD) dimer SG3199. ABT-700-SG3199 exhibited superior potency and efficacy in CRC models compared to the clinical-stage MET-targeting ADCs ABBV-399 and ABBV-400, which use the same antibody backbone conjugated to different payloads. Treatment with ABT-700-SG3199 increased LGR5 expression, and the combination of ABT-700-SG3199 with 8E11-CPT2 enhanced CRC cell-killing efficacy, reinforcing the rationale for a dual-targeting approach. In patient-derived xenografts, combined administration of 8E11-CPT2 and ABT-700-SG3199 markedly delayed tumor relapse and prolonged survival compared with single-agent treatment. Taken together, these findings reveal a reciprocal regulation between MET and LGR5 in response to LGR5- or MET-targeting ADCs in CRC models and support a LGR5/MET dual-targeting therapeutic strategy to enhance efficacy and potentially overcome resistance and relapse.
affiliations: University of Texas Health Science Center Houston (corresponding author)

papers.title: Alternative organelle targeting of OPA1 mediates fatty acid release from lipid droplets
papers.abstract: Mitochondria and lipid droplets (LDs) are functionally coupled to coordinate fatty acid utilization and storage. However, a comprehensive understanding of mitochondria-LD alliances remains elusive. We have identified a previously unrecognized role for optic atrophy 1 (OPA1), a mitochondrial fusion factor, in the regulation of fatty acid release from LDs. We demonstrated that OPA1's exon 4 adapts an amphipathic helix to target OPA1 to LDs. OPA1 localized to LDs promotes fatty acid release by facilitating the recruitment of lipases to LDs. In addition, OPA1's residence on LDs competes with its mitochondrial entry, influencing mitochondria fusion and connectivity. Furthermore, the S158N polymorphism within OPA1's exon 4 exhibiting attenuated fatty acid release from LDs is associated with altered circulating lipid levels in pediatric cancer survivors. Altogether, our findings reveal that OPA1 actively mediates fatty acid release from LDs and provide a mechanistic link between OPA1 and human metabolism.
affiliations: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital (corresponding author)

papers.title: Notch-dependent left-right asymmetry in β-catenin-TCF activity instructs anteroposterior positioning of motor neurons in the C. elegans ventral nerve cord
papers.abstract: The precise organization of motor neurons along the neuroaxis is essential for nervous system connectivity and function. In newly hatched C. elegans, the ventral nerve cord (VNC) contains 22 motor neurons of three classes, DD, DA, and DB, whose cell bodies are arranged in a stereotyped pattern along the anteroposterior (AP) axis. However, the mechanisms that control motor neuron positioning during nerve cord assembly are not fully understood. Here, we uncover a left-right asymmetry in {beta}-catenin-TCF transcriptional activity that regulates AP motor neuron positioning. Loss of bar-1/{beta}-catenin or pop-1/TCF causes a shift of motor neuron cell bodies toward the anterior, while loss of pry-1/Axin shifts them toward the posterior. We further find that POP-1/TCF activity is asymmetric between the left and right sides of the VNC in a BAR-1-dependent manner. Increasing BAR-1 levels on both sides of the VNC causes a posterior shift in motor neuron cell body placement. During VNC assembly, asymmetric Notch signaling promotes PRY-1 expression in left-side neurons, thereby restricting BAR-1 accumulation to right-side motor neurons, presumably through degradation by the destruction complex. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized pathway in which an initial Notch-dependent left-right asymmetry establishes asymmetric {beta}-catenin-TCF activity to regulate the AP positioning of motor neuron cell bodies along the VNC.
affiliations: Ottawa Hospital Research Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Impact of the N-glycosylation on full-length IgG2 and IgG4 antibodies: a comparative study using molecular dynamics simulations.
papers.abstract: Like other proteins, monoclonal antibodies - important biodrugs- are subject to post translational modifications, especially the N-glycosylations. However, the effect of the N-glycosylations remains poorly studied and atomistic details about their influence are rarely available. . Moreover, the few existing studies focus on the prevalent immunoglobulin G1. To go further in the understanding of the impact of glycosylations, we have carried out a comparative exploration of the effect of N-glycosylations on two different classes of antibodies, namely Mab231, an IgG2 and the pembrolizumab, an IgG4 . The two antibodies differ by their sequences, their length, their 3D structure but also by the location and composition of the glycans. In the present work, detailed and important information were gained through molecular dynamics simulations where both monoclonal antibodies were studied without and with the presence of their glycans. The results of 1.5 microseconds of sampling for each system show that glycosylation does not drastically alter the overall conformational landscape of either antibody, whatever the metrics considered. However, it measurably modulates local flexibility, inter-domain correlated motions, and the relative orientation of the Fab arms with respect to the Fc domain, with statistically significant shifts in key geometric descriptors. Importantly, contact analysis reveals that glycan interactions extend beyond the Fc region to reach Fab residues. The allosteric network calculations demonstrate that the influence of Fc-bound glycans propagates even until the Fab framework regions in both mAbs, which could impact the antigen binding. The nature and magnitude of these effects are subclass-dependent, reflecting differences in glycan composition, hinge architecture, and three-dimensional organization Our findings challenge the prevailing view that Fc glycosylation uniformly promotes CH2 domain opening. More importantly, it underscores the necessity of considering full-length structures and IgG subclass diversity in glyco-engineering strategies.
affiliations: Universite Paris Cite and Universite de la Reunion, INSERM, EFS, BIGR U1134, DSIMB Bioinformatics Team, F-75015 Paris, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: Sequence-dependent conformational and mechanical landscapes of double-stranded nucleic acids
papers.abstract: The sequence-dependent mechanical landscapes of double-stranded nucleic acids (dsNAs) remain largely unexplored beyond canonical dsDNA.
