Four additional IncC plasmids from other species were included, for a total of 32 IncC plasmids. IncC type 2 predominated among V. cholerae plasmids, and five novel core genome sequence types (cgSTs) were identified. Antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) occurred within diverse genetic structures inserted at specific sites in the conserved IncC backbone. Despite remarkable diversity in ARGs and associated genomic islands, the IncC backbone remained stable over five decades. These findings highlight the dynamic evolution and adaptability of IncC plasmids in 7PET under antimicrobial selection.
affiliations: Institut Pasteur (corresponding author)

papers.title: Antimicrobial resistance in a warmer world: selection and transfer of kanamycin resistance is temperature dependent in E. coli.
papers.abstract: Climate warming consistently correlates with increased antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Understanding the biological mechanisms underpinning this relationship is important for both prediction and mitigation of the future burden of antibiotic resistance in a warmer world, especially given AMR can spread through both selection and horizontal gene transfer. Here, we experimentally measure how temperature alters susceptibility to kanamycin, selection and spread of resistance in Escherichia coli MG1655 carrying the natural plasmids R1 and RP4. We predict that susceptibility should be lowest - and plasmid transfer highest - at maximal growth rate. Thermal performance of bacterial growth peaked at 40{degrees}C and we detected a small plasmid cost - for RP4, but not R1 - in the absence of kanamycin. The thermal performance of plasmid transfer did not mirror that of bacterial growth, instead, R1 transfer peaked at 35{degrees}C with a much narrower thermal tolerance. Susceptibility to kanamycin decreased with increasing growth rate until 31{degrees}C, before increasing again as temperatures approached and exceeded optimal growth temperature. Increasing susceptibility coupled with high growth rates meant that selection was strongest at the highest measured temperature, but the shape of the relationship changed with kanamycin concentration. In mixed populations of resistant and susceptible bacteria, we found that AMR spread most where selection was strongest, irrespective of plasmid transfer. Our findings suggest increased AMR at higher temperatures is predominantly driven by higher growth rates and increased susceptibility, resulting in stronger selection. Our study provides a framework to uncover generalities across antibiotic classes, strains, species, and plasmids, laying the foundation for improved prediction of AMR selection in the environment.
affiliations: University of Exeter (corresponding author)

papers.title: Bat-borne influenza A H9N2 virus shows species-specific replication and transmission
papers.abstract: Bat-borne H9N2 IAV (bat H9N2), initially detected in bat feces in Egypt in 2017, has recently attracted attention because of its unexpected pre-pandemic properties, including airborne transmission between ferrets and efficient replication in human lung explant cultures. However, its host range and potential reservoir hosts remain poorly defined, particularly with respect to additional bat hosts and mammalian or avian mixing-vessel species. Here, we compare the susceptibility of two pteropodid bat species, Rousettus aegyptiacus and Eidolon helvum, and additionally assessed pigs and quails following intranasal inoculation with bat H9N2. Juvenile R. aegyptiacus showed only low-level viral replication and shedding, largely restricted to the upper respiratory tract, and did not show transmission to contact bats. In contrast, both juvenile and adult E. helvum, despite showing no clinical signs, showed high-level viral replication and shedding in the upper respiratory tract, with efficient and early transmission to contact bats. Viral RNA was most abundant in the respiratory turbinates, the nasopharyngeal meatus and the tracheal epithelium, where it was associated with moderate to severe necrotizing rhinitis and tracheitis. The lower respiratory tract was less involved, with viral RNA confined to scattered bronchioles and associated with focal necrotizing bronchiolitis. Other organs, including the gastrointestinal tract, lacked histologic lesions and viral RNA labeling. In pigs and quails, intranasal inoculation did not result in detectable replication, transmission, or seroconversion. Our findings demonstrate marked differences in the susceptibility to bat H9N2 between the two fruit bat species tested and identify E. helvum as a highly susceptible host capable of rapid and efficient transmission. Conversely, pigs and quails were not susceptible, suggesting that additional viral adaptations may be required to allow for a productive infection in these species.
affiliations: Ludwig Boltzmann Gesellschaft (corresponding author)

papers.title: Rapid RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a detection of Vibrio coralliilyticus for coral aquaculture disease surveillance
papers.abstract: Coral aquaculture is expanding globally to support both the ornamental aquarium trade and reef-restoration initiatives, yet disease outbreaks remain a threat to production, causing potential substantial coral mortality and economic losses. Effective disease management requires early pathogen detection; however, conventional molecular diagnostics are labor-intensive and poorly suited to time-sensitive aquaculture operations. Here, we developed a rapid diagnostic assay for the coral pathogen Vibrio coralliilyticus by implementing recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/Cas12a-based fluorescent signaling for sensitive and specific detection. The assay was optimized and validated against DNA from seven V. coralliilyticus strains and seven non-target Vibrio species, demonstrating high specificity and a detection limit <10 target copies per reaction within 30 minutes following DNA extraction. Performance of the assay was further evaluated using water from flow-through aquaria containing healthy and diseased Acropora tersa colonies, and results independently validated using droplet digital PCR (ddPCR). Although RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a consistently detected V. coralliilyticus across the tanks holding both healthy and diseased corals, ddPCR indicated substantially higher pathogen abundance in diseased tanks, suggesting that pathogen load rather than the presence alone is a more reliable indicator of disease risk. Incorporating rapid semi-quantification of pathogen abundance in future assay development could therefore improve disease prediction and management. This study demonstrates the potential of CRISPR-based diagnostics as a fast, sensitive, and field deployable tool for routine coral aquaculture biosecurity, enabling earlier intervention and more effective mitigation of disease outbreaks.
affiliations: James Cook University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A staged evidence chain identifies a recent horizontal transfer of a HET-domain gene into a Fusarium tricinctum strain from a lineage related to the Fusarium oxysporum species complex
papers.abstract: Genes encoding the heterokaryon incompatibility (HET) domain form fast-evolving, highly paralogous families, which makes horizontal gene transfer (HGT) among them hard to separate from duplication, loss and annotation artefacts. We describe a staged evidence chain for testing a single HGT candidate and apply it to the strongest signal in the HET-domain view of a 109-genome similarity graph of 8,815 HET-domain (PF06985) proteins. Each stage is a separate test with a decision rule fixed before it was run: (i) a gene tree with ultrafast-bootstrap support; (ii) a species-tree check that donor and recipient lie in different clades; (iii) a genome-wide identity background and a contamination screen of the recipient assembly; (iv) a sister-species control that removes genes conserved by vertical descent; and (v) a tblastn search of whole genome assemblies, so that absence is tested in the DNA rather than in the gene annotation. We identify a recent horizontal transfer of a HET-domain gene into one F. tricinctum strain (MPI-SDFR-AT-0068) from a lineage related to the F. oxysporum species complex (FOSC). The F. tricinctum copy is 98.4% identical to its best FOSC hit (local protein identity), against a genome-wide median of 83%, and its synonymous divergence from the FOSC copies (median dS 0.11) is lower than that of 99.6% of F. tricinctum genes from their best F. oxysporum hits and of 91% of F. tricinctum genes from their best hits in the sister species, which argues strongly against vertical descent, hidden paralogy and shared ancestral alleles. Protein gene trees group it with the FOSC copies (UFBoot 96-98), and a nucleotide tree of the gene region places it as sister to all sampled FOSC copies (UFBoot 98). F. tricinctum and the F. oxysporum strains belong to different species complexes (species-tree patristic distance 0.075, about 22 times the distance between F. oxysporum strains). The gene is absent from the assembly of F. tricinctum's sister species, F. avenaceum (best locus 49% identity), and from 14 of 15 further F. avenaceum genomes, from 23 of the 26 assemblies of Fusarium species outside the FOSC and the F. tricinctum complex, and no other sequenced genome of the recipient strain's own lineage carries it; close copies (at least 90% identity) occur only in 7 of 9 FOSC strains and in one metagenome-assembled Fusarium genome from neither complex. In F. tricinctum the gene sits in an approximately 6-kb strain-specific island on a putative accessory scaffold with F. oxysporum-affine gene content, whereas in the FOSC it occupies one conserved, subtelomeric locus of a core chromosome. Assembly contamination was excluded, and single long reads span the gene and its flanks. The donor lineage remains unresolved, and formal reconciliation is still needed. The evidence chain is cheap and uses only public assemblies; each stage targets a specific alternative explanation, and synonymous divergence against the genome background proved the most decisive test.
affiliations: Iowa State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Molecular Characterization of Gene-Product Relationships in the Wheat Gluten Complex for Reduced Immunogenicity Wheat Development
papers.abstract: Immune-mediated reactions to wheat gliadins, including celiac disease and wheat allergies, affect ~1% of the U.S. population and are prevalent worldwide. Reducing the risk of inadvertent gluten exposure for individuals with celiac disease or wheat allergies requires the development of reduced immunogenicity wheat varieties which are suitable for human consumption. This study was designed with a view to improve our understanding of gene protein relationships at the complex wheat Gli1/Glu3 and Gli2 loci, and to develop genetic and molecular resources for breeding reduced-immunogenicity wheat lines. We conducted comprehensive genomic, biochemical, and immunological analyses of diverse wheat genetic resources, including aneuploid stocks, chromosome deficiency and interstitial deletion lines, Wasko omega null, the landrace San Pastore, Pegaso near isogenic lines lacking Gli1/Glu3/Gli2 loci, and progenies derived from a Wasko mega null X Pegaso(6A/6D) alpha null. Genomic characterization involved the targeted GlutEnSeq approach and PCR based DNA markers while biochemical and immunological analyses employed acid-urea PAGE, SDS PAGE, and ELISA. Integration of these complementary approaches resolved gliadin gene protein relationships at an unprecedented level. Notably, two F2; lines exhibited substantial reductions (both omega and alpha gliadins) due to the successful stacking of parental mutations. The resulting F2; progenies and associated DNA markers represent valuable resources for breeding wheat for reduced immunogenicity
affiliations: Clemson university Pee Dee Research and Education Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Compact Regulatory Logic Governs Fibroblast Cell State Plasticity in Fibrosis
papers.abstract: Fibroblast activation drives organ failure across human diseases, yet its regulatory basis remains largely undefined. Here, we repressed 280 conserved disease-activated enhancers using CRISPR droplet sequencing (CROP-seq) in ~550,000 fibroblasts, constructing a regulome of 15 gene programs governing the profibrotic state. Systematic TF perturbation converged on MEOX1 as a central regulator, and fibroblast-specific Meox1 deletion in mice improved cardiac function, reduced fibrosis, and rewired profibrotic fibroblasts toward quiescence in heart failure. Effector gene perturbation in human cardiac fibroblasts revealed distinct regulators of contractility, migration, and inflammatory signaling, and these programs were conserved across profibrotic states in human lung, liver, and skin. Simultaneous repression of just six enhancers using a multiplexed dCas12a-KRAB system collapsed the profibrotic network, suppressed migration and contraction, and rewired fibroblast paracrine signaling to attenuate macrophage inflammation. These findings define the regulatory logic of fibroblast plasticity and establish a new framework for reprogramming profibrotic cell states in disease.
affiliations: Gladstone Institutes; San Francisco, CA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mechanism-guided Discovery of Fluoroacetate Dehalogenase (FAcD) Variants for Enzymatic PFAS Defluorination
papers.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent anthropogenic "forever chemicals" whose strong C-F bonds (~460-533 kJ mol-1) resist defluorination, and the recast EU Drinking Water Directive sets parametric values of 0.10 ug L-1 for the sum of 20 specified PFAS and 0.50 ug L-1 for total PFAS. Here, we present DeFluorX, a mechanism-first pipeline that uses Boltz-2 to co-fold 2,150 bacterial fluoroacetate dehalogenase (FAcD) variants with 26 PFAS and fluoroacetate, generating uniformly high model confidence (rho = +0.08) but poorly tracked catalytic competence. Thus, the complexes were ranked and tiered by SN2-defluorination geometry based on the known mechanism of control of FAcDs RPA1163 with fluoroacetate: Odelta...C-alpha distance and Odelta-C-alpha-F angle; relay; carboxylate clamp; F-stabiliser; F-cradle; and penalties for scissile bond strength, backside occlusion, beta-fluorination and bond multiplicity. The tiering identified eight complexes (med angle 173.2 degrees, distance 2.91 A) with a high probability of degradation, including Alphaproteobacterial enzymes, with mono-, di- and trifluoroacetate attacking at 172-178 degrees versus 163 degrees for the control. We performed WaterMap, restrained 1 us Desmond MD, MM-GBSA and scans of the three WaterMap-aware best MD frames per complex using B3LYP/6-31G** QM/MM. All 12 frames exhibited product-end C-F cleavage with barriers ranging from 1.1 to 11.8 kcal mol-1, and the departing fluoride carried -0.43 to -0.63 e. The Laboratory validation is ongoing.
affiliations: Section of Plant Glycobiology, Department of Plant and Environmental Sciences, University of Copenhagen, Frederiksberg C-1871, Denmark. (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Evolving Bileome: A Pan-Repository Landscape of Expanded Bile Acid and Related Steroidal Signatures
authors: van der Hooft, J. J. J.
papers.abstract: Bile acids and related steroidal metabolites are among the most studied biomolecules, yet recent work has revealed far greater structural diversity than previously recognized, much of it shaped by the microbiome. We previously introduced a repository-scale bile acid MS/MS library built from queries targeting C24 bile acid fragmentation, limited to Orbitrap Q Exactive datasets within GNPS/MassIVE. Here we announce a major expansion of this library: a bile acid and steroidal MS/MS spectral library assembled across three major metabolomics repositories, now capturing C23, C24 (including alkamine), C26 (C-C bonded aceto derivatives), and C27 bile acids, as well as C28 bile alcohols. The expanded libraries comprise 640,141 unique MS/MS spectra, of which 120,293 (18.8%) match 2,529 reference spectra, leaving most of this steroidal chemical space structurally unassigned. Linked to harmonized pan-repository metadata, the library provides a starting point for classifying MS/MS spectra as likely bile acids or related steroids, with two example analyses illustrated here. This resource allows researchers to flag candidate bile acid and steroidal signatures in their own data for further characterization.
affiliations: Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: MassBank Human: The annotated human metabolome
papers.abstract: Mass spectrometry-based metabolomics is essential for deciphering human metabolic functions and metabolite dark matter. However, the dark matter of the human metabolome is intricately hidden. Therefore, we developed MassBank Human, a curated library that distills 36,512,540 MS2 spectra from 76 public human datasets into 203,886 high-quality spectra via spectral averaging, recalibration, and filtering to achieve high mass accuracy. We further used three metabolite annotation tools and developed a Zipf-Bayesian rank aggregation framework to aggregate their rankings with false discovery rate control. This framework assigned molecular formulas, chemical classes, and planar structures to 55,564, 22,619, and 14,198 spectra, respectively. Approximately half of the annotated structures potentially originated from food, pollutants, or gut microbiota. In a metabolome analysis of colorectal cancer cells, MassBank Human doubled structural annotation coverage (10.6% to 21.2%), identifying acetylated polyamines as markers of metabolic rewiring. This community resource provides an annotated foundation for exploring human metabolomes.
affiliations: Department of Bioinformatic Engineering, Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, The University of Osaka (corresponding author)

papers.title: ELiAH2: update of the atlas of E3 ligases in human tissues by integrating tissue-specificity and docking properties of ligands for targeted protein degradation
papers.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD), including proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), requires coordinated selection of E3 ligases, target proteins, and ligands to achieve efficient and tissue-selective degradation. However, current TPD resources provide limited support for integrating tissue-specific transcriptomic evidence with structural compatibility during early candidate prioritization. Here, we present ELiAH2, an expanded database for transcriptome- and structure-guided prioritization of TPD candidates. ELiAH2 integrates GTEx RNA-seq profiles across 24 human tissues to characterize tissue-specific expression patterns of E3 ligases and target genes. Compared with the previous version, ELiAH, current update presented over 200% of expansion for the number of covered tissues and samples. Previously, E3 ligase-target gene associations were inferred using mutual information-based network analysis, enabling users to explore transcriptomic relationships. To further support structural evaluation, ELiAH2 provides large-scale docking datasets comprising 827,385 E3 ligase-target protein pairs and 7,800,521 protein-ligand docking models, including E3 ligase-ligand and target protein-ligand interactions. Docking scores, ranked interaction tables, gene and ligand identifiers, and downloadable PDB structures are incorporated into the web interface. By combining tissue specificity, E3-target association, protein-protein docking, and protein-ligand docking, ELiAH2 provides a comprehensive resource for narrowing the TPD search space and supporting rational degrader design. ELiAH2 is freely available at https://eliahdb.org.
affiliations: UST (corresponding author)

papers.title: BioMINTREL expands biological problem solving through cross-disciplinary representations
papers.abstract: Biological research agents often rely on familiar analytical methods, limiting the questions explored in existing data. We introduce BioMINTREL, an AI agent that finds methods from other disciplines and connects them to biological measurements. It can draw on relationships among datasets and complementary ideas from several methods to develop new questions and analyses. We evaluate it on BioMDC-Bench, which assesses 228 possible applications of computational methods to biological tasks. Compared with GPT-5.4 mini and Qwen3.6-35B, BioMINTREL improves F1 agreement with human experts by up to 45.3 percentage points and increases coverage of applications supported by studies published in subsequent years by up to 58.8 percentage points. Four case studies on real data go beyond previous analyses to reveal dose-specific variant effects, constraints on spatial cell communication and routes through perturbation-response states, and identify the sampling needed to test whether rare high-state cells predict later lineage size. These results highlight BioMINTREL's potential to expand questions in existing data and suggest directions for subsequent research.
affiliations: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: To mix or to de-mix?: Cation-π suppresses heterogeneity in local structure and dynamics of heterotypic Condensates
papers.abstract: Heterotypic biomolecular condensates can exhibit pronounced spatial and dynamic heterogeneity because chemically distinct components compete between self- and cross-association. Here, we use coarse-grained simulations to investigate how cation-{pi} interactions modulate this competition in condensates formed by peptides with systematic variation of hydrophobicity-to-charge ratios in binary peptide pairs. By independently tuning sequence heterogeneity, peptide composition, and cation-{pi} interaction strength, we establish how an additional short-range interaction reshapes condensate stability, internal organization, and molecular dynamics. In the absence of cation-{pi} interactions, highly heterogeneous peptide pairs form distinct core-shell architectures, with charge- and hydrophobicity-rich sequences preferentially occupying different regions of the condensate. Introducing cation-{pi} interactions progressively enhances phase stability and promotes molecular mixing, with stronger interactions substantially increasing the critical temperature and condensate density. Energetic analysis reveals that cation-{pi} interactions partially compensate for the loss of electrostatic and hydrophobic stabilization, providing an additional and tuneable source of cohesive interactions. This enhanced cross-association also suppresses spatial and dynamic heterogeneity, yielding more homogeneous peptide distributions, slower translational diffusion, and more uniform chain reconfiguration within the dense phase. Collectively, our results demonstrate that cation-{pi} interactions provide a molecular mechanism for coupling condensate stability to spatial organization and internal dynamics, enabling sequence heterogeneity and composition to be translated into distinct condensate states.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur NH 62 Nagaur Road Karwar 342030 Jodhpur District Rajasthan India. (corresponding author)

papers.title: hnRNPA1 Remodels SARS-CoV-2 Genomic G-Quadruplexes through Its UP1 Domain
papers.abstract: The single-stranded RNA genome of SARS-CoV-2 contains several predicted G-quadruplex (G4) forming sequences. Pharmacological stabilisation of these structures has been shown to suppress viral replication, suggesting that their resolution may be required for efficient viral replication. However, the roles of host proteins in stabilization or destabilization of G4 structures have remained largely unexplored. Human hnRNPA1, one of the most abundant RNA-binding proteins in eukaryotic cells, is a G-quadruplex unfolding protein and has independently been identified as a SARS-CoV-2 genome-binding protein. However, whether it acts on the G-quadruplexes within the SARS-CoV-2 genome has not been examined. Here, we screened eight putative G-quadruplex forming sequences conserved across SARS-related coronaviruses and identified two sequences that fold into G4 structures, confirmed by circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy and thioflavin T (ThT) fluorescence-based experiments. Furthermore, we showed that the UP1 and UP1+RGG domains of hnRNPA1 specifically bind and unfold these two viral RNA G-quadruplexes. Both UP1 and UP1+RGG unfold viral RNA G-quadruplexes to similar extent, indicating that recognition and unfolding of these viral G-quadruplexes are mediated mainly by the UP1 domain of hnRNPA1. Together, these findings identify hnRNPA1 as a host factor capable of binding and remodelling SARS-CoV-2 genomic RNA G-quadruplexes and suggest a mechanism by which the virus may exploit an abundant host protein to resolve G4 structures within its genome.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Science (corresponding author)

papers.title: Modeled Oxidative Lesions Remodel the ABCB1 Linker: A Hypothesis for Transporter Regulation
papers.abstract: Multidrug resistance mediated by P-glycoprotein (P-gp; ABCB1) remains a major barrier to chemotherapy. Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has increased drug responsiveness in resistant cancer models, but the molecular link between plasma-derived oxidative chemistry and ABCB1 regulation remains unresolved. We investigated whether site-specific oxidative lesions remodel the intrinsically disordered linker connecting nucleotide-binding domain 1 to transmembrane domain 2. Native-ensemble exposure analysis identified contrasting oxidation candidates: dynamically exposed Met653 and persistently exposed Trp698. Met653 oxidation to methionine sulfoxide and Trp698 oxidation to kynurenine were examined individually and together using a balanced 2 by 2 molecular-dynamics design with a mechanically tethered linker construct. Analyses integrated global descriptors, residue-resolved mobility, backbone order, native-state occupancies, projected breadth, and conformational switching. Trp698[->]KYN produced the dominant response: all seven global descriptors shifted toward restriction, accompanied by distributed mobility changes, compaction, and increased intramolecular hydrogen bonding. In the radius-of-gyration/end-to-end-distance projection, compact-state occupancy increased from 46.9% to 99.7%, switching decreased from 6.50 to 0.07 transitions per 10 ns, and projected breadth contracted. Met653[->]SME produced weaker, heterogeneous effects, while the double-modified linker remained restricted but showed greater projected exchange than Trp698[->]KYN alone. In this model, Trp698[->]KYN generated a compact, low-exchange projected ensemble in the tethered ABCB1 linker. These findings identify oxidation-site-specific linker remodeling as a candidate molecular intermediate that could influence linker-mediated domain coordination, while requiring experimental validation of lesion formation, transporter activity, and multidrug resistance outcomes.
affiliations: Amir Kabir University of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Collateral effects of bacteriophage resistance on antibiotic sensitivity in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Collateral effect (CEs) of phage resistance can alter antibiotic sensitivity, leading to collateral sensitivity (CS). CS of phage resistance can potentially be used to design more effective phage--antibiotic combination treatments, yet insufficient knowledge on the occurrence of such phage resistance associated CS is currently available. Here, we characterized CEs across diverse Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains, antibiotics, and phages. For each of eight strains (seven clinical isolates and PAO1), we generated mutants resistant to phage PAO1-1 and, separately, mutants resistant to each of six antibiotics. Phage-resistant mutants were also generated using four additional phages (M32, NP1, NP3, and PNM), and double phage- and antibiotic-resistant mutants from one strain. We measured growth curves across antibiotic concentration ranges after which the area-under-the-curve (AUC) was quantified as a measure of bacterial burden. Dose-response curves for AUC against antibiotic concentrations were constructed to estimate a fold change in EC50 of mutants relative to their parental strains. PAO1-1-resistant mutants showed significant CS to colistin and polymyxin B. For other antibiotics, CEs varied by phage and parental strain: PAO1-1-resistant mutants showed CS to tobramycin, whereas mutants resistant to the other four phages tested were associated with CR. For double phage- and antibiotic resistant mutants we found CS to colistin and tobramycin relative to the parental strain. Resistance mutations occurred predominantly in genes involved in metabolism, virulence, and DNA replication. Antibiotic-resistant mutants also showed increased phage sensitivity, with the strongest effect in colistin-resistant mutants. In conclusion this study demonstrates collateral effects of phage resistance are most specific to both strain- and antibiotic-specific.
affiliations: Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research, Leiden University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Evolution of SARS-CoV-2 reshapes upper airway immunity in children
papers.abstract: Children were relatively protected from severe COVID-19 during the early pandemic a phenomenon linked to rapid and heightened innate immune responses in the upper-airways. Although adult upper-airway antiviral responses varied across successive SARS-CoV-2 waves, whether viral evolution similarly reshaped pediatric mucosal immunity remains unclear. Here we used single-cell transcriptomics to profile 229,533 upper-airway cells from 68 unvaccinated children including 17 uninfected controls, spanning the wild-type SARS-CoV-2, Alpha, Delta and Omicron waves. Epithelial interferon responses were primarily determined by time since symptom onset but were, unlike in adults, independent of disease severity. During early infection, anti-viral responses differed across variants without following a progressive pattern of attenuation. Alpha and Delta elicited the strongest interferon programs across epithelial and immune cell populations, whereas Omicron exhibited a shift towards macrophage cytokine signaling and T-cell cytotoxicity. These findings reveal variant-specific remodeling of pediatric upper-airway immunity that fundamentally differs from that described in adults.
affiliations: Berlin Insitute of Health at Charité (corresponding author)

papers.title: Single-cell profiling of physically interacting immune cells using image-guided sorting
papers.abstract: Single-cell transcriptomics of cell-cell complexes offers key insights into in vivo immune interactions, yet distinguishing true physical contacts from artifacts remains challenging. Here, we integrated spectral imaging cell sorting with physical cell deconvolution to separate circulating T cell-monocyte doublets from tuberculosis patients into physically interacting (in-contact) and non-interacting (coincidental) populations. Single-cell sequencing of individual cell partners revealed that physical contact is associated with robust signatures distinct from singlets, including unidirectional monocyte-to-T cell RNA transfer, heightened metabolic activity and T cell cytotoxicity, and a trend toward antigen-specific enrichment. These signatures spanned all T cell and monocyte subpopulations, reflecting a global program of T cell-monocyte engagement. Coincidental doublets displayed intermediate transcriptional profiles between singlet and in-contact states, suggesting the presence of recently disrupted or forming physical pairs. This framework provides high-fidelity deconvolution of cellular interactions, uncovering signatures governing T cell-monocyte communication in human disease.
affiliations: La Jolla Institute for Immunology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Diverse stresses converge on bacterial periplasmic expansion through distinct physiological mechanisms
papers.abstract: Diverse environmental and antibiotic stresses induce localized periplasmic expansion, the separation of the inner membrane from the cell wall and outer membrane, in Gram-negative bacteria, yet whether these morphologically similar responses arise through a common mechanism remains unclear. Here, we compare periplasmic expansion induced by sudden starvation, ciprofloxacin, mitomycin C, and globomycin in Escherichia coli. We find that these perturbations produce similar morphologies through distinct physiological and mechanical routes. Ciprofloxacin- and mitomycin C-induced periplasmic expansion coincides with loss of turgor, whereas starvation requires water efflux, and globomycin leads to unequal expansion of the inner and outer membrane as a result of aberrant inner membrane-cell wall crosslinking. Outer membrane stiffness modulates expansion during ciprofloxacin treatment. Despite these distinct mechanisms, robust periplasmic expansion during starvation and treatment with ciprofloxacin or globomycin requires UDP-glucose synthesis. Together, these findings establish periplasmic expansion as a convergent physical outcome of diverse stresses and reveal the remarkable plasticity of the Gram-negative cell envelope.
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis (corresponding author)

papers.title: Retroviral CA subdomains encode their immature assembly properties independently of strict subdomain co-pairing
papers.abstract: Retroviral capsid (CA) proteins display a conserved two-domain architecture consisting of independently folded N-terminal (CA-NTD) and a C-terminal (CA-CTD) subdomains. Despite a strong CA protein fold conservation, different retrovirus species are employing remarkably variable geometrical solutions to stabilize the CA lattices that form the immature virus particle. For instance, while HTLV-1 has been reported to use the CA-NTD to stabilize its immature lattice, HIV-1 relies on a contiguous structural unit formed of the CA-CTD together with the short spacer peptide 1 (SP1). This raises the question whether immature assembly phenotypes are modular features encoded independently into individual CA subdomains, or if they are emergent features requiring strict co-pairing or co-evolution between CA subdomains of a given species. To test for these two options, we have designed chimeric proteins pairing the CA subdomains of HTLV-1 and HIV-1. Our results show that the CA subdomains of HIV-1 and HTLV-1 can be clearly distinguished into assembly-passive and assembly-driving categories. Moreover, pairing assembly-driving subdomains from the two retrovirus species still allows them to independently form their native immature contacts, while at the same time trying to impose their preferred curvature on each other. Mutations of either subdomain within the chimeric context do not disrupt assembly, but rather shift the phenotype balance while relieving curvature strains, demonstrating that all immature assembly properties can be encoded into a single subdomain. Our results therefore highlight that the two-domain architecture of retroviral capsid is a result of a division of labor approach built on structural modularity, where, at least for immature assembly, one of the subdomains is the key driver for assembly competence while the other could serve more regulatory functions.
affiliations: Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Receptor-like kinase RLK15 binds a fungal RNase effector to enhance autophosphorylation and activate host defense
papers.abstract: Fungal pathogens secrete diverse effectors to suppress host immunity, yet the plant receptors that perceive these virulence factors often remain elusive. Here, we identify Ss1624, a secreted RNase from the sugarcane smut pathogen Sporisorium scitamineum, and show that it is recognized by the plasma-membrane-localized CrRLK1L-family receptor kinase RLK15. This recognition triggers canonical immune outputs, including reactive oxygen species burst, callose deposition, defense gene activation, and induces hypersensitive cell death. Mechanistically, Ss1624 physically interacts with the receptor-like kinase RLK15, which is required for Ss1624-triggered cell death. Functional assays indicate that this interaction enhances RLK15 autophosphorylation in a kinase activity-dependent manner, suggesting that Ss1624 can act as an elicitor. Transcript profiling further reveals coordinated expression patterns of Ss1624 and RLK15 during infection, and perturbation of Ss1624 expression alters RLK15 transcript levels and pathogenic outcomes. Extending these findings to rice, the ortholog OsRLK15 contributes positively to resistance to bacterial and fungal diseases without yield penalty in rice. Our results support a model in which a secreted RNase effector is directly sensed by a receptor kinase to initiate broad-spectrum immune responses, providing insights into host-pathogen interactions and identifying RLK15 as a candidate for crop improvement.
affiliations: Integrative Microbiology Research Center, Engineering Research Center of Biological Control, Ministry of Education, College of Plant Protection, South China Agr (corresponding author)

papers.title: Leveraging synthetic environmental covariates to explore crop genotype by environment interactions
papers.abstract: Environments are unpredictable. Genotype by environment interactions (GEI) further complicate any assessment of genotype performance or stability across diverse environments posing a challenge for plant breeders. Several approaches exist to address this challenge. However existing approaches present a trade-off between scale and interpretability often acting in a 'black box' manner. Here we extend the Finlay-Wilkinson regression on synthetic environmental covariates of Piepho and Blancon (2023) to dissect GEI at the level of individual developmental windows, resolving which growth stages drive GEI and how genotype stability varies across them. Yield data for 961 genotypes from a barley breeding program, tested across 12 environments, is used as a case study to illustrate how this approach can provide valuable insight into the GEI present. Exploring the dynamic impact of environmental variables across growth stages revealed that environmental factors during early grain fill contributed the most to yield GEI variance. Stability was found to be dynamic across development windows, presenting growth-stage-specific yield stability as a new potential breeding target. This approach yields new, growth-stage-resolved measures of yield stability and a new means of dissecting GEI in complex traits, while also opening a route to environmental clustering based on stage-specific GEI patterns.
affiliations: The University of Queensland (corresponding author)

papers.title: Nanopore sequencing reveals the DNA replication timing programme of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum
papers.abstract: The DNA replication timing programme, defined as the temporal order in which genomic loci replicate, is of fundamental importance to maintaining genome stability. In human cells, replication timing is routinely measured using Repli-seq which reveals that the human genome is divided into replication timing domains that replicate in early or late S-phase. These timing domains are associated with gene expression, chromatin compaction, and three-dimensional genome organisation. In particular, late-replicating domains can be hotspots of genomic instability under replication stress. Because of the parasite's unusual cell cycle, Repli-seq cannot be used in the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum, leaving the open question as to whether its genome is divided into replication timing domains and how this might impact evolution of the parasite. Here, we leverage the power of Oxford Nanopore Technologies long-read DNA sequencing together with DNAscent to determine, for the first time, the replication timing programme of P. falciparum. We show how it relates to elevated rates of DNA breaking and replication fork stalling, and predict that these stalls are predominantly transient.
affiliations: University of Cambridge (corresponding author)

papers.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Assay-Aware Drug-Target Binding Affinity Prediction
papers.abstract: Machine learning models for molecular discovery often train on bioactivity data from heterogeneous assays, yet assay context is rarely explicitly represented. We investigate whether natural-language assay descriptions provide predictive information beyond molecular and protein representations. We develop ACL-DTI (Assay-aware Contrastive Learning-based Drug Target Interaction) and MAMMAL-AsAP, an assay-context extension of MAMMAL-DTI. Across five triplet-disjoint random splits, assay-aware models achieve competitive or improved performance over assay-agnostic baselines. Among the evaluated models, MAMMAL-AsAP achieves the highest (R^2) of 0.7198 +/- 0.0085. Masking experiments show that ACL-DTI is robust to incomplete assay descriptions, exhibiting the smallest reductions in R^2 among the evaluated models when masking the target name, assay technique, or both: 0.0228 +/- 0.0064, 0.0406 +/- 0.0113, and 0.0620 +/- 0.0190, respectively. These results indicate that assay descriptions contain predictive information not fully captured by molecular structures and protein sequences, and reveal architecture-dependent differences in how this information is exploited.
affiliations: Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology Delhi (corresponding author)

papers.title: Insulin fails to mitigate amyloid pathology but modulates intestinal morphology in the 5xFAD model revealed by synchrotron-based XPCT
papers.abstract: Intranasal insulin has been investigated as a metabolic intervention in Alzheimers disease (AD), but its effects across the brain-gut axis remain unclear. We combined multiscale synchrotron X-ray phase-contrast tomography (XPCT), amyloid-{beta} immunofluorescence, and fecal metaproteomics to examine structural and molecular responses in 5xFAD mice. Twenty-four mice representing wild-type and 5xFAD genotypes, saline and insulin conditions, and terminal ages of 2 and 6 months received insulin at 1 U/mouse/day for 5 weeks. Micro-XPCT visualized plaque-like deposits, nanoXPCT revealed their heterogeneous internal organization, and MOAB-2 labeling provided qualitative support for amyloid pathology. Detectable plaque burden was not lower after treatment: deposits occurred in two of three treated versus none of three untreated 5xFAD mice at 2 months, and treated animals had higher descriptive regional means at 6 months. In the ileum, insulin was associated with lower villus length and crypt depth in 6-month-old 5xFAD mice, whereas no significant differences were detected at 2 months. Fecal profiles retained broad taxonomic overlap but differed in functional annotations, with hydrolase-associated fractions of 81%, 92%, 96%, and 93% across untreated wild-type, treated wild-type, untreated 5xFAD, and treated 5xFAD conditions, respectively, within the selected peptide subset. Thus, lower ileal dimensions coexisted with non-reduced detectable brain plaque burden and a fecal protein profile distinct from untreated wild type. Together, these findings reveal contrasting central and peripheral patterns following intranasal insulin treatment in 5xFAD mice: no detectable reduction in cerebral plaque burden, alongside attenuation of selected ileal structural alterations and distinct fecal metaproteomic profiles. Although exploratory, the findings raise the possibility that intranasal insulin alters amyloid compartmentalization or plaque detectability rather than promoting amyloid clearance, while producing distinct peripheral remodeling.
affiliations: RIKEN IMS (corresponding author)

papers.title: Persistently activated virus-specific CD8 T cells indicate antigen-driven immune aberrations in long COVID
papers.abstract: Long COVID (LC) affects millions of people worldwide, yet its driving mechanisms remain incompletely defined and no treatment has been approved. Persistence of SARS-CoV-2 and reactivation of herpesviruses have been implicated in LC, but direct detection of these viral antigens in blood and tissues has been challenging. T cells are exquisitely sensitive to viral antigens, survey organs throughout the body, and can be readily sampled in peripheral blood. Using high-dimensional spectral flow cytometry and single-cell sequencing approaches with multiplexed peptide/HLA tetramers, we profiled virus-specific T cells from hundreds of people with LC and recovered controls. We identified a subset of people with LC that maintained elevated activation of CD8 T cells targeting SARS-CoV-2 spike and/or lytic antigens from Epstein-Barr virus, but not other viral specificities. Spike-specific cells in LC expressed genes linked to TCR stimulation, terminal effector differentiation, and exhaustion and demonstrated reduced functionality upon cognate peptide stimulation ex vivo. Thus, T cells from a subset of people with LC are likely chronically stimulated by persistent SARS-CoV-2 antigens. These findings establish the use of T cells as biosensors of persisting antigen in LC and other disease settings and may help develop new therapeutic strategies for LC.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: An ancestral mitochondrial DNA insertion disrupts RNAi and enables persistence of a novel mycovirus in Cryptococcus neoformans
papers.abstract: RNA interference (RNAi) is a widely conserved genome-defense mechanism that protects eukaryotes against viruses and transposable elements. We previously showed that RNAi loss can lead to hypermutation and antifungal drug resistance in the human fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans, illuminating the potential clinical relevance of this pathway. In this study, we identified another function of RNAi in C. neoformans: mycovirus restriction. By screening known RNAi-deficient C. neoformans isolates, we identified a novel dsRNA mycovirus of the Orthototiviridae family, which we named CnTV1. We subsequently detected CnTV1 in three additional RNAi-deficient isolates. All CnTV1-positive isolates shared an ancestral nuclear mitochondrial DNA segment (NUMT) insertion that disrupts the gene encoding Argonaute (Ago1). Restoration of RNAi in sexually produced zygotes efficiently eliminated CnTV1. RNAi rescue by CRISPR-Cas9-mediated allele exchange eliminated CnTV1 during vegetative growth, further demonstrating RNAi is sufficient for mycoviral control. Loss of the RNA helicase Ski2 or the exoribonuclease Xrn1 increased CnTV1 abundance, revealing RNAi-independent restriction of the virus. Restoration of RNAi cleared the virus even in the absence of Ski2 or Xrn1, indicating a dominant role for RNAi in antiviral defense. To investigate the biological implications of CnTV1 infection, we developed a cytoplasmic-mixing approach and generated isogenic strain pairs in an RNAi-deficient background that differ only in viral infection status. Leveraging these strains, we show that CnTV1 infection leads to coordinated, low-magnitude transcriptomic changes and that strains lacking the mycovirus were moderately less virulent in a murine infection model. Our findings reveal that RNAi serves as a dominant antiviral defense system in C. neoformans and suggest that naturally occurring RNAi deficiency may be more prevalent than previously appreciated. This work highlights mycovirus persistence as an important consequence of RNAi loss in this WHO-designated critical priority fungal pathogen.
affiliations: Duke University Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: The (implicit) force is with you: an application of the implicit function theorem for automatic protein force fields reparametrization
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics simulations are powerful tools for studying protein behavior, yet their accuracy remains limited by the approximations of molecular force fields and the difficulty of determining their parameters. Moreover, existing force fields are largely optimized for globular proteins and can perform poorly on structurally distinct systems. Developing a universal force field that accurately describes all existing protein structures may be beyond reach with current physical models. Instead, we propose shifting generality from the force field itself to the method used to assign its parameters, enabling systematic reparameterization for restricted, structurally homogeneous classes of proteins. We formulate this task as a bilevel optimization problem and solve it using the implicit function theorem. We demonstrate this approach by reparameterizing AMBER for amyloid fibrils, optimizing its parameters to improve agreement with experimentally determined structures and enhance fibril stability during molecular dynamics simulations.
affiliations: Montpellier University (corresponding author)

papers.title: SLAFIT: Viral fitness inference and structural variant detection from TGS data
papers.abstract: Evolution is driven by genetic variation at multiple scales, from single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) to structural variants (SVs). Within populations, nonrandom associations among SNVs, quantified by linkage disequilibrium (LD), must be considered when inferring fitness from sequencing data. Characterizing SVs, SNVs, and the LD between SNVs therefore provides complementary insights into the genetic basis of evolutionary change. Although third-generation sequencing technologies facilitate the characterization of genomic variation, finite read lengths often limit the resolution of LD across entire genomes. Here, we present SLAFIT, a pipeline for linkage-aware fitness inference and SV detection from third-generation sequencing data. The pipeline reconstructs genome-wide haplotypes and their frequencies from third-generation sequencing reads to infer SNVs and estimate LD. When time-series data are available, it also infers fitness. An established SV detection tool is incorporated into the same workflow. Simulations support accurate LD and fitness inference under tested conditions, with reduced computation time through parallelization. Applications to enterovirus C104 and herpes simplex virus 1 reveal selection signals in predicted epitopes and recover a known inversion, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of SLAFIT for studying viral evolution through complementary analyses of fitness and structural variation.
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (corresponding author)

papers.title: Billi: Accurate and Scalable Bubble Detection in Pangenome Graphs
papers.abstract: A key application of pangenome graphs is the characterization of small and large genomic variants by enumerating bubble-like structures in the graph. Several formalizations of bubbles have been proposed. Superbubbles and ultrabubbles are two such formalizations, but both exclude cyclic subgraphs. Representing cyclic structures is essential for capturing complex genomic variation, such as inversions. Other definitions that accommodate cycles do not guarantee that overlapping bubbles are strictly nested. This makes it difficult to organize variants hierarchically and distinguish complex variants from their constituent subvariants. We introduce two formalizations, called panbubble and hairpin, that accommodate cyclic subgraphs. We prove that both satisfy the strict nesting property. In our theoretical analysis and algorithm design, we leverage an auxiliary undirected graph representation derived from the bidirected pangenome graph, enabling us to exploit established graph-theoretic algorithms and properties. We then present an exact O(|V|^2(|V| + |E|)-time algorithm for detecting all panbubbles and hairpins in a bidirected graph G = (V, E). In addition, we propose a heuristic that produces the same output as the exact algorithm on all tested graphs and scales to both the first and second releases of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium. We implemented our algorithms in the tool Billi. At a known recurrent inversion locus on the human Y chromosome, Billi recovers the inversion together with its nested variants, whereas existing bubble-detection methods miss part of the variation or fail to correctly represent the nesting relationships among variants.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Science (corresponding author)

papers.title: SpectroBird: Event-Level Vocalization Detection and Curation for Avian Ecology
papers.abstract: Passive acoustic monitoring often summarizes long recordings as fixed-window presence predictions, but many ecological questions require records of individual vocal events: how many occurred, when they occurred, whether they overlapped, how long they lasted, what frequency band they occupied, and whether each event was complete enough for structural measurement. We address this event-level measurement problem with SpectroBird, a spectrogram-based method for localizing and curating avian vocalizations in noisy field recordings. SpectroBird first applies a detection-localization model to identify candidate vocalizations as time-frequency boxes. An event-consolidation step merges repeated detections from overlapping windows while preserving overlapping vocalizations as separate events. A completeness-curation model then classifies each consolidated event as complete or incomplete before downstream event-level analysis. We demonstrate SpectroBird on breeding-season Hume's Leaf Warbler buzz vocalizations recorded in the Himalaya across a 3,200-3,800 m elevational gradient. Under shared window-level scoring, the detection-localization model remained competitive with AST and YOLOv11-cls baselines while retaining event timing and frequency bounds; event-level evaluation achieved AP > 0.999 for complete buzzes. Applied to two field seasons, the resulting event records showed that duration of complete buzzes declined with elevation, complete-buzz occurrence showed no simple elevation trend, and relative day-of-year occurrence patterns were strongly correlated between years. These results show how event-level detection and curation can support ecological analyses that depend on individual vocalizations rather than fixed-window presence alone.
affiliations: School of Biological Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, United States (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genomic classification and immune profiling define mucosal melanoma
papers.abstract: Mucosal melanoma is a rare, lethal melanoma subtype with distinct genetics and limited benefit from immunotherapy. To define features associated with mucosal melanoma clinical outcomes, we assembled a large, multimodally profiled cohort spanning primary and metastatic disease. Compared with cutaneous melanoma, primary mucosal melanoma showed greater genomic heterogeneity, ploidy and aneuploidy, and a more dedifferentiated, proliferative transcriptional state. Analysis of genomic sequencing of 339 patients with mucosal melanoma identified four mutually exclusive genomic subtypes: CDK4/MDM2/CCND1, SF3B1-mutated, TP53/ATRX, and mucosal melanoma Triple WT, associated with distinct anatomic sites but similar outcomes. In the tumor microenvironment, we observed reduced T cell infiltration and increased CD163+ tumor-associated macrophages in mucosal melanoma relative to cutaneous melanoma. In matched longitudinal samples, CD163+ tumor-associated macrophages increased with disease progression and immunotherapy resistance. CD163+ tumor-associated macrophages engaged non-regulatory T cells through GAL9-TIM-3 interactions, nominating TIM-3 blockade as a therapeutic strategy for mucosal melanoma. These findings define the distinct aggressive biology of mucosal melanoma and highlight potential therapeutic targets and mechanisms of immune resistance.
affiliations: Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) Cancer Center, Boston, MA, USA. (corresponding author)

papers.title: Enzyme-Constrained Metabolic Modeling of the Tripartite Synapse Links Astrocyte-Neuron Lactate Shuttle to Lipid Trafficking and Redox Homeostasis
papers.abstract: Neuron-astrocyte metabolic coupling sustains synaptic function through coordinated substrate exchange, redox homeostasis, and lipid handling, yet the systems-level mechanism remains poorly understood. Here, we developed an enzyme-constrained, genome-scale metabolic model of the mouse tripartite synapse to test whether protein allocation can reproduce the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle (ANLS). Starting from the iMM1865 mouse metabolic model, we corrected mass and charge imbalances, expanded fatty acid and lipid pathways, and standardized annotations to obtain a high-quality, generic mouse model, improving the MEMOTE score from 46% to 83%. Cell type-specific astrocyte and neuron models were reconstructed using the integrative metabolic analysis tool (iMAT) with cell type-resolved mouse brain proteomics, and were further extended to represent the tripartite synapse. Enzyme-constrained resource allocation models (RAMs) were reconstructed for the astrocyte and neuron models using the GECKO 3.0 pipeline and integrated into a tripartite synapse community model via a modified SteadyCom framework. In the stoichiometry-only model, minimum lactate exchange remained at zero under ATP-maintenance and biomass objectives, indicating no coupling between astrocyte lactate secretion and neuronal uptake arising from the metabolic network itself. Imposing enzyme constraints made lactate secretion obligatory, with corresponding neuronal lactate uptake. Across 100 turnover-number bootstrap parameterizations, lactate coupling became obligatory under both objectives, with median onsets at 0.770 of maximal ATP-maintenance demand and 0.879 of maximal growth. This indicates that protein limitation can drive astrocyte-neuron lactate coupling consistent with ANLS, independent of modeling assumptions. Incorporation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and lipid peroxidation pathways demonstrated that the brain-type fatty acid binding protein (FABP7) knockout redistributed flux away from astrocytic detoxification, increased neuronal ROS burden, and produced cell-type-specific changes in lipid-associated reporter metabolites, with prostaglandin J2 as the highest-ranked reporter metabolite. Model predictions, including lactate shuttling and lipid metabolic shifts in FABP7 knockout, align with published experimental studies, supporting the biological relevance of this framework. These findings indicate that ANLS emerges, at least in part, from enzyme limitation in the tripartite synapse model and that FABP7-mediated lipid trafficking is essential for lipid-redox homeostasis at the tripartite synapse.
affiliations: Washington State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A membrane-impermeant nucleic acid dye converts bacteriophage plaque assays into a machine-readable format for automated counting
papers.abstract: Plaque assays remain the gold standard for bacteriophage quantification, but routine plaque counting is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and poorly suited to large experiments or automated workflows. Conventional plaque images also often provide insufficient contrast for simple software-based counting, especially when plaques are small, faint, or heterogeneous. Here we show that a membrane-impermeant nucleic acid dye (SYTOX) can convert standard bacteriophage plaque assays into a high-contrast, machine-readable format compatible with simple automated counting. In a soft-agar overlay workflow, fluorescent labeling enabled plaque detection and automated enumeration using an open-source ImageJ pipeline based on Find Maxima. In a representative benchmark using a large language model (LLM), conventional transmitted-light images were not counted accurately, whereas fluorescent SYTOX images brought both Fiji- and LLM-based counts within Poisson counting uncertainty of the manual count. Because the method improves the image contrast of the assay itself, it may also provide improved input for future machine-learning or other advanced automated counting workflows. The method was evaluated across diverse phage-host systems spanning dsDNA, ssRNA, filamentous, and enveloped phages, including T7, MS2, M13, and phi6. In lytic systems, fluorescent signal emerged prior to or alongside conventional plaque visibility and yielded automated counts that agreed closely with manual counting. M13 exhibited delayed fluorescence consistent with its chronic, nonlytic lifestyle, yet remained machine-countable at the conventional next-day endpoint. A Gram-positive Leo2-Bacillus safensis system revealed an important compatibility limit: dye incorporation at plating inhibited plaque formation. Follow-up experiments indicated that SYTOX did not measurably reduce free Leo2 recovery or alter host-dependent depletion of free phage in liquid culture, arguing against simple direct phage damage or a large liquid-phase adsorption defect under the tested conditions. While we were unable to identify the exact cause of the plaquing defect, a post-labeling workflow restored detectability and automated counting. Together, these results show that membrane-impermeant dye labeling can make plaque assays more computationally tractable while preserving the accessibility of standard phage methods. This approach provides a practical path toward higher-throughput, statistically rigorous phage biology in both low-resource and automation-oriented laboratories.
affiliations: Sandia National Labs (corresponding author)

papers.title: Fragmented landscapes of mobile transposable element families bolster the diversity of large-effect alleles in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are powerful endogenous mutagens, but our understanding of the 'mobilome' - the set of mobile TEs at the species level - has largely been shaped by the study of a single reference genome. To overcome this reference-centric view, we produced long-read genome assemblies for 91 Arabidopsis thaliana strains and performed a reference-free pangenomic graph analysis of structural variants. Our analysis revealed the presence of twice as many TE families with recent mobilization activity as previously described. These >200 newly identified TE families are ancestral, with a third experimentally shown to be mobile and although they are often characterized by the presence of full-length copies in only a few rather than in most strains, they nonetheless contribute significantly to the generation of large-effect alleles. These findings uncover a much more fragmented and impactful mobilome than previously documented and highlight how pangenome approaches dramatically improve the study of genetic diversity.
affiliations: Institut de Biologie de l Ecole Normale Superieure, ENS-PSL, UMR 8197 CNRS (corresponding author)

papers.title: Advisory Board and Contents
Subscription and Copyright Information
The pianist who never played
PhD students who write dissertation with AI less likely to stay in academia
Precision RNAi for fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva in mice using a combinatorial unimolecular allele selective approach
Market Integration Pathways for Enhanced Geothermal Systems in Europe
papers.abstract: Enhanced geothermal systems can provide constant, reliable electricity and heat with minimal emissions, but high drilling costs and uncertain cost reductions leave their future unclear. We explore scenarios for the future adoption of these systems in a carbon-neutral, multi-sector European energy system. Here we show that in a net-zero system, heat (co-)generating enhanced geothermal plants at current cost can support 20–30 gigawatts (GW) of thermal capacity in Europe, primarily driven by district heating demands. If drilling costs were to decrease by approximately 60% relative to 2020 costs, the technology would become competitive in electricity markets, greatly expanding its market opportunity. However, the spatially dispersed rollout of district heating stands against the confined overlap of high geological potential with low potential for other renewables, which conditions the competitiveness of electricity-generating plants. This results in a challenge where the majority of the market potential depends on pan-European technology learning for cost reductions, emphasising that coordination is crucial in stakeholders’ efforts.

papers.title: Structural basis for loop-dependent inhibition by AcrIIC1 anti-CRISPR proteins
Hydroxy artificial water channels enable ultraselective reverse osmosis membranes for N-nitrosamine removal in water reuse
Temporary carbon storage can mitigate slow-responding climate changes
papers.abstract: Carbon removal and storage is central to many net-zero commitments, yet its durability, particularly for nature-based methods, is uncertain due to disturbance risks. Previous work shows that carbon storage-years (the time-integrated quantity of carbon storage) are proportional to time-integrated avoided warming, which in turn causes avoided changes in slow-responding climate variables. Here, we show that temporary carbon storage results in avoided changes in inertial climate variables. Avoided changes in 2100 are proportional to carbon storage-years across a range of storage amounts and emissions scenarios for permafrost carbon, ocean carbon, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, ocean temperature, and thermosteric sea-level rise. By 2300, proportionality persists in some variables, notably sea-level rise, ocean temperature, and ocean carbon. Temporary storage therefore has climate benefits that extend beyond the duration of the storage, with some persistence of benefits even on multi-century timescales. We find that these climate benefits are greatest when temporary storage is paired with ambitious mitigation.

papers.title: Cobalt-catalyzed alkyne migratory hydroboration to access β-alkenylboronates via catalytic zipper-like alkyne translocation
From fragmentation to fault zone architecture as a structural framework for fault weakening
A smart photothermal microneedle system for dual-targeted therapy of osteoarthritis via MMPs inhibition
Coordinated inhibition of SOX9 and cell-cycle progression by microRNA-200 restricts sebaceous gland fate specification
papers.abstract: The microRNA-200 family (miR-200s) is known for inhibiting epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and cell-cycle progression in cancer, but its function in epithelial development remains unclear. Here we show that miR-200s are highly enriched in hair matrix progenitors but absent from the upper hair follicle (HF), where sebaceous gland (SG) and HF stem cells are specified. Ectopic miR-200 induction abolishes SG specification while preserving hair morphogenesis. Genome-wide identification of miR-200 targets reveals direct repression of negative regulators of WNT signaling and cell-cycle regulators. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses uncover mutually exclusive domains of WNT activity and SOX9 expression in the upper HF that is disrupted by miR-200 induction. Genome-wide mapping of SOX9 targets further uncovers a lipogenic and fatty-acid metabolic program required for SG specification. Together, these findings show that miR-200 blocks SG fate by inhibiting SOX9 function and restricting cell proliferation, defining a spatially organized regulatory network essential for SG development.

papers.title: Only time will tell
papers.abstract: Chronotherapy promises to improve medicine by aligning treatment with the body’s internal clock. As this idea moves into clinical trials, a high-profile retraction reveals the ups and downs of circadian medicine.

papers.title: Conversational brain AI for adaptive epilepsy care
papers.abstract: A small study shows that patients can help fine-tune their own seizure detectors by chatting with an AI agent. However, the more difficult challenge ahead is to build AI that responds appropriately.

papers.title: EGFR-targeted antibody−toxin conjugate in recurrent glioma: a phase 1 trial
papers.abstract: Results of a phase 1 trial of the antibody−toxin conjugate D2C7-ATC targeting EGFR/EGFRvIII in patients with recurrent malignant glioma show encouraging safety and efficacy signals, with translational analyses of patient samples indicating intratumoral and systemic immune activation.

papers.title: Real-world, digital-first delivery of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy in women
papers.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated substantial weight reduction and cardiometabolic benefit in randomized trials; however, prospective implementation evidence from digital care models and female sex community populations remains limited. Here we report outcomes from an observational study of 8,127 women initiating GLP-1RA therapy (99.8% tirzepatide) through a structured digital program incorporating mandatory biochemical monitoring, weekly video-supported follow-up and clinician-guided dose titration in the UK. Mean weight reduction was 16.1 kg (95% confidence interval 15.9 to 16.2; P − 1 (95% confidence interval 3.1 to 3.4; P − 1 , low-density lipoprotein cholesterol of 0.61 mmol l − 1 and triglycerides of 0.47 mmol l − 1 ). Retention was 91.4% at 6 months, with no serious treatment-related adverse events. These findings support the feasibility of delivering structured, digitally enabled obesity pharmacotherapy at scale and provide prospective real-world implementation evidence for this care model. Interpretation is limited by the observational design, absence of a comparator group, self-pay population and 6-month follow-up.

papers.title: Recent developments of fluorescent proteins and biosensors driven by cross-disciplinary insights
papers.abstract: This Review summarizes recent developments in fluorescent protein technology, including the engineering of fluorescent biosensors.

papers.title: AmpliconSuite: an end-to-end workflow for analyzing focal amplifications in cancer genomes
papers.abstract: Here we present AmpliconSuite, a toolkit for focal amplification analysis from cancer whole-genome sequencing that identifies extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), breakage–fusion–bridges and other amplification modes. Its ecContext module categorizes ecDNA structures to understand formation mechanisms. Validation across 175 metaphase fluorescence in situ hybridization-probed genes in 72 models demonstrated accurate predictions. Analysis of 6,506 patient pan-cancer samples revealed ecDNA-mediated oncogene co-amplification preferences. To democratize data sharing, we created AmpliconRepository, a community-contributable platform, enabling investigation of results across >15,000 publicly hosted samples.

papers.title: NAD+ precursor treatment prevents cardiomyopathy but disrupts erythroid maturation in mitochondrial progeria
Stereochemical preorganization directs triple-helical assembly of Au4 nanoclusters
papers.abstract: Translating local stereochemical information into higher-order helical architectures is a central challenge in materials design. Now it has been shown that stereochemically preorganized Au4 nanoclusters assemble into homochiral triple helices through directional aurophilic interactions, providing a design strategy for chiral nanocluster materials with amplified chiroptical responses.

papers.title: Unidirectional rotation in a molecular motor driven by angular-momentum transfer via helical orbitals
papers.abstract: Molecular motors typically rotate by cycling through excitation and relaxation to ground states. Now it has been shown that a molecular motor can be driven by angular-momentum transfer. Circulating positive and negative currents flowing through orbitals of opposite helicity along a carbon–carbon triple bond enable unidirectional rotation.

papers.title: Localization accuracy in single-molecule fluorescence microscopy
papers.abstract: The two prevalent methods to determine the position of individual fluorophores in the focal plane of a microscope rely either on the centroid of the fluorescence pattern produced by the fluorophore on a camera or on targeting the fluorophore's coordinate with a spatially controlled illumination minimum, as realized in MINFLUX. In both methods, (sub)nanometer localization precisions have been reached, but little is known about their accuracy, i.e., the deviation of the obtained coordinate from its ground truth. Here we report a theoretical and experimental comparison of the accuracy provided by these two strategies. We quantify substantial systematic errors in camera-based localization due to the interplay of two difficult-to-control parameters: the orientation of the fluorophore in space and its axial deviation from the focal plane (defocus). For example, within an axial range of {+/-}120 nm around the focus, the median distance between two fluorophores on a nanobody measured by camera-based localization varies by 26.5 nm. Under the same conditions, a commercial MINFLUX system yields a median variation in distance of 1.4 nm, indicating an improvement in accuracy by an order of magnitude. The accuracy of MINFLUX localization can be further improved to (sub-)[a]ngstrom levels by reducing the average distance between the coordinates targeted by the illumination minimum and the fluorophore. As it delivers unrivaled precision and accuracy for mapping fluorophores and their distances, we consider coordinate-targeted localization essential for studying labeled cells at the sub-10 nm level and for exploring structural and conformational changes of labeled biomolecules.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: Targeting TMPRSS2-ERG Fusion-Driven Prostate Cancer using Novel HBS-α-Helicomimics
papers.abstract: Gene fusions between the androgen receptor (AR)-responsive gene TMPRSS2 and ERG occur in approximately 50% of prostate cancers (PCa), thereby promoting tumorigenesis through aberrant ERG expression. Therapeutic targeting of transcription factor-DNA interfaces remains a formidable challenge, largely owing to the entropic penalty associated with peptide folding during target engagement. Here, we describe the structure-guided design and preclinical evaluation of hydrogen-bond surrogate (HBS)-constrained alpha-helicomimics targeting the ERG-DNA recognition interface. Structural analysis of ERG-DNA complex revealed that DNA binding induces elongation of recognition helix H4 from approximately 2.5 to 4.0 helical turns. To stabilize the bioactive conformation, we incorporated an N-terminal HBS macrocycle, introduced D363E and S366E mutations to enhance DNA binding and structural stability, and added dual NLS-TAT tags to facilitate cellular delivery. Biochemical and cellular assays demonstrated that the lead compound, ERG helicomimics, competitively inhibited ERG binding to ETS motifs, disrupted ERG association with AR and other cofactors, leading to suppressed ERG transcriptional activity. Chromatin immunoprecipitation-qPCR confirmed reduced ERG occupancy at regulatory regions of canonical target genes, accompanied by downregulation of ERG-driven transcriptional programs. ERG helicomimics also reduced proliferation, migration, and invasion in ERG-positive PCa cells. In a murine xenograft model of TMPRSS2-ERG-positive PCa, systemic ERG helicomimics treatment suppressed tumor growth without overt toxicity and reduced Ki-67 expression compared with the designated control peptide. Collectively, our findings support HBS-constrained ERG helicomimics as a rational strategy for targeting ERG-driven PCa and warrant further therapeutic optimization.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur (corresponding author)

papers.title: Growth costs of protein allocation in models of growing cells
papers.abstract: Microbial growth depends on how cells allocate their limited proteome among competing functions. Although many proteins are expressed near levels that maximize growth, deviations from these optima are common and can impose substantial fitness costs. Modeling the growth costs of suboptimal protein allocation remains challenging because protein expression influences growth through multiple interacting mechanisms, including biosynthetic demands, enzyme kinetics, and limits on cellular density. Here we analyze these effects using growth balance analysis (GBA), a nonlinear framework that predicts steady-state growth and biomass composition of coarse-grained microbial models from basic cellular constraints. The optimal biomass compositions predicted for these models include not only protein concentrations but also the reactant concentrations required to saturate enzymes through nonlinear rate laws, thereby capturing more complex resource trade-offs than in conventional linear resource allocation models. Using these GBA models, we compute optimal biomass compositions with individual proteins fixed at suboptimal levels. The resulting relationships between suboptimal protein allocation and growth rate are consistent with qualitative experimental patterns in bacteria, with growth effects depending on protein function (including idle proteins), environmental conditions, toxic byproducts, and alternative reactions. These results indicate a practical and tractable approach for modeling growth costs arising from suboptimal protein allocation, and suggest a basis for predictive modeling in metabolic engineering and synthetic biology.
affiliations: Institute of Analytical Chemistry, University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Mechanistic Model of Caspase-mediated Apoptosis Signaling Reveals Regulators of Drug Resistance in Prostate Cancer Cells
papers.abstract: Anticancer drug resistance remains a major barrier to effective treatment because both intrinsic and acquired resistance mechanisms can suppress apoptotic cell death. The growing incidence of castration-resistant prostate cancer highlights the need for therapeutic strategies that remain effective, independent of hormonal signaling. Here, we developed a parsimonious, data-calibrated ordinary differential equation model of caspase-mediated apoptosis signaling in prostate cancer. Rather than representing the full complexity of the apoptotic network, the model incorporates a reduced set of key apoptotic regulators required to capture experimentally-observed apoptotic responses. Model parameters were estimated using published data from three pro-apoptotic agents (Tocopheryloxybutyrate, Narciclasine, and Celecoxib), and global sensitivity analysis was used to identify determinants of treatment response and resistance. The model accurately reproduced experimental observations and revealed that variability in specific signaling components can produce substantial differences in response to pro-apoptotic drug treatment. Simulations identified key regulators of apoptotic commitment, predicted conditions under which resistance may be overcome through combination therapies, and suggested candidate mechanisms underlying heterogeneous responses among cancer cells. Together, these findings demonstrate that a reduced mechanistic framework can generate biologically meaningful insight into apoptotic drug response while identifying testable hypotheses regarding therapeutic vulnerabilities.
