Together, scMTG provides a unified generative framework for reconstructing cellular dynamics and uncovering regulatory programs that shape development, differentiation, and disease progression. scMTG is available as open-source software at https://github.com/liuq-lab/scMTG.
affiliations: Yale University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Joint Variable Selection for Omic Biomarkers in Time-to-Event Data
papers.abstract: The incidence of the vast majority of neurodegenerative, cancer, and metabolic diseases generally increases exponentially with age. In large-scale biobanks, linking time-to-diagnosis information in electronic health records to multiple genomic (``multiomics'') measures has the potential to reveal the genes and biological pathways involved in the disease onset and progression. To date, association testing has commonly been conducted by testing one variable at a time using semiparametric Cox proportional hazards (CoxPH) models, which ignores correlation structure and increases the risk of false discoveries. To address these issues, we introduce a novel fully parametric Bayesian computational method, vampW, based on the Vector Approximate Message Passing framework applied to a Weibull model. vampW jointly models correlated features, while providing an interpretable hazard structure, producing a continuous survival curve, and incorporating prior knowledge. In an extensive simulation study, we demonstrate that joint modeling of omics data and time-to-event outcomes with vampW, substantially reduces false discoveries in comparison to marginal testing and other forms of joint CoxPH models. In 53,018 individuals from the UK Biobank, vampW identifies 219 protein associations with 24 disease outcomes, most of which are not among the top marginal discoveries. We further correct protein levels for exponential age effects, identifying 1,308 associations and highlighting the sensitivity of the analysis to age-correction methodology. Our findings replicate in independent cohorts using different measurement technologies, within data from Iceland and a novel Generation Scotland proteomics dataset. vampW also achieves significant improvement in the prediction of disease onset times: across 14 outcomes, it reduces the root mean squared error by over 30% and 26%, when compared to CoxPH variants and the deep learning approach DeepSurv, respectively, while maintaining predictive utility in minority populations. In summary, vampW offers accurate and interpretable variable selection and out-of-sample prediction within a single computational framework, making it a powerful tool for dissecting the genomic architecture of common complex disease onset.
affiliations: Institute of Science and Technology Austria (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multivalent Surface Search Dynamics Shape Bacteriophage Adsorption Efficiency: A Stochastic Model of Tail Fiber Optimization
papers.abstract: Phages must locate and bind to bacterial surface receptors to initiate infection. Their tail fiber configuration critically influences this process. We develop a stochastic model describing surface search as a renewal process, incorporating attachment, detachment, and target-finding steps. Using both numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we quantify how tail fiber number, attachment-detachment rates, and geometric constraints impact the mean and the distribution of time to successful adsorption. Notably, the search efficiency shows a nonmonotonic dependence on tail fiber number, governed by a trade-off between binding stability and diffusion-mediated mobility. This optimum shifts depending on the effective bacterial density, target radius, and fiber reach. Short fiber reach imposes severe geometric constraints, reducing mobility at high tail fiber counts and leading to performance degradation. Our findings suggest that phage adsorption strategies are shaped by a balance between anchoring and exploration, with evolutionary implications for tail fiber design and infection efficiency.
affiliations: University of Copenhagen (corresponding author)

papers.title: Programming Targeted Immune Cell Migration Using Orthogonal Chemokine-Receptor Pairs
papers.abstract: Chemokines orchestrate the migration of immune cells throughout the body, but harnessing chemokine signaling to engineer targeted cell trafficking is challenging because of their overlapping interactions and broad expression patterns. Here we used structure-guided protein design to engineer orthogonal chemokine-receptor pairs with minimal crosstalk to native systems. T cells engineered with an ortho-receptor selectively infiltrated tissues producing the ortho-chemokine, in vitro and in vivo. By engineering T cells that both sense and secrete the ortho-chemokine, we generated collective swarming behavior in which pioneer cells attract follower cells via an ortho-chemokine gradient self-organized by positive feedback. By providing orthogonal genetic control over both the generation and sensing of chemokine gradients, this system enables the construction of autonomous spatial targeting programs in engineered cells.
affiliations: University of California, San Francisco (corresponding author)

papers.title: 13C-Metabolic Flux Analysis of Substrate Co-Metabolism in the Methylotrophic Acetogen Eubacterium limosum.
papers.abstract: Acetogens are promising microbial catalysts for the sustainable production of fuels and chemicals, metabolizing a range of renewable single-carbon (C1) compounds with high energetic efficiency. The major challenge is their energy-limited anaerobic lifestyle, which results in slow growth and a limited product spectrum on individual C1 substrates. We previously showed in the acetogen Eubacterium limosum that co-metabolism of glucose-methanol or CO-methanol mixtures results in substantial improvements in growth and acetate productivity. To investigate the underlying mechanism(s), here we conducted 13C metabolic flux analysis (13C-MFA) of E. limosum grown on a glucose-methanol mixture, as well as in single-substrate controls. The results suggest that the main benefit of glucose cofeeding is not provision of additional ATP, but rather a reduction of flux through the ferredoxin-dependent and kinetically challenging reactions of the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway. Subsequent RNAseq analysis showed no significant differences in the expression level of genes involved in methanol metabolism between cofeeding and methanol-only controls, suggesting this reduction of flux is controlled post-transcriptionally. Most surprisingly, we found that under all growth conditions, flux through pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) was in the oxidative direction, with cysteine (added as a reducing agent) providing all required gluconeogenic carbon flux under CO2-fixing conditions. This work provides critical insights into the metabolic network of an emerging model acetogen that will facilitate future metabolic engineering efforts to channel flux to value-added products, and highlights the under-appreciated role of cysteine as a carbon source in acetogenic fermentations.
affiliations: Northeastern University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Bringing large scale top-down metabolic modelling to eukaryotes with PhotoEukStein: a meta-model for unicellular phototrophs
papers.abstract: Defining biological functional traits for unicellular organisms relies on comprehending the set and combination of the biochemical reactions their genomes encode for. This network of biochemical reactions defines the metabolic strategy organisms and communities use. Understanding the functional traits of unicellular organisms involves studying the combination of biochemical reactions encoded in their genomes. These reactions determine the metabolic strategy that organisms and communities use to grow in a specific environment. While prokaryotes have been extensively studied for their metabolic networks, eukaryotes have lagged behind due to the complexity of their genomes and the need for a better understanding of their metabolism. We have created PhotoEukstein, a meta-metabolic model for unicellular phototrophic eukaryotes. This meta-model enables quick and automated derivation of Genome-Scale Metabolic models directly from genomes. We have used it to analyse 533 environmental genomes and marine eukaryotic unicellular plankton transcriptomes. These models can help predict functional traits that cannot be purely deducted from taxonomic information or the listing of metabolic reactions encoded by the genome. They provide the opportunity to build connections with Earth System Models to pinpoint environmental parameters to capture specific functional traits.
affiliations: Génomique Métabolique UMR8030 Genoscope, Institut de Biologie François Jacob, CEA, CNRS, Univ Evry, Université Paris-Saclay, Evry, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cirrhosis-associated immune dysfunction reflects impaired intestinal CD8ab⁺ intraepithelial lymphocyte compartmentalization
papers.abstract: Bacterial infections drive decompensation and mortality in cirrhosis, yet the mechanisms underlying cirrhosis-associated immune dysfunction remain unclear. Current models invoke adaptive immune exhaustion, whereas intestinal intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs), which mediate epithelial surveillance and microbial containment, remain unexplored. We combined spectral flow cytometry of paired duodenal biopsies and blood, plasma proteomics, immunofluorescence and single-cell RNA sequencing in healthy volunteers and patients with compensated or decompensated cirrhosis. The healthy duodenal epithelium was dominated by CD8 alpha beta IELs, which were depleted in cirrhosis, whereas innate cytotoxic populations expanded. CD8 alpha beta IEL loss correlated with plasma markers of bacterial translocation. Residual IELs showed attenuated antimicrobial programs, confirmed by reduced granulysin protein, and enriched cytotoxic pathways. IEL depletion was accompanied by reduced CCR9 on circulating and mucosal CD8 T cells and elevated plasma CCL25. Exposing blood mononuclear cells to patient-level CCL25 concentrations reduced surface CCR9, indicating ligand-driven desensitization. In contrast, circulating lymphocytes retained functional competence and lacked exhaustion markers. Cirrhosis-associated immune dysfunction thus reflects failed intestinal compartmentalization of CD8 alpha beta T cells, linked to disruption of the CCL25-CCR9 axis, rather than systemic exhaustion.
affiliations: KU Leuven Department of Chronic Diseases and Metabolism; Hepatology Research Unit, Laboratory of Mucosal Biology, Leuven, Belgium. (corresponding author)

papers.title: Bacterial vitamin sharing emerges from a balance between release and uptake
papers.abstract: Many microbes use vitamins they cannot synthesize. As a result, vitamin availability impacts microbial community composition and productivity. Yet how vitamins become available to users remains poorly understood. To understand the basis of vitamin sharing, we quantified vitamin B12 synthesis and uptake in over 200 soil, freshwater, and marine bacterial isolates. We reveal the existence of four strategies demarcated by all combinations of high or limited B12 synthesis and uptake. B12 synthesis, but not uptake, was predictable from genomes without pathway knowledge. Among synthesizers, the fraction of vitamin that was extracellular varied over 100-fold. Extracellular B12 was quantitatively predicted from a dynamic model capturing only release via death and reuptake by living cells. A subset of synthesizers rapidly reclaim released B12, resulting in limited sharing, while retainers exhibit limited release or uptake, and providers release without reuptake. Thus, extracellular B12 availability is governed not by synthesis alone, but by the balance between release and uptake.
affiliations: University of Chicago (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genes controlling polysaccharide synthesis, protein folding and basic metabolism ensure intra-host cell adaptation and replication of Yersinia enterocolitica
papers.abstract: Pathogenesis of yersiniosis comprises cell-invasive events in which the bacteria subvert the endocytic-autophagolysosomal pathway of infected host cells to create an intracellular niche for bacterial replication. To determine potential virulence factors that enable intracellular proliferation of Yersinia enterocolitica, we performed a high-throughput transposon-directed insertion site sequencing approach (TraDIS) with infected epithelial HeLa cells. In this screen, we identified seven particular genes that have either metabolic activities in disulfide bond formation (dsbA), glutamine synthesis (glnA), and energy generation (acnB), or dictate synthesis of enterobacterial common antigen ECA (webB/C/F) and LPS (wzx). Individual knockout of the identified genes impaired intracellular replication of Yersinia. Furthermore, these mutants differentially affected host cell autophagy and the acidification of Yersinia-containing vacuoles (YCVs). The results indicate that glnA, acnB, dsbA, wecB, and wecC support autophagy-promoted, intracellular replication of Yersinia. Folding of yet to be defined proteins dependent on dsbA seems to be most critically required for mediating these events. A wzx-controlled LPS synthesis pathway appears implicated in preventing YCV acidification. These results suggest that autophagy induction and adjustment of Yersinia to the intravacuolar environment result from a multifactorial adaptation process that involves formation of a protective carbohydrate envelope and basic metabolic enzymes needed for the refinement of productive intracellular replication.
affiliations: University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf, Universitatsklinikum Hamburg-Eppendorf (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ctcf deficiency in myofibers induces pathological genome reprogramming toward the spontaneous development of myopathy
papers.abstract: How perennial, postmitotic multinucleated tissues, such as skeletal myofibers, maintain their identity and transcriptional adaptation to homeostatic perturbations through adult life is an outstanding question. To address this issue, we investigated the consequences of loss of 3D-genome architecture in skeletal muscles by generating myofiber-specific Ctcf-deficient (CtcfmKO) mice. CtcfmKO mice did not exhibit muscular phenotype at birth but spontaneously developed a severe myopathy. Integrated analysis of snRNAseq, ATACseq and promoter-capture Hi-C revealed both common and fiber-type specific patterns of dysregulated gene expression associated with alterations in chromatin accessibility and promoter-based interactions in Ctcf-deficient myonuclei at distinct stages of myopathy development. Decreased chromatin accessibility at promoters and changes in their connectivity with distal elements were observed across all myonuclei as a direct consequence of Ctcf deficiency at early stages and associated with downregulation of genes implicated in myofiber contraction and anabolism, metabolism, adhesion and neuromuscular transmission. Conversely, at later stages, upregulation of genes leading to persistent activation of ER stress/UPR and catabolism resulted from global reconfiguration of chromatin structure and connectivity, partly as indirect consequence of Ctcf deficiency. Notably, type-IIB myonuclei exhibited specific alterations in gene expression that culminated in loss of fiber-type identity and ectopic expression of inflammatory genes. These results reveal a requirement of Ctcf for maintenance of fiber-type identity and transcriptional adaptation in vivo, through multilayered control of 3D genome integrity. They also indicate an unprecedented association between Ctcf deficiency in myofibers and susceptibility to develop myopathies, whereby Ctcf dispensability for developmental myogenesis confers vulnerability to develop myopathic syndromes.
affiliations: SanfordBurnhamPrebys Medical Discovery Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Single-cell RNA-seq using UltraMarathonRT expands the known transcriptome
papers.abstract: The ability to map messenger RNA (mRNA) molecules from individual cells using next-generation sequencing technologies, known as single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq), is transforming biology by redefining cellular identities with unmatched detail. However, all current protocols depend on copying RNA into complementary DNA with a single reverse transcriptase (RT) derived from murine leukemia virus, which is an RT enzyme known for low processivity and limited ability to unfold complex RNA structures. Here, for the first time, we introduce a group II intron reverse transcriptase, UltraMarathonRT (uMRT), to perform scRNA-seq, a protocol we coined scMarathon-seq. We demonstrate that this enzyme reveals an unexpected transcriptomics landscape by capturing additional genes and other genomic features that conventional RTs miss. We also combined uMRT with metabolic RNA labeling, nucleoside conversion and scRNA-seq to explore genome-wide transcriptome dynamics at the single-cell level. Overall, we establish uMRT as a transformative biotechnological tool for single-cell transcriptomics.
affiliations: Helmholtz Institute for RNA-based Infection Research (HIRI), Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research (HZI), Wuerzburg, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: The nuclear membrane protein Samp1 links peripheral genome organization to the myogenic transcriptional program
papers.abstract: Samp1 is an inner nuclear membrane protein required for myogenic differentiation and involved in chromatin organization at the nuclear periphery. Here, we investigated whether these functions are connected by studying the effects of Samp1 depletion during C2C12 myogenic differentiation using immunofluorescence microscopy, RNA sequencing, FRIC, and chromosome-positioning analysis. Samp1-depleted cells showed strongly reduced MyHC expression and virtually abrogated multinucleated fiber formation. Although cell-cycle withdrawal was not prevented, the transcriptional program driving differentiation was drastically perturbed, with reduced muscle-associated transcripts and incomplete repression of genes normally downregulated during myogenesis. Samp1 depletion also disrupted peripheral chromatin organization and prevented the accumulation of peripheral heterochromatin typically seen during differentiation. In addition, radial chromosome distribution was disrupted, evidenced by the failure of chromosome 8 to reposition to the nuclear periphery during differentiation. Together, these findings link the requirement for Samp1 in myogenic differentiation to its role in genome organization at the nuclear periphery.
affiliations: Stockholm University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Rapid, reversible RNA/DNA precipitation using rare earth ion coordination
papers.abstract: Efficient recovery and removal of nucleic acids remain major challenges in molecular biology, diagnostics, and viral-vector manufacturing. Conventional precipitation methods often require organic solvents, low temperatures, and extended centrifugation, while nuclease-based contaminant removal can be incomplete and/or is incompatible with downstream workflows. Here, we evaluate NADA, a trivalent rare earth-based reagent, for rapid, solvent-free precipitation of RNA and DNA, and ALGO-mediated recovery of the full range of properties of unmodified RNA. Using hepatitis B virus pre-genomic RNA, lambda bacteriophage DNA, and the HBV nucleocapsid as model systems, we show that NADA rapidly sequesters both ssRNA and dsDNA from solution, reducing Midori Green nucleic acid fluorescence and UV absorption to baseline levels. The NADA complex prevents HBV core protein binding to the HBV pgRNA, and therefore triggering of nucleocapsid formation, even when added simultaneously with core protein, suggesting that lanthanide ion coordination, out-competes the cognate Cp for viral RNA-binding interactions. Recovery with ALGO restores pgRNA integrity and functionality, enabling subsequent assembly of the expected T=4/T=3 nucleocapsids. In contrast, pre-assembled nucleocapsids resist NADA-ALGO treatment, demonstrating coat protein capsid-mediated protection of encapsidated pgRNA. Similar outcomes for lambda dsDNA establish NADA/ALGO as a rapid, reversible, and selective alternative platform for nucleic acid precipitation, with potential applications in viral particle purification, contaminant removal, and RNA handling workflows.
affiliations: University of Leeds (corresponding author)

papers.title: High-plex protein imaging across thick tissue by synchronized amplification
papers.abstract: High-plex protein imaging is essential for decoding complex tissue organization, yet it remains largely confined to thin sections. Current approaches in millimeter-thick samples suffer from poor signal penetration and depth-dependent, uneven signal amplification. Even with specialized instrumentation to facilitate probe diffusion, iterative millimeter-thick tissue workflows can take more than four days per staining round, and reported eleven-marker experiments extend beyond a month. We introduce Amplification by Cyclic Extension (ACE), a DNA-barcoded, synchronized in situ amplification strategy that uses thermally controlled cyclic extension to coordinate DNA concatemer growth across tissue depths. By synchronously activating and coordinating reaction progression throughout the sample, ACE enables controlled, uniform signal amplification across tissue depths. Using ACE, we demonstrate 63-plex protein and RNA imaging in thin sections, 22-plex protein imaging in 200 m mouse brain sections, and 16-plex protein imaging in 1 mm-thick brain tissue encompassing over three million cells. For millimeter-thick tissues, ACE reduces per-round target-switching time from multiple days to less than eight hours, shifting volumetric high-plex protein imaging from months to days. Together, these results establish ACE as a synchronized amplification strategy that enables scalable high-plex protein imaging in thick tissues.
affiliations: Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering, Harvard University, Boston, MA, 02215, USA; Department of Systems Biology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, (corresponding author)

papers.title: Hydrogel microneedle patch for low-cost, colorimetric, continuous glucose monitoring
papers.abstract: Diabetes is a chronic condition characterized by dysregulated blood glucose levels. Continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) enable minimally invasive, real-time monitoring of glucose levels, but broader access requires devices that are both effective and affordable. Popular CGMs such as Dexcom and FreeStyle Libre have high accuracy and are integrated with mobile applications to display real-time data and alerts but are limited by high cost. We developed a low-cost, electronic-free, microneedle hydrogel patch CGM that utilizes colorimetric detection to continuously monitor glucose levels. The proposed patch penetrates the skin and absorbs interstitial fluid (ISF) containing glucose. This glucose reacts with glucose oxidase (GOx) enzyme embedded in the hydrogel, producing gluconic acid and decreasing the pH of the hydrogel. As glucose levels increase, decreasing pH levels are reported by the loaded pH indicator bromocresol purple (BCP) via a color change from purple to yellow. This system was validated through a combination of in vitro experiments and COMSOL computational modeling to assess performance at physiologically relevant glucose concentrations. The resulting hydrogels demonstrated reversible and dynamic color changes in response to glucose levels ranging from 3.5-10 mmol/L (63-180 mg/dL), supporting their potential for continuous monitoring applications. A quantitative, image-based analysis method enabled estimation of glucose concentration from photographs, demonstrating strong predictive performance (RMSE=8.59 mg/dL, R2=0.94). Although optimization of mechanical strength and diffusion kinetics remain necessary, these findings highlight the promise of integrating colorimetric sensing with microneedle-based sampling for affordable, user-friendly glucose monitoring.
affiliations: Duke University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Individual-Specific Gaussian Graphical Models for Heterogeneous Populations with Application to Epigenetic Gene Regulation in Lung Adenocarcinoma
papers.abstract: Inter-patient molecular heterogeneity is a fundamental challenge in precision oncology: population-level multi-omics networks reveal average biology aggregated across the population but obscure individual variations that drive differential clinical outcomes. We introduce SIREN (Sample-specific Inference via Regularized Empirical-Bayes Networks), a method that estimates one partial correlation network per sample across omics layers by combining a population-level empirical Bayes prior with a rank-1 individual-specific update. Since a sample-specific precision matrix cannot be estimated from a single observation, SIREN uses a conjugate Inverse Wishart prior whose mean is the Oracle Approximating Shrinkage estimator, yielding closed-form individual-specific posteriors without MCMC. On simulated heterogeneous populations, SIREN achieves superior edge recovery over population-average methods including OAS, Ledoit-Wolf, and graphical Lasso, while remaining competitive in homogeneous settings. Applied to paired transcriptomic and methylomic profiles from lung adenocarcinoma, SIREN identifies individual-specific gene-methylation regulatory edges that stratify patients by survival in ways population-level analysis cannot, implicating chromatin remodeling and WNT signaling pathways in epigenetic heterogeneity. SIREN is computationally scalable and available as a Python package.
affiliations: Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health (corresponding author)

papers.title: Learning Dynamic Protein Representations at Scale with Distograms
papers.abstract: Protein function and other biological properties often depend on structural dynamics, yet most machine-learning predictors rely on static representations. Physics-based molecular simulations can describe conformational variability but remain computationally prohibitive at scale. Generative models provide a more efficient alternative, though their ability to produce accurate conformational ensembles is still limited. In this work, we bypass expensive simulations by leveraging residue-residue distance probability distributions (distograms) from structure predictors such as Boltz-2. Our approach provides a scalable way to encode dynamic information into protein representations, aiming to improve function prediction without explicit conformational sampling. All code required to reproduce the experiments presented in this work is publicly available at https://github.com/anonymous-research-world/distodyn.
affiliations: Institut Pasteur - CNRS (corresponding author)

papers.title: A multimodal precision oncology platform integrating genomics,single-cell transcriptomics, and functional drug screening expandstherapeutic options in pediatric brain tumors
papers.abstract: Precision oncology for pediatric brain tumors mainly relies on clinically validated, targetable genomic alterations, which are often sparse, yield few matched therapies, and do not guide chemotherapy selection. We developed a tiered framework in which deep whole-genome sequencing and single-cell RNA sequencing extend targeted-therapy selection, with ex vivo functional drug screening supporting selection of both targeted therapies and chemotherapies. We applied it to 17 children with malignant CNS tumors. The approach expanded recommendations beyond genomics: functional screening provided every patient with at least one high-confidence targeted-therapy or chemotherapy nomination, while single-cell RNA sequencing identified an average of 37 druggable gene targets per patient, producing a fourfold increase in high-confidence targeted-therapy recommendations. In an exploratory analysis, functional classifications were directionally consistent with outcomes in 8 of 10 evaluable cases, although combination treatments and radiation precluded causal attribution. Single-cell profiling also identified subclone-specific vulnerabilities, supporting prospective evaluation of the platform's feasibility and predictive utility.
affiliations: University of Utah (corresponding author)

papers.title: Dysregulation of epithelial differentiation architecture underlies field cancerization in head and neck cancer
papers.abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) has exceptionally high recurrence rates, exceeding 50%, contributing to mortality and morbidity. This recurrence rate is proposed to be due to field cancerization, a phenomenon where tumor-adjacent "field" tissue that appears histologically normal harbors molecular changes that prime it for subsequent tumor growth. Current models attribute field cancerization to shared driver mutations between tumors and adjacent at-risk tissue, but this assumption has never been directly tested. To comprehensively characterize this phenomenon, we profiled patient-matched tumor, normal-adjacent field (NAF), contralateral normal, and blood samples from HPV-negative HNSCC patients using whole genome sequencing, targeted driver gene sequencing, single-nucleus multiome profiling, spatial transcriptomics and functional proliferation assays. While histologically normal NAF tissues did harbor expanded mutant clones, these mutations rarely overlapped with paired tumors and were not shared across patients, suggesting molecular features beyond mutations are altered in NAF. Single-cell multiomics revealed that NAF epithelium loses its normal organizational hierarchy: basal stem cell markers persist in differentiated cells, while terminal differentiation programs fail to activate, with reconfiguration of both gene regulatory networks and cell-cell interactions. Proliferating cells appeared in tissue layers normally restricted to post-mitotic cells, a pattern typically seen only in overt dysplasia. Within this disrupted hierarchy, a distinct epithelial state arose in NAF that expressed both normal epithelial and tumor-associated markers, which we localized to the parabasal layers using immunofluorescence and spatial transcriptomics. Together, our findings demonstrate that field cancerization operates through epithelial hierarchy disorganization that disrupts differentiation, generates cells with tumor-like features, and may create a permissive environment for the expansion of cancer-associated mutations, all within tissue that appears histologically normal.
affiliations: Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Biomarker-driven and gene-enhanced viral therapy for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor
papers.abstract: Background: High-grade malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNST) frequently lose Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), reducing the repressive histone mark, H3K27me3. We hypothesized that H3K27me3 loss sensitizes MPNST to oncolytic HSV due to impaired transcriptional resistance. HSV replication is also restricted by the integrated stress response, normally countered by HSV ICP34.5, representing an additional resistance pathway to ICP34.5-attenuated HSV. Methods: PRC2 loss-of-function was evaluated as a biomarker of HSV G47{Delta} ({Delta}ICP34.5) susceptibility in MPNST using isogenic, pharmacologic inhibition, and genetic rescue models. CUT&RUN and RNA-sequencing defined PRC2-dependent viral and host responses. We engineered a G47{Delta}-derived vector (G47{Delta}2) with tumor-regulated ICP34.5 expression [G47{Delta}2,ins(BIRC5>ICP34.5)] and evaluated efficacy in MPNST xenografts. Results: H3K27me3 deficiency increased G47{Delta} sensitivity and viral spread in vitro. CUT&RUN demonstrated PRC2-dependent H3K27me3 accumulation on the viral genome, explaining G47{Delta} activity in H3K27me3-deficient MPNST. RNA sequencing of G47{Delta} infected MPNST cells revealed heightened integrated stress response activity and blunted induction of translation-associated programs in the PRC2-deficient state (both p<0.001), consistent with compensatory resistance at the level of viral protein translation. Accordingly, tumor-regulated ICP34.5 HSV limited daily tumor-volume growth to 0.6% (95% CI, -2.9-4.2%), improving upon both G47{Delta}2 (8.3%; 4.5-12.2%) and controls (22.5%; 17.4-27.8%). A murine gastrointestinal toxicity phenotype reduced all-cause event-free survival, indicating vector and dosing optimizations are needed to widen the therapeutic window. Conclusions: H3K27me3 loss creates a paradoxical antiviral state that tumor-selective ICP34.5 overcomes to rescue HSV anti-tumor activity, supporting biomarker-driven viral engineering to exploit the permissive transcriptional state of H3K27me3-deficient MPNSTs.
affiliations: University of Minnesota (corresponding author)

papers.title: A low-androgen environment sustains redox-active sGC states required to restrain castration-resistant prostate cancer growth via elevated cGMP levels
papers.abstract: Castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) remains incurable and fatal, creating a dire need for new safe and effective treatment strategies. We recently reported that the soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) stimulator, riociguat, cooperates with standard-of-care androgen deprivation (AD) to inhibit castration-resistant tumor burden by oxygenating hypoxic tumor niches and inducing tumor apoptosis. We further found that AD restores the sensitivity of CRPC cells to riociguat, which requires a redox-active functional sGC complex to stimulate cyclic GMP (cGMP) production. As redox reprogramming is a feature of the low-androgen PC milieu, to better establish the parameters of riociguat efficacy, we wished to determine whether redox-inactive forms of sGC persist in the castrate setting. To do so, we treated CRPC LNAI tumor-bearing animals with cinaciguat, an sGC activator which preferentially acts on the oxidized sGC complex. We found that, compared to riociguat, cinaciguat did not significantly increase intratumoral or systemic cGMP levels in the castrate setting. Nor did cinaciguat treatment significantly decrease tumor burden or oxygenate the hypoxic CRPC tumors. Given the preferential activity of cinaciguat on the redox-inactive sGC complex, our results indicate that the low-androgen castrate setting maintains the sGC complex in its functionally reduced state, affirming the critical benefit of AD for riociguat efficacy in the lethal castration-resistant disease stage.
affiliations: University of Miami Miller School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: LuTuFlow: a deep learning-based pipeline for quantitative characterization of mouse lung tumors in CT imaging
papers.abstract: Computed tomography (CT) is a widely used, non-invasive imaging tool to monitor tumor growth. Tumor identification and volumetric quantification are crucial for assessing tumor burden, whereas tracking individual tumors by aligning scans from multiple time points reveals disease progression. However, these processes remain largely dependent on manual analysis, limiting the accuracy, reproducibility, objectivity, and scalability of tumor characterization. Several deep learning models have enabled automated segmentation and object identification. However, open-source, integrated software platforms that cover the entire workflow - including processing raw CT images, annotating and tracking tumors through time, and generating data reports and visualizations - are still needed. Here, we present LuTuFlow, a computer vision pipeline incorporating a nnU-Net-based deep learning model, configured for murine lung segmentation and tumor analysis. We integrated these modules into a Napari plugin, allowing researchers to apply the entire automated workflow to transform raw CT scan datasets into quantitative readouts and interactive visualizations in a simple graphical user interface. The resulting model, iteratively refined using expert-corrected annotations, generated reliable quantitative estimates of tumor burden.
affiliations: EPFL (Swiss Fed. Inst. of Technology Lausanne) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Predicting resistance to synthetic lethal therapies in cancer
papers.abstract: Background Synthetic lethality (SL) occurs when an alteration in one gene renders cells vulnerable to inhibition of another, offering a strategy for targeted cancer therapy. PARP inhibitors represent the first clinically approved synthetic lethal therapy, and numerous additional candidates are now in clinical trials. Unfortunately, resistance to these therapies is common and impairs their overall effectiveness. Although there is a growing understanding of the factors that predict synthetic lethal interactions, the prediction of mechanisms driving resistance to these effects remains largely unstudied. Here, we sought to determine whether SL resistance could be predicted a priori using protein-protein interaction networks integrated with additional molecular profiles. Methods We curated genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 chemogenetic resistance screens spanning ten unique SL biomarker-target pairs. For each pair, we extracted resistance genes and computed features capturing protein-protein interactions, gene expression, and essentiality. We compared these features between resistance and non-resistance genes and developed a random forest classifier to predict resistance. Model performance was assessed using random-split and structured leave-one-out schemes based on biomarkers, targets, and SL pairs to ensure robust generalisation. Independent validation of the model was performed by assessing its ability to predict resistance to two SL therapies currently in clinical trials, MTAP-PRMT5 and ATM-ATR. Results Resistance genes were significantly enriched among the protein-protein interaction partners of SL pairs across multiple datasets, suggesting functional interaction networks can aid the prioritisation of resistance mechanisms. Resistance genes tended to be more co-expressed with their associated target and also displayed distinct essentiality patterns. Although no individual feature was strongly predictive, integrating all features in a random forest model improved discrimination between resistance and non-resistance genes. Under leave-one-SL-pair-out cross-validation - our most stringent test of generalisation - the model achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.72 across ten pairs (range 0.57-0.91; mean average precision ~9%); a random train-test split gave a higher AUROC (~0.78) that we treat as an optimistic upper bound, since biomarkers and targets are shared across folds. Average precision remained low in absolute terms, reflecting the inherent challenge of predicting extremely rare resistance events (<1% of genes). Conclusions Resistance to synthetic lethal therapies arises, at least in part, from predictable patterns of network connectivity, transcriptional coordination, and context-dependent essentiality. Our integrative framework provides a computational approach for anticipating resistance mechanisms across the expanding landscape of synthetic lethal therapies, offering a foundation for designing more durable and effective combination treatments.
affiliations: University College Dublin (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cytoplasmic FKBP7 reflux sustains NFE2L1 levels in an adaptive response to chemotherapy in prostate cancer cells
papers.abstract: Understanding how cancer cells adapt to chemotherapy is essential for overcoming drug resistance. Here, we identify a mechanism of taxane resistance in prostate cancer mediated by FKBP7, a poorly characterized cis-trans prolyl isomerase resident in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Using cell fractionation, we show that FKBP7 undergoes proteasome-independent retrotranslocation from the ER to the cytosol. This cytosolic pool is increased in docetaxel-resistant cells, which have also developed an enhanced capacity to counteract chemotherapy-induced oxidative stress. In the cytosol, FKBP7 associates with the translation machinery, interacting with multiple regions of the scaffolding protein eIF4G1, including its C-terminal HEAT3 domain, as well as with the 40S ribosomal subunit and polysomes. Polysome profiling and RNA sequencing after FKBP7 silencing revealed that FKBP7 loss leads to translation buffering of a large set of mRNAs, many of which are targets of the transcription factor NFE2L1, a master regulator of the oxidative stress response. Consistently, FKBP7 sustained NFE2L1 protein levels, and both proteins were required for the survival of docetaxel-resistant cells. Pharmacological inhibition of NFE2L1 activation suppressed the growth of docetaxel-resistant cells. We further report the first structural characterization of the FKBP7 catalytic domain by NMR, showing that it is a well-folded protein that binds rapamycin and everolimus, but not FK506. Together, these findings uncover a moonlighting function for an ER-resident chaperone in cytosolic translational control and oxidative stress adaptation and identify the FKBP7-NFE2L1 axis as a potential therapeutic target to overcome chemoresistance.
affiliations: Gustave Roussy (corresponding author)

papers.title: Engineered cells that sense and respond to interleukin-23 with neutralizing therapy for autoimmunity
papers.abstract: Engineered cell sensors are powerful tools for monitoring biomarkers and delivering timely therapy. Here we create an engineered cell sensor of interleukin-23 (IL-23), a critical biomarker in many autoimmune diseases, and a therapeutic delivery platform for autoimmune disease management. We utilized Modular Extracellular Sensor Architecture (MESA), a promising platform given its modularity and previously developed cell sensors for immune targets such as IL-10. First, we developed a library of IL-23 MESA receptors by incorporating IL-23-specific nanobody binders and performed high-throughput functional screening. We achieved further receptor optimization by modifying the extracellular linker length and the ratio of receptor chain expression. Receptor performance was highly correlated with predicted geometric features such as binder pair distance and degree of transmembrane domain dimerization. The receptors were limited by poor surface expression and functioned most effectively as sensors for intracellular IL-23. Finally, we modified the IL-23 sensing circuit to output an IL-23 neutralizing nanobody with the potential to reduce inflammation triggered by IL-23 secretion. This sense-and-respond architecture can be utilized for dynamic therapeutic treatment to meet the dynamic relapse-remitting pattern of many autoimmune diseases.
affiliations: University of Michigan (corresponding author)

papers.title: Comprehensive calculation of product and ATP yields for glucose fermentation
papers.abstract: Lignocellulose sugars are degraded anaerobically by microbial communities as part of the carbon cycle, yielding short- and medium-chain fatty acids as intermediates and carbon dioxide and methane as final products. The underlying metabolic network is branched and its product yields depend on environmental conditions. We compiled a pan-catabolic network of the anaerobic digestion of glucose into 11 fermentation products, including alcohols, acids, and ketones. It consists of 75 reactions and incorporates energy conservation via substrate-level phosphorylation and transport-coupled phosphorylation, with ferredoxin, NADH, and quinol as electron carriers. We calculated all net conversions of glucose into fermentation products and their ATP yields. We find 195,629 unique conversions (about 50% with non-zero ATP yield), including known and many novel ones. Conversions with identical product stoichiometry can differ in ATP yield: glucose to propionate and acetate is achieved by different subnetworks with 23 distinct ATP/glucose yields, and even glucose to lactate shows 12 yields ranging from 0 to 4.5. The driving force of the conversions decreases with ATP yield, whereas the number of reactions used does not correlate with it. The known catabolic conversions underlying anaerobic digestion might thus be only the tip of the iceberg.
affiliations: VU Amsterdam (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Single-Cell Atlas of PVOD Across the Lifespan Reveals Cellular and Molecular Therapeutic Targets
papers.abstract: Rationale Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease (PVOD) is a progressive and lethal disease cured only lung transplant. While genetic mutations in EIF2AK4 have been identified in some cases, 70% of PVOD patients have no known etiology. Objectives To construct a single-cell atlas to define the cellular and molecular constituents driving pathophysiology in PVOD. Methods Lung samples were collected from four idiopathic non-EIF2AK4 mutation pediatric and adult PVOD patients and age-matched controls. Analyses of single-cell RNA sequencing, Xenium spatial transcriptomics, and immunohistochemistry were performed to identify cell state changes and differential gene expression between controls and PVOD and subsequent transcriptome comparison between our PVOD and published pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) datasets. Measurement and Main Results The single-cell atlas reveals marked changes in the PVOD endothelium compared to controls. EndMT and ectopic COL15A1+ systemic venous shunts and pulmonary vein endothelium are hallmarks of PVOD. Molecular analyses reveal activation of the integrated stress response (ISR)/ATF4, TGF{beta} signaling, MAPK signaling, and BRD4 are potential key players in the pathophysiology of PVOD. While PVOD and PAH share both pathological and some molecular mechanisms, ISR and TGF{beta} signaling are more prominent in PVOD than PAH. Conclusions These data indicate that endothelial dysfunction is a primary etiology in the development of PVOD with activation of multiple pathways with druggable targets.
affiliations: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Anisomycin-induced ribosome collisions follow a dose-dependent positional rule, distinct from the UV-induced collision landscape
papers.abstract: Ribosome collisions trigger stress pathways such as the ribotoxic stress response (RSR), yet how different ribosome-impairing stimuli shape where collisions form on mRNAs remains unclear. Here, we combine monosome- and disome-resolved ribosome profiling with proteomics of collided-ribosome fractions to compare anisomycin- and UV-induced ribosome impairment in mouse embryonic stem cells. Low-dose anisomycin, a widely used collision-inducing paradigm, does not generate collisions dispersed along transcripts but a post-initiation collision zone, with stalled monosomes and disomes accumulating within the first ~70 nucleotides of coding sequences across most translated mRNAs. High-dose anisomycin, commonly considered collision-poor, produces the same pattern shifted closer to the start codon and reduced in amplitude. These observations support a single dose-dependent positional rule, in which drug occupancy determines how far ribosomes progress before arrest and ongoing initiation supplies trailing ribosomes. In contrast, 30 min after UV irradiation, collisions are detectable biochemically but appear more dispersed, with few recurrent hotspots and preferential accumulation on highly translated mRNAs. Collided-ribosome fractions share enrichment of the collision sensor EDF1 across conditions, whereas recruitment of ZNF598 and initiation factors is most evident after UV. Our results refine the interpretation of anisomycin-based collision paradigms and show that collision landscapes depend on the nature of the stimulus.
affiliations: Universite de Lausanne (corresponding author)

papers.title: Host Plant and Light Regime Shape Limited, Whole-Body Transcriptional Rhythmicity in the Bird Cherry-Oat Aphid (Rhopalosiphum padi)
papers.abstract: Background Daily cycles in environmental conditions shape the biology of plants and their insect herbivores. Because aphids feed nearly continuously from the phloem to sustain rapid population growth, they maintain prolonged, direct contact with their hosts, which exposes them to plant-derived daily rhythms in addition to those arising from the environment. We investigated whole-body transcriptional rhythmicity in the bird cherry-oat aphid (Rhopalosiphum padi) under light-dark (LD) and constant darkness (DD) conditions while aphids fed on either wheat or an artificial diet sachet, sampling transcript expression every 4 h over a 48 h window. Results Only a small fraction of the transcriptome in R. padi displayed 24 h rhythms, and this fraction declined further as light and host cues were removed. Unexpectedly, more transcripts were rhythmic in DD than in LD on wheat. This trend was not present in diet-fed aphids and was not consistently detected across rhythmic detection tools or significance thresholds. Transcripts that were rhythmic in aphids feeding on wheat hosts had higher amplitudes compared to those feeding on diet. Peak expression (i.e., phase) for rhythmic transcripts clustered near dawn and pre-dusk (zeitgeber time, ZT0 and ZT12), except for transcripts detected as rhythmic in darkness-only on wheat, which peaked approximately 4 h later. Rhythmic transcripts detected in this study were functionally enriched for processes relevant to plant-aphid interactions, including carbohydrate metabolism and detoxification. Subsequent promoter analysis found E-box motifs in both rhythmic and non-rhythmic transcripts, and de novo promoter motif discovery on rhythmic transcripts identified recurring Mad/SMAD- and PAR-bZIP-like motifs. Conclusions Whole-body transcriptional rhythmicity in R. padi is limited in scope and appears strongly dependent on environmental and host-derived cues. The candidate transcripts and regulatory pathways identified in this study provide clear targets for tissue-specific, functionally minded follow-up studies to investigate the extent and regulatory mechanisms of endogenous physiological and behavioral rhythms in R. padi.
affiliations: Colorado State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A massively parallel reporter screen defines the syntax of SECReTE, a secretion-enhancing cis regulatory targeting element, in mammalian cells
papers.abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) localization to specific subcellular regions is crucial for proper protein translation and localization. Potential means to localize mRNAs include cis-acting or structural motifs embedded within the sequence. We previously identified a secretion-enhancing cis regulatory targeting element (SECReTE) enriched in mRNAs encoding secreted proteins from prokaryotes, eukaryotes, and viruses, found to enhance both protein synthesis and secretion by localizing mRNAs to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. Defined as at least 10 consecutive NNY triplets (where N is any nucleotide and Y is a pyrimidine), this highly degenerate motif can be specified by approximately ~10^15 different sequence combinations. Yet, some combinations may prove more efficient than others in regulating mRNA localization and protein secretion. To better understand SECReTE syntax and to identify robust combinations, we designed and synthesized a library of ~5 x 10^4 variants and inserted them into the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of two reporter genes, green fluorescent protein (GFP) and immunoglobulin light chain. We expressed each variant in Chinese hamster ovary cells and assayed their activity using parallel assays to measure the effect of each variant upon mRNA partitioning between the ER and cytoplasm, and protein secretion. Our results reveal that ER-associated mRNAs are enriched with SECReTE elements of a defined syntax. Notably, RRY repeats (where R is purine) were superior to NNY repeats. Variants conferring a high mRNA ER localization score consistently enhanced protein secretion, confirming the mechanistic relationship between mRNA targeting to the ER and secretion efficiency. The correlation between variant performances across both reporters suggests a shared regulatory mechanism. Additional analysis identified a novel secretion-promoting cis element, called "split NNS" (where S is G or C). This work refines the syntactic definition of mRNA localization motifs that regulate protein secretion in both natural and heterologous expression systems.
affiliations: Weizmann Institute of Science (corresponding author)

papers.title: A mysterious jelly seems to be left behind by toads
Inundated AI conferences impose submissions caps
Whistleblowing in universities is ‘extraordinarily risky’: stronger protections are needed
Diversify Nobel-prize nominations before it’s too late
Atomic-scale spin sensing of a 2D d-wave altermagnet via helical tunneling
Selective, Catalytic Oxidation of Polyethylene Surfaces
Author Correction: Parkinson’s disease as a somato-cognitive action network disorder
Can GLP-1s heal the brain? Obesity drugs get a makeover for addiction and depression
Lead-tainted teeth reveal medieval mines’ unequal toll
Current aviation roadmaps are not within planetary boundaries
papers.abstract: Aviation decarbonization roadmaps predominantly rely on replacing fossil kerosene with alternative jet fuels, yet the systemic impact of these alternatives on planetary boundaries other than climate change has not been quantified. Here we integrate prospective life-cycle inventories with the planetary boundaries framework to evaluate the absolute impacts of aviation roadmaps as time-dependent trajectories, rather than endpoint snapshots. Across scenarios to 2050, we find that fuel-switch-centered roadmaps do not achieve sustainability, persistently transgress the climate change and biosphere integrity core boundaries, and exert large demands for energy, land, freshwater and CO 2 capture that challenge their feasibility. Slower traffic growth brings aviation closer to its share of the safe operating space in terms of lowering energy demand, but respecting additional planetary boundaries requires air traffic to decline by at least 7.2% yr −1 . Our results show that aligning aviation with Earth’s safe operating space cannot be achieved through fuel substitution alone and requires governance strategies that combine supply-side solutions with explicit demand-side measures.

papers.title: Securing critical rare-earth supply through end-of-life NdFeB magnets recycling via molten salt electrolysis with consumable Mg-cathode
Author Correction: Engineered CRISPR-OsCas12f1 and RhCas12f1 with robust activities and expanded target range for genome editing
Epitaxial-strain engineering of supported tensile noble metallene oxides for enhanced oxidation catalysis
papers.abstract: Supported two-dimensional noble metal oxides (metallene oxides) hold great promise for heterogeneous catalysis owing to their maximized surface exposure and tunable electronic structures. However, their high surface energy and low oxidation potentials make them intrinsically unstable under reaction conditions. Here, we report an epitaxial strain strategy to stabilize and modulate the electronic structure of supported PtO 2 metallene oxide. By employing rutile TiO 2 and rutile SnO 2 supports with distinct lattice parameters, we achieve epitaxial growth of PtO 2 metallene oxide layers with controlled strain states, where the larger-lattice SnO 2 substrate imposes biaxial tensile strain on PtO 2 . The tensile-strained PtO 2 /SnO 2 exhibits a reconfigured Pt–O electronic environment that simultaneously improves structural resilience and enhances the intrinsic reactivity of PtO 2 , delivering markedly improved methane oxidation performance with a T 90 of 370 °C (versus 434 °C for PtO 2 /TiO 2 and 469 °C for PtO x /Al 2 O 3 ) and

papers.title: Population-resolved single-emitter spectroscopy
A multi-stage engineering framework for feasible scheduling of large-scale energy batch transport systems
Colossal visible birefringence and ultraviolet hyperbolicity in wide bandgap semiconductor CuAlO2
Controlled crosslink cleavage and phase separation enable highly stretchable and strong 3D-printed hydrogel for soft robotics
Gamma-alumina as a highly active hydrogenation catalyst deciphered by molecular nitrogen
Disrupting the NAD+/NAM metabolic ratio driven by IL-1β inflammatory response potentiates chemotherapy and chemoimmunotherapy in mice
Metabolically reprogrammed blastoids from totipotent-like stem cells exhibit enhanced tissue-specific organ-like development and placental formation
Wireless, optoelectronic, multimodal skin sensor for simultaneous monitoring of mechanical stress and vascular responses
CD200+ fibroblasts prime the immunoregulatory function of granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells in inflammatory arthritis
papers.abstract: Granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (G-MDSCs) are immunoregulatory cells of the neutrophil lineage. Here, we show that immunoregulation by G-MDSCs is imprinted by the joint tissue microenvironment in patients with axial spondyloarthritis and in animal models of inflammatory arthritis. We demonstrate that the suppressive function of G-MDSCs is significantly enhanced in the joint tissue, but not in the circulation. Analysis of public single-cell RNA sequencing datasets was consistent with Cd200r1 high Hmgb2 + precursors differentiating into G-MDSCs following interaction with Cd200 + fibroblasts. In hTNFtg/ Il23mc mice, treatment with a CD200R1 agonist promoted an immunoregulatory signature associated with PD-L1 expression, whereas CD200 blockade reversed the phenotype. Following adoptive transfer of G-MDSC precursor cells into arthritic mice, administration of a CD200-blocking antibody impaired the differentiation of PD-L1 + G-MDSCs and exacerbated disease severity. These findings reveal a tissue-intrinsic program that facilitates resolution of inflammation through fibroblast-myeloid crosstalk that enhances G-MDSC function.

papers.title: Precise construction of antiparallel-stacked 2D imine covalent organic frameworks for atmospheric water harvesting
High average and linear scaling of Ecological Footprint in cities
Characterizing the onset and progression of cancer cachexia using routine clinical data
papers.abstract: In 52,236 patients with cancer, cachectic weight loss episodes were linked to lower survival rates, occurred at times of disease progression, and carried a consistent serological signature across routine laboratory markers. Specific tumor genotypes, including TP53 mutations, were also positively associated with cachexia risk. Statistical models were trained to predict a patient’s impending risk of cachexia.

papers.title: Autologous and broadly neutralizing antibodies drive ART-free HIV control
papers.abstract: A secondary analysis of trial data shows that both host antibodies and infused antibodies against HIV help to delay viral rebound after interruption of antiretroviral therapy (ART), which could inform approaches to durable, ART-free HIV control.

papers.title: Human–artificial intelligence collaboration for comanaging epilepsy in real time
papers.abstract: A small epilepsy monitoring study shows that a moderated, large language model-based chat interface lets patients converse with their electroencephalography monitoring in real time, using a smartphone, and patient feedback cut seizure-detector false alarms by about 80% without clinician input.

papers.title: Author Correction: Monocyte-derived galectin-1hi cells provide innate immune help in the generation of functional memory CD8+ T cells
Targeting ribosome biogenesis
papers.abstract: New work reveals a small-molecule inhibitor of the human ribosome biogenesis AAA-ATPase NVL that shows high selectivity and anti-proliferative activity. This holds promises for the development of better cancer drugs that target ribosome biogenesis.

papers.title: A selective NVL inhibitor suppresses tumor growth by targeting ribosome biogenesis
papers.abstract: Guo, Tao and Cruz et al. identified a selective inhibitor named MM17 of nuclear valosin-containing protein-like (NVL), an AAA+ ATPase responsible for assembly of large ribosome subunit (60S). A bioavailable derivative, MM927, blocks 60S biogenesis, activates p53 and suppresses tumor growth, suggesting NVL as a potential therapeutic target.

papers.title: Rare k-mers reveal centromere haplogroups underlying human diversity and cancer translocations
papers.abstract: By defining centromere haplogroups from rare k-mer variation, Shiraishi et al. uncover extensive hidden diversity and link centromere structure to human evolution and disease-associated genomic instability.

papers.title: A high-dimensional population code in the bat motor cortex during natural dexterous flight
papers.abstract: Bats use their hand-like wings to reproduce natural flights with wingbeat-level precision. Rather than mainly tracking the wingbeat cycle, the wing motor cortex generates sparse, distinct population states with little shared variance across wingbeats, resulting in a high-dimensional code distinct from that typically observed in constrained tasks.

papers.title: Mechanisms of transcription control by distal enhancers from single-gene nanoscopy
papers.abstract: High-resolution real-time imaging of enhancer-promoter communication reveals how the two genomic loci are actively brought together through cohesin-mediated loop extrusion and how E-P interactions are temporally coordinated with transcriptional bursts. Unexpectedly, components of the RNA Pol II general machinery form nanoscale clusters at distal enhancers, and embedding the promoter into such clusters boosts GTF activities and triggers burst initiation.

papers.title: PTPRS mediates invasion of tetanus neurotoxin into the central nervous system
papers.abstract: Tetanus neurotoxin enters the central nervous system through motor neurons. This study identifies PTPRS as the long-sought retrograde transport receptor that directs toxin trafficking in motor neurons into the spinal cord, uncovering a host pathway that can be targeted for post-exposure treatment and for drug delivery into the central nervous system.

papers.title: The nerve rings twice
Astrocytes go into presenter mode
Multidimensional view of immunotherapy
papers.abstract: The introduction of immune checkpoint blockade revolutionized cancer treatments. Since then, the field of immunotherapy has expanded exponentially, both in therapeutic innovations and applicable disease contexts. Investigators across disciplines discuss how they are reimagining strategies to drive the immune system in contexts of cancer, autoimmunity, and beyond.

papers.title: Viral deISGylation holds the key to the metabolic kingdom
Regulatory B cells: Induced, inspired, and ready to soothe neuroinflammation
The narrow path to CD8+ T cell recognition of mutant p53
The matrix remembers
Transposable element splicing reveals a tumor-enriched class of gene-independent transcripts
papers.abstract: Li et al. systematically map splicing within and between transposable elements (TEs) across cancers and define TEtrans, a tumor-enriched class of gene-independent transcripts. TEtrans display distinct regulatory programs and can function as oncogenic RNAs or encode immunogenic tumor antigens, expanding the functional landscape of TE reactivation in cancer.

papers.title: Structural basis of directionality control in large serine integrases
papers.abstract: Shin et al. present cryo-EM structures of the SPβ integrase along the integration and excision pathways that provide mechanistic insights addressing the long-standing questions of how large serine integrases enforce highly directional DNA recombination and how the cognate recombination directionality factor leads to a complete reversal of directionality.

papers.title: Reverse transcribed ssDNA derepresses translation of a retron antiviral protein
papers.abstract: Retrons help bacteria defend against phage by initiating a toxic response to restrict viral propagation. Here, Zhang et al. describe the non-canonical mechanism of Retron-Vpa2, which accumulates msDNA in response to phage triggers and regulates its toxic response on a translational level through a highly structured hybrid RNA.

papers.title: A feedback mechanism of m6A via PARP1-mediated ADP ribosylation of METTL3/METTL14
papers.abstract: Bai et al. reveal a PARP1-mediated m6A feedback mechanism involving IGF2BPs and the METTL3/METTL14 writer complex. They further show that combined targeting of ADP ribosylation and m6A leads to synergistic anti-tumor effects, providing a potential therapeutic strategy for cancer treatment.

papers.title: Anterior cingulate feedback facilitates rapid global context modulation in primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: Peterka et al. show that sensory processing as early as primary visual cortex is modulated not just by recent stimuli but by learned patterns and global probabilities. They go on to demonstrate that this modulation depends on feedback inputs from a higher brain region, consistent with predictive coding hypotheses.

papers.title: Proprioceptive sensory-driven mechanisms shape Clarke’s column development
papers.abstract: Sensory feedback from muscles does more than report body position—it helps build the circuits that process it. Song et al. find that proprioceptive sensory neurons are required for the postnatal development of Clarke’s column, a key relay carrying movement information from the spinal cord to the cerebellum.

papers.title: USP9X promotes the degradation of trapped translation factors on collided ribosomes
papers.abstract: Teodorowicz et al. show that USP9X, in conjunction with the E3 ligases RNF14 and RNF25, is required to promote the VCP-dependent proteasomal degradation of eRF1 and eEF1A1 trapped in the ribosomal A-site and identify 4EHP as a mediator of translational shutdown following translation factor clearance.

papers.title: Human organ chip models recapitulate FRC-driven high endothelial venule differentiation, immune recruitment, and cancer-induced disruption
papers.abstract: Oh et al. develop human high endothelial venules (HEVs) on a chip, specialized immune-recruiting blood vessels found in lymph nodes. The study shows that FRCs drive HEV specialization and functional T-cell adhesion, while cancer cells disrupt these processes, providing a platform for studying HEV function and dysfunction in disease.

papers.title: Structural basis of an endoplasmic reticulum EMC:Spf1 insertase–dislocase complex
papers.abstract: Most eukaryotic membrane proteins are inserted into the membrane at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). This essential process relies on molecular quality control machineries to prevent mistargeting and incorrect structure formation. Here, we show that the ER membrane protein complex (EMC) forms an evolutionarily conserved supercomplex with the P5A-ATPase Spf1/ATP13A1. Biochemical, structural and cellular analyses demonstrate that the EMC and Spf1 associate in a stoichiometric manner and retain their individual catalytic activities, the transmembrane domain (TMD) insertase function of the EMC and the TMD dislocase activity of Spf1. Our cryo-electron microscopy structures show that the EMC insertase cavity and the Spf1 dislocase cleft are positioned in close proximity within the membrane and reveal that the ATPase cycle of Spf1 remodels the interface between the two machineries and alters cytoplasmic accessibility of both substrate-binding cavities. Together, our study provides structural insights into how membrane protein insertion and extraction machineries can be spatially coordinated at the ER membrane, suggesting that functionally distinct proteostasis factors can assemble into hubs to support membrane protein biogenesis and quality control.

papers.title: Ligand-dependent G protein dynamics underlying opioid efficacy
papers.abstract: Deutsch et al. show how μ-opioid receptor agonists exert long-range allosteric control over bound G proteins, providing an additional mechanism for encoding opioid signaling outcomes.

papers.title: μ-Opioid ligands tune G-protein opening kinetics
papers.abstract: There is a thin line between opioids acting to relieve pain and causing life-threatening adverse effects, yet the mechanistic basis separating these outcomes is not fully understood. A study suggests that the difference is encoded in the motions of the G-protein α-helical domain that gates GDP release.

papers.title: Single-cell CRISPR screen maps epigenetic regulators of lineage specification and malignancies in human HSPCs
papers.abstract: Yuan et al. establish a scalable single-cell CRISPR platform in primary human HSPCs, linking 322 regulator perturbations to cell states and gene programs. The atlas identifies regulators associated with long-term repopulation and lineage-biased outputs and nominates PRDM10 as a candidate AML dependency.

papers.title: Rapid CAR-T manufacturing with low-intensity priming enhances CAR-T cell fitness and limits inflammatory programming in a phase 1 study
papers.abstract: Yang and colleagues show that low-intensity priming during rapid chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T manufacturing preserves T cell fitness while restraining inflammatory programming. PrimeCAR cells maintain stemness-associated and proliferative responses with reduced myeloid-activating inflammation, and early-phase studies in B cell malignancies demonstrate encouraging clinical activity with few severe cytokine release syndrome (CRS) or immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) events.

papers.title: Cancer-cell-derived fumarate suppresses the anti-tumor capacity of CD8+ T cells in the tumor microenvironment
TNF compromises intestinal bile-acid tolerance dictating colitis progression and limited infliximab response
Structural basis and rational engineering of a thermophilic Cas13a for robust RNA detection
papers.abstract: Oladeji et al. determined the cryo-EM structure of the TccCas13a ternary complex and leveraged structural insights to engineer a thermophilic Cas13a variant with 100-fold enhanced sensitivity. The engineered nuclease retains programmability and thermostability, enabling highly sensitive RNA detection in different biological matrices.

papers.title: Atomic, structural and molecular insights into GPCR ligand binding and signalling
papers.abstract: This Review explores the atomic, structural and molecular basis of G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR)-mediated signalling, highlighting recent insights into conformational changes associated with ligand recognition and interaction with downstream adaptors, and underscoring their importance for the development of therapeutics.

papers.title: Chemokine-induced cell swelling fluidises the plasma membrane to regulate CD8+ T cell migration
papers.abstract: T cell migration is primarily viewed as a cytoskeletal process. Here, we show that chemokine-stimulated CD8+ T cell migration is modulated by a volume-driven biophysical switch at the plasma membrane (PM). We found that chemokine-induced cell swelling creates an adhesion-dependent gradient of high PM fluidity at the leading edge. External chemical fluidisation of the PM using membrane modulators enhances migration similar to chemokine-induced fluidisation without the need of cell-swelling. Together, our findings identify PM fluidity as a tuneable biophysical gatekeeper that controls T cell migration, potentially providing a novel mechanical tool for optimising adoptive cell therapies in restrictive tissue microenvironments.
affiliations: Karolinska Institutet (corresponding author)

papers.title: Asymptomatic colonization by Botrytis cinerea reveals polarized plant-fungus interfaces before widespread disease
papers.abstract: Botrytis cinerea is a necrotrophic pathogen whose destructive growth is typically studied under conditions that rapidly generate visible disease. Yet symptomless associations are well documented, the fungal and host processes operating before widespread tissue collapse remain poorly resolved. We developped an intact Arabidopsis thaliana seedling pathosystem that extends the interval between infection establishment and widespread visible disease. Fungal colonization was quantified using qPCR and a constitutively bioluminescent reporter strain, together with longitudinal plant phenotyping, hormone profiling and multiscale fluorescence microscopy. Substantial fungal colonization occurred while seedlings remained largely green and continued to grow, whereas robust whole seedling accumulation of salicylic and jasmonic acids occurred later. During this interval, B. cinerea displayed diverse tissue-associated infection morphologies. At individual contact sites, fungal walls showed heterogeneous exposure of chitin-associated epitopes, while host cells exhibited focal plasma-membrane polarization toward fungal contact sites, together with cortical actin reorganization. These results show that the interval preceding widespread visible disease is an active and spatially heterogeneous interaction state, in which substantial fungal development and highly organized local host responses are already established. Intact seedlings therefore provide a powerful system for resolving plant-pathogen interactions that are largely obscured in rapid disease assays.
affiliations: Université Lyon 1, CNRS, INSA, Bayer SAS, MAP, UMR5240, Lyon, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: In vitro-generated murine monocyte-derived dendritic cells habor a unique identity compared to other mononuclear phagocytes, largely conserved with their human and putative in vivo counterparts.
papers.abstract: Whether the cells differentiating in vitro from total murine bone marrow (BM) cultures with GM-CSF +/- IL-4 are homologous to the human cells derived in vitro from purified circulating monocytes (Mo) cultured with GM-CSF and IL-4, mostly correspond to monocyte-derived dendritic cells (moDCs) or rather to macrophages (MFs), and have in vivo counterparts, is debated. It has been proposed to define cell types based on their ontogeny, leading to the proposal of excluding from the dendritic cell (DC) family the cells that do not arise from the common DC progenitors (CDP). However, recent discoveries support defining cell types rather by functions, or, as a surrogate, their instructive molecular networks. Indeed, Langerhans cells, Rorgt+ DCs, some cDC2As and human in vitro-derived moDCs do not arise from the CDP but exert hallmark DC functions instructed by specific transcriptomic modules shared with cDCs. Actually, the study of both LCs and moDCs has been key for dissecting DC biology. Yet, the existence of moDCs is put into questions. The functions once attributed to moDCs are now proposed to be exerted by type 2B conventional DCs (cDC2Bs) or type 3 DCs (DC3s) that have been characterized recently, harbor strongly overlapping phenotypes with moDCs and a similar mixed expression of genes from both the cDC and Mo/MF lineages, but a different ontogeny. To clarify these issues, we generated a transcriptomic atlas of in vitro-derived mononuclear phagocytes (MNPs). We show that moDCs are the only DC type arising in BM cultures in the presence of GM-CSF and IL-4. They express a unique transcriptomic and phenotypic signature, different from those of cDC2Bs and DC3s that are produced in FLT3-L cultures and appear to correspond to the same DC type differentiating though two different but converging ontogenetic paths. By harnessing the phenotypic and transcriptomic signatures identified from the analysis of our in vitro MNP atlas, we are able to identify in vivo a population of putative DCs differentiated from monocytes derived from the common monocyte-granulocyte progenitor (GMP), in a respiratory allergy model, specifically in the lungs of mice sensitized to house dust mite (HDM). Using the model of thioglycolate-induced peritonitis, we also characterized the CD226+ Mo-derived cells that have been reported to be moDCs or small cavity MFs (SCM) depending on studies. We showed that these cells are mainly differentiated from monocytes derived from the MDP, and split into two populations, one resembling MFs (SCMs) and the other one closer to lung moDCs but expressing distinct genes suggesting a different functional potential. Collectively, we show that the generation and characterization of specific MNP types in vitro can be harnessed to rigorously define their in vivo counterparts based on phenotypic analysis and gene module assessment, as we demonstrate for moDCs.
affiliations: CNRS (corresponding author)

papers.title: PZLS-1/PDZRN controls muscle polarity downstream of Wnt-Ror-Dvl signalling in C. elegans muscles
papers.abstract: Non-canonical Wnt pathways provide directional cues for cell polarity, but the mechanisms that translate these cues into asymmetric cellular organisation remain incompletely defined. We previously showed that a non-canonical EGL-20/Wnt-CAM-1/Ror-DSH-1/Dishevelled pathway establishes polarised membrane compartments in Caenorhabditis elegans body wall muscles. However, how EGL-20/Wnt signalling is translated into muscle polarity remains unknown. Here, we identify PZLS-1, the C. elegans ortholog of human PDZRN3, PDZRN4 and PDZD4, as a regulator of muscle polarity. Although PDZRN proteins are known targets of non-canonical Wnt-Ror signalling, how they are spatially organised within polarised cells and how their protein domains contribute to their function remain largely unknown. We reveal that PZLS-1 is itself asymmetrically localised by Wnt-Ror-Dvl signalling, and is closely associated with DSH-1. PZLS-1 and DSH-1 colocalise in intracellular puncta and are mutually required for their localisation. In vivo structure-function analyses reveal conserved protein motifs that differentially control PZLS-1 localisation, abundance and function. This includes a previously uncharacterized highly conserved sequence that regulates PZLS-1 abundance in a DSH-1-dependent manner. We further show that PZLS 1 and DSH-1 control the abundance and polarised localisation of VAB-8/KIF26b, another conserved target of Wnt-Ror signalling. Together, these findings indicate that Wnt-Ror-Dvl signalling can control the spatial organisation and abundance of PDZRN- and KIF26B-family proteins in vivo, providing a mechanism to translate extracellular polarity cues into intracellular asymmetry.
affiliations: Universite Lyon 1, CNRS, INSERM, MELIS, UMR 5284, UMR S1314, Lyon, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: Human caspase-4 and caspase-5 assemble into non-canonical inflammasomes in response to overlapping and distinct LPS structures
papers.abstract: Innate immune sensing of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is critical to host defense, but a dysregulated response can lead to sepsis, a life-threatening condition associated with multiple organ failure and shock. LPS is sensed at the cell surface by Toll-Like Receptor 4 (TLR4) and in the cytosol by mouse caspase-11 (Casp11) or its human orthologs, caspase-4 and 5 (CASP4/5). In response to cytosolic LPS, Casp11 oligomerizes in a catalytically dependent manner into supramolecular organizing centers (SMOCs). We demonstrate that CASP4 and CASP5 also form catalytically dependent SMOCs in response to bacterial LPS in macrophages. Furthermore, we find that CASP4 and CASP5 differentially respond to distinct LPS structural variants that fail to activate CASP11 and that only activating LPS structures induce SMOC formation by the corresponding caspase.
