papers.title: Targeting Cardiac Fibrosis with Chimeric Antigen Receptor Neutrophils Derived from Human Pluripotent Stem Cells
papers.abstract: Heart failure remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, with cardiac fibrosis contributing to disease progression. Following myocardial injury, activated cardiac fibroblasts orchestrate adverse extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, which leads to tissue stiffening and compromised contractility. Despite the clinical importance of cardiac fibrosis, current pharmacological interventions modulate disease progression without directly eliminating activated fibrogenic cells. To target these cells directly, we engineered human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived neutrophils expressing a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) directed against fibroblast activation protein (FAP). In vitro, FAP CAR neutrophils exhibited increased reactive oxygen species-associated fluorescence during fibroblast co-culture and dose-dependent cytotoxicity in 2D cultures, while reducing fibroblast-associated fluorescence in 3D cardiac organoids without a significant reduction in cardiomyocyte-associated cardiac troponin T staining. FAP CAR neutrophils also showed increased iNOS and decreased Arginase-1 expression compared with unmodified neutrophils, consistent with a shift toward an N1-associated polarization profile. Analysis of public cardiac single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing datasets identified temporal patterns of immune-associated expression and fibroblast activation that informed treatment timing. In a murine myocardial infarction (MI) model, mice treated systemically with FAP CAR neutrophils showed higher day 7 left ventricular ejection fraction than PBS-treated mice in an exploratory comparison. Together, these findings support further evaluation of hPSC-derived FAP CAR neutrophils as an immunotherapeutic approach to cardiac fibrosis.
affiliations: Purdue University (corresponding author)

papers.title: An RFX-driven ciliogenic cell state defines ex vivo FGFR-inhibitor sensitivity in colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Genomic stratification leaves most patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) without opportunities for targeted therapy. Seeking tumour state-linked drug sensitivities, we combined image-based ex vivo drug profiling with matched transcriptomics in 127 prospectively collected patient biopsies across CRC stages and molecular subtypes. Network-level integration identified a ciliogenic cell state defined by upregulation of cilia related genes with selective sensitivity to the FGFR inhibitor erdafitinib. This ciliogenic signature was associated with poor progression-free survival (hazard ratio 2.28; adjusted p=0.0098), even in early-stage colorectal cancer. Furthermore, knockdown of the transcriptional regulators RFX2 and RFX3, upstream of the ciliogenic cell state, attenuated erdafitinib sensitivity. Orthogonal bulk and single-cell analyses across normal, primary and metastatic tissues contextualised the ciliogenic programme along a transition from canonical epithelial states towards fetal and non-canonical tumour states, concomitant with Wnt-related remodelling, FGFR1/FGFR2 upregulation, and loss of intestinal epithelial identity. Together, these findings define a tumour-intrinsic ciliogenic cell state as a feature of CRC progression, revealing a patient-stratified repurposing opportunity for targeted therapy beyond the current CRC treatment paradigms.
affiliations: Botnar Institute of Immune Engineering (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tumour-derived factors prime microglia for immune checkpoint-mediated T-cell regulation
papers.abstract: Tumour-associated microglia are major regulators of the immune microenvironment in brain malignancies, yet the early mechanisms by which tumour-derived signals shape their immune phenotype remain poorly understood. We used quantitative proteomic analysis on microglia upon tumour exposure and observed extensive remodelling of the microglial proteome following exposure to tumour-conditioned media, indicating that soluble mediators represent the dominant drivers of early microglial activation. Microglia reprogramming was characterized by coordinated upregulation of inflammatory mediators together with proteins involved in antigen presentation and T-cell regulation, including MHC-I, PD-L1 and Galectin-9. Flow cytometric validation using multiple murine and human cell models confirmed the increased expression of PD-L1 and MHC-I on microglia following exposure to tumour-derived conditioned media. Subsequently, tumour-conditioned microglia promoted expression of the inhibitory receptors PD-1 and TIM-3 on T-cells after coculture. Importantly, integration of publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing datasets and cell-cell communication analysis further demonstrated that this immune-regulatory program is recapitulated in microglia from patients with brain tumours. Together, our findings identify an early, soluble factor-driven microglial activation program that precedes direct tumour contact and integrates inflammatory activation with immune checkpoint regulation. These results provide a mechanistic framework for the early establishment of an immunosuppressive brain tumour microenvironment and highlight microglial immune checkpoint pathways as potential targets for therapeutic intervention.
affiliations: University of Cologne (corresponding author)

papers.title: Catabolism of extracellular glutathione is a driver of metastasis formation
papers.abstract: Metastasizing cancer cells require metabolic plasticity to adapt to the microenvironment of the target organ. Analyzing metabolites in interstitial fluids, we found that the liver microenvironment is devoid of cystine but contains high concentrations of glutathione (GSH). Detailed mechanistic analysis revealed that cancer cells degrade extracellular GSH utilizing gamma-glutamyl-transferase (GGT) activity for provision of cysteine to support proliferation and prevent ferroptosis under cystine-free conditions. This was independent of system Xc- but required activity of glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCLC). GGT1 expression was associated with poor survival and upregulated in liver metastases of human breast cancer patients. Overexpression of Ggt1 in murine breast cancer cells enhanced their capacity for liver colonization and promoted lung metastases after orthotopic implantation. This identifies extracellular GSH catabolism as driver of metastasis that supports proliferation and oxidative stress resistance in metabolically challenging microenvironments.
affiliations: Division of Tumor Metabolism and Microenvironment, German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) and ZMBH-DKFZ Alliance; Heidelberg, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: THERAPY RESISTANCE IN MELANOMA DRIVES CILIOGENESIS AND GLUTAMINE/ASPARTATE METABOLISM DEPENDENCY
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable success of new therapeutic approaches, a considerable number of melanoma patients still relapse on conventional therapies within two years and develop resistance. Alterations in metabolism, including amino acid availability and regulation of metabolic processes, have been implicated in acquired drug resistance. In this study, we developed in vitro and in vivo models of target therapy resistance (TTR) and identified a translational program that supports primary ciliogenesis in drug-resistant BRAF melanoma. We established that drug resistance enhances primary ciliogenesis, which is needed to respond and survive to combination therapy (CT). Mechanistically, impairing cilia formation (IFT88KO) rewires glutamine and aspartate metabolism. Overall, we provide a new molecular mechanism underlying therapy resistance that should be considered to tailored therapeutic strategies.
affiliations: University of Padua (corresponding author)

papers.title: A 21-Color Spectral Flow Cytometry Panel for Comprehensive Immunophenotyping of Rat Tissues and a Companion 9-Color T-Cell Functional Assay
papers.abstract: Although rats are crucial translational research models due to their immunological homology and surgical feasibility, the scarcity of conjugated antibodies has hampered high-dimensional immune profiling. To bridge this gap, we created a synergistic two-panel method that uses full-spectral flow cytometry: a 21-color comprehensive immunophenotyping panel and a 9-color intracellular cytokine staining (ICS) panel. The 21-color panel navigates the limited fluorophore pool and maps innate and adaptive lineages at high resolution. While it can be used to profile neutrophils and monocytes in peripheral blood it reaches its full potential in lymphoid organs, allowing for the simultaneous evaluation of tissue-resident macrophages, dendritic cells, T cell differentiation (including Tregs), and APC function. Based on this phenotypic paradigm, the 9-color ICS panel dissects effector T cell activation and Th1/Th2/Th17 cytokine production. Furthermore, we reserved the PE color during panel creation, allowing for the use of antibodies and probes with PE or comparable fluorophores in conjunction with this panel, hence increasing overall flexibility. This combination technique, designed for rat peripheral blood, spleen, and lymph nodes, combines panoramic phenotyping with functional analysis, offering an adaptable foundation for complicated tissue microenvironments in tumor immunology, rheumatology, and autoimmunity research.
affiliations: Center of Basic Medical Research, Institute of Medical Innovation and Research, Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China. (corresponding author)

papers.title: NOD2 restrains probiotic-mediated TLR2-dependent antitumor immunity
papers.abstract: The gut microbiota influences cancer immunotherapy, but how interactions among host microbial sensors determine the activity of individual bacteria remains unclear. Here, we show that NOD2 restrains TLR2-dependent antitumor immunity induced by Lactiplantibacillus plantarum. Oral administration of live or heat-killed L. plantarum enhanced immune checkpoint blockade efficacy in mouse tumor models. This activity required host TLR2 signaling and was diminished by disruption of bacterial lipoprotein. In contrast, NOD2 deficiency enhanced tumor control, intratumoral interferon-associated programs, and T cell activation. NOD2 deficiency also amplified chemokine and interferon-associated responses to L. plantarum and the synthetic TLR2 agonist Pam3CSK4 in myeloid cells. Genetic loss or pharmacological inhibition of NOD2 improved Pam3CSK4-mediated tumor control in combination with checkpoint blockade. These findings identify NOD2 as a functional checkpoint on TLR2-driven antitumor immunity and demonstrate that interactions between host microbial-sensing pathways shape the therapeutic activity of commensal bacteria and innate immune agonists.
affiliations: Scripps Research (corresponding author)

papers.title: The mitochondrial transaminase GOT2 supports Japanese encephalitis virus replication in neuronal cells
papers.abstract: Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is the leading cause of viral encephalitis in Asia, yet the host pathways that sustain its replication in the central nervous system remain poorly defined, and no antiviral therapies exist. Here we combine time-resolved transcriptomics and proteomics in mouse neuroblastoma (Neuro-2a) cells with time-resolved proteomics of infected mouse brain, integrated using directionality-penalized p-value merging. JEV infection was accompanied by progressive induction of interferon-stimulated proteins and by changes in the abundance of enzymes of central carbon and energy metabolism, spanning the tricarboxylic acid cycle, glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation and glutaminolysis. Temporal clustering of the brain proteome linked oxidative phosphorylation remodelling to a dependence on glutamine metabolism. Glutamine antagonism with DON reduced viral RNA, whereas glycolytic inhibition and AKT modulation did not significantly alter it under the conditions tested. Silencing of the mitochondrial transaminase GOT2 reduced JEV RNA, viral protein, and infectious virus production in human SH-SY5Y cells. Our findings identify a glutamine-GOT2 axis as a metabolic dependency of JEV and a candidate host-directed antiviral target.
affiliations: Karolinska Institutet (corresponding author)

papers.title: RTK signaling and epidermis remodeling instruct dendrite regrowth after pruning in the Drosophila PNS
papers.abstract: Morphology and function of many neuron types must be adapted to the current developmental stage through neurite pruning and regrowth. Pruning and regrowth occur during defined temporal windows, but how these are defined is often unclear. Drosophila peripheral c4da neurons prune their larval sensory dendrites in an ecdysone-induced manner during metamorphosis. They subsequently regrow adult-specific dendrites, but how dendrite regeneration is linked to pruning is not known. We show that dendrite regrowth requires two receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), the insulin receptor InR and Ret, and present evidence that RTK ligands are derived from the adjacent epidermis. The Drosophila epidermis is extensively remodeled during metamorphosis through ecdysone-dependent apoptosis of larval epidermal cells and expansion of adult so-called histoblasts. We find that this occurs during a time window between dendrite pruning and regrowth, and that preventing epidermis remodeling inhibits dendrite remodeling. Furthermore, the two processes might also be evolutionarily linked. We propose that dendrite pruning and regrowth are part of a biphasic response to ecdysone, where a delayed regrowth signal is via the epidermis to ensure coordination of tissue developmental processes.
affiliations: University of Muenster (corresponding author)

papers.title: HIV-1 envelope glycan loss links receptor adaptation and innate immune escape in SHIVs
papers.abstract: Simian-human immunodeficiency viruses (SHIVs) are widely used to model HIV-1 infection in macaques, yet most SHIVs encoding circulating HIV-1 envelope glycoproteins (Env) replicate poorly because of inefficient use of macaque CD4 and sensitivity to host antiviral responses. During adaptation to macaques, Env is therefore subject to multiple selective pressures to improve receptor utilization while maintaining function in the face of host immune restriction. Type I interferon (IFN) is a major component of the host antiviral response during acute infection, and IFN resistance increases during SHIV adaptation to macaques through serial passage. However, the viral determinants of this resistance have remained unclear. Here, we show that serial passage of a lineage of SHIVs in macaques selected Env variants with markedly increased resistance to IFN- and enhanced replication in macaque CD4+ T lymphocytes. IFN- resistance mapped principally to loss of two highly conserved N-linked glycans at N197 and N276 near the CD4-binding site. Glycan loss altered the conformational landscape of virus-associated Env, enhanced macaque CD4-dependent entry and membrane fusion without increasing human CD4-dependent entry, and reduced incorporation of the IFN-inducible restriction factors IFITM3 and IFITM3A into progeny virions. Depletion of IFITM3/3A rendered the parental SHIV highly resistant to IFN- and abolished differential IFN- sensitivity among parental, adapted, and glycan-loss viruses. These findings reveal that loss of receptor-proximal Env glycans can simultaneously improve utilization of a heterologous CD4 receptor and promote escape from IFN-mediated restriction, linking receptor adaptation and innate immune evasion during lentiviral adaptation to a new host.
affiliations: NC State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: HSF1 inhibition potentiates the antifungal activity and proteome instability induced by the fungal Hsp110 inhibitor 2H
papers.abstract: Fungal infections remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide; however, therapeutic options are limited and are increasingly compromised by antifungal resistance. Heat Shock Protein 110 kDa (Hsp110) is an essential molecular chaperone required for protein homeostasis (proteostasis) and fungal viability and has recently emerged as a promising antifungal target. We previously identified 2H, a first-in-class inhibitor of fungal Hsp110 proteins that exhibits broad-spectrum antifungal activity through disruption of proteostasis. Heat Shock Transcription Factor 1 (HSF1), the master regulator of cellular stress responses and chaperone expression, has also been proposed as a potential antifungal target, although direct pharmacological evidence supporting this strategy remains limited. Here, we investigated the effects of combining the HSF1 inhibitor DTHIB with the fungal Hsp110 inhibitor 2H in Cryptococcus neoformans and Candida albicans. Although DTHIB alone exhibited minimal antifungal activity, it significantly enhanced the growth-inhibitory and fungicidal effects of 2H. Notably, this potentiating effect was specific to 2H and was not observed with fluconazole. Consistent with the roles of Hsp110 and HSF1 in proteostasis, 2H induced extensive accumulation of detergent-insoluble protein aggregates in C. neoformans, whereas HSF1 inhibition further increased both the abundance and diversity of aggregated proteins. Quantitative proteomic analyses demonstrated that 2H induces proteome-wide protein aggregation, impacting proteins involved in a broad range of essential cellular processes, with high-molecular-weight proteins exhibiting particular susceptibility. Together, these findings provide pharmacological evidence supporting HSF1 as a promising antifungal sensitization target and demonstrate the utility of 2H as a chemical probe for studying Hsp110-dependent proteostasis. Simultaneous disruption of both HSF1-mediated stress responses and Hsp110-dependent proteostasis promotes extensive proteome instability and enhances antifungal activity, highlighting a potential new strategy for antifungal drug development.

papers.title: Pharmacokinetics and Efficacy of the FimH Inhibitor Sibofimloc in Preventing Necrotizing Enterocolitis in Preterm Piglets
papers.abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a disease in preterm infants associated with an increased abundance of Enterobacteriaceae. FimH, a mannose-binding adhesin on Enterobacteriaceae type 1 fimbriae, mediates mucosal attachment and TLR4-dependent inflammatory cascades. We evaluated the safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy of an oral FimH inhibitor (Sibofimloc) to reduce Enterobacteriaceae colonization and prevent NEC in preterm piglets. We performed a 9-d dose-escalation safety study (10, 25, 50 mg/kg BID) assessing absorption and tolerability and a 10-d randomized efficacy study. Piglets in the efficacy study received an infant formula diet with or without oral sibofimloc (40 mg/kg BID), or donor human milk (DHM) as a healthy control. NEC incidence, tissue histopathology, and gut microbiota composition via metagenomic whole-genome sequencing (WGS) were evaluated. Systemic exposure data reveal that sibofimloc was dose-dependently absorbed, while plasma levels decreased from postnatal day 2 to day 8, indicating reduced drug absorption with maturation of the intestinal barrier. Treatment with sibofimloc did not reduce NEC incidence (100% in sibofimloc in formula controls) or severity, whereas DHM-fed piglets experienced 0% NEC. Sibofimloc-treated animals exhibited significantly reduced crypt depths, demonstrating heightened mucosal injury and impaired regenerative capacity. WGS revealed that sibofimloc-treated animals maintained a gut luminal microbiota composition similar to untreated formula controls, dominated by Clostridium perfringens (C. perfringens). Selective targeting of FimH-expressing Enterobacteriaceae was insufficient to prevent NEC or alter the gut microbiota in this preterm piglet model, underscoring the complexity of NEC-associated microbial communities and suggesting that additional microbial targets and other colonization mechanisms may contribute to disease development.
affiliations: USDA/ARS Children's Nutrition Research Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Single-site DNA methylation activates retron defence by enabling effector tetramerisation
papers.abstract: Retrons are unique among bacterial defence systems in using DNA to sense phage infection. They achieve this by producing multicopy single-stranded DNA (msDNA) that monitors the activity of DNA-targeting phage proteins. Although we understand how extensive msDNA perturbations such as degradation activate retrons, activation by subtle chemical modifications remains enigmatic. Here, we used a structure-function approach to elucidate how single-site msDNA methylation activates Retron-Sen2. The cryo-EM structure of Retron-Sen2 features RcaT, the most prevalent retron effector, sequestered as an inactive dimer within a four-component assembly of previously undescribed architecture. Methylation by DNA adenine methyltransferase disrupts the RcaT-msDNA interaction and exposes a previously occluded interface that enables RcaT dimers to form tetramers, leading to retron disassembly. We show that RcaT dimer-dimer assembly is essential for its toxicity. To assess whether this is a conserved RcaT feature, we characterised additional homologues. RcaTs capable of tetramerisation or higher-order oligomerisation are toxic and form distinct phylogenetic clades from RcaTs that remain dimeric and are non-toxic. Together, our findings provide a paradigm for retron activation by single-site msDNA modifications and showcase how variation in an intrinsic protein property can diversify the toxicity of the same bacterial defence effector during evolution.
affiliations: European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Allyl chloride respiration by Dehalobacter shapes the fate of 1,2,3-trichloropropane
papers.abstract: The synthetic compound 1,2,3-trichloropropane (1,2,3-TCP) is a persistent groundwater contaminant and probable human carcinogen for which effective detoxification pathways remain limited. Under anoxic conditions, microbial transformation of 1,2,3-TCP typically stalls at the intermediate allyl chloride, preventing complete detoxification. Here, we report the enrichment and characterization of Dehalobacter restrictus strain XRTCP, a bacterium capable of coupling dichloroelimination of 1,2,3-TCP with subsequent hydrogenolysis of allyl chloride to propene. While dichloroelimination to allyl chloride has been previously observed, the ability to utilize allyl chloride as a respiratory electron acceptor represents a previously unrecognized metabolic capability. This transformation was linked to microbial growth, with cell densities increasing by up to 74-fold during 1,2,3-TCP reduction and 15.8-fold during allyl chloride transformation. Metagenomic and metaproteomic analyses revealed a diverse repertoire of reductive dehalogenases (RDases), with expression patterns that differed between 1,2,3-TCP and allyl chloride amendments. Notably, a tcpA-like RDase was expressed under both 1,2,3-TCP and allyl chloride conditions, while distinct RDases were preferentially expressed under each substrate, indicating functional specialization within the dechlorination pathway. Despite this metabolic capability, propene formation remained limited due to rapid abiotic transformation of allyl chloride, primarily via reactions with reduced sulfur species, highlighting a critical branching point between biotic and abiotic pathways. These findings demonstrate that allyl chloride can function as a growth-supporting respiratory electron acceptor. More broadly, this work reveals how interactions between microbial metabolism and geochemical processes govern contaminant fate, with implications for improving both monitored natural attenuation and engineered bioremediation strategies for chlorinated solvents.

papers.title: Tropism of Drosophila innubila Nudivirus in Cell Culture and in Tissues
papers.abstract: Most viruses are successful because they can infect and exploit specific host tissues for reproduction and transmission. As a result, we often classify viruses by their ability to infect different tissues: respiratory, reproductive and gut, for example. Thus, knowing the tissue and cellular tropism of a virus may elucidate aspects of its biology including routes of transmission and virulence. We studied tropism of the Drosophila innubila Nudivirus (DiNV) in cells and infected hosts. DiNV is a nudivirus, a family of viruses related to the baculoviruses that are relatively large (150-200 nm), contain large double-stranded DNA genomes, and infect different host tissues. Cultured cells stained with an antibody against the DiNV nucleocapsid demonstrated punctate staining in the cytoplasm by confocal microscopy. Electron micrographs of infected cells, on the other hand demonstrated that virions are present in the nucleus. After purification, DiNV was often associated with multimembrane-like vesicles as described for Oryctes rhinoceros nudivirus. We examined tropism in hosts first by sagittal section and found most virus associated with the gut and, to a lesser extent, reproductive tissues. Upon dissection and electron microscopy, we found that DiNV in the gut is primarily in the visceral muscle of the gut and not the lumen as might be expected for a virus if transmitted fecal-orally.
affiliations: University of Kansas (corresponding author)

papers.title: Long terminal repeats influence deletion propensity and genome instability in proviruses across major retroviruses
papers.abstract: A hallmark of retroviral infection is integration of viral genomes into host chromosomes to form proviruses. Most proviruses are defective, particularly in people with HIV receiving antiretroviral therapy, with large internal deletions as a dominant outcome. The contribution of retroviral long terminal repeats (LTRs) in the formation of large internal deletions remains unclear. We used dual-fluorophore reporters based on HIV-1, HIV-2, and HTLV-1 LTRs, integrated at AAVS1 by CRISPR/Cas9, to test whether LTRs influence proviral integrity in the absence of reverse transcriptase or integrase. Cerulean expression was driven by the LTR and mCherry by an independent human promoter. Double-positive (Cerulean/mCherry) cells were a proxy for intact vectors, whereas single mCherry cells indicated latent and/or defective proviruses. Double-positive cells harboured intact vectors for all constructs. Non-inducible single mCherry populations were enriched for extensively deleted proviruses with HIV-1, HIV-2, or HTLV-1 LTRs, whereas the LTR-deficient reporter yielded few single mCherry cells, all with intact proviruses. The presence of LTRs was significantly associated with deleted genomes. HIV-1 and HTLV-1 showed higher observed deletion rates than HIV-2, but this was not statistically significant owing to limited sequence numbers. Single Cerulean populations across all constructs showed recurrent deletions affecting the mCherry cassette and upstream promoter, with short direct repeats at deletion junctions. These likely reflect microhomology-mediated end joining as a contributing repair mechanism during CRISPR/Cas9-mediated integration, in which LTRs may not directly contribute. Together, these data identify retroviral LTRs as contributors to the formation of large internal deletions in proviruses.
affiliations: University of Zurich and University Hospital Zurich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Staphylococcus aureus enhances influenza A virus replication through modulation of host cell vesicular transport
papers.abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) is a major respiratory pathogen that causes substantial morbidity and mortality worldwide. A significant complication of primary IAV infection is secondary bacterial co-infection. Here, we report that Staphylococcus aureus enhances IAV replication through the activity of the surface protein fibronectin-binding protein A (FnbA). The pro-viral activity of FnbA is conserved across multiple IAV strains and is associated with reduced abundance of the host vesicular trafficking proteins VPS26A and VTA1. FnbA does not substantially increase viral protein abundance or alter intracellular distribution. Instead, pro-viral activity is associated with a greater proportion of infectious progeny particles and increased release of infectious virions from infected cells. Thus, we identify FnbA as a bacterial factor that enhances IAV replication and demonstrate that S. aureus can manipulate host cell processes to promote the production and release of infectious virus.
affiliations: University of Victoria (corresponding author)

papers.title: RNA evidence supports clinical stage antibody drug targets in oncology
papers.abstract: Background: The selection of efficacious and safe antibody-based oncology targets depends on tumor specificity and normal-tissue expression, and remains challenging. Bulk RNA-seq can identify tumor-enriched surface genes, but may obscure tumor specificity and normal-cell expression patterns that are relevant to the therapeutic window. We evaluated whether single-cell RNA-seq-derived expression features improve retrospective prioritization of clinically pursued antibody targets. Methods: We developed a bulk and single-cell RNA expression-based ranking framework across six solid tumor indications. 4,532 candidate surfaceome targets were scored using tumor Specificity, normal Safety, and blood Sink features derived from bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, or a combined modality. Ranking performance was evaluated against a curated validation set of tumor-associated antibody-based oncology targets using logistic regression, with odds ratios (ORs) reported per one-standard-deviation increase in score. Results: Higher Specificity scores were associated with clinical-stage target selection across all modalities. In cross-indication meta-analysis, single-cell Specificity showed higher ORs than bulk Specificity across clinical phase thresholds, including Phase [≥] 1 (OR 2.56 versus 1.81), Phase [≥] 2 (OR 2.77 versus 1.88), Phase [≥] 3 (OR 3.53 versus 2.04) and Approved targets (OR 3.51 versus 1.74). Combined bulk-and-single-cell Specificity showed intermediate enrichment. Specificity score alone did not consistently show a significant single-cell advantage over bulk in paired indication-level comparisons, except for Phase [≥] 3 targets. After adding normal-cell Safety and blood Sink features, the single-cell general score showed the strongest enrichment across thresholds (Phase [≥] 1 OR 3.61, Phase [≥] 2 OR 4.16, Phase [≥] 3 OR 5.57, and Approved targets OR 4.25). This general score also showed consistently significant single-cell advantage over bulk in paired indication-level comparisons. Safety contributed most strongly in the single-cell modality, increasing meta-analytic ORs by an average of ~36% across thresholds compared to Specificity alone. Performance varied by indication, with breast cancer showing weaker Specificity-based enrichment. Conclusion: Expression-derived ranking features are retrospectively enriched among clinically pursued tumor-associated antibody targets. Single-cell evidence is most informative when tumor Specificity is combined with normal-cell Safety information, supporting its use as an interpretable component of early antibody target prioritization. These findings are in alignment with recent evidence that single-cell RNA-based cell-type specificity supports clinical-stage targets and demonstrate that expression-driven ranking can systematically recover clinically relevant oncology targets.
affiliations: Genmab (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ontology-Driven Annotation of Key Events Enables Transcriptomics-Based Assessment of Adverse Outcome Pathway Networks
papers.abstract: Chemical safety assessment is moving towards new approach methodologies (NAMs) to improve human safety and reduce animal testing. The Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) is a NAM framework describing toxicity as a chain of Key Events (KEs). Many AOP-Wiki KEs describe molecular, cellular, or tissue-level processes and can therefore be assessed with gene expression data, making transcriptomics of human in vitro models a NAM data generator. In AOP-Wiki, KEs are described by Key Event Components (KECs). A gene set can be derived when the biological process (BP) component carries a Gene Ontology (GO) term. Most KEs carry no such term, so their perturbation cannot be assessed using omics data. We assigned GO BP terms to the unmapped BP component across the brain, lung, liver and kidney AOP networks. We also replaced obsolete and direction-carrying terms in the pre-existing mapping with current, direction-neutral ones. For liver, we reviewed all pre-existing terms and replaced overly broad terms with better-matched alternatives. We then applied this approach to pesticide-induced hepatotoxicity, using Open TG-GATEs transcriptomics data from primary human hepatocytes exposed to cycloheximide, 2,4-dinitrophenol, hexachlorobenzene, and rotenone. KE perturbation was scored using single-sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (ssGSEA). Annotation increased the proportion of transcriptomics-linkable KEs in the liver network from 53% to 77%, enhancing identification of perturbed KEs after exposure. The KEs perturbed by all four compounds fell into five functional categories associated with hepatotoxicity. Our approach resulted in a more relevant AOP network for transcriptomics-based assessment of KE perturbation. These findings show molecular perturbation rather than direct proof of KE activation or causal progression through an AOP. When validated on larger and independent datasets, such networks will support mechanistic interpretation of transcriptomics data in chemical safety assessment.
affiliations: Department of Translational Genomics, NUTRIM, Maastricht University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Prospective discovery of LasB inhibitors by integrating generative design, free energy ranking, and experimental validation
papers.abstract: Identifying synthetically accessible, potent ligands from vast chemical space remains a major challenge in drug discovery, particularly because experimental synthesis and testing are costly and low throughput. Here, we present a fully open-source computational-experimental workflow that integrates fragment-based de novo molecular design with rigorous alchemical absolute binding free-energy calculations to enable physics-based prioritization before chemical synthesis. We apply this strategy by targeting the virulence-associated zinc metalloprotease LasB from Pseudomonas aeruginosa. From ~40,000 diverse compounds generated through multi-objective optimization, a small subset was prioritized and experimentally evaluated, leading to the discovery of three previously unreported nanomolar inhibitors (IC50 22-53 nM) with excellent metabolic and plasma stability. This work demonstrates a general and scalable framework for coupling generative molecular design with quantitative binding affinity prediction, improving decision-making and reducing the cost, time, and risk associated with early-stage drug discovery.
affiliations: Saarland University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Branching Suppresses Self-Aggregation while Preserving Membrane Association in SET-M33: An Atomistic Molecular Dynamics Study
papers.abstract: Branched antimicrobial peptides offer a promising strategy for improving the stability and activity of membrane-active peptides, but how branching alters self-association and membrane binding remains unclear. We used all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to compare tetra-branched SET-M33 with its linear branch sequence Q33 (KKIRVRLSA) in water and at an anionic bacterial-membrane model, to do this, systems containing equivalent numbers of Q33 sequence units were simulated. Q33 formed dimers and higher-order oligomers, particularly at the membrane interface and under hydration-tuned enhanced sampling. In contrast, SET-M33 remained more dispersed, as the branched scaffold and its high cationic charge limited peptide-peptide association while allowing multivalent membrane binding. Both architectures associated rapidly with the bilayer but remained predominantly surface-bound, without persistent pore formation or complete insertion. Q33 showed stronger membrane-induced helical stabilization, whereas SET-M33 retained a more heterogeneous conformational ensemble. Overall, branching primarily altered lateral peptide organization while preserving close membrane association, suppressing uncontrolled self-aggregation and providing an atomistic rationale for the distinct behavior of SET-M33 relative to Q33.
affiliations: Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cell Painting PLUS reveals phenotypic signatures for nephrotoxicity profiling in human RPTEC/TERT1
papers.abstract: Multiplex high-throughput phenotypic profiling offers a cost-effective approach to monitor how chemical perturbations alter cellular morphology, thereby contributing to a mechanistic, human-centred hazard assessment with new approach methodologies in the context of Next Generation Risk Assessment (NGRA). In this study, we employed Cell Painting PLUS (CPP), an expanded high-content imaging assay that adds spatially resolved channels for mitochondria, lysosomes, actin, Golgi, RNA, DNA, and the endoplasmic reticulum, to renal RPTEC/TERT1 cells to evaluate nephrotoxicity. We profiled a set of nephrotoxic agents together with well-annotated reference chemicals encompassing diverse cellular targets to identify specific morphological profiles associated with distinct mechanisms of action (MoAs). Benchmark concentration modelling, correlation analysis, and hierarchical clustering of RPTEC/TERT1 CPP data captured specific morphological signatures of more than 300 tested compounds and enabled discrimination between closely related and opposing phenotypes. Comparison with CPP data generated in bone osteosarcoma U2OS cells highlighted cell-type-specific differences: despite lower overall activity, RPTEC/TERT1 resolved biologically relevant nephrotoxicity-associated phenotypes, highlighting the importance of using physiologically relevant cell models for contextspecific phenotypic profiling. Overall, these findings establish RPTEC-based CPP as a valuable phenotypic profiling platform supporting mechanistic nephrotoxicity assessment for integration into NGRA.
affiliations: German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Stemness overcomes IFNγ-induced antitumour exhaustion in human macrophages
papers.abstract: Macrophages hold great promise for antitumour therapies (1-4), particularly owing to their ability to infiltrate solid tumours (5). Yet therapeutic success has been limited (6,7), because macrophages exhibit rapid exhaustion of antitumorigenic activity in the tumour (5,8,9). Here, we induced a stem-like self-renewal programme in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived macrophages by deleting the self-renewal restricting transcription factors MAFB and MAF (MAF-DKO). Human MAF-DKO macrophages showed activated stem cell signatures, increased clonogenicity and proliferative potential. Increased self-renewal capacity was accompanied by enhanced mitochondrial fitness and invigorated energy metabolism. Importantly, these stemness features prevented exhaustion, cellular aging-associated parameters and loss of energy efficiency that are typically associated with proinflammatory macrophage activation. In addition, activated MAF-DKO macrophages showed a broad loss of IFN{gamma}-triggered immunosuppressive pathways (10,11), induced a super-activated state with robust cytotoxic activity and resisted exhaustion upon tumour cell exposure. Consequently, activated MAF-DKO macrophages showed intratumoral persistence with a stable antitumoral phenotype in vivo, conferred robust reduction of tumour burden and extended survival of tumour-bearing mice. Together, this demonstrates that the induction of stemness in human macrophages can overcome critical roadblocks of antitumour therapy by conferring resistance to activation-triggered exhaustion of antitumour activity in the TME.
affiliations: TU Dresden, Center for Regenerative Therapies Dresden (CRTD), 01307 Dresden, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: Bacteriophage susceptibility in clinical Enterococcus faecalis reflects host genomic background and Epa-associated phage adsorption
papers.abstract: Cytolysin-positive Enterococcus faecalis has been implicated as a disease-associated pathobiont in alcohol-associated hepatitis, motivating development of selective bacteriophage-based strategies. However, strain-level determinants of phage susceptibility remain incompletely understood. We characterized the host range of three E. faecalis phages, {Phi}Ef2.1, {Phi}Ef2.2, and {Phi}Ef2.3Ev, across 45 clinical isolates and investigated bacterial and phage factors associated with adsorption and productive infection. Isolates were characterized by whole-genome sequencing, cytolysin status, antimicrobial resistance determinants, and predicted anti-phage defense systems. Phage susceptibility was measured by efficiency of plating (EoP) and adsorption assays. Thirty-five of the 45 isolates (77.8%), including all 15 cylLs-positive isolates, were susceptible to at least one of the three phages at EoP [≥]0.01. {Phi}Ef2.1 and {Phi}Ef2.2 showed greater activity against cylLs-positive isolates, which also carried higher burdens of predicted antimicrobial resistance determinants and anti-phage defense system types. Analysis of 367 complete E. faecalis RefSeq genomes classified the variable region of the enterococcal polysaccharide antigen (epa) locus into 15 recurrent architecture groups that were associated with phage-specific adsorption patterns. Efficient adsorption did not always result in productive infection, indicating additional post-adsorption barriers. AbiD emerged as a candidate factor associated with reduced {Phi}Ef2.2 productivity, although this signal was prediction-tool dependent, while unexplained post-adsorption blocks suggest the involvement of additional uncharacterized mechanisms. These findings link naturally occurring epa architecture to phage adsorption and highlight distinct post-adsorption constraints on host range, providing a framework for rational phage selection against clinically relevant E. faecalis populations.
affiliations: Department of Medicine, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, California, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Root exudates enhance the ecological fitness of a non-native PGPR and reshape rhizosphere microbiome assembly
papers.abstract: Root exudates play critical roles in rhizosphere microbiome assembly. Nevertheless, the molecular mechanisms by which plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) perceive these signals, adapt to the rhizosphere, and influence native microbial communities remain poorly understood. Here, using maize (Zea mays cv. Early Golden Bantam) and the rhizobacterium Priestia aryabhattai AB211, we took a multi-omics approach combining metabolomics, bacterial transcriptomics and proteomics, and rhizosphere metagenomics to elucidate the mechanism underlying this process. Maize root exudates were enriched in diverse carbon and nitrogen metabolites that promoted bacterial growth and induced extensive molecular reprogramming of pathways involved in nutrient acquisition, chemotaxis, motility, stress adaptation, and plant growth promotion, thereby enhancing rhizosphere competence. In field-conditioned soil, AB211 persisted as a core member of the maize rhizosphere microbiome, promoted early seedling growth, and reshaped microbial community composition and function. Root exudates-primed (RE-primed) AB211 further enhanced the enrichment of microbial functions associated with nutrient cycling, quorum sensing, plant growth promotion, and rhizosphere fitness, highlighting the role of root exudates in modulating the rhizosphere-adaptative potential of beneficial bacteria. These findings establish a mechanistic framework linking root exudates composition with PGPR adaptation and microbiome assembly, providing a foundation for engineering ecologically adapted microbial inoculants to improve crop productivity and sustainable agriculture.
affiliations: Bose Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: A silent intergenic locus for efficient and versatile transgene expression in Plasmodium falciparum
papers.abstract: Genetically modified Plasmodium falciparum parasites expressing transgenes such as fluorescent markers are crucial tools for malaria research. However, current reporter lines often rely on integrated transgene constructs that disrupt the coding sequence of a native gene, potentially affecting progression in the life cycle of the tool parasite line. We identified six candidate Silent Intergenic Loci (SILs): putatively editable intergenic regions without transcriptional activity, where gene insertions occurred in P. falciparum after its divergence from Plasmodium berghei and Plasmodium vivax. We characterised the largest candidate SIL on chromosome 12, SIL12, by integration of a constitutively expressed cytosolic mScarlet reporter. The resulting PfRed12 parasites progressed normally throughout the life cycle, from asexual blood-stage replication to mosquito stages and subsequent liver infection. Importantly, they infected both Anopheles stephensi and Anopheles coluzzii mosquitoes. PfRed12 parasites displayed bright fluorescence in both blood and mosquito stages, making them well suited for live visualisation of parasite transmission. In addition, we used two CRISPR-Cas9 target sites in the mScarlet cassette, one of which we purposely added, to perform efficient re-editing of the transgene. As a proof of concept, we re-edited PfRed12 parasites and integrated an apicoplast metabolic bypass construct, an inducible gametocyte producer construct, and two mNeonGreen reporter constructs. Together, our findings demonstrate that SIL12 permits stable transgene expression without compromising parasite development throughout the life cycle. We established PfRed12 as a new reporter line to study blood- and mosquito-stage development and as a versatile parental line for further genetic engineering.
affiliations: Radboudumc (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genomic and physiological characterization of Neobacillus ammoniipjilus sp. nov. reveals versatile inorganic nitrogen utilization and ammonia-mitigation potential
papers.abstract: A novel bacterial strain (KR4-4T), was isolated from soil in the Republic of Korea and subjected to polyphasic taxonomic and functional characterization. Phylogenetic analysis based on the 16S rRNA gene sequence placed strain KR4-4T within the genus Neobacillus. Phylogenomic analysis based on 92 bacterial core genes further supported its distinct taxonomic position. Average nucleotide identity and digital DNA-DNA hybridization values between KR4-4T and related Neobacillus type strains were 69.76-82.31% and 18.3-25.9%, respectively, supporting its recognition as a distinct species. Cells were Gram-stain-positive, non-motile, facultatively anaerobic rods, with growth occurring at 15-45 {degrees}C, pH 6.0-8.0, and 0-2.0% (w/v) NaCl. The major cellular fatty acids were iso-C15:0 and anteiso-C15:0, while the major polar lipids included diphosphatidylglycerol, phosphatidylglycerol, and phosphatidylethanolamine. Genome analysis revealed genes associated with inorganic nitrogen transport, nitrate and nitrite reduction, and ammonium assimilation. In liquid culture, KR4-4T removed NH4+-N under aerobic conditions and was able to utilize ammonium, nitrate, and nitrite as individual nitrogen sources, with removal efficiencies of 86.5%, 69.35%, and 62.9%, respectively. The strain also contributed to the reduction of gaseous NH3 in a closed-flask assay. Together, these physiological and genomic characteristics indicate a versatile capacity for inorganic nitrogen utilization and transformation and suggest potential for further evaluation in biological ammonia-mitigation applications. Based on phylogenetic, genomic, phenotypic, and chemotaxonomic evidence, strain KR4-4T represents a novel species of the genus Neobacillus, for which the name Neobacillus ammoniiphilus sp. nov. is proposed. The type strain is KR4-4T (= KACC 24003T = CCTCC AB 2025077T).
affiliations: Kyonggi University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Quantitative host-response mapping enables phenotypic profiling of viruses detected by virome sequencing
papers.abstract: Animal-derived viruses have repeatedly caused human outbreaks, motivating efforts to identify and characterize viruses circulating in animals. Virome sequencing has accelerated animal virus discovery, but phenotypic characterization remains difficult to scale. Although generated for viral detection, virome RNA-seq data also capture host transcriptional responses to infection. Here, we developed ViroChart, a comparative transcriptomic framework that quantifies activities across biological pathways and maps diverse mammalian host responses into a common, interpretable low-dimensional space. ViroChart enables clustering of infected samples by host response pattern and quantitative assessment of host response similarity between samples. In virome data sets from wild and farmed animals, some lung samples infected with poorly characterized betacoronaviruses showed host responses resembling those induced by viruses capable of causing fatal disease. ViroChart also revealed host-response heterogeneity in natural infections: among rats with zoonotic rodent-borne viruses, most showed weak responses, consistent with asymptomatic infection, but some showed pronounced inflammation characteristic of acute infection. ViroChart thus enables phenotypic characterization and prioritization of newly detected viruses by leveraging the same RNA-seq data from which their genomes were detected.
affiliations: The University of Osaka (corresponding author)

papers.title: Concentration-dependent inhibition of Streptococcus mutans metabolic activity by purified Croton lechleri latex (sangre de grado) in vitro
papers.abstract: Background. Chlorhexidine is the reference chemical antiplaque agent, but its adverse effects motivate the search for plant-derived alternatives. The proanthocyanidin-rich latex of Croton lechleri (sangre de grado) is a candidate, yet quantitative concentration-response data against Streptococcus mutans are scarce. Methods. In this exploratory in vitro study, ethanol-purified C. lechleri latex was tested at working concentrations of 3-100% v/v (final in-well concentrations 0.6-20% v/v) against S. mutans ATCC 25175 in a 96-well resazurin assay with dual-wavelength reading (570/600 nm) and correction for medium and latex color. Chlorhexidine 1% (0.2% in-well) was the positive control. Each condition was run in technical triplicate within a single experiment. Data were analyzed by one-way ANOVA, Tukey's test with simultaneous 95% confidence intervals (CI) and four-parameter logistic regression. Results. Metabolic activity decreased monotonically with concentration, from 101.3 +/- 1.7% (vehicle) to 54.0 +/- 4.7% (12%), 15.5 +/- 4.0% (50%) and 8.6 +/- 7.7% (100%), compared with 3.1 +/- 2.8% for chlorhexidine (F(7,16) = 160.7, p < 0.001). The lowest concentration that differed from the vehicle was 6% (difference 17.6 percentage points, 95% CI 2.1-33.1). The estimated half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) was 12.3% v/v (95% CI 9.5-15.1). Differences from chlorhexidine at 50% and 100% were not statistically significant, but their confidence intervals were compatible with differences of up to 28 and 21 percentage points, respectively. Conclusions. Purified C. lechleri latex inhibited the metabolic activity of planktonic S. mutans in a concentration-dependent manner. These preliminary findings do not establish equivalence with chlorhexidine and warrant replication in independent experiments with chemically standardized extracts expressed in mg/mL, determination of MIC/MBC and biofilm models.
affiliations: Universidad Católica de Santa María (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cardioselective β-blocker Therapy Resolves Staphylococcus aureus Toxin-Induced Innate Immunoparalysis
papers.abstract: During Staphylococcus aureus sepsis, the pore-forming -toxin (Hla) triggers lytic platelet death and provokes the release of catecholamines that modulate leukocyte effector function. The resulting surge in catecholaminergic action paralyzes host antimicrobial capacity by upregulating interleukin-10 (IL-10), profoundly suppressing the protective interferon (IFN) response to orchestrate innate immunoparalysis. Here, we deconvolute a multi-cellular regulatory pathway in the blood and highlight a pivotal immunological checkpoint, where pharmacological intervention with cardioselective {beta}-blockers uncouples the immunosuppressive cascade, restores host antimicrobial function, and significantly improves survival outcomes.
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pan-cancer estimation of prognostic immune biomarkers from histopathology using artificial intelligence
papers.abstract: Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) assays such as ImmunoProfile provide standardized quantification of prognostic immune markers but are costly and not routinely used in clinical settings. We developed a weakly-supervised AI model, HistoProfile, to estimate intratumoral cell densities of key immune biomarkers (CD8, FOXP3, PD-1, and PD-L1) and the PD-L1 tumor proportion score from routine H&E-stained whole-slide images. Trained on a large pan-cancer cohort with paired H&E and mIF data, HistoProfile discriminated biomarker-high from biomarker-low tumors in held-out samples and tumor-specific subgroups (AUROCs of 0.78-0.89 across biomarkers). Critically, the estimated biomarkers preserved prognostic stratification in downstream survival analyses, and showed cancer-specific survival associations across TCGA cohorts where mIF is unavailable. These findings support scalable H&E-based estimation of key immune biomarker measurements for large-scale immune profiling and risk stratification.
affiliations: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: ALBIS: simulation of multi-resolution and multi-dimensional spatial transcriptomics data
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies has been accompanied by substantial growth in computational methods, creating an increasing need for systematic and reliable benchmarking, particularly as analyses increasingly extend from individual tissue sections to three-dimensional (3D) tissue reconstruction. Existing benchmarks often rely on a small and similar set of experimentally-derived datasets because they offer a reliable ground truth label, which is hard to find in practice. Simulated or synthetic data provide an alternative, yet most existing simulators either adapt single-cell RNA-sequencing models to spatial coordinates or generate individual sections in a two-dimensional (2D) space at predefined resolutions. More recent approaches can simulate 2D and 3D tissues, but generally do not derive multiple spatial resolutions from the same molecular realization. Here, we introduce ALBIS (A muLti-resolution Biological In-silico Simulator for spatial transcriptomics), a statistically grounded and highly customizable framework that generates synthetic ST data from an in silico 3D tissue. ALBIS defines spatially structured cell populations with corresponding markers for gene expression, then initializes individual mRNA molecules in 3D space to create cell-level information with a ground truth 3D coordinate for each molecule and cell. From this common realization, ALBIS cuts the 3D tissue into multiple 2D tissue sections with cell-, bin-, and spot-level measurements, enabling direct comparison across spatial resolutions. Properties of the simulated data, including spatial domains, cell type composition, gene-expression effects, batch effects, measurement resolution, and tissue scale, can be systematically varied, enabling rigorous stress-testing of computational methods under known and increasingly challenging conditions.
affiliations: Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health (corresponding author)

papers.title: Lack of adoption of computational gene-panel-selection tools in targeted spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Targeted spatial transcriptomics requires selecting a gene panel before any experiment is run. Choosing well across tens of thousands of candidate genes under platform-specific probe, panel-size, and sensitivity constraints is difficult to do manually, and impossible to correct once a panel has been used. A growing number of computational tools to automate this selection have been designed, yet it remains unclear whether they are adopted in practice. Several factors could limit uptake: validation uncertainty about panel performance, workflow friction between a ranked gene list and a submission-ready panel, limited platform awareness in tools developed for dissociated single-cell data, and the cost advantage of vendor panels. We analyzed 18 computational tools for gene-panel selection from two angles: their citation landscape and their use across a targeted spatial transcriptomics corpus. Across 540 full-text-classified records, only 35 (6.5%) reported using the cited tool for panel design; most came from computational, benchmark, review, or non-spatial papers, or papers that cited but did not use it. In an independent corpus, only 34 of 479 (7.1%) involved a computational tool, alone or in a hybrid workflow; most used manually curated, premade vendor, or modified vendor panels. Both lines of evidence point the same way: computational selection is rarely part of the reported experimental workflow, and it more often supplemented manual curation than replaced it. Adoption is unlikely to turn on further benchmark gains alone; it will depend on reducing the validation uncertainty and workflow friction that keep users on established panel-design practice.
affiliations: Katholieke Universiteit Leuven (corresponding author)

papers.title: Interlaboratory benchmarking of differential scanning fluorimetry reveals sources of variability in protein thermal stability parameters
papers.abstract: Differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) is widely used to assess protein thermal stability and to compare protein variants, ligands, or formulations with limited sample consumption. Yet, the reproducibility of DSF derived parameters across laboratories, instruments and analysis workflows remains poorly defined. Here, we report a two phase interlaboratory benchmark using a shared VHH sample across 26 laboratories, 28 instruments and seven DSF instrument models. In Phase 1, participants applied their routine acquisition and analysis workflows, whereas in Phase 2, acquisition conditions were harmonised. Datasets were analysed locally and then centrally reprocessed with MoltenProt. Participant reported apparent melting temperatures (Tm) showed good within instrument repeatability but moderate inter instrument dispersion. Harmonisation of acquisition conditions did not substantially reduce this dispersion. Conversely, centralised reprocessing narrowed the distribution among retained datasets, indicating contributions from analysis workflows and data acceptance criteria in addition to instrument dependent factors. Comparison with differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) further showed that apparent Tm depended strongly on the fluorescence readout. For this VHH, single wavelength fluorescence at 350 nm showed the closest agreement with the DSC transition temperature, whereas the 350/330 nm ratio and barycentric mean generally yielded higher values. Furthermore, DSF derived apparent unfolding enthalpies were more variable than apparent Tm. Together, these findings show that DSF can be highly repeatable within a defined instrument and workflow, but that quantitative comparability across instruments depends on instrument specific effects, the choice of fluorescence readout and analysis strategy. Improved comparability will require transparent reporting of acquisition and analysis conditions, explicit data quality criteria, and well characterised reference materials to monitor instrument dependent offsets.
affiliations: Institut Pasteur; Universite Paris Cite (corresponding author)

papers.title: An inspectable Grover algorithm-based amplitude-amplification workflow for k-mer discovery and motif scanning with genomic coordinate traceability
papers.abstract: Motif discovery and motif scanning remain core primitives in genomics, but both tasks face combinatorial growth as k-mer length increases and as mismatch-tolerant searches expand the candidate space. In this work, we present MotifQu, a Python package and command-line tool that maps two common motif-analysis workflows-(i) scanning a genome for a user-specified consensus motif and (ii) de novo discovery of recurrent k-mers above a user-defined count threshold-onto Grover-style amplitude amplification circuits executed reproducibly via Qiskit Aer statevector simulation. We evaluate MotifQu on the SARS-CoV-2 reference contig (29,903 bp) and S. cerevisiae S288C reference genome, where the classical census identifies strongly non-uniform motif frequencies dominated by A/T-rich 5-mers and returns explicit coordinate lists across the full genome span. We further execute the same logical 10-qubit search on IBM hardware showing that while end-to-end execution is feasible, transpilation-induced circuit depth and entangling-gate volume produce a diffuse measurement distribution whose probabilities remain close to the uniform 1/1024 scale, limiting observable amplitude concentration under current NISQ constraints. Finally, we demonstrate the full discovery workflow on the S. cerevisiae S288C reference genome (12,157,105 bp) to illustrate search results (ranked motifs, probability summaries, circuit diagrams, and position plots) and to highlight the regime where a large, marked set reduces the sharpness of Grover amplification.
affiliations: MIT Vishwaprayag University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chromatin Acetylation Overrides Substrate Stiffness-Dependent Mechanoresponse and Lineage Specification in Human Mesenchymal Stem Cells
papers.abstract: Human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) exhibit a stiffness dependent cellular phenotype and lineage bias. Cells on soft substrate display reduced cell spreading, less cellular traction, smaller and fewer focal adhesions and decreased actin stress fibre organization, whereas cells on stiff substrate exhibit the converse behaviour. Further, hMSCs preferentially undergo adipogenic differentiation on soft substrate and osteogenic differentiation on stiff substrate. These stiffness dependent changes are accompanied by global chromatin condensation/decondensation on soft/stiff substrates. Despite these well documented correlations, it remains unclear whether modulating chromatin condensation alone can be sufficient to reprogram stiffness dependent cellular phenotype. To answer whether chromatin organization acts as an active regulatory element in rigidity sensing, we induced chromatin condensation/decondensation in hMSCs cultured on soft/stiff polyacrylamide gels using histone deacetylase inhibitor (HDACi) and histone acetyltransferase inhibitor (HATi) respectively. We found that across conditions, phenotypic outcomes including nuclear localization of mechanosignalling protein YAP correlated strongly with chromatin compaction state rather than with substrate stiffness when the cells were presented with combination of signals. Mechanistically pharmacological inhibition of ERK phosphorylation attenuated chromatin dependent lineage specification while leaving chromatin compaction unchanged, indicating that ERK phosphorylation operates downstream of chromatin state. Collectively, these findings suggests an inside-out signalling mechanism in which chromatin compaction state reprograms the stiffness dependent mechanoresponse and fate decisions in hMSCs. Altogether, this works provides a fundamental framework for integrating mechanical and epigenetic cues in designing biomaterial microenvironment for controlling hMSCs fate in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Bombay (corresponding author)

papers.title: When label-free morphology is sufficient for targeted cellular measurements
papers.abstract: Label-free morphology captures cellular responses, but its ability to substitute for targeted cellular measurements depends on the intended use. We assess measurement sufficiency using nearly 10 million paired phase-reporter observations across 1,000 gene knockouts, 52 fluorescent reporters and 73 A549 screens. Ten predictors differed in recovery across held-out fields, genes and screens. Same-cell pairing controls identified reporter-state information beyond perturbation averages and measured covariates. Perturbation ranking often persisted despite reduced variation in predicted response magnitudes. Predictions of held-out knockout responses retained a median 79% of the strongest hits, whereas functional-term retention varied. Atlas-derived criteria identified 30 quantitative and 7 ranking proxies for a fixed ensemble, with reference reproducibility constraining interpretation. In independent primary-hepatocyte data, brightfield predictions prioritized 10 of the 11 compounds with the largest measured metabolic-activity losses among 217 held-out compounds. Measurement sufficiency therefore depends on target, predictor, context and scientific task, beyond predictive correlation alone.
affiliations: Shenzhen Loop Area Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Response representation shapes AlphaGenome enhancer-gene prediction in human astrocytes
papers.abstract: Background: Sequence-to-function models predict regulatory perturbation responses, but their added value beyond established enhancer-gene predictors and across prediction tasks remains unclear. We evaluated whole-enhancer deletion and sparse variant responses in human astrocytes. Results: We analyzed 2,307 CRISPR-interference-tested relations, including 133 expression-decreasing hits. Adding deletion responses increased fully nested EGrf average precision from 0.5475 to 0.6137. The paired increment was 0.0662 (enhancer-cluster 95% interval 0.0144-0.1181). In a separate exploratory analysis, sparse Atlas responses were combined with seven-input logistic and random-forest comparators by equal-weight rank fusion. Atlas magnitude fusion exceeded absolute-deletion fusion by 0.0519 and 0.0637 in average precision. Enhancer-cluster 95% intervals were 0.0098-0.0957 and 0.0220-0.1094, respectively. Standalone Atlas magnitude reached average precision 0.5570, but its advantage over absolute deletion remained uncertain. Signed Atlas fusion performed worse than either comparator alone. Incremental value for within-enhancer target choice and in the external WTC11 MHC evaluation remained uncertain. The reported performance intervals use one-way clustering of fixed predictions; Atlas analyses were exploratory within the same cohort. Conclusions: In AstroREG, whole-enhancer deletion responses increased observed retrieval performance beyond a fully nested chromatin-based predictor. Sparse variant responses were more informative as magnitudes than as signed averages. Improved within-enhancer target choice and external transfer were not established.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: PanTEon: a cross-kingdom framework to guide the design of transposable element classifiers
papers.abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genome evolution, yet their annotation and classification remain inconsistent and hard to reproduce across species. Fragmented repeats, lineage-specific mutations, and the use of heterogeneous taxonomies across databases and tools make comparative analyses difficult and hamper progress in TE biology. To address this, we developed PanTEon, a cross-kingdom deep learning framework for reproducible TE classification that combines a harmonized database with an open, modular benchmarking platform. The PanTEon Database is an automatically curated, taxonomically broad TE repository spanning animals, plants, and fungi. The PanTEon platform standardizes training, evaluation, and inference across nine machine learning methods, while being extensible to user-defined architectures. We use this framework to benchmark state-of-the-art machine learning-based TE classifiers and find that performance varies markedly across TE superfamilies and major eukaryotic lineages. Ensemble approaches and phylum-specific models improve predictive F1 scores, but cross-species generalization remains challenging. Together, the PanTEon Database and platform provide a reproducible, scalable, and extensible foundation for TE classification, enabling standardized evaluation of future AI methods and supporting community-driven annotation efforts.
affiliations: Life Science Department, Barcelona Supercomputing Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: REMAG: recovery of eukaryotic genomes from metagenomic data using non-contrastive self-supervised learning
papers.abstract: Metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) are central to exploring microbial communities. Yet, despite the relevance of protists and fungi to diverse ecosystems, eukaryotic MAG recovery lags behind that of prokaryotes. A major bottleneck is that most state-of-the-art binning pipelines exclusively rely on prokaryotic single-copy core gene reference databases and are optimized for smaller genomes. To address this gap, we present REMAG (Recovery of Eukaryotic MAGs), a tool designed to recover high-quality eukaryotic genomes suited for long-read metagenomic data. REMAG uses a fine-tuned HyenaDNA genomic foundation model to efficiently filter eukaryotic contigs. It then employs a dual-encoder Siamese network trained with the non-contrastive Barlow Twins loss to learn a shared embedding space by integrating contig composition and differential coverage. Finally, high-quality bins are extracted using greedy iterative Leiden clustering optimized with eukaryotic single-copy core gene constraints. In benchmarks based on simulated mixed prokaryotic/eukaryotic communities and real datasets of varying sizes and origin, we demonstrate REMAG's ability to recover more near-complete eukaryotic genomes than existing state-of-the-art tools, which often produce highly fragmented eukaryotic bins. REMAG provides an automated eukaryotic binning method that scales effectively with the increasing size and sequencing depth of metagenomic datasets.
affiliations: Earlham Institute, Norwich Research Park, NR4 7UZ Norwich, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural model of the blood protein vitronectin bound to lipid and HDL
papers.abstract: Vitronectin (Vn) is a multifunctional blood glycoprotein involved in cell adhesion and migration, blood coagulation, and inflammation. It is a component of the high-density lipoprotein (HDL) proteome also found associated with the calcified, lipid-rich, protein deposits that are a hallmark of age-related macular degeneration, Alzheimer's disease, atherosclerosis and other aging-related diseases. Here we explored the molecular basis for lipid binding and HDL association by Vn. Using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we identify a hydrophobic groove on the surface of the Vn hemopexin-like (HX) domain, that is capable of binding phospholipids. Key residues mediate the association of VnHX with phosphatidylcholine (PC) via hydrophobic and polar contacts. Lipid binding is guided by interactions with positively charged and hydrophobic residues that organize the lipids in a tail-to-tail bilayer-like arrangement within the groove. MD simulations of PC-bound VnHX combined with an MD structural model of discoidal HDL, show that VnHX associates with HDL in a lipid-mediated manner and at the exposed edge of the discoidal HDL lipoparticle where the terminal helices of the scaffolding protein ApoA1 flip away. Collectively, the data establish a comprehensive structural model for Vn association with PC and HDL. They expand the range of protein-lipid interactions observed within the structurally and functionally diverse collection of HDL particles.
affiliations: Medical College of Wisconsn (corresponding author)

papers.title: Alcohol, Tobacco, and HPV exposure synergistically regulate promoter methylation of PD-L1 related genes in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
papers.abstract: Although alcohol, tobacco and human papillomavirus (HPV) are established risk factors for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), the molecular effects of their co-occurrence remain poorly understood. DNA methylation may link exposure history to regulation of the PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint pathway, whose therapeutic blockade benefits only a subset of patients with recurrent or metastatic HNSCC. We stratified primary tumors from The Cancer Genome Atlas HNSCC cohort by all combinations of these exposures and examined promoter methylation across seven interferon-{gamma}-PD-L1 signaling genes at single-CpG resolution, with region-level validation. Triple-exposure tumors exhibited coordinated methylation changes involving CD274, IRF1, JAK1, PDCD1, MIR33A and MIR34A, with differentially methylated regions overlapping PDCD1, MIR34AHG and JAK1. CD274 promoter methylation is inversely correlated with gene expression. Significant methylation differences occurred only in HPV-positive subgroups, suggesting HPV may be necessary for this phenotype, while concurrent exposures may modify its extent. Transcriptomic analysis and immune deconvolution further suggested greater estimated immune infiltration alongside downregulation of innate and adaptive immune activation pathways, consistent with an inflamed but functionally suppressed tumor microenvironment. These findings suggest combined exposure history may help contextualize checkpoint pathway regulation in HNSCC.
affiliations: UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA, SAN DIEGO (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cyclical content exchange in hydrogel-core synthetic cells
papers.abstract: Synthetic cells lack the complex protein machinery that living cells use to control molecular traffic across their membranes, making programmable exchange with the environment a central challenge in bottom-up synthetic biology. Here, we introduce a protein-free approach for dynamic content exchange in liposome-based synthetic cells through a membrane-hydrogel composite architecture. We assemble the synthetic cell by crosslinking a polymer hydrogel within the lumen of giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) and chemically tethering it to the inner membrane leaflet. The resulting mechanical coupling enables a previously unexplored response through which the membrane can be reversibly permeabilized and re-sealed upon osmotic swelling and de-swelling of the hydrogel. This mechanism of membrane remodeling enables cyclic exchange of small molecules and macromolecules, offering a versatile route for dynamic regulation of intracellular biochemistry that does not rely on reconstituted protein pores.
affiliations: Institute of Science Tokyo (corresponding author)

papers.title: Characterization of Stress Tolerance and Probiotic Traits of Streptococcus salivarius Strains Isolated from Wildflower Honey
papers.abstract: Honey represents a distinctive microbial habitat that imposes physicochemical stresses on its resident microbiota while also serving as a potential source of beneficial microorganisms. Two Streptococcus salivarius strains, DOW-5A and DOW-10, isolated from Korean wildflower honey were identified through phenotypic observation and 16S rRNA sequencing. Comprehensive evaluation, including 5 safety assessments and 14 functional assays, was conducted to reveal distinct potential probiotic characteristics in the two isolates. Both strains exhibited no gelatinase or hemolytic activity and showed no significant cytotoxicity toward Caco-2 cells. While DOW-5A maintained higher viable counts during the simulated gastric phase, DOW-10 showed an increase after an initial decline during the simulated intestinal phase. Both strains also exhibited growth under stress conditions involving phenol or hydrogen peroxide. Among the cell-surface and adhesion-related characteristics, DOW-5A exhibited greater mucin adhesion and cell-surface hydrophobicity, whereas DOW-10 showed higher autoaggregation at 6 and 12 h. Both strains exhibited DPPH radical-scavenging activity, with no significant difference from that of the reference probiotic strain, Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG. Atypical and crystalline-like colony morphologies, suggestive of EPS production, were observed when sucrose was supplied as the carbon source. Furthermore, both strains formed biofilms in a crystal violet staining assay, while DOW-5A showed a marked increase in biofilm biomass upon sucrose supplementation. These findings highlight strain-specific variation in stress tolerance and probiotic-associated traits between the two honey-derived Strep. salivarius isolates and support their further investigation as probiotic candidates.
affiliations: Department of Life Science, Handong Global University, Pohang, 37554, Republic of Korea (corresponding author)

papers.title: SCAMP - an open-source tool for the quantification of calcification in fish larvae
papers.abstract: Quantifying skeletal mineralization phenotypes in larval fish is complicated by the natural curvature of the notochord and by sample-to-sample variability in orientation, staining and imaging. Consequently, many studies rely on summary measures such as vertebral counts or total stain intensity. Here we present SCAMP (Spinal Calcification & Mineralization Profiler), an open-source, GUI-based Python tool that computationally straightens the curved notochord of Alizarin Red S-stained fish larvae and generates standardized ARS-based mineralization profiles along the spinal axis. This approach reduces positional and shape variability, allowing direct quantitative comparison of Alizarin Red S fluorescence patterns within experimental cohorts processed and imaged under matched conditions, without requiring programming expertise. We validate SCAMP using a zebrafish model of Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (abcc6aelu15/elu15), recovering genotype-specific differences in the intensity, extent and spatial distribution of ectopic calcification. Using SCAMP, we further show that inorganic pyrophosphate supplementation reduces ectopic intervertebral Alizarin Red S signal, alters the anterior-posterior distribution of mineralized regions in homozygous mutants, and increases signal at physiological chordacentrum positions. We also show that methylene blue, a routine antifungal additive in fish medium, is associated with reduced baseline Alizarin Red S-based mineralization endpoints, with the most pronounced effects observed in heterozygous controls. SCAMP is freely available and has the potential to be adapted to other fish species used in skeletal and mineralization research.
affiliations: Department of Genetics, ELTE Eötvös Loránd University, Budapest, Hungary (corresponding author)
