papers.title: Biobank-scale genotyping of Robertsonian translocations reveals hidden structural variation on the human acrocentric chromosomes
authors: del Castillo del Rio, S. O.
papers.abstract: Balanced Robertsonian translocation (ROB) is the most common chromosomal rearrangement in humans, with an estimated occurrence of 1 in 800 in newborn studies. Carriers are at increased risk of cancer and often diagnosed at fertility clinics after facing recurrent miscarriages, infertility, or aneuploid offspring. Genotyping carriers with DNA sequencing has been challenging because of gaps and misrepresentation of the translocation fusion site in the human reference genome. Only recently, telomere-to-telomere (T2T) human genomes successfully revealed sequences of the acrocentric short arms, including the most common ROB fusion site. A ROB results in loss of two ribosomal DNA (rDNA) arrays and its adjacent distal sequences, including the highly conserved distal junction (DJ). Here, we present a new method to type ROB carriers directly from short and long sequencing reads by estimating DJ copy number. We demonstrate that our method successfully genotypes ROBs using a reference-free approach or alignments to either T2T-CHM13v2 or GRCh38. Applying this method to a cohort of healthy newborns and family members (n=4,172) as well as the UK Biobank (n=490,416), we find candidate ROBs at a frequency consistent with the previously reported incidence (0.11-0.12%). In addition to ROB carriers, we report the frequency of one DJ loss (9, 2.8-3.4%) or gain (11+, 8.4-9.3%) from the two cohorts and the 1000 Genomes Project (n=3,202), and characterize the underlying structural variation in near-T2T genome assemblies from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium. Importantly, we provide the first screening method for ROB carriers using low-coverage sequencing data, enhancing its clinical applicability and enabling new studies of structural variation on the acrocentric chromosomes.
affiliations: Genome Informatics Section, Center for Genomics and Data Science Research, NHGRI, NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: CPIExtract: A software package to collect and harmonize small molecule and protein interactions
papers.abstract: Summary: The binding interactions between small molecules and proteins are the basis of cellular functions. Yet, experimental data available regarding compound-protein interaction are not harmonized into a single entity but rather scattered across multiple institutions, each maintaining databases with different formats. Extracting information from these multiple sources remains challenging due to data heterogeneity. Here, we present CPIExtract (Compound-Protein Interaction Extract), a tool to interactively extract experimental binding interaction data from multiple databases, perform filtering, and harmonize the resulting information, thus providing a gain of compound-protein interaction data. When compared to a single source, DrugBank, we show that it can collect more than ten times the number of annotations. The end-user can apply custom filtering to the aggregated output data and save it in any generic tabular file suitable for further downstream tasks such as network medicine analyses for drug repurposing and cross-validation of deep learning models. Availability: CPIExtract is an open-source Python package under an MIT license. CPIExtract can be installed from https://pypi.org/project/cpiextract and downloaded from https://github.com/menicgiulia/CPIExtract. The package can run on any standard desktop computer or computing cluster.
affiliations: Harvard Medical School/Brigham and Women's Hospital (corresponding author)

papers.title: Targeting MAT2A-S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) Axis Attenuates DNA Damage Response and Cancer Stemness to Increase Platinum Sensitivity in Ovarian Cancer
papers.abstract: Abstract Metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming drives development of platinum resistance and disease recurrence in high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSC), a major clinical challenge in the field. S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) is the universal methyl group donor, synthesized by methionine adenosyltransferase 2A (MAT2A) from methionine. Prior studies have linked altered SAM-dependent DNA methylation to acquired platinum resistance in HGSC, connecting metabolism and epigenetic regulation. However, how MAT2A-driven SAM synthesis coordinates the metabolic-epigenetic remodeling axis to affect platinum sensitivity remains unclear. Here, we report that MAT2A-driven SAM synthesis is required for platinum-induced alterations in DNA methylation and the enrichment of ovarian cancer stem cells (OCSCs). We found that MAT2A upregulation correlated with poor progression-free survival in OC patients, and both pharmacological inhibition and genetic knockdown of MAT2A increased sensitivity to cisplatin. To investigate the underlying epigenetic mechanism, we profiled genome-wide changes in DNA methylation using OVCAR3 treated with cisplatin (15M, 16hr) and/or MAT2A siRNA (48hr), which showed that MAT2A knockdown reversed platinum-induced DNA methylation dynamics. Subsequent analysis revealed enrichment of pathways associated with platinum resistance, DNA repair, and stemness. Mechanistically, inhibiting MAT2A abrogated both the platinum-induced hypermethylation at promoter regions and the SAMTOR-mTOR-S6K-FANCD2 signaling axis, resulting in accumulated R-loops, attenuated DNA repair activation in response to platinum, and enhanced platinum-induced DNA damage and cell death. Using a functional DNA damage reporter assay, we directly showed that MAT2A knockdown reduced DNA repair through homologous recombination (HR) and non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) pathways. By detecting key DNA damage response kinases governing HR and NHEJ signaling, we further demonstrated that MAT2A inhibition abrogated DNA repair activation in response to platinum. Furthermore, single-sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis of paired primary and recurrent tumors from HGSC patients revealed an association between MAT2A expression and increased OCSC features in recurrent tumors. In vitro, MAT2A inhibition prevented cisplatin-induced enrichment of OCSCs, reduced stemness markers, and inhibited spheroid-forming ability, all of which were rescued by SAM supplementation. Together, our study reveals a previously unrecognized mechanism linking metabolism to epigenetic regulation through platinum-induced remodeling and establishes the MAT2A-SAM axis as a promising therapeutic target to enhance platinum sensitivity by abrogating DNA damage response and OCSC enrichment and ultimately reduce OCSC-driven disease recurrence in HGSC.
affiliations: Indiana University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: MDL-001: an Oral, Direct-Acting Broad-Spectrum Antiviral for Influenza-Like Illness (ILI) and Chronic Hepatitis In Vivo
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Endemic viral respiratory illnesses caused by influenza, RSV, and coronaviruses impose a global disease burden of hundreds of millions of infections and hundreds of thousands of deaths annually. Chronic hepatitis B and C infections persist in 254 million and 58 million people worldwide, respectively. No approved therapy addresses these viruses simultaneously. MDL-001 is an oral, direct-acting, broad-spectrum antiviral targeting the Thumb-1 allosteric site of viral polymerases. Methods: Here we evaluated the antiviral activity of MDL-001 in vitro in influenza A/B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2, endemic human coronaviruses, and hepatitis B/C/D. We next evaluated MDL-001 antiviral activity in vivo in H1N1, SARS-CoV-2, HCV, and HBV. MDL-001's in vivo efficacy was compared head-to-head versus standards of care including oseltamivir, remdesivir, sofosbuvir, and tenofovir alafenamide, or through literature comparison with nirmatrelvir and molnupiravir. Lastly, we evaluated the pharmacokinetics, metabolism, tolerability, and safety profile of MDL-001. Results: Here, we report MDL-001 inhibits influenza A/B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2, endemic human coronaviruses, and hepatitis B/C/D viruses with nanomolar EC90 potency in vitro. MDL-001 demonstrated equivalent in vivo efficacy to oseltamivir against mouse-lethal influenza A virus infection, reducing lung viral load by 2.6 log10 and preventing weight loss and mortality. MDL-001 demonstrated equivalent symptom reduction to subcutaneous remdesivir after SARS-CoV-2 infection. MDL-001 reduced SARS-CoV-2 lung viral titers by 2.9 log10, superior to literature reported 1.4 log10 and 1.0 log10 reductions for nirmatrelvir and molnupiravir, respectively. MDL-001 reduced HCV viremia by 3.3 log10, equivalent to sofosbuvir. Oral MDL-001 reduced plasma HBV surface antigen by 2.5 log10, superior to tenofovir alafenamide from Day 8 through Day 21. MDL-001 demonstrated an in vitro EC50 of 79.4 nM against infection with RSV strain A2, a 416-fold improvement over literature-reported ribavirin. Oral pharmacokinetics studies demonstrate MDL-001 is rapidly absorbed and partitioned into Lung (Kp=39-52) and Liver (Kp=71-104) tissues. MDL-001 produced no treatment-related tolerability adverse events across 376 animals and showed no hERG, Ames genotoxicity, or micronucleus safety issues. Conclusions: These findings support MDL-001 as a broad-spectrum, direct-acting non-nucleoside antiviral clinical candidate.
affiliations: Model Medicines (corresponding author)

papers.title: Beyond Conveyance: Assessing the Contribution of Process-Critical Bacteria from Urban Sewer Systems to Wastewater Treatment Plants
papers.abstract: The sewer microbiome is known to be the main source of process-critical bacteria involved in nitrogen and phosphorus removal in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) and is thus crucial for the assembly of activated sludge (AS) microbial communities. However, the extent of these bacterial loads arriving at WWTPs currently lacks scientific attention. We provide a quantitative description of the biomass loads from sewer systems to WWTPs by coupling microbial community data by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing from the Aalborg municipality sewer catchment with mass balances and biomass production across gravity and pressure sewer systems. Accounting for microbial transformations in sewer wastewater, biofilm and sediments under steady state dry weather flow conditions, gravity sewers were found to produce higher biomass loads than pressure systems, with loads of 1.57 and 0.27 kgCOD m-3 d-1 respectively. A key feature of our sewer model is its ability to estimate biomass loads from specific taxa, such as polyphosphate accumulating organisms (PAOs). Using Aalborg West WWTP as a case study, model estimations correlated well with figures calculated based on influent wastewater data monitoring. The model-estimated loads for the PAOs Azonexus and Ca. Accumulibacter were 2.10 kg day-1 and 1.80 kg day-1, compared to the influent wastewater monitoring-based loads of 1.77 kg day-1 and 1.20 kg day-1, respectively. While providing a framework for further research on sewer microbial dynamics, this study offers a tool for gaining insights into microbial immigration, generating valuable information for improving microbial communities management in WWTPs, optimizing nutrient removal, and enhancing WWTP design.
affiliations: Aalbor University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Nucleic acid 3D structure search and alignment with GTalign
papers.abstract: Structural comparison of nucleic acids, particularly RNA, is critical for understanding evolutionary and functional relationships beyond sequence similarity, yet efficient tools for large-scale 3D structure search and alignment remain scarce. We extend GTalign to support nucleic acid structures, enabling unified, high-performance alignment across macromolecules. Benchmarking on diverse nucleic acid datasets demonstrates improved alignment accuracy and substantially lower runtimes compared to existing methods. GTalign thus provides a scalable solution for nucleic acid structure comparison and database search. Availability and Implementation: https://github.com/minmarg/gtalign_alpha
affiliations: Institute of Biotechnology, Vilnius University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tensorizing Pairwise Structural Analysis: GPU-Accelerated RMSD and FCC Clustering in HADDOCK3 Without Structural Regression.
papers.abstract: Integrative macromolecular docking pipelines generate thousands of candidate structural decoys, relying on downstream pairwise ensemble analysis, including Root-Mean-Square Deviation (RMSD) matrices and Fraction of Common Contacts (FCC) clustering, to identify biologically relevant binding poses. However, pairwise structural comparisons scale quadratically (O(N^2)), and canonical workflows in HADDOCK3 historically rely on disk-bound trajectory serialization and iterative CPU set operations, creating a quadratic computational and storage bottleneck for large ensembles. Here, we demonstrate that these operations can be reformulated as continuous linear algebra on GPU-resident tensors: structural superposition via batched Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and residue contact overlap via binary matrix multiplication (M = A A^T). Across empirical benchmarks spanning N = 200 to 10,000 models (evaluating up to 49,995,000 decoy pairs), our GPU implementation achieves a 6.41-fold compute speedup on Apple Silicon (MPS) and up to 12.2-fold end-to-end acceleration in an N = 5,000 ablation on NVIDIA CUDA by eliminating trajectory disk I/O. Crucially, the implementation achieves zero downstream structural regression relative to canonical baselines, preserving identical cluster assignments (Adjusted Rand Index ARI = 1.0000, zero differing assignments) with sub-microangstrom RMSD concordance (Delta_max <= 4.07 x 10^-7 Angstrom on single-precision MPS; machine-precision Delta_max <= 8.88 x 10^-16 Angstrom on double-precision CUDA). The accelerated code, test suites, and benchmarking workflows are openly accessible on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license.
affiliations: University of Ghana (corresponding author)

papers.title: A simple platform for in situ DNA-PAINT optimization enables improved multiplexed super-resolution imaging in Gram-negative bacteria
papers.abstract: DNA-PAINT enables super-resolution imaging with high multiplexing capacity, yet it is rarely used in nanoscale bacteriology. A likely reason is the lack of straightforward protocols and of systematic characterization of imager-docking strand pairs inside intact bacterial cells, whose envelope and dense cytoplasm differ markedly from both the DNA origami in vitro systems used to develop them, and eukaryotic cells. In this work, we establish a screening platform based on RNA-FISH, in which we extend the 16S rRNA-directed EUB338 probe with docking sequences of choice. This allows imager-docking pairs to be benchmarked directly inside Escherichia coli cells and characterized for parameters such as specificity, binding kinetics, and localization precision. We screened 12 different DNA-PAINT sequences and used an optimized set to perform four-target 3D Exchange-PAINT in single E. coli cells. We further applied our strategy to image three effector mRNAs in the Gram-negative pathogen Yersinia enterocolitica and quantified RNA clusters and their 3D distribution. Our work provides a framework and practical guidelines for high-quality 3D DNA-PAINT imaging in Gram-negative bacteria and should facilitate its broader adoption in nanoscale bacteriology.
affiliations: Rudolf Virchow Center, University of Wuerzburg (corresponding author)

papers.title: Covariance Nonstationarity is Evident in Spatial Transcriptomics and Provides a New Categorization of Spatially Varying Genes
papers.abstract: Gaussian process models underlie many spatial transcriptomics tools but typically assume stationary covariance. To test this assumption, we use approximate Bayes factors from R-INLA to compare stationary and non-stationary Matern covariance functions across 12 Visium datasets; covariance non-stationarity is substantially evident as it appears in 3% to 50% of genes across datasets. We find that gene sets associated with effector functions are enriched among genes favoring non-stationary spatial covariance.
affiliations: University of Victoria (corresponding author)

papers.title: Assembly and activation of the AAA+ motor of the multi-subunit cobaltochelatase
papers.abstract: Cobalamin is a complex yet essential cobalt-containing cofactor synthesized exclusively by prokaryotes and archaea. Aerobic cobalamin biosynthesis requires the CobNST multi-subunit class I cobaltochelatase for cobalt incorporation. Cobalt chelation is dependent on the energy transfer from the CobST AAA+/VWA motor unit to the substrate-binding catalytic unit (CobN). However, the mechanism for assembly and function of CobNST cobaltochelatase remains poorly understood. Here, we used cryo-EM to solve the structures of the AAA+ motor CobS, in the absence and presence of ATP and its VWA-partner protein CobT. Our data reveal that the AAA+ CobS assembles into various conformations, including hexameric planar rings and different spiral left-handed assemblies: hexamers, double rings and filaments. In the absence of nucleotide, the CobT N-terminal domain interacts with CobS left-handed oligomers, remaining in a half-assembled, nonfunctional motor unit. In the CobST complex, ATP induces conformational rearrangement of CobS from left-handed helical oligomers to a right-handed closed hexamer. The simultaneous repositioning of the CobT VWA domain to the AAA+ central pore shifts the motor unit to a functional state, ready-to-drive CobN-catalyzed chelation reaction. These findings define the mechanism for assembly and activation of the class I cobaltochelatase CobST motor.
affiliations: Department of Biology/Chemistry - Structural Biology of Photosynthetic Microorganisms, University of Osnabrueck, Osnabrueck 49076, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: Is this idea from AI or humans? A detector claims it can tell
In the AI era, coding means thinking like a systems architect
Preserve research data for tomorrow’s AI-enabled integrity checks
When microbes degrade plastic, where does it go?
Why not every global problem can be tackled by an IPCC-like organization
Decentralized AI needs more evidence on energy use
What’s the secret sauce for happy scientists at work? These eight countries offer some clues
Admire another researcher’s work? Tell them about it
Scellmate enables contamination aware curation and host mobilome linkage analysis of large SAG datasets
papers.abstract: In this study, the authors develop a computational framework, Scellmate, that curates and analyzes large-scale microbial single-cell datasets from complex environments, and show that this helps to reveal microbial diversity and infer microbe–plasmid and microbe–phage associations in sewage.

papers.title: Soil proteogenomics uncover microbial strategies for soil depth-specific carbon cycling under whole-soil warming conditions
papers.abstract: Soils are Earth’s largest carbon reservoir, yet microbial mechanisms controlling decomposition, and their warming response, remain poorly resolved, especially in subsoils. Using genome-resolved proteogenomics within a replicated whole-soil warming experiment (0–90 cm, +4 °C, 7.5 years) we map microbial traits, their depth stratification, and warming responses. Depth is the dominant driver of microbial community and trait structure. Depth-wise, metabolism converge on low-molecular-weight and C1 compounds, challenging glucose-centric models, with surface soils enriched in methanol oxidation and deep soils in alcohol fermentation, CO oxidation and N₂ fixation. Abundant sialidases in deep soils implicate glycoproteins as a key carbon source. Warming effects are smaller and decrease over time but are depth-specific: surface soils show enhanced amino sugar and sugar alcohol transport, phosphorus mobilization, and stress tolerance, whereas mid- and deep soils exhibit stimulated C1 metabolism, CO oxidation, and altered nitrogen turnover. These depth-specific microbial trait shifts may critically influence soil carbon–climate feedbacks.

papers.title: Reinforcement learning guided robotic platform that investigates and discovers asymmetric reactions
papers.abstract: Autonomous robotic platforms accelerate chemical discovery by coupling automated experimentation with algorithmic decision-making, but most lack integrated support for chirality and the sequential decision-making required to explore asymmetric reaction spaces with unknown reactivity and stereochemical outcomes. Here, we report a bespoke robotic platform guided by deep reinforcement learning that autonomously navigates a defined asymmetric reaction space by scouting reaction conditions, discovering chiral products, screening catalysts and mapping substrate scope. The structure-agnostic workflow is enabled by a digital twin of asymmetric catalysis, in which control policies are trained before transfer to the laboratory. We validate the approach in chiral phosphoric acid catalysis: over 30 days, the system made more than 3,000 decisions and uncovered four highly enantioselective transformations, including an axially chiral molecule and three allene syntheses, one involving the enantioselective functionalization of a pyrrolopyrrole moiety. These results highlight deep reinforcement learning-guided autonomy as a strategy for discovery in complex catalytic systems.

papers.title: Unmet care needs at the end-of-life among older adults with activity limitations
papers.abstract: Formal end-of-life care expansion in the US, Europe, and South Korea has not fully compensated for declining informal care, resulting in care gaps. Demographic transitions interact with development contexts to create distinct care landscapes.

papers.title: NiCLIP: neuroimaging contrastive language-image pretraining model for predicting text from brain activation images
papers.abstract: Researchers developed NiCLIP, an AI model that decodes cognitive tasks, concepts, and domains from brain activation patterns. Trained on over 23,000 papers, NiCLIP excels at group-level decoding, outperforming traditional decoders.

papers.title: Multi-day recalibration-free electrophysiology interface based on carbon nanotube thin film dry electrodes
papers.abstract: Electrophysiological signals provide crucial and reliable information for decoding behavioral and cognitive human states. However, existing electrode interfaces are susceptible to artifacts or drift over time, thereby requiring frequent machine-learning model retraining. Here we present an end-to-end design of dry electrodes based on carbon nanotube (CNT) thin films, synthesized by a roll-to-roll floating catalyst chemical vapor deposition process. By balancing structural and electrical properties, we achieved low electrode-skin impedance, high signal fidelity, minimal motion artifacts, high breathability, and biocompatibility, outperforming the gold standard wet electrodes. In a multichannel myoelectric interface demonstration, these CNT electrodes maintained stable signals and consistent task performance across 14 days using only minutes of training data and no further model retraining. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a multi-day recalibration-free dry electrode system under naturalistic conditions, achieved by stable electrode–skin interface, rather than ongoing algorithmic adaptation.

papers.title: Author Correction: Improved pharmacodynamics of epidermal growth factor via microneedles-based self-powered transcutaneous electrical stimulation
Mitochondria-localized circRNA BRAKE restrains adipogenesis under nutrient overload by disrupting ATP synthase assembly in mice
papers.abstract: Impaired adipogenesis contributes to obesity-associated metabolic disorders, in which mitochondrial dysfunction plays an important role. Emerging evidence suggests that mitochondria-localized circular RNAs (circRNAs) influence mitochondrial function; however, whether they regulate adipogenesis and systemic metabolism is unclear. By profiling circRNAs in mitochondria isolated from the white adipose tissue (WAT) of obese male mice, we observe an upregulation of Birc6 -circRNA Repressing Adipogenesis and Krebs-cycle Energy (BRAKE) in mitochondria. In vivo, adipocyte-specific circRNA BRAKE knockdown in male mice reduces body weight, restricts fat expansion, and improves insulin sensitivity. In vitro studies show that circRNA BRAKE inhibits adipogenesis. Mechanistically, circRNA BRAKE binds ATP5A and disrupts ATP synthase assembly, thereby reducing ATP production and mTORC1 signaling and suppressing adipogenesis. In omental WAT (oWAT) of patients with obesity, mitochondrial circRNA BRAKE levels are elevated and inversely correlated with mitochondrial bioenergetic function. Collectively, our data identify a mitochondria-localized circRNA that regulates energy metabolism and adipogenesis, suggesting that circRNA BRAKE may represent a potential therapeutic target for obesity-related metabolic diseases.

papers.title: Proteomic aging clocks go to trial
papers.abstract: Six proteomic aging clocks are deployed in a clinical trial for the first time, revealing more about the clocks than about the drug.

papers.title: In vivo engineering of CAR natural killer cells for immunotherapy using ligand-directed lipid nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor natural killer cells to treat autoimmune disease and cancer are generated in vivo.

papers.title: The companion website
papers.abstract: How biologists can make the most of supplementary materials for impact.

papers.title: Near-infrared photochromic miniprotein enables photoacoustic molecular imaging of acute inflammation and intracellular antigens
papers.abstract: Using near-infrared photoswitchable photochromic genetically encoded probes, differential photoacoustic tomography (PAT) enables deep-tissue imaging with high resolution and sensitivity; however, current bacteriophytochrome-based probes are bulky multidomain proteins exceeding 55 kDa, which constrains their use for designing PAT molecular reporters. Here we engineer rsmiRFPnano, a compact cyanobacteriochrome-derived photoswitchable PAT probe. With a molecular weight below 19 kDa, rsmiRFPnano efficiently incorporates biliverdin, exhibits high extinction coefficients in both photochromic states and demonstrates robust performance in live cells. We established rsmiRFPnano-based reporters for NF-κB and AP-1 pathways, which display low basal activity and strong activation-dependent responses. These reporters effectively visualized acute inflammation using noninvasive PAT in vivo, further validated through cellular-level spatial omics mapping. We then created photoswitchable nanobody probes, rsNIR-Fbs, stabilized upon antigen binding and rapidly degraded otherwise, enabling selective photoacoustic immuno-imaging of intracellular antigens in vivo. Together, these results establish rsmiRFPnano as an ultracompact and versatile platform for molecular PAT.

papers.title: A unique and equity-driven approach to immunology education in low- and middle-income countries
papers.abstract: We present a model for education that has proven transformative for faculty and students, fostering mentorship, inclusion and cross-border collaboration. By embedding training in local contexts, our framework builds confidence, skills and leadership among early-career scientists. These elements foster scientific autonomy and enable sustainable global engagement.

papers.title: Clonal heterogeneity in human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and its impact on tumor progression
papers.abstract: This study uses single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma tumors to investigate tumor heterogeneity and clonal evolution, providing a valuable resource for this aggressive cancer.

papers.title: Repurposing adult AI radiograph models for neonatal care through continual learning: an international multicentre study
papers.abstract: Despite growing clinical adoption of artificial intelligence in radiology, fewer than one in five commercially available models are cleared for paediatric use. Existing systems are trained predominantly on adult data and generalize poorly to neonates, yet efficient strategies for repurposing them without data sharing or large-scale local data curation are lacking. Here we present an international retrospective study of neonatal chest radiographs from 30 neonatal intensive care units across 20 countries and territories, evaluating continual learning as a privacy-preserving approach to adapt a deep learning model for adult endotracheal tube assessment to neonatal care. Each hospital contributed 50 radiographs for sequential model retraining without centralized data pooling. Continual learning achieved lower anatomical landmark localization error (0.67 cm versus 1.29 cm for hospital-specific fine-tuning and 4.30 cm for adult-only models) at 29 of 30 sites, with improved detection of deep intubations at 27 of 30 sites. These findings demonstrate that privacy-preserving collaborative learning can address critical gaps in paediatric AI deployment.

papers.title: Interpretable AI model reveals spatial codes of cell recruitment in tissues
papers.abstract: A fully interpretable multi-instance learning framework, SPACER, helps elucidate which molecular signals recruit specific cells to their precise locations by decoding gene-level recruitment rules from spatially resolved transcriptomics data.

papers.title: Untranslated region rewiring defines a novel class of oncogene fusions
papers.abstract: Cerqua et al. identify a previously unrecognized class of oncogene fusions in which native oncogene 5′ untranslated regions (5′ UTRs) are replaced by donor-derived 5′ UTRs. This rewiring of translational control increases expression from intact protein-coding sequences and extends across multiple oncogenes.

papers.title: Macrophage-induced ferritin expression protects pancreatic cancer cells from ferroptosis
papers.abstract: Cheung et al. show that pancreatic cancer cells recruit macrophages that secrete IL-6, which promotes increased expression of the iron-binding protein ferritin in the cancer cells. As a result, the cancer cells become more resistant to ferroptosis, thereby allowing them to survive under conditions of oxidative stress.

papers.title: A systemic circadian nicotinic acid riboside (NaR) signal engages the unfolded protein response and adipogenesis via the prefoldin complex
papers.abstract: Vlassakev et al. show that circadian regulation of circulating nicotinic acid riboside (NaR), driven by the liver clock, engages the unfolded protein response (UPR) and adipogenesis. Rhythmic, but not chronic, NaR exposure regulates CEBPA expression and promotes lipid accumulation, identifying NaR as a systemic circadian signal regulating lipid metabolism.

papers.title: Quantifying the impact of genetic mutations on enhancer dynamics
papers.abstract: Genetic perturbations alter both enhancer activity and gene expression. Das et al. measure enhancer responses to genetic perturbations to identify regulatory programs and sequence grammar that remain hidden from gene expression changes alone.

papers.title: Molecular mechanisms of promoter silencing by transcriptional readthrough
papers.abstract: Shipman et al. propose a model of transcriptional interference to define how transcriptional readthrough leads to stable gene silencing. By dissecting the contributions of antisense transcription, H3K36me3, and DNA methylation, they describe a hierarchical silencing cascade in which transcription initiates local chromatin remodeling and DNA methylation stabilizes the repressed state.

papers.title: Cingulate thrombospondin 4 protects against neuropathic pain and comorbid anxiodepression via interaction with EAAT2
papers.abstract: Liu et al. find that nerve injury-mediated THBS4 downregulation in the ACC impairs THBS4-EAAT2 interaction in astrocytes, leading to extracellular glutamate accumulation and aberrant synaptic plasticity, ultimately exacerbates pain hypersensitivity and aversive emotions, indicating THBS4-mediated neuron-astrocyte crosstalk as a mechanism underlying the neuropathic pain and comorbid anxiodepression.

papers.title: Spatial distribution of blood-brain barrier membrane proteins is controlled by sorting motifs and physiological signals in vivo
papers.abstract: Amick et al. establish a method for measuring polarized protein sorting in brain endothelial cells in vivo. This approach is used to measure the spatial distribution of blood-brain barrier membrane proteins, identify protein-intrinsic motifs that regulate localization, and observe a spatial shift in CD31 distribution between rest and active periods.

Mouse Cutaneous Melanoma Induced by Mutant BRaf Arises from Expansion and Dedifferentiation of Mature Pigmented Melanocytes
Ubiquitin phosphorylation opens a hatch to a code still largely undeciphered
papers.abstract: The discovery of ubiquitin phosphorylation as a mitophagy activator pointed to ubiquitin being at the heart of a broad signalling code.

papers.title: Scaling up measurements of the interactions that build condensates
papers.abstract: Condensate partitioning by mRNA-display (CPmD) enables high-throughput assessment of protein (domain) propensity for condensate formation.

papers.title: Viral dispersal drives changes in population composition
papers.abstract: In an acute viral infection, a small seeding population expands rapidly over several orders of magnitude, then declines. This vast population growth is accompanied by spatial expansion as infection spreads to new anatomical sites within the host. Evolutionary theory predicts that spatially expanding populations experience more extreme stochastic losses of genetic diversity than spatially unstructured populations. To test this prediction in the context of viral dynamics, we evaluated the impact of spatial expansion on viral population genetic structure and assessed how modulators of viral dispersal affected this structure. To this end, we developed a means of implementing the spatial expansion of influenza A virus in cell culture and applied it to a viral population carrying a diverse genetic barcode. Across this simplified cellular landscape, we found that spatial expansion produces a patchwork of distinct viral subpopulations. We then evaluated the consequences for population structure of two modulators of viral dispersal: extracellular viscosity and a common polymorphism in the viral attachment protein. Both physical constraint and viral phenotype altered the extent of genetic bottlenecking and spatial heterogeneity that developed during expansion, indicating that environmental features and viral traits that modulate dispersal also modulate viral population composition, diversity and evolution.
affiliations: Emory University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reversible fixation of microbial cells for targeted genomics
papers.abstract: Phylogeny- or activity-based fluorescent labelling of microorganisms coupled with fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) is a powerful approach to rapidly isolate cells of interest from complex communities for targeted genomics. However, the method has not been widely adopted because standard paraformaldehyde or ethanol fixation procedures hamper nucleic acid recovery and/or long-term sample storage. Here, we present dithiobis(succinimidyl propionate) (DSP) as a reversible fixative for microbial cells that enables fluorescence imaging and DNA extraction and amplification for sequencing. DSP fixation is compatible with widely used fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) approaches and bioorthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging, and can be applied to diverse sample types, where it consistently performed as well as paraformaldehyde. Furthermore, high-quality genomes were obtained from individual and multiple bacterial cells selectively extracted from complex samples using FISH-FACS. Thus, DSP is a dual-use fixative for microbiome imaging and sequencing, improving targeted microbial genomics.
affiliations: School of Environment and Life Sciences, University of Portsmouth, Portsmouth, United Kingdom. (corresponding author)

papers.title: Do LLM Proposers Improve Budgeted Search for Ionizable Lipids?
papers.abstract: Efficient lipid design under limited experimental budgets is a central challenge in computational chemistry and drug discovery. We introduce LEAF (Lipid Evolutionary Adaptive Framework), a matched-budget protocol for testing whether language-model proposers improve combinatorial molecular search relative to classical baselines. The study uses a 30,044-candidate ionizable-lipid space, a frozen Gaussian-process oracle fitted to experimental potency labels, and a separate active-learning surrogate. Four language models evaluated over eight seeds and three splits show no significant improvement over genetic-algorithm or random-search baselines. For Llama 8B, 79.1% of acquisition-selected queries repeat previously evaluated archive members. Removing duplicates reduces the performance gap on some splits but increases proposal cost and can prevent budget exhaustion. Larger models reduce duplication without establishing superiority or equivalence. Exploratory scored prompts and stricter novelty controls yield positive median differences against the genetic algorithm, yet wide intervals and shared-seed dependence preclude stronger conclusions. A validated single-assay reanalysis preserves the chemotype-cold deficit at a smaller numerical scale, and exploratory expected hypervolume improvement does not reverse the result. Follow-up checks address whether proposers genuinely use injected evidence. These checks include a zero-shot leakage probe, rank-only and chain-of-thought-rationale prompts, a score-shuffle perturbation, an evidence-conflict probe, and a genuine reasoning-mode proposer. They show measurable engagement with supplied information without a corresponding performance gain. LEAF isolates proposal quality as the experimental variable and documents a concrete failure mode of zero-shot LLM proposers under controlled budgets.
affiliations: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Shiv Nadar University, Delhi-NCR, India (corresponding author)

papers.title: BioMod: Biological Module Tokenization for Single-Cell Foundation Modeling
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models typically represent cells as flat sequences of individual genes, requiring higher-order biological organization to be inferred implicitly from sparse expression profiles. Similar to the evolution from character-level to semantic tokenization in natural language processing,we hypothesize that cellular states can be more efficiently represented using biologically meaningful intermediate units. Here we present BioMod, a 50-million-parameter single-cell foundation model that introduces biological modules as representation units between genes and cells. BioMod constructs an overlapping vocabulary of 660 biological modules derived from curated pathways and data-driven gene programs, replacing thousands of gene-level inputs with compact module representations. Pretrained on approximately 73 million human cells using high-ratio module masking with an asymmetric decoder, BioMod achieves state-of-the-art performance across cell-type annotation, zero-shot batch integration, perturbation-response prediction and drug-response forecasting while maintaining a compact architecture that enables efficient inference on a single GPU. Module-level analyses further demonstrate that BioMod captures biologically meaningful cellular programs and preserves pathway-level organization.
affiliations: Shenzhen Loop Area Instutite (corresponding author)

papers.title: Apoptotic Cells Promote Tim4+ Macrophage Differentiation Through Direct and Indirect Signaling Pathways
papers.abstract: Tissue macrophages are the primary cells responsible for efficiently clearing apoptotic cells, yet how professional efferocyte populations are established remains unclear. Tim4 marks a subset of macrophages across multiple tissues that are highly efferocytic, but the mechanisms governing Tim4 acquisition are poorly understood. Here, we show that monocyte-derived macrophages progressively differentiate into Tim4 macrophages in homeostatic and pathological settings. We identify a cell-autonomous pathway in which efficient apoptotic cell clearance promotes Tim4 acquisition in macrophages, as combined deficiency of CD11b and MerTK impairs both efferocytosis and Tim4 acquisition. Surprisingly, excessive apoptotic cell burden enhanced Tim4 acquisition independently of these receptors. We demonstrate that serial exposure to apoptotic cells induces a type 2 immune response characterized by expansion of IL-4-producing populations and that IL-4R-STAT6 signaling is sufficient and required to drive Tim4 acquisition. These findings support a model in which Tim4 acquisition in macrophages integrates direct signals associated with apoptotic cell clearance and indirect signals generated by apoptotic cell burden. We propose that these complementary mechanisms enable tissues to dynamically adjust the size and function of the professional efferocyte compartment to meet changing demands for apoptotic cell clearance.
affiliations: The Wistar Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Anti-inflammatory macrophages limit endothelial inflammation and restrict neutrophil recruitment through Gas6/AXL signaling
papers.abstract: Neutrophil extravasation requires coordinated interactions between the endothelium and surrounding cells, including tissue resident macrophages. Macrophages adopt distinct polarization states in the tissue environment, positioning them as regulators of vascular inflammation. However, how these states influence barrier function and neutrophil extravasation remains unclear. Here, we polarized macrophages in the matrix surrounding an endothelial vessel, in a three-dimensional inflammation-on-a-chip model developed only from primary human cells. We found anti-inflammatory macrophages limited endothelial inflammation, reducing ICAM-1 upregulation, maintaining VE-Cadherin expression, halving permeability relative to pro-inflammatory devices, and reducing neutrophil extravasation and migration relative to macrophage-free devices. Secretome profiling identified Gas6, an AXL ligand, as a potential regulator of these effects. Inhibiting AXL increased extravasation in devices with anti-inflammatory macrophages, and soluble Gas6 reduced extravasation in macrophage-free devices, implicating Gas6 as a mediator of this regulation. This indicates macrophages regulate endothelial inflammation and the neutrophil response via Gas6 signaling.
affiliations: University of Colorado Boulder (corresponding author)

papers.title: BCR repertoire analysis and cloning of antibody candidates targeting native and Asp7-isomerized β-amyloid
papers.abstract: Computational approaches are increasingly used to prioritize monoclonal antibody (mAB) candidates from BCR-seq datasets. However, the reliable identification of B cells encoding antibodies against rare antigenic epitopes remains challenging. We employed a repertoire-guided workflow combining antigen-tetramer sorting of B cells from immunized mice, followed by low-input bulk BCR-seq, which yielded informative clonal repertoires. Clustering analysis allowed us to prioritize IGH and IGK clonotypes potentially targeting {beta}-amyloid and the isoAsp7 proteoform (isoD7-A{beta}1-16), implicated in Alzheimer's disease. We observed recurrent IGHV8-12 and IGKV1-117 usage, consistent with canonical mouse anti-A{beta} responses. Focusing on isoD7-A{beta} -associated candidates, we selected fourteen candidate IGH--IGK combinations for recombinant expression including variants containing IGKV8-21, IGKV8-19, IGKV2-112 together with IGHV1-75, IGHV10-1 or IGHV8-12. Several recombinant mABs showed detectable binding activity to isoD7-A{beta}, including a candidate with preferential recognition of isoD7-A{beta}, supporting the feasibility of the approach but underscoring the challenge of accurate chain pairing. These results provide proof of principle that repertoire-guided analysis can prioritize candidate IGH and IGK chains and propose possible heavy-light chain combinations based on their co-representation across samples while experimental testing remains necessary to identify antibodies with preferential recognition of isoD7-A{beta}.
affiliations: Institute of Translational Medicine, Pirogov Russian National Research Medical University, 117513, Moscow, Russia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Fever-range temperature enhances B cells in vitro but is dispensable for the germinal center in vivo
papers.abstract: Fever is a conserved physiological response to immune activation characterized by elevated body temperature. While hyperthermia enhances innate and T cell immunity, its role in shaping the B cell compartment remains poorly defined, despite B cells' role in long-term protection. Understanding how temperature modulates B cell physiology is relevant to vaccine strategies, particularly fever management around immunization. Therefore, we investigated the influence of fever-range thermal changes on humoral immunity. To decipher the direct effects, primary B cells from C57BL/6 mice were stimulated in vitro under mild hyperthermic conditions (~1.5{degrees}C increase). Fever-range temperature enhanced B cell activation, facilitated entry into cell division, and increased antigen presentation to CD4+ T cells, while transcriptomic analysis revealed enrichment of pathways involved in protein synthesis and mitochondrial respiration. To determine whether these intrinsic effects translated into altered humoral immunity in vivo, we developed a novel tunable implant-based system to induce localized, 48-hour hyperthermia around a draining lymph node in awake mice without altering core body temperature. Following subcutaneous NP-OVA/alum immunization, localized hyperthermia localized hyperthermia did not enhance antigen-specific germinal center B cell expansion, antibody titers or IgG affinity on day 9. Moreover, heating during priming did not affect the recall humoral response after a booster on day 21. Thus, fever-range temperature directly modulates murine B cell function in vitro but does not enhance humoral immunity in vivo, indicating that the biological consequences of intrinsic B cell thermosensitivity depend on its integration within the multicellular and inflammatory signals shaping germinal center responses.
affiliations: Université Paris Cité and Université Sorbonne Paris Nord, INSERM, LVTS, F-75018 Paris, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: Spatiotemporal analysis of sporozoite maturation and infectivity
papers.abstract: Plasmodium sporozoites must undergo tightly regulated developmental transitions to become infectious and be successfully transmitted from the mosquito vector to a mammalian host. While transcriptomic studies have revealed stage-specific changes across sporozoite populations, the functional consequences of these transitions remain unclear. Here, using P. berghei, we characterised over time the infectivity of sporozoite forms collected from the midgut, haemolymph, salivary glands and saliva. We show that salivary gland invasion is required but not sufficient for sporozoite optimal infectivity, with the acquisition of hepatocyte cell traversal and invasion progressively increasing until a plateau from 18 days post-infection onwards. Using a stage-specific fluorescent reporter to track maturation, we found that fluorescence increased over time and correlated with infectivity within each compartment, yet maximal infectivity was reached only in salivary gland sporozoites. Notably, our data suggest that salivated sporozoites, the natural transmission form, exhibit enhanced infectivity relative to gland-resident forms both in vitro and in vivo early after salivary gland invasion. This difference decreases following optimal maturation inside the glands over time. These observations show a crescent gradient of sporozoite maturation and infectiveness from the midgut to the saliva, in which pre-salivary gland forms retain limited infectivity but do not reach the competence of mature salivary gland-associated parasites.

papers.title: Supplementation with a Limosilactobacillus fermentum K73 synbiotic modulates gut microbiota function and behavior in gnotobiotic mice transplanted with microbiota from children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder
papers.abstract: Gut dysbiosis has been implicated in numerous pathological conditions, including neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. Recently, dietary interventions targeted at restoring microbial balance have therefore gained attention as potential therapeutic strategies. We recently demonstrated that an encapsulated synbiotic containing high-oleic palm oil and Limosilactobacillus fermentum K73 can modulate the metabolic activity and composition of human-derived gut microbiota in an in vitro batch bioreactor. Here, we extended this work through an in vivo supplementation pilot study using gnotobiotic mice colonized with gut microbiota from Colombian pediatric patients diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) or age-matched neurotypical (NT) donors. Behavioral assessments and analyses of gut microbiota composition and function were performed before and after synbiotic supplementation. First, we found that the gut microbiota from Colombian ASD patients exhibited significantly reduced richness relative to NT donors, consistent with reports from other geographical regions, and displayed distinct compositional features unique to this population. Humanization of the gnotobiotic mice with this donor microbiota was successful, with murine gut communities reflecting features of their corresponding donor microbiota. Notably, synbiotic supplementation induced significant increases in the abundance of beneficial taxa and the production of short chain fatty acids that were more pronounced in mice colonized with ASD-derived microbiota, with concurrent behavioral changes associated with beneficial modulation of gut microbiota. Overall, we provide evidence that supports synbiotic supplementation as a viable strategy to positively modulate gut microbiome in conditions of dysbiosis. Our study also expands the body of knowledge of gut microbiome to understudied populations such as Latin America.
affiliations: University of Florida (corresponding author)

papers.title: VPS34 regulation in pulmonary arterial vascular smooth muscle cells in pulmonary hypertension
papers.abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is characterized by the hyperproliferative phenotype of pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cells (PAVSMCs) and extensive extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. Vacuolar protein sorting 34 (VPS34), a Class III Phosphatidylinositol-3 Kinase (PI3K), regulates cell proliferation, but its specific function in pulmonary vascular remodeling remains poorly understood. We aim to determine the role of VPS34 activation and regulation in PAVSMC proliferation, matrix deposition, and the progression of PAH. First, we found a marked decrease in the inhibitory phosphorylation of VPS34 at Ser164 (P-S164-VPS34), indicative of constitutive VPS34 activation, in remodeled pulmonary arteries (PAs) from human PAH patients and male mice exposed to Sugen/Hypoxia (SuHx). In human PAH PAVSMCs, siRNA-mediated knockdown of VPS34 or pharmacological inhibition via the selective inhibitor SAR405 significantly blunted cell proliferation and reduced the production of fibronectin, a major component of the remodeled ECM. Mechanistically, we found that Akt activation in PAH PAVSMCs promotes VPS34 activation; Protein Phosphatase 1 Catalytic Subunit Alpha is a potential effector in VPS34 activation; and active VPS34 led to the activation of the mTOR/S6 signaling pathway with tuberous sclerosis complex 2 downregulation. Finally, in vivo treatment with SAR405 attenuated right ventricular systolic pressure, right ventricular hypertrophy, and pulmonary vascular remodeling in SuHx mice, while concurrently decreasing vascular fibronectin deposition. Our study demonstrates that VPS34 activation, driven by an Akt-mediated loss of the inhibitory P-S164, is crucial in PAVSMC proliferation and fibrotic vascular remodeling in PAH. Targeting the VPS34 axis represents a promising anti-remodeling therapeutic strategy for the treatment of PAH. Keywords: Pulmonary arterial hypertension, vacuolar protein sorting 34, pulmonary vascular remodeling, pulmonary arterial vascular smooth muscle
affiliations: School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences, Binghamton University, Johnson City, NY, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: A single epigenetic repressor controls opposing developmental tempos in human neural and cranial neural crest lineages
papers.abstract: The precise timing of lineage specification is essential for embryonic development, yet the epigenetic mechanisms enforcing human developmental tempo remain poorly understood. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in ZNF462 cause Weiss-Kruszka syndrome (WKS), a pleiotropic disorder characterized by neurodevelopmental delays and craniofacial dysmorphisms. Here, we show that ZNF462 acts as an epigenetic gatekeeper that coordinates human developmental tempo across divergent lineages by repressing cell lineage-specific gene enhancers. In human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), ZNF462 maintains self-renewal by recruiting the G9A/GLP histone methyltransferase complex to silence primate-specific retrotransposon-derived enhancers. Upon neural lineage commitment, ZNF462 redirects to hominoid-specific LTR5_Hs elements and divergent lineage-specific enhancer programs, where its loss produces opposing kinetics. In neural progenitor cells (NPCs), ZNF462 enforces G9A/GLP-dependent repression of ZIC-driven neural enhancers, and loss of this repression traps NPCs in a progenitor state, slowing cortical neurogenesis without impairing terminal neurogenic capacity. In neural crest cells (NCCs), ZNF462 targets repressive chromatin to silence SOX9 family-driven enhancers. Here, ZNF462 haploinsufficiency triggers premature activation of definitive NCC specifiers, accelerating differentiation. These findings establish that a single repressor can simultaneously decelerate and accelerate developmental tempo by gating lineage-specific enhancers, placing Weiss-Kruszka syndrome into the emerging class of human developmental timing disorders.
affiliations: Department of Cancer Biology, Keck School of Medicine, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, 90033, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Single-cell variant landscape of the human mitochondrial genome reveals cell type-specific functions and disease mechanisms
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) heteroplasmy is a significant source of cellular genetic diversity and can cause disease yet its distribution and functional importance across different human cell types are poorly understood. Here we present scMOCHA (Single-Cell Mitochondrial Omics for Cellular Heteroplasmy Analysis), a scalable computational framework that resolves highconfidence, single-cell resolution mtDNA heteroplasmy directly from standard single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. Using this tool to interrogate publicly available scRNA-seq datasets from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and bone marrow (BM) uncovered the single-cell landscape of mtDNA single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) and heteroplasmy across ages in human hematopoietic cell types. PBMCs and BM share many inherited homoplasmic and highly heteroplasmic SNVs, whereas somatic SNVs are tissue- and cell type-specific and distributed across the mtDNA genome, suggesting that they arise largely stochastically. mtDNA replication error is a dominant force shaping homoplasmic variants, while oxidative stress potentially drives a significant portion of heteroplasmic and somatic mutations. Importantly, we discover previously unknown cell type-specific and human disease-associated mtDNA SNVs. By coupling mtDNA genotypes with matched single-cell nuclear transcriptomes and structural modeling, we uncover potential molecular mechanisms by which disease-associated mtDNA SNVs impact cellular processes such as inflammation and contribute to disease. Together, these findings define the single-cell variant landscape of the human mitochondrial genome and reveal previously unrecognized lineage- and disease-associated patterns of mtDNA variation in the human hematopoietic system.
affiliations: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: Convergent genome evolution reveals shared routes to salt tolerance in flowering plants
papers.abstract: Transitions to saline environments pose formidable challenges to plants, yet halophytism has evolved independently across many flowering plant lineages. We assembled a comparative angiosperm gene catalog of ~10 million protein-coding genes from 232 genomes spanning 55 families, with similar representation of halophytes and salt-sensitive relatives, to identify convergent genomic signatures of halophytism. Halophytes show remarkable convergence with recurrent genomic trends in salt-response genes, including lower copy numbers, higher basal expression, more constrained expression variation, distinct evolutionary rates, and independent positive selection on select genes at the same amino acid sites across multiple halophyte lineages. Crops and their wild halophytic relatives differ in gene family evolution, particularly in stress-response pathways. These findings reveal repeatedly tested evolutionary routes to halophytism and establish a genomic foundation for translating convergent adaptations into salt-tolerant crops.
affiliations: Louisiana State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mid-Infrared Photothermal Imaging Unveils Altered Stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD) Activity in Ovarian Cancer Cells
papers.abstract: Stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD)-catalyzed fatty acid desaturation plays a key role in cancer metabolism reprogramming. While existing approaches enable quantification of SCD expression, directly monitoring in situ SCD enzymatic activity alterations remains challenging. Here, we report a strategy to measure intracellular SCD activity alterations and SCD product distributions by mid-infrared photothermal (MIP) imaging. Fully deuterated palmitic acid (PA-d31) is repurposed here as a chemical probe to report the SCD activity via a new peak at 2246 cm-1, corresponding to the stretching of D-C=C-D bonds in the SCD product. The MIP intensity ratio between the product-associated signal and the total C-D signal defines the apparent SCD activity index. By visualization of SCD-catalyzed metabolic conversion, our approach reveals altered SCD activity in cisplatin-treated ovarian cancer cells, ovarian cancer stem cells and cells fed with oleic acid. Non-uniform distributions of the SCD product are also observed. These results establish bio-orthogonal MIP microscopy as a platform for studying intracellular enzymatic reactions in living systems.
affiliations: Boston University (corresponding author)

papers.title: LOCALE: Local-Alignment Embeddings for Noise-Robust DNA Search at Scale
papers.abstract: Searching petabase-scale repositories of raw sequencing data such as the NIH Sequence Read Archive (SRA) could unlock biological insights that remain inaccessible. Existing sequence-search methods either do not scale well or rely on exact $k$-mer matching that is brittle to genomic variation, which is high both within and across species and is further compounded by sequencing error. We recast sequence search as dense retrieval: we learn sequence embeddings whose inner-product similarity ranks locally aligned sequences above unaligned ones. We introduce LOCALE, an encoder trained with an InfoNCE objective on biologically informed augmentations: overlapping crops of parent sequences corrupted with substitutions, insertions, and deletions. This training recipe, rather than a specialized architecture, consistently induces variation-robust representations across four encoders spanning three tokenization schemes, improving Recall@$R_q$ by 7--39 points at 10% genomic variation. On a 50-accession SRA benchmark LOCALE retains 63.2% Recall@$R_q$ at 10% variation while existing k-mer indexes and DNA embedding methods fall below 35%, and on the full 4,571-accession MetaGraph benchmark (296 Gbp, 2.06 billion vectors) it achieves 4.5x the AUPRC of MetaGraph, the state-of-the-art k-mer index, with a single-node GPU IVF-PQ index retaining a 3.6x advantage at MetaGraph's query latency. Our encoder and training strategy generalize to real biological variance: on a cross-genotype Hepatitis B task, querying reads from one genotype against accessions of another with >8% natural divergence, LOCALE reaches 0.813 Recall@R_q versus 0.518 for MetaGraph.
affiliations: University of Maryland (corresponding author)

papers.title: AlphaFold3 and Intrinsically Disordered Proteins: Reliable Monomer Prediction, Unpredictable Multimer Performance
papers.abstract: AlphaFold3 represents a major advance in protein structure prediction, yet its performance on intrinsically disordered proteins remains uncharacterized. We present the first systematic evaluation of AF3 on disordered systems, revealing a striking dichotomy. For monomers, AF3's pLDDT scores reliably predict disorder (MCC: 0.693), matching AlphaFold2 and rivaling dedicated predictors. This consistency across fundamentally different architectures confirms that disorder prediction emerges from training data, not model design. For multimers, the picture grows complex. Despite comparable aggregate performance (mean DockQ: 0.563 vs 0.571), AF3 and AF2 achieve these results through fundamentally different mechanisms. Conventional structural features explain 58% of AF2's variance but only 42% of AF3's. Users cannot predict when AF3 will succeed or fail from interface properties alone. On disorder-to-order transitions (MFIB benchmark), both models perform equally well, successfully predicting final folded states. Yet seed variance analysis reveals AF3's failures are deterministic: the model converges to identical structures across independent runs, whether correct or incorrect, indicating rigid structural priors override available information. Our findings establish AF3 as reliable for the prediction of monomer disorder but unpredictable for multimers. Architectural innovation alone cannot overcome training data bias. Progress demands disorder-enriched datasets and ensemble sampling, not merely novel architectures.
affiliations: University of South Florida (corresponding author)

papers.title: Imputing relative abundances via Gaussian random fields
papers.abstract: Longitudinal studies with human participants frequently face the challenge of missing samples, which lead to incomplete trajectories of participant biomarkers and a reduction in data size. Existing approaches focus on single-variable imputation or model features one at a time, while neural networks typically require a large number of parameters and substantial training data. To address these challenges, we present an explainable model for multiple imputation of compositional samples based on a Gaussian random field (GRF). The model is specifically designed for longitudinal data: it incorporates participant-specific information and accounts for both temporal dependence across repeated observations and within-sample correlations, while using a moderate number of parameters. By coupling the GRF with sparse activation functions, the framework outputs sum-constrained compositions and explicitly models zero inflation. Under the Aitchison and Jensen--Shannon distances, our framework achieves imputation accuracy comparable to that of an observation-carrying baseline, while overcoming its static nature by modeling temporal trajectories and multivariate correlations. The resulting multiple imputations allow us to reconstruct complete datasets for downstream analysis and uncertainty quantification. We demonstrate the practical utility of our framework on gut microbiome datasets, restoring incomplete time series and achieving a balanced accuracy of 0.72 in predicting food allergy in infants (sensitivity 0.8) and of 0.64 in forecasting postpartum depression.
affiliations: Uppsala University, Science for Life Laboratory (corresponding author)

papers.title: Leptin receptor deficiency suppresses gastric tumorigenesis by limiting stromal activation and tumor microenvironment development.
papers.abstract: Leptin receptor (LEPR) signaling has been implicated in multiple malignancies; however, its role in gastric tumors remains poorly defined. We previously demonstrated that mice with gastrointestinal epithelial cell-specific deletion of suppressor of cytokine signaling 3 (SOCS3 cKO), a negative feedback regulator of LEPR signaling, develop gastric tumors due to aberrant leptin production and LEPR activation. Here, we demonstrate that concurrent deletion of both Socs3 and Lepr (double knockout; DKO) under the same promoter substantially suppresses gastric tumorigenesis and markedly prolonged survival. Whereas SOCS3 cKO mice exhibited early stromal activation, increased TGF-{beta}1 production, accumulation of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and collagen deposition, these tumor-promoting alterations were substantially attenuated in DKO mice. Additionally, DKO mice showed reduced inflammatory cytokine and chemokine signaling, decreased the accumulation of Gr-1+CD11b+ myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and reduced LEPR and TGF-{beta} signaling. Analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas stomach adenocarcinoma cohort revealed high LEPR expression in the chromosomal instability and genomically stable subtypes, correlating with poor prognosis. Moreover, LEPR expression was mutually exclusive with CLDN18 and ERBB2, two major therapeutic biomarkers, and positively correlated with a CAF-related transcriptional signature. Our findings identify LEPR signaling in epithelial cells as a key driver of gastric tumorigenesis through promotion of stromal activation and tumor microenvironment development. They further highlight LEPR as a promising therapeutic target for patients with gastric cancer who are unlikely to benefit from current ERBB2/HER2- or CLDN18-directed therapies.
affiliations: Fujita Health University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Framework for Comparing Mouse Neoantigen Immunogenicity
papers.abstract: Cytotoxic CD8+ T cell responses targeting tumor neoantigens are critical for immunotherapy efficacy and are widely studied across different preclinical mouse tumor models. Defined neoantigens are commonly identified or introduced into mouse tumors to enable tracking of tumor-specific T cell responses. However, these neoantigens differ in immunogenicity and variation in their composition may produce immune phenotypes that are mistakenly attributed to tumor-intrinsic mechanisms and complicate comparison across studies. Here, we sought to create a framework for comparing neoantigen immunogenicity by determining relative peptide-major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) affinity (KD) and stability (Koff) and in vivo neoantigen-targeted vaccine responses for 25 commonly used mouse tumor-derived and model neoantigens. We found that in silico prediction of pMHC affinity moderately stratified strong versus weak in vivo immunogenicity but could not accurately predict rank order; experimental measurements of affinity did not improve prediction. In contrast, experimental measurement of pMHC stability closely correlated with the relative magnitude of vaccine responses demonstrating strong predictive value. Thus, we report the relative stability of commonly used neoantigens as a resource and provide a simple method to benchmark novel neoantigens against this library. This tool allows contextualization of the level of immunogenicity of newly identified neoantigens and aids in comparative interpretation of tumor-immune phenotypes across studies.
affiliations: Oregon Health & Science University (corresponding author)

papers.title: AT1R-Selective Negative Allosteric Modulator Targeting the Epitope for Pathogenic Autoantibody Activation
papers.abstract: A major therapeutic strategy for managing cardiovascular and renal diseases is the use of angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs). These drugs block both pathogenic and physiological signaling by the angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) by preventing angiotensin II (AngII) binding to orthosteric pocket in transmembrane portion of AT1R. However, in many autoimmune diseases, AT1R activation is chronically driven by pathogenic autoantibody binding to a distinct extracellular surface located allosteric site. Currently, there are no allosteric inhibitors of AT1R available to mechanistically prevent the autoantibodies and preserve the orthosteric hormonal functions of AngII. Here, we report the structure-guided hit-to-lead optimization of TP1, a first-in-class AT1R allosteric chemotype and negative allosteric modulator (NAM) with improved potency and drug-like properties. Computational docking and site-directed mutagenesis identified a TP1 binding mode that is distinct from the orthosteric-site binding of ARBs and AngII. Synthetically pure TP1 significantly reduced the capacity of AT1R to bind AngII without affecting AngII binding to AT2R, demonstrating an AT1R selective effect. TP1 reduced AngII-induced calcium signaling and migration in AT1R-expressing cells, arterial contraction, and increases in blood pressure in AngII-infused mice, demonstrating its activity as a NAM. Crucially, TP1 blocked binding of pathogenic autoantibodies to AT1R-expressing cells from the serum of patients with preeclampsia and dilated cardiomyopathy, a function distinct from ARBs. Together, these findings establish TP1 as a proof-of-concept, AT1R-selective NAM chemotype with therapeutic potential for AT1R autoantibody-driven conditions such as preeclampsia, where ARBs are strictly contraindicated. Developing AT1R-targeted NAM antihypertensive drugs may offer therapeutic advantages over ARBs and expand the pharmacological toolkit for this important CVD receptor. Key words: AT1R, AngII, AT1R-AAb, NAM, Allosteric ligand, GPCR, blood pressure, pharmacokinetics, antihypertensives
affiliations: Cleveland Clinic Lerner College of Medicine at Case Western Reserve University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Microbial Dynamics Across Commercial Spaceflights of Varying Duration
papers.abstract: Spaceflight introduces environmental stressors that can alter human microbiomes and immune responses. We analyzed 259 and 17 biospecimens for microbiome and single-cell studies from n=6 astronauts across two commercial ISS missions: Axiom 2 (10-day mission) and Axiom 3 (21-day mission). Samples included saliva, stool, urine, and body swabs from 10 anatomical sites, profiled via 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene amplicon sequencing. Gut and oral microbiomes remained stable, while skin-associated communities exhibited transient diversity shifts post-flight. Taxonomic analysis revealed individual and site-specific patterns, as well as from the spaceflight/ISS environment. Cytokine profiling from single-cell data indicated immune activation, with IL-32 and IL-16 transcripts elevated in Axiom 2 and Axiom 3. Microbiome and interleukin correlation analyses found 14 significant associations in Axiom 2 data. These findings provide an integrated view of microbiome individuality. Our study represents a descriptive comparison of two missions, informing strategies for crew health on future long-duration missions.
affiliations: Human Genome Sequencing Center, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, TX, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Direct 3D isolation in gelatin methacryloyl microbeads versus conventional 2D isolation and culture: a trade-off between mesenchymal stromal cell purity and niche-associated transcriptional profiles
papers.abstract: Bone-marrow mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) isolation typically couples plastic-adherence selection to planar expansion. Therefore, the recovered cells may reflect culture adaptation as much as native stromal biology. Direct isolation within a three-dimensional matrix could reduce planar selection, but its effects on cellular recovery, composition and MSC transcriptional profiles remain insufficiently resolved. We therefore developed a gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) workflow progressing from bulk hydrogels to medium-surrounded GelMA microbeads (GMBs) and compared 3D-derived cells with conventional 2D cultures. Qualitative live/dead staining with calcein acetoxymethyl ester (CAM) and propidium iodide (PI) and 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) imaging established cellular activity in both GelMA formats. In bulk GelMA cultures from four human donors, CD73-, CD90- and CD105-associated flow-cytometric readouts did not increase from day 7 to day 21. At day 21, the combined marker readout was numerically higher in donor-matched 2D cultures than in bulk 3D cultures, which retained heterogeneous marker-defined populations. GMBs enabled cell recovery and flow-cytometric characterization and motivated an exploratory one-donor single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis. The final dataset contained 37,784 cells across four samples and 23 annotated populations. MSC-focused re-embedding resolved 13,175 cells into two 3D and four 2D clusters. A pooled comparison identified 4,840 differentially expressed genes (DEGs, false discovery rate [FDR]<0.01, |log2FC|[≥]1), indicating a broad method-associated expression shift. The 3D C1 cluster combined progenitor-, extracellular-matrix-, adhesion-, cytokine-, hypoxia/glycolysis- and predicted-interaction-associated programmes, whereas 2D clusters showed mitochondrial, cytoskeletal/mechanoadaptive and proliferative programmes. Thus, 2D culture yielded a more strongly represented and compositionally purer MSC compartment, while 3D isolation contained rare MSC clusters with niche-associated transcriptional profiles within a heterogeneous marrow environment. These findings support a testable native-associated tendency for 3D, but donor replication, matched recovery and direct native-reference mapping are required before inferring greater in-vivo similarity or functional superiority.
affiliations: Leibniz University Hannover (corresponding author)

papers.title: Benchmarked sequencing methods reveal hidden mosaic variation in the human brain
papers.abstract: Mosaic variants (MVs) record cellular lineages, but their recovery is strongly method-dependent. Here, we benchmarked four duplex sequencing methods alongside bulk and single-neuron genome sequencing in matched human brain tissue. The methods differed in genome representation, MV yield and mutational profiles, with limited caller-level concordance. However, read-level interrogation revealed substantially greater cross-method molecular support. To systematically recover this evidence, we developed Read-level Integration for Variant Evidence Recovery (RIVER), expanding the pool of cross-method-supported candidates by approximately two orders of magnitude relative to caller-level overlap. Orthogonal sequencing at ~10,000x across brain and peripheral tissues validated approximately half of the tested RIVER-rescued candidates. MVs recovered from a single brain region resolved broadly distributed and regionally restricted clones and provided lineage information among individual neurons. These findings show that RIVER substantially expands the pool of endogenous lineage markers available to investigate human development, aging, disease-associated mosaicism and clonal evolution.
affiliations: Department of Neurosciences, School of Medicine, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA 92093, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: A telomere-to-telomere genome of Holstein cattle resolves chromosome-end architecture and the genetic basis of telomere length
papers.abstract: Telomeres safeguard chromosome-end integrity, yet population-scale dissection of telomere-length genetics has been largely restricted to humans. Here, we report a 3.01-Gb telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome of Holstein cattle that resolves repeat-rich chromosome ends and centromeres and enables telomere-length quantification at single-chromosome-end resolution. Holstein chromosome ends show marked telomere-length asymmetry and end-specific variation in telomere variant repeats, subtelomeric tandem repeats, GC/CpG composition, and DNA methylation. Using sequencing-depth-corrected telomere-length phenotypes from 9,591 cows, teloGWAS identifies major loci encompassing RTEL1, CTC1, and TERT, while multi-tissue eQTL, sQTL, TWAS, and co-expression analyses prioritize CTC1 and implicate DNA replication, DNA repair, and stress-response networks. Together, these findings extend population-scale telomere genetics beyond humans and establish a sequence-resolved framework for chromosome-end biology and telomere-informed livestock genomics.
affiliations: Key Laboratory of Animal Genetics, Breeding and Reproduction of Shaanxi Province, College of Animal Science and Technology, Northwest A&F University, Yangling, (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pocket-Conditioned Generation and Down-Selection of Non-Oxime Reactivators
papers.abstract: Acetylcholinesterase reactivation is a structure-constrained design problem in which chemical plausibility, access to central nervous system, pocket compatibility, and reactivation geometry must be considered together. We report a computational workflow for generating and down-selecting candidate non-oxime reactivators in the paraoxon-inhibited human acetylcholinesterase pocket. For generating the candidates, the first-round utilitezed pocket-conditioned DrugFlow, but due to solubility issues, the second-round candidates were output form FlexFlow, DrugFlow-OOD, DrugFlow preference alignment, and pocket-specified BoltzMol-1. A property-guided DrugDiff output provided a protein-unconditioned baseline. Although 93.9% of the DrugDiff subset passed Lipinski criteria for druglikeness, its median synthetic accessibility (SA) score signalled that it was difficult to synthesize compared against other generative approaches. A strict predicted blood-brain barrier and solubility gate retained 31.0% of Base DrugFlow, 61.0% of FlexFlow, 27.5% of DrugFlow-OOD, 3.8% of DrugFlow-PA, and 35.1% of BoltzMol-1. The second-round top-ten lists had lower SA scores and higher quantitative estimate of drug-likeness (QED) values than the DrugDiff shortlist, while DrugDiff had fewer aggregate heuristic violations. This work compares the best performing generative drug discovery models with suggested down sleection approaches for human acetylcholinesterase reactivation.
affiliations: Johns Hopkins Applied Physic Laboratory (corresponding author)

papers.title: Matrix-modulated Air-liquid Interface Microenvironments Reveal Architectural Control of Lung Tumor Phenotypes
papers.abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma evolves within a highly structured microenvironment shaped by air exposure, basement-membrane ligands and three-dimensional (3D) organization, yet standard in vitro models capture only fragments of this architecture.
