papers.title: Circadian phase alignment promotes survival under predictive oxidative stress
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks are endogenous time-keeping mechanisms that continue to oscillate with a period that approximates 24 h in the absence of cyclic environmental cues. This free-running period (FRP) varies from species to species and can vary within species across latitudinal clines. Because natural environments provide daily cues that reset circadian clocks to exactly 24 h, the importance of the FRP length is unclear. Using the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus we show that the FRP length alters the alignment of a biological process with an environmental reference, known as phase angle of entrainment, across seasonal photoperiods, thereby repositioning stress response programs relative to the external environment. This phase relationship affects the overall fitness of the organism: strains that position stress-response programs to peak at the time at which the stressor peaks outcompete their early- or late-peaking counterparts. Our results suggest that the FRP length is selected for its ability to adjust the phase angle of entrainment across seasonal photoperiods: the wild-type FRP length was uniquely plastic in its ability to adjust stress-response programs to coincide with the stressor in all photoperiod conditions.
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (corresponding author)

papers.title: Isoindole-benzohydrazide derivative potentiates colistin activity to overcome resistance conferred by MCR-1 variants in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Polymyxin antibiotic resistance mediated by the mobilized colistin resistance (MCR) enzyme threatens the last-resort treatment of deadly multidrug-resistant pathogens, including Acinetobacter baumannii, and calls for urgent mitigation efforts. We used a multifaceted approach involving computational and wet-lab techniques to identify an isoindole-benzohydrazide derivative, JNAL-042, which potentiates colistin activity in an Escherichia coli MCR-resistance phenotype screening model. JNAL-042 lacked intrinsic antibiotic activity but potentiated that of polymyxin antibiotics at 12-24 mug/ml, as demonstrated by bacterial growth susceptibility screens. Cell viability counts and time-kill assays corroborated these findings, demonstrating complete abolition of MCR-mediated resistance by the antibiotic-adjuvant combination at concentrations mirroring those of empty vector controls. Post-induction treatment with this combination similarly prevented the propagation of the resistance phenotype, albeit at a higher antibiotic dose. This landmark study presents JNAL-042 as a promising antibiotic adjuvant to combat MCR-mediated resistance and offers a viable solution to preserve last-resort polymyxin antibiotics.
affiliations: Miami University (corresponding author)

papers.title: From dynamic transcripts to stable proteins: multi-omics revealed regulatory buffering of Candidatus Accumulibacter under cyclic conditions
papers.abstract: Enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR) relies on polyphosphate-accumulating organisms that experience dynamic fluctuations in redox conditions and substrate availability. How these organisms regulate metabolism across molecular layers under cyclic operation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated molecular regulation in a long-term, stable aerobic granular sludge system dominated by Candidatus Accumulibacter. We combined metagenomics, time-resolved metatranscriptomics, and matched metaproteomics across three consecutive operational cycles. Genome-resolved metagenomics revealed an Accumulibacter-dominated community encoding canonical EBPR functions. Time-resolved metatranscriptomics revealed extensive and reproducible transcriptional dynamics affecting hundreds of genes. These dynamics did not align with discrete EBPR phases or instantaneous environmental transitions, but instead unfolded gradually over the cycle. Despite pronounced transcript-level heterogeneity, aggregation at the functional level revealed strong consolidation, with only a limited number of KEGG orthologs exhibiting coherent temporal regulation. Quantitative metaproteomics revealed a stable proteome across EBPR cycles, with no individual proteins or functional categories showing significant differential abundance despite direct transcript-protein mapping and time-matched sampling. This indicated that transcriptional dynamics did not translate into measurable changes in protein pool size on the time scale of individual cycles, consistent with slow, growth-coupled proteome turnover relative to cycle duration. Together, these results support a hierarchical model of regulation in Candidatus Accumulibacter, in which dynamic transcriptional responses are buffered at both the functional and protein levels. This organization provides a plausible basis for stable EBPR performance under predictable cyclic operation and demonstrates how time-resolved multi-omics can be used to resolve regulatory dynamics across molecular layers in engineered microbial ecosystems.
affiliations: Laboratory for Environmental Biotechnology, Ecole Polytechnique Federale de Lausanne (EPFL) (corresponding author)

papers.title: High temperature ligation enables in vitro assembly of eukaryotic genes
papers.abstract: Our ability to efficiently construct synthetic DNA products is essential to studying and engineering biology. There is an abundance of widely adopted DNA assembly technologies suitable for generating synthetic constructs from diverse DNA inputs, but these techniques suffer from low specificity of connection during assembly, which decreases the accuracy, efficiency, and throughput of construction. Here we propose a broadly applicable paradigm for DNA assembly, High Temperature (HighT) assembly, that lowers misconnection rates by ligating complementary single strand DNA overhangs at reaction temperatures significantly higher than their predicted melting temperatures. By expanding the concept of melting temperature to demarcate smaller association fractions of DNA duplexes, we characterize HighT and demonstrate 40 percentage points increase in accuracy, and 4 orders of magnitude increase in yield of transformants when applying the technique to conventional assembly technologies. HighT is then applied to develop cloning pipelines for the development of efficient assembly-to-integration protocols, the construction of specific low-abundance isoforms of medically relevant proteins from human gDNA and oligos, and the de novo construction of a 10 kb, GC rich genomic region from the functionally extinct Northern White Rhinoceros created entirely in vitro.
affiliations: California Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Release of BEC-1 from CED-9 stimulates lysosome tubulation in C. elegans by engaging Class III PI3K complex I
papers.abstract: The anti-apoptotic protein CED-9 and the autophagy protein BEC-1 have been linked to autophagy regulation, but how their interaction modulates this process is not fully understood. Here, we find that the physical dissociation of BEC-1 from CED-9 influences lysosomal morphology in addition to autophagic activity in Caenorhabditis elegans. We present evidence that when autophagy is stimulated via dietary restriction, BEC-1 is released from CED-9 and assembles with VPS-34 and other members of the PI3K complex I to promote PI3P enrichment at lysosomal membranes and subsequent membrane tubulation. Mutation of two hydrophobic amino acids within a predicted BH-3 like motif of BEC-1 is sufficient to disrupt its interaction with CED-9, thereby constitutively inducing lysosomal tubulation and increasing autophagic cargo turnover. This phenotype is dependent on VPS-34 activity, linking the CED-9/BEC-1 dissociation to PI3K-dependent lysosomal remodeling. Collectively, our work identifies the CED-9/BEC-1 interaction as a molecular switch that governs apoptosis, autophagy, and lysosomal morphology.
affiliations: Louisiana State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Single-Cell Proteo-Transcriptomic Profiling Uncovers Post-Translational Regulatory Layers in Human Hematopoiesis
papers.abstract: Background: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) have the unique ability to produce all mature cell types in the blood and understanding the mechanisms governing their differentiation and renewal is a driving question in stem cell biology. While single-cell RNA sequencing has transformed our view of human hematopoiesis, mRNA abundance represents an incomplete proxy for functional cell states. Here, we apply single-cell multimodal profiling to simultaneously measure 280 surface and intracellular protein targets alongside whole transcriptomes within individual adult human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. Results: By directly coupling modalities within single cells, we show that protein-RNA correlations peak dynamically in transitioning intermediate progenitors across lineages, consistent with pervasive post-transcriptional mechanics underlying lineage choice. Furthermore, key transcription factor proteins maintain multilineage co-expression longer into commitment than their transcripts, demarcating a possible window of fate decision reversibility. Moreover, low and flat CTNNB1 mRNA levels mask late-erythroid {beta}-catenin protein enrichment, apparently pairing with E-cadherin expression and suggesting post-translational stabilization at the cell membrane. Conclusions: This dataset enables the observation of translational dynamics and RNA-protein relationships throughout the differentiation landscape at an unprecedented level of granularity. Together, our findings demonstrate that transcriptomics alone misses fundamental regulatory programs, establishing single-cell proteo-transcriptomics as a powerful tool for decoding human stem cell fate.
affiliations: University of Cambridge (corresponding author)

papers.title: Spatial proteomics identifies altered thick ascending limb cells as drivers of kidney disease through uromodulin retention
papers.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is increasingly prevalent and is a leading cause of mortality. Recent transcriptomic studies have identified the persistence of injury-induced renal tubular epithelial cell states, yet the cell populations that drive CKD remain unresolved. Uromodulin (UMOD) is the most abundant urinary secreted protein expressed exclusively in thick ascending limb (TAL) epithelial cells in the kidney. UMOD is strongly associated with CKD risk in genome-wide association studies, suggesting a broader, yet unexplored role of UMOD and TAL cells in CKD pathogenesis. Here, using spatial proteomics, we identified an injury-induced TAL cell state marked by intracellular UMOD accumulation. Spatially resolved multimodal integration revealed that UMOD accumulation occurred without transcriptional upregulation. Impaired urinary UMOD secretion further supported pathological intracellular retention. These altered TAL cells with UMOD retention exhibited inflammatory signaling, formed profibrotic niches enriched with M2-like macrophages across renal compartments, and were associated with CKD progression in multiple experimental models. Reducing the burden of UMOD retention diminished altered TAL cells and their profibrotic microenvironments, and attenuated CKD development. A similar altered TAL state was identified in human kidney disease and was associated with worse kidney function. Together, we identify pathological UMOD retention and altered TAL cells as key drivers of CKD development and potential therapeutic targets. This study also highlights that protein-level alterations can redefine disease-associated cell states beyond transcript profiling.
affiliations: Indiana University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Developmental rewiring of EHMT1 function during human cortical neurogenesis
papers.abstract: Ubiquitously expressed chromatin regulators orchestrate cell-type-specific gene expression programs, yet how they acquire distinct regulatory functions during development remains fundamentally unresolved. Using temporally controlled protein depletion during human cortical neurogenesis in vitro, we show that the autism-associated histone methyltransferase EHMT1 is developmentally repurposed from epiblast to cortical neurons. Broadly expressed zinc finger proteins recruit EHMT1 to distinct cis-regulatory elements within changing chromatin landscapes associated with lineage-specific transcription factor activity, with extensive remodeling of EHMT1 enhancer occupancy during neural induction dependent on ZNF462. This genomic rewiring is accompanied by a fundamental shift from restraining premature developmental gene expression in pluripotent cells to supporting neuronal programs, with distinct transcriptional consequences of EHMT1 loss across neural progenitors and excitatory and inhibitory neuronal subtypes. Timed depletion and recovery experiments identify the neural progenitor stage as the onset of a developmental period during which EHMT1 is required for faithful neuronal maturation. Remarkably, EHMT1 can re-engage stage-specific targets after prolonged deficiency, allowing extensive transcriptional recovery with only limited molecular scarring. These findings reveal how ubiquitous epigenetic machinery acquires developmental specificity while demonstrating the resilience of developmental gene regulatory programs to prolonged disruption, with implications for neurodevelopmental disorders.
affiliations: Weill Cornell Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Alignment-Aware Genomic Coordinate Encoding for Long-Range DNA Modeling
papers.abstract: Existing genomic foundation models (GFMs) are adept at capturing local, sequential dependencies in DNA. However, their architectures often struggle to efficiently model gene regulation features, such as sparse motifs and distal regulatory elements that operate beyond linear proximity. Moreover, standard positional encodings fail to fully exploit the reference genome coordinate system. Therefore, we present USM-AA, an alignment-aware genomic foundation model that incorporates reference genome coordinates through a non-contiguous positional encoding, Alignment-Aware Rotary Position Embedding, and an alignment embedding module encoding chromosome, strand, and Compact Idiosyncratic Gapped Alignment Report (CIGAR) information. To improve long-range sequence modeling, USM-AA leverages a reverse-complement masked learning strategy. Pretrained on alignment-aware genomic sequences spanning cross-species evolution and human population variation, USM-AA consistently outperforms existing models across multiple downstream tasks, highlighting the importance of alignment-aware representations for genomic sequence modeling.
affiliations: AI for Life Sciences Lab, Tencent (corresponding author)

papers.title: Directed evolution of laccase from Thermus thermophilus HB27 reveals a variant with enhanced high temperature catalytic activity and electrochemical properties
papers.abstract: Laccases belong to the multicopper oxidase family (MCO). Compared with fungal laccases, bacterial laccases have high stability and activity under extreme pH and temperature conditions. Because of these characteristics, bacterial laccases have become highly impactful in industrial processes. In the present work, we engineered the Thermus thermophilus HB27 laccase (Tth-Lac) by directed evolution. The library had a size of 1.2 x105 colonies, and we screened mutants by malachite green decolorization on solid medium. The results showed that Q36H mutant exhibited higher catalytic activity than Tth-laccase (WT) at 90 degrees Celsius. Both enzymes showed similar pH profiles, but the activity at 90 degrees Celsius of Q36H mutant was X-fold higher than that of the wild-type enzyme. In contrast, the kinetic constants were similar for both enzymes. In the voltammetric responses, at 61.5 degrees Celsius, the Q36H mutant showed increased current, and the T1 copper potential shifted by 100 mV relative to the tth-Lac. These results suggest that the Q36H mutation has high potential for industrial applications because replacing a glutamine (Q) with a histidine (H) at position 36 enhances the enzyme's structural stability, allowing it to function efficiently under extreme temperature conditions.
affiliations: Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pre-catalytic activation pathway of the Smc5/6 complex
papers.abstract: The Smc5/6 complex (Smc5/6) preserves genome stability through ATP-dependent DNA organization, but the structural details that prime the complex for productive DNA engagement remain unknown. Here, we combine cryo-electron microscopy and conformational heterogeneity analysis to define the pre-catalytic activation pathway of Smc5/6. We show that in the absence of ATP and DNA, Smc5/6 exists as a heterogeneous conformational ensemble composed predominantly of two conformations termed Bridge and Cross. In the presence of DNA alone, Smc5/6 adopts a Juxtaposed conformation that brings the ATPase heads into proximity, aligning them for nucleotide engagement. With both ATP and DNA associated, Smc5/6 establishes an Engaged architecture, within which DNA stabilizes its head-associated binding cavity through local remodeling of the complex. Conformational heterogeneity analyses suggest a continuous structural transition between the Cross and Juxtaposed states, while anisotropic network modeling identifies the Bridge-Cross-Juxtaposed-Engaged sequence as the mechanically favored pathway connecting the four experimentally observed conformations. Together, these findings support a pre-catalytic conformational pathway for Smc5/6 activation and provide a structural framework for understanding how conformational heterogeneity gives rise to an activation-competent motor state.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute of Biophysics (corresponding author)

papers.title: Benchmarking single-cell foundation models reveals an advantage in the low-data regime for cell-type and disease-state prediction
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models perform well on cell-type classification, but their value for disease-state prediction and their advantage over classical representations remains unclear. We benchmarked cell-representations from four foundation models using logistic regression, on 868 disease-prediction tasks (82 datasets) and 65 cell-type datasets from CELLxGENE. With full data, the baseline (log-normalized counts) outperformed the best model (TranscriptFormer-Sapiens) for cell type and matched it for disease. However, with few labeled cells, TranscriptFormer-Sapiens significantly outperformed the baseline in both tasks up to ~102 samples per class. Our comprehensive zero-shot benchmark identifies the data-scarce regime as a domain where Single-cell foundation models truly show advantage.
affiliations: The Institute for Medical Research Israel-Canada, Department of Developmental Biology and Cancer Research, Jerusalem, Israel (corresponding author)

papers.title: Activation of Disease-Associated Polycystin-1 Mutants by Binding of Stalk-derived Agonist Peptides
papers.abstract: Polycystin-1 (PC1) functions as an atypical G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) with an autocatalytic GAIN domain that cleaves PC1 into extracellular N-terminal (NTF) and membrane-embedded C-terminal (CTF) fragments. Mutations in PC1 are responsible for 85% of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) cases. Activation of signaling by PC1 CTF has been shown to be allosterically mediated by a stalk tethered agonist (TA) and to be prevented by mutations of the stalk. Soluble, synthetic peptides derived from the PC1 stalk were also shown to re-activate signaling by a stalkless CTF mutant. Here, we have investigated the ability of selected stalk peptide agonists p9, p15 or p17 to re-activate signaling by PC1 CTF with ADPKD-associated missense mutations, G3052R or R3063C. Biochemical experimental data showed that each of the three stalk peptides was able to significantly reactivate signaling by the CTF-R3063C mutant. In contrast, signaling by CTF-G3052R could only be rescued by treatment with p17. In parallel, we employed peptide docking and novel Peptide Gaussian-accelerated Molecular Dynamics (Pep-GaMD) simulations to elucidate the binding conformations of p9, p15 and p17 to the PC1 mutants. The simulation findings were highly consistent with experimental data. Furthermore, Pep-GaMD revealed binding conformations of the agonist peptides and important low-energy conformational states of the PC1 CTF, as well as their critical residue interactions. Overall, our complementary approach provides important mechanistic insights into the re-activation of PC1 disease-associated mutants by stalk-derived peptide agonists. Such insights are expected to be valuable for the future design and development of peptide modulators targeting PC1 for an effective ADPKD therapeutic treatment.
affiliations: Department of Pharmacology and Computational Medicine Program, Bioinformatics and Computational Biology Program, University of North Carolina - Chapel Hill (corresponding author)

papers.title: Predicting cyanobacterial oxic diazotrophy and prioritizing candidate protein families beyond known Nif proteins
papers.abstract: Diazotrophic cyanobacteria must reconcile oxygenic photosynthesis with the oxygen sensitivity of nitrogenase. Engineering studies have demonstrated nitrogenase activity in a non-diazotrophic cyanobacterium while highlighting the importance of accessory functions and oxygen management. Robust aerobic nitrogen fixation remains challenging, motivating systematic identification of candidate support functions beyond the canonical Nif machinery. We modeled nifHDK-defined diazotrophic potential from protein-family presence or absence in 426 cyanobacterial assemblies. Four classifiers evaluated with genus-blocked cross-validation achieved mean ROC AUCs of 0.853 to 0.893, with purity and genus-breadth filters fitted within training folds. Restricting the panel to 401 assemblies with current NCBI status gave AUCs of 0.806 to 0.881. Family-content logistic regression outperformed a genome-size-only baseline across ten genus partitions. Two inventories describe candidates across the full panel: 981 high-purity families and 473 families with positive residual associations (accompanied by three ubiquitous controls). Model importance orders the residual-association inventory. A separate heuristic score combines inventory membership with proteomics, condensate-driver ranks and genus-based morphotype proxies to prioritize 167 families for experiments. Proteomics annotations tracked detection opportunity; the condensate contrast between inventories attenuated after prevalence adjustment. These annotations help choose experiments but do not independently validate accessory functions. Protein-family content predicts nifHDK-defined diazotrophic potential, with performance sensitive to assembly inclusion, taxonomy, genome size and taxonomic weighting. The two candidate inventories distinguish high carrier purity from residual association, providing complementary resources for prioritizing previously uncharacterized functions associated with cyanobacterial oxic diazotrophy.
affiliations: University of South Dakota (corresponding author)

papers.title: Horizontal transfers can reveal ghost birth events and complete species trees
papers.abstract: Extinct and unsampled species vastly outnumber the species typically included in phylogenetic studies. Most of these so-called ``ghost lineages'' are unknown and, among them, those that are extinct may have left no trace in the fossil record. Horizontal gene transfers (HGTs), however, provide a potential source of information about these missing lineages, because transfers can connect sampled ancestral species to lineages outside the sampled species tree. Such transfers may leave observable signatures in gene trees. Here, we formalize this signal under idealized models of duplication, transfer, and loss, and characterize the information that can be retrieved about the complete species tree (containing ghost and non-ghost lineages) thanks to sampled gene trees and sampled species trees (containing only the non-ghost lineages). We establish four identifiability results, assuming an infinite number of gene families and errorless dated gene trees. First, transfers identify the lineage through time (LTT) curve of the complete tree, averaged over each time interval induced by the nodes of the sampled species tree. Second, in the presence of transfers, the distribution of node heights in sampled gene trees uniquely determines the internal speciation times of the complete species tree, including ghost speciations. Third, these hidden speciation times suffice to restore identifiability of birth-death-sampling parameters, through a reduction to a recent theorem of Dieselhorst and Stadler. Finally, when duplication, transfer, and loss rates are known constants and the transfer rate is non-zero, the distribution of sampled gene trees almost surely uniquely determines the topology and branch lengths of the complete species tree, including all ghost branches. These results provide a theoretical basis for using signatures left by HGTs in gene trees to recover information about extinct and unsampled lineages, and suggest ways in which this signal could be exploited in practice.
affiliations: Universite Claude Bernard Lyon 1, LBBE, UMR 5558, CNRS, VAS, Villeurbanne, 69622, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: BioMeBar Indian Gut Reference Atlas: A Harmonised Multi-Cohort Healthy Microbiome Baseline and the Indian Gut Health Index
papers.abstract: Population-scale gut microbiome reference databases exist for Western and East Asian cohorts, yet no harmonised healthy baseline has been available for India's 1.4 billion inhabitants, whose diets span extreme geographic and cultural gradients. Western-derived reference ranges risk systematic misclassification when applied to Indian subjects. We harmonised eight published Indian healthy-gut microbiome cohorts (1,672 samples from 1,456 unique individuals , 20 geographic locations, six zones) onto a common NCBI family-level taxonomy axis. Raw 16S rRNA amplicon data were reprocessed through a uniform QIIME 2 / DADA2 / SILVA 138.1 pipeline where raw sequences were available; author-provided taxonomic tables from MetaPhlAn, HITChip, and RDP-based pipelines were retained and mapped via a four-step resolution cascade (exact match, synonym lookup, genus-to-family fallback, Unassigned). We defined the Indian Gut Health Index (IGHI), a four-component composite score (diversity, taxon balance, core membership, community typicality) calibrated against geography-stratified healthy Indian norms. The unified matrix comprised 380 bacterial families, of which 17 constituted the pan-Indian core ([≥]80% prevalence; Lachnospiraceae 100%, Prevotellaceae 99.5%). PERMANOVA confirmed significant compositional differences across geographies (pseudo-F = 43.4, p = 0.001) and cohorts (pseudo-F = 89.6, p = 0.001). Variance partitioning revealed that geography and cohort effects were deeply confounded (shared variance 30.4%; pure geography 4.1%, pure cohort 4.7%, residual 60.9%). Restricted permutation PERMANOVA confirmed city-level geographic signal after cohort correction (p = 0.001), but zone-level signal did not survive (p = 0.896). Two community types were identified: a Prevotellaceae-dominant type (69%) and an Oscillospiraceae-dominant type (31%), contrasting with the Western three-enterotype model. A Random Forest zone classifier achieved 68.4% balanced accuracy (null 16.6%), with Northeast subjects most distinguishable (F1 = 0.92). IGHI zone means ranged from 67.6 to 72.9 (inter-zone range 5.3 points), confirming effective geographic normalisation. Weight sensitivity analysis showed IGHI rankings were robust to moderate perturbation (Spearman {rho} [≥] 0.88 for five of six alternative schemes). The BioMeBarTM Indian Gut Reference Atlas provides the first pan-Indian harmonised healthy microbiome baseline, and the IGHI offers a population-calibrated scoring framework for gut health assessment in Indian individuals. The atlas, scoring model, and analysis code are openly available at https://github.com/TusharParihar128/BioMeBar_Indian_Healthy_Cohorts_datasets.
affiliations: BioMeBar Health and Wellness Solutions Pvt Ltd (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reformulating Protein Corona Prediction as Universal Protein-conditioned Learning
papers.abstract: When nanoparticles enter biological environments, their surfaces are rapidly coated by proteins, forming a protein corona that governs their biological identity and downstream responses. Existing computational methods treat each protein as an independent prediction task, preventing the learning of shared adsorption principles and limiting generalization beyond experimentally characterized proteins. Here we introduce NanoPCT, a universal protein-conditioned learning framework that jointly models nanoparticle physicochemical properties and protein sequence representations. Using frozen ESM-2 embeddings and a joint interaction transformer, NanoPCT learns transferable representations of nano-bio interaction patterns across hundreds of proteins and maintains robust performance as protein diversity increases. The learned protein representation further enables zero-shot prediction for previously unseen proteins and biologically distinct protein groups through classifier reconstruction in embedding space. Beyond prediction, NanoPCT supports large-scale in silico inverse design and reveals consistent adsorption preferences between observed and unseen protein populations, suggesting that it captures transferable interaction patterns rather than protein-specific memorization. NanoPCT provides a unified framework for protein corona prediction, zero-shot generalization, and rational nanomaterial design.
affiliations: State Key Laboratory for Quality Ensurance and Sustainable Use of Dao-di Herbs, Artemisinin Research Center, and Institute of Chinese Materia Medica, China Acad (corresponding author)

papers.title: Representing biological concepts as directions in foundation model embeddings
papers.abstract: Biological foundation models encode rich information about protein structure, function, and cellular state in high-dimensional embeddings, but accessing specific biological properties typically relies on additional, task-specific prediction models. Here, we show that diverse biological properties can be mapped to interpretable, reusable directions in embedding space. In the Concept Activation Vector (CAV) approach, examples representing a concept are distinguished from a background set using a linear model, and the resulting weight vector defines the CAV for that concept. In protein embeddings, CAVs recover Gene Ontology and Enzyme Commission annotations, localize Pfam domains, reveal novel structural relationships, and capture DNA-binding and protein-interaction interface specificity. In single-cell embeddings, CAVs isolate cancer-associated expression transitions, and gene variation along these axes substantially agrees with conventional differential-expression analysis despite being a distinct computational approach. Together, these results establish concept directions as a common representation, enabling diverse biological features to be compared, localized, and manipulated.
affiliations: The University of Arizona (corresponding author)

papers.title: AnnZarro: scalable, interactive exploration of cell-by-cell and gene-by-gene relationships in single-cell data
papers.abstract: Cell-by-cell and gene-by-gene relationships, such as kernels and correlations, shape most single-cell analyses but are rarely inspected directly due to a lack of visualization tools that display them. AnnZarro is a point-and-click browser viewer that shows these matrices linked to an AnnData object's cells x genes data. Using AnnZarro, experimental biologists can explore data without code and computational biologists can probe the relationships behind their analyses. One focused cell and one focused gene drive every panel. Clicking a cell paints its row of any cell-by-cell matrix over an embedding or spatial coordinates; clicking a gene paints its row of any gene-by-gene matrix over a gene plot such as a volcano. The focus also links genes to the cells where they change, and cells to the genes that distinguish them. AnnZarro reads only the matrix rows and columns each panel displays from zarr stores and hence users can explore matrices far larger than memory on a laptop or a shared server. Large datasets open on a reproducible subset, and users step through the remaining cells in parts. On a laptop, a 100,000-cell part of Tahoe-100M opens in 4 s and stays interactive. With the subset switched off, AnnZarro draws all 95.6 million cells in one plot in about 5 to 7 s. This tutorial prepares a dataset with Kompot differential abundance and expression, a diffusion kernel and gene correlations, then explores it in six worked examples.
affiliations: Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Fluid shear magnitude, mechanical history and actin-sensitive coupling shape Piezo1 signalling
papers.abstract: Mechanical forces shape cell behaviour, yet how Piezo1-associated responses encode force magnitude, recent mechanical history and cytoskeletal context under repeated fluid shear remains unclear. We combined defined fluid shear stress (FSS) with GenEPi, a genetically encoded reporter of Piezo1-proximal Ca2+ entry, in engineered XLGenEPi-HEK293T monolayers to resolve mechanically evoked responses at single-cell and population scales. GenEPi responses increased with FSS magnitude but showed diminishing response gain at higher shear. Repeated submaximal FSS produced history-dependent attenuation and reduced temporal coordination, with higher FSS accelerating the early phase of attenuation. Low-dose Latrunculin A, without significantly reducing bulk F-actin abundance, converted sustained FSS-evoked signalling into a brief, decay-dominated response while largely preserving peak responses to Yoda1. These findings show that Piezo1-associated signalling is shaped over minutes by force magnitude, recent mechanical history and actin-sensitive mechanical coupling, providing a quantitative framework for understanding mechanotransduction under sustained and repeated mechanical stimulation.
affiliations: Imperial College London (corresponding author)

papers.title: DNA nullomers as a statistical phenomenon
papers.abstract: Nullomers are sequences absent from a certain genome. Due to their unexpected occurrence in short sequences, a hypothesis is that they are avoided for evolutionary reasons or because they might have lethal consequences on organisms. However, we present evidence that the occurrence and frequency of nullomers in genomes is expected as a stochastic consequence of uneven base pair combination distributions in the genetic code. This is done by artificially constructing whole genomes from statistics with a Markov chain model. The number of nullomers in these artificial genomes is in good agreement with the nullomer counts in reference genomes. Additionally, we investigated the nullomers of over 200 human genomes and found large deviations in the nullomers between individuals, further supporting the hypothesis that a vast majority of nullomers is very unlikely to have lethal effects.
affiliations: University of Kassel (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural Basis for the Rational Design of UAMC-1110-Based FAP Radiopharmaceuticals
papers.abstract: Radioligands targeting fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) are promising tools for cancer diagnosis and therapy. However, the molecular binding mode of clinically established UAMC-1110-derived ligands such as FAPI-46 remains insufficiently characterized. To simplify synthesis while preserving key binding properties, we designed two novel derivatives - FAP-DD-101 (short aminoalkyl linker) and FAP-DD-102 (extended aminohexanoic acid spacer) - and evaluated them alongside FAPI-46 using molecular docking and all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Across all derivatives, we identified a highly stable, energetically favorable charge-anchored binding mode, in which the 2-cyano-4,4-difluoropyrrolidine head anchors in a negatively charged subregion formed by Glu202, Glu203, and Glu204, mimicking the binding architecture observed in the FAP-linagliptin complex. MD trajectories confirmed that FAPI-46 and FAP-DD-101 maintain exceptional stability in this pose, with several non-anchored FAPI-46 trajectories spontaneously evolving toward engagement with this electrostatic subregion. For FAP-DD-102, linker elongation slightly reduced pose robustness, yet initial charge-anchored states still yielded superior average binding energies and vector stability compared to non-anchored poses. Overall, these findings elucidate the key structural determinants of FAP recognition, establishing a rational framework for designing synthetically accessible FAPI radiotracers with retained binding stability.
affiliations: Forschungszentrum Juelich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Lipid diffusion enhanced by molecular motors
papers.abstract: An experimental study of myosin I motors on a supported lipid membrane with a nematic actin filament layer is presented. The activities of myosin I motors re-organize the actin layer, in particular the morphology of +1/2 nematic defects. Data from single-particle tracking (SPT) of lipid molecules reveal two interesting features. First, the distribution of average lipid speed over a track shows two groups of lipids (high-speed and low-speed), and the proportion of lipids to be high-speed is higher in regions rich in actin. Second, by classifying short-time movement of the lipids into normal diffusion, directed motion, confined motion, and subdiffusion states, we found that lipids in regions rich in actin have a lower probability to stay in the confined and subdiffusion states and more likely to perform normal diffusion. Furthermore, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) measurements show that the diffusion of lipids in the actin-rich regions is enhanced. The SPT and FRAP results suggest that myosin I motor activities turn low-speed lipids to high-speed ones, and affect the lipid moving state by reducing confined and subdiffusive motion. As a result, lipid diffusion is enhanced by motor activities.
affiliations: National Central University, Taiwan (corresponding author)

papers.title: PINPOINT enables non-destructive nanoscopic quality control of individual lipid nanoparticles and their mRNA cargo
papers.abstract: Quality control of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) is central to development of mRNA therapeutics, yet ensemble measurements obscure critical heterogeneity in particle morphology and mRNA cargo loading. Here we introduce PINPOINT (Profiling Individual Nanoparticles with Precise Observation of INternalized Therapeutics), a single-particle nanoscopy platform for non-destructive, multiparametric profiling of preformulated LNP samples. Super-resolution imaging with Nile Red resolves size and morphology, while an optimized permeabilization strategy provides selective access to encapsulated mRNA without compromising LNP integrity. Single-particle fluorescence measurements, including RiboGreen and sequence-specific probes, enable quantification and validation of mRNA loading and identity. Comparative analyses of bare and encapsulated mRNA reveal kinetic and structural features, exposing heterogeneity masked by bulk assays. By integrating structural and molecular readouts at the single-particle level, PINPOINT establishes a quantitative framework for assessing of LNP composition and payload distribution, offering actionable insights for improving batch consistency and guiding the rational design of next-generation mRNA delivery systems.
affiliations: University of Michigan (Ann Arbor) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Radiotherapy Reshapes the 3D Genome in Medulloblastoma Cells
papers.abstract: Radiotherapy is central to medulloblastoma treatment, yet the molecular and three-dimensional (3D) genome responses to irradiation remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated RNA sequencing, proteomics, and Micro-C to characterise the response of ONS-76 medulloblastoma cells to clinically relevant radiation exposures. A single 2 Gy dose induced widespread transcriptional and proteomic changes, including altered cell adhesion, migration, DNA replication, and ribosome biogenesis pathways. Integrated analysis identified LAMB3 and AKR1B10 as candidate mediators of radioresponse that remained elevated following fractionated irradiation. Micro-C profiling following single and repeated 2 Gy exposures revealed radiation-induced 3D genome remodelling. While global genome organisation remained largely stable, irradiation promoted shifts towards active A compartments, new TAD boundary formation, and transient boundary strengthening. Together, these findings provide the first genome-wide characterisation of radiation-induced 3D chromatin reorganisation in a medulloblastoma model and identify molecular and structural features associated with radioresponse.
affiliations: University of Tasmania (corresponding author)

papers.title: A reference-calibrated spatial-statistical framework for quantifying stroma-tumor cell spatial associations from histology and its geometric limits
papers.abstract: Quantifying interactions in biological tissues requires determining whether an interaction exists, the distance over which it operates, and its strength. Existing spatial-statistical approaches can characterize spatial organization but often require interaction range or interaction models to be specified a priori, making them less suited to settings where these quantities are themselves unknown. Here, we present a practical framework that recovers the presence, range, and association strength of spatial bias toward a tissue structure directly from segmented histology. The framework combines four complementary statistics, the resource selection function, nearest-structure distance distributions, the cross J-function, and the radial distribution function, with specimen-specific reference states that preserve tissue stromal architecture while spanning a continuum of known spatial biases. Across controlled in silico tissues, we show that tissue stromal architecture imposes geometric limits on the range of recoverable interactions and that event fraction independently constrains statistical sensitivity. These spatial associations establish fundamental bounds on inference and demonstrate that spatial statistics must be interpreted relative to tissue-specific reference states rather than absolute scales. We apply the framework to proliferating tumor cells relative to CAF-rich stroma during tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy in an ALK+ NSCLC model and identify a strong stroma-associated proliferation bias extending approximately 30-60 micrometers. The framework broadly applies to any histological setting where events and reference structures can be defined, providing a practical approach to quantify localized interactions directly from tissue stromal architecture.
affiliations: H. Lee Moffitt Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Positive selection and structural disruption of KCNA5 by mutation in colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Ion channels regulate cell proliferation, survival and migration, but the functional consequences of many ion channel mutations in cancer are unknown, and electrophysiological characterisation at scale is impractical. Here we use the mutational landscape of colorectal adenocarcinoma as a functional filter to identify potassium channel mutations under selection. A dN/dS screen of 16 potassium channels expressed in the large intestine identified KCNA5 (Kv1.5) as the strongest candidate under positive mutational selection. These mutations cluster in the T1 tetramerisation, S1-S4 voltage-sensor and pore domains, yet avoid the selectivity filter, indicating that selection does not favour loss of conduction. Within the pore region, the observed mutations occupy a biophysical space distinct from known C-type inactivation, activation-gate and toxin-binding mutations. In the voltage sensor, mutations affect gating-charge arginines. In the T1 domain, mutations fall on inter-subunit interfaces conserved across the KCNA family, and saturation mutagenesis energy calculations predict that they destabilise subunit contacts or the folding of the domain. Molecular dynamics simulations of D166N and G128R show loss of coordinated interface dynamics and distortion of the local backbone, respectively. Transcriptomic analysis of KCNA5-mutant tumours shows reduced expression of cell-cycle, KRAS-related and inflammatory pathways, and we observe differences between transcriptional effects induced by T1 and S1-S4 domain mutations. These changes are not reproduced by low KCNA5 expression alone, consistent with an effect specific to the mutant protein. Together, these computational results highlight that KCNA5 is under mutational selection in colorectal adenocarcinoma, and that these mutations are likely functional and induce phenotypic effects on tumors.
affiliations: University College London (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reduced emerin expression marks gastric cancer progression and invasive nuclear remodeling
papers.abstract: Altered nuclear morphology is a defining diagnostic feature of malignancy, and nuclear structure is increasingly recognized as a functional regulator of cancer cell invasion. The inner nuclear membrane protein emerin maintains nuclear architecture and restrains invasive phenotypes in breast cancer models, but whether emerin expression is similarly altered in gastric cancer has not been established. Here, we analyzed emerin protein expression, nuclear morphology, and impeded migration in nonmalignant and malignant gastric cell lines. In parallel, emerin protein expression and nuclear envelope localization across gastric cancer was determined using patient tissue microarrays. Emerin was abundant at the nuclear envelope in cancer-adjacent and noncancerous gastric epithelium but was reduced across multiple gastric cancer histologies, including adenocarcinoma, signet-ring cell carcinoma, mucinous adenocarcinoma, neuroendocrine carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and metastatic lesions. Reduced emerin at the nuclear envelope was most strongly associated with higher-grade tumors, with grade 2 and grade 3 cancers exhibiting significantly lower nuclear envelope scores than noncancerous tissue and grade 1 tumors. Consistent with the patient tissue data, the gastric cancer cell lines AGS and MKN1 expressed less emerin protein than noncancerous gastric epithelial control cells HFE-145. Consistent with studies in breast cancer cells, gastric cells with reduced emerin expression also had smaller nuclei and increased impeded migration through 8 micron pores. These findings support a model in which reduced nuclear envelope emerin is a conserved feature of invasive epithelial tumor progression and a candidate biomarker of gastric cancer nuclear remodeling.
affiliations: Cooper Medical School of Rowan University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Efficacy of Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields) in triple negative breast cancer cells and synergy with PARP inhibitor talazoparib
papers.abstract: Breast cancer is the most diagnosed cancer worldwide. Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a subtype with a poor prognosis because of its aggressiveness and high likelihood of relapse, making its treatment particularly challenging. We explored the effect of Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields) as a novel treatment option for breast cancer, which can be used together with other therapies, such as PARP inhibitors. TTFields use alternating electric fields to inhibit cell growth and induce cellular damage. Our findings indicate that TTFields increase expression of the universal cell cycle CDK inhibitory protein p21(WAF1)/CDKN1A independently of TP53 mutational status. Moreover, when used together with the PARP inhibitor talazoparib, the combination further upregulates p21 protein. Both TTFields alone and together with talazoparib induce cell death as documented by PARP cleavage while reducing markers of cell growth and anti-apoptotic proteins, including p-STAT3, STAT3, and MCL-1. Additionally, TTFields together with talazoparib induce DNA damage, as indicated by increased {gamma}H2AX expression. The combination of talazoparib plus TTFields treatment decrease PDL-1 levels and given its utility in predicting response to PD-1/PD-L1 by mediating immune evasion, this raises the possibility of future combination for immune modulation in cancer therapy. Our preclinical results suggest TTFields alone or together with PARP inhibitors such as talazoparib as a promising therapeutic approach for further development for the treatment of breast cancer.
affiliations: Brown University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Malignant and stromal partial EMT programmes and cetuximab outcome in head and neck cancer
papers.abstract: Partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (pEMT) was defined in single malignant cells of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma but is usually scored in bulk tumours. In three single-cell datasets, its laminin-332 and hemidesmosome genes were expressed by malignant cells (the malignant arm) and its fibrillar collagens and vimentin by fibroblasts (the stromal arm). In bulk tumours the stromal arm dominated co-expression, so standard pEMT scores mainly measure stroma. We recovered the malignant arm with a classifier trained on single cells and a 12-gene core. In 40 patients treated with platinum and cetuximab, both malignant measures were higher in those with long progression-free survival (area under the curve 0.78 and 0.82), and the stromal arm was not. The malignant arm was inseparable from the Basal subtype, whose score did as well or better in these patients (0.93) and in two xenograft panels. Bulk pEMT scores should be read by cell of origin.
affiliations: Milner Therapeutics Institute, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom (corresponding author)

papers.title: A conditional upper-bound design map for rhodopsin-augmented electro microbial CO2-to-biomass conversion
papers.abstract: The value of rhodopsin proton pumps as light harvesters in electro-microbial CO2-to-biomass conversion depends on molecular photophysics, pathway energetics and reactor light delivery. We couple these scales for Cupriavidus necator, comparing Calvin-Benson-Bassham (CBB) and reductive glycine (rGlyP) assimilation. The model predicts a 17.9% dark rGlyP yield advantage, close to 16.5% measured in chemostats. At 568 nm, 100 PPFD and 45% membrane occupancy, light-derived ATP raises yield by 17% for rGlyP and 14% for CBB. Charging CO2 capture and formate electrosynthesis, a retinal-only reactor reaches 3.29% efficiency versus 2.56% in the dark. A carotenoid antenna raises this to 3.52% at the model-derived 70% transfer estimate and helps in 93.2% of uncertainty samples, but lowers efficiency at the thermodynamic limit by diverting photons from photovoltaics. Point-source CO2 cuts the relative light benefit from 38% to 8%. Rhodopsin is therefore most useful when upstream formate is energy-intensive, not as a general efficiency boost.
affiliations: University of Oxford (corresponding author)

papers.title: The immunogenic 33-mer gliadin peptide attenuates flagellin-induced TLR5/NF-κB signaling
papers.abstract: Wheat gluten is the main trigger of gluten-related disorders such as celiac disease, in which the proteolysis-resistant, 33-mer peptide is a key immunodominant factor. It has been reported that the 33-mer forms oligomers and thin-plate superstructures that accumulate in the Caco-2 intestinal epithelial cell line, although their biological effects remain only partially understood. Here, we screened the effects of these nanostructures on Toll-like receptors in Caco-2 cells to investigate their effect on the early innate immune response. Our findings showed a specific upregulation of TLR5 mRNA in response to 33-mer gliadin superstructures, although no inflammatory response was detected based on CXCL1 and CXCL8 levels. Moreover, immunofluorescence analysis revealed partial co-localization with TLR5. We further found that the 33-mer superstructures attenuate flagellin-induced TLR5/NF{kappa}B signaling in reporter cells, similar to a blocking anti-hTLR5-IgA2 antibody. Molecular docking suggested that the 33-mer peptide occupies the concave region of TLR5 as well as 54% of the TLR5-TLR5 dimerization interface. The interference with the TLR5 dimerization domain could explain the experimental attenuation of flagellin-mediated TLR5 activation. Given that TLR5 contributes not only to inflammation but also to intestinal homeostasis, our findings suggest that the formation of 33-mer nanostructures upon its accumulation may increase the local concentration of 33-mer, interfering with TLR5-mediated mucosal immune responses. These findings provide a rationale for investigating the role of TLR5 and 33-mer aggregates in clinical samples from patients with celiac disease and other gluten-related disorders.
affiliations: Bielefeld University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mice immunized with N1 neuraminidase in a single cycle infectious virus or in a recombinant nanoparticle vaccine are protected against lethal challenge with highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 influenza
papers.abstract: The recent spillover of highly pathogenic (HP) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b into dairy cattle and other mammalian species has been concerning. Vaccine candidates that can be rapidly synthesized and implemented are key countermeasures for protecting the human population against emerging pathogens. Here we examine the use of a pH1N1 virus lacking the genetic material for hemagglutinin (HA), limiting the infection to a single cycle (sciIAV) or Cobalt lipid-porphyrin nanoparticles decorated with neuraminidase (NA) of HPAI H5N1 (N1-CoPoP) as vaccine candidates. C57BL/6 mice that were inoculated intranasally with a single dose of pH1N1 sciIAV did not differ in serum NA antibody compared to uninoculated mice. However, mice that were inoculated intramuscularly with the N1-CoPoP alone or in combination with pH1N1 sciIAV had increased N1 IgG antibodies. Upon lethal challenge with HPAIV H5N1, all mice inoculated with either pH1N1 sciIAV or N1-CoPoP were protected from weight loss, unlike unvaccinated mice with substantial body weight losses that succumb to viral infection between 7 and 10 days post infection (dpi). Both pH1N1 sciIAV and N1-CoPoP immunization minimized viral infection such that only one mouse receiving pH1N1 sciIAV had detectable viral titer in the lungs at 4 dpi. By 6 dpi, no mouse inoculated with pH1N1 sciIAV and/or N1-CoPoP had detectable virus in nasal turbinates, lungs or the brain, unlike the high viral titers found in uninoculated mice. Both pH1N1 sciIAV and N1-CoPoP were protective and should be investigated further as alternative vaccine candidates.
affiliations: University of Alabama at Birmingham (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mechanistic prediction of fecal microbiota transplant engraftment and Clostridioides difficile colonization resistance with μODE
papers.abstract: Shotgun metagenomics routinely resolves microbial community composition down to the strain level via metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), but translating these static catalogs into mechanistic, time-resolved understandings of ecosystem dynamics remains a critical computational bottleneck. Here, we present muODE, a fully automated framework that converts MAGs into dynamical simulations of community metabolism equipped with a composable, literature-grounded ecology layer, fundamentally designed to serve as a mechanistic hypothesis-testing engine. It employs dynamic flux balance analysis (dFBA) coupled to a shared extracellular pool and integrates a composable ecology layer capturing pH inhibition, time-varying antibiotic pharmacokinetics, bile-acid transformations, and spore dormancy. To evaluate the core engine, we cross-validated the dFBA machinery to machine precision against an independent reference implementation. We provide native export to the established COMETS engine for third-party verification. Benchmarking against two independent experimentally validated datasets confirmed that while monoculture growth is robustly captured, overflow secretion and directed community composition remain strictly bounded by the flux-routing limitations of max-biomass FBA. However, when applied to rate-modifying ecological feedback, muODE mechanistically and quantitatively reproduces bile-acid-mediated colonization resistance against Clostridioides difficile. With a single rate parameter calibrated so that baseline deoxycholate matched its measured physiological concentration, the framework reproduced the uncalibrated antibiotic-induced collapse of deoxycholate, with the calibrated inhibitor concentration coinciding with the independently set inhibitory threshold of the pathogen and driving a ~44x shift in the simulated pathogen-susceptibility ratio; bile-acid transformation is represented in the composable ecology layer rather than in the genome-scale stoichiometry. Finally, applying muODE end-to-end to a real longitudinal fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) yielding 139 de novo genome-scale metabolic models, the framework successfully recovered the clinical direction of treatment. By transparently diagnosing the structural competitive-exclusion bias that limits precise compositional prediction, muODE motivates the necessity of community-objective extensions while transitioning microbiome modeling from descriptive taxonomy toward testable, quantitatively-validated dynamic hypothesis testing, laying the essential mechanistic groundwork for the predictive engineering of safe, targeted ecological therapeutics. muODE is freely available at https://github.com/cumbof/muODE.
affiliations: Cleveland Clinic Foundation (corresponding author)

papers.title: Interdependent mode of RNA recognition by the interacting KH-domain proteins KhpA and KhpB
papers.abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are central regulators of gene expression. In bacteria, two KH domain-containing proteins, KhpA and KhpB, are increasingly recognized as globally-acting RBPs, including in pathogens that lack well-studied RBPs, such as Hfq and ProQ. While KhpA and KhpB interact with various RNAs in diverse bacteria, their crosstalk and molecular basis of RNA recognition remain poorly understood. Here, we explored the mutual dependence between KhpA and KhpB in the food-borne pathogen Campylobacter jejuni. We demonstrate KhpA and KhpB interact in vivo, and their individual global RNA recognition is largely dependent on the presence of the partner protein. Using RNA co-immunoprecipitation, we reveal that KhpA requires a conserved KH domain motif for RNA binding, whereas KhpB relies on an atypical R3H domain. Moreover, mutating the RNA-binding domain of one protein compromises the RNA interactome of the other. Overall, we demonstrate an interdependent RNA-binding mode of KhpA and KhpB and anticipate that such KH-proteins have co-evolved to elicit joint RNA regulation in bacteria.
affiliations: Department of Molecular Infection Biology II, Institute of Molecular Infection Biology (IMIB), University of Wuerzburg, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: 2C-RT Quantifies Genome-Wide DNA Replication Perturbationsand Redefines RIF1-CDC7 Regulation of Replication Timing
papers.abstract: Replication timing (RT) coordinates DNA synthesis with genome organization and influences mutation rates, cancer evolution, and developmental plasticity. Current methods infer S-phase timing from DNA content, an assumption that obscures responses to replication perturbations and limits accurate comparisons of RT changes. Here, we develop 2C-RT, a multiplexed sequencing approach that uses DNA content-independent markers for robust RT profiling across S phase. Combining 2C-RT with imaging, we resolve distinct layers of human RT control and identify local and genome-wide responses to drugs and genetic perturbations. We find that RIF1 spatially restricts CDC7 activity and that its loss does not neutralize RT per se but advances replication across most RIF1-sensitive regions. A conserved MCM5 bob1 mutation lowers the origin-activation threshold and reveals a role for CDC7 in establishing local origin dominance. These findings support a revised model in which CDC7 primes early origins, CDK promotes permissive origin firing genome-wide, and RIF1 counteracts CDC7 in distinct chromatin states and peripheral nuclear domains.
affiliations: Department of Medical Biochemistry and Biophysics, Karolinska Institutet, 171 77 Stockholm, Sweden (corresponding author)

papers.title: Dog-human gene network colocalization links synaptic signalling and ubiquitination to compulsive disorders
authors: Nordic OCD and Related Disorders Consortium (NORDiC),
papers.abstract: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is highly polygenic, and the largest genome-wide association study (GWAS), with 53,660 cases and 2,044,417 controls, identified only 30 loci, a small fraction of loci estimated to explain its heritability - too few to resolve biological pathways. Pet dogs develop a compulsive disorder (dogCD) similar to OCD. In a GWAS of dogCD with 2,584 dogs from the community science project Darwin's Ark, each dog locus explains at least 40-fold more phenotypic variance than each human OCD locus, giving power equivalent to the human GWAS with 80-fold fewer individuals. Combining the two GWAS identifies a 165-gene network undetectable in humans at current sample sizes. This network is enriched for genes expressed in neurons, particularly in the amygdala and cortex, and comprises four biological processes: excitatory-inhibitory synaptic transmission, axon guidance and neuron recognition, protein ubiquitination, and adenylyl cyclase-activating G-protein-coupled receptor signaling. Like most complex human traits, dogCD risk is likely driven by regulatory variation: fine-mapped dogCD SNPs are non-coding, and dogCD loci are enriched in candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) in a new dog epigenomic atlas spanning eight brain regions. The cross-species network implicates an inherited risk architecture largely outside current OCD pharmacotherapy, and establishes pet dogs as a model for gene network discovery, particularly for conditions underpowered in human studies.
affiliations: Uppsala University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Nose-to-Knee Transplantation for Osteochondral Regeneration: A Proof-of-Concept Study in Sheep Employing Ceramic-Hydrogel Osteochondral Grafts
papers.abstract: Osteochondral defects remain a major clinical challenge, frequently progressing to osteoarthritis and ultimately requiring joint replacement. Despite advances in regenerative strategies, current approaches often fail to restore the structural and functional complexity of the osteochondral unit, resulting in poor integration and limited long-term performance. Here, we developed autologous osteochondral grafts combining mechanically mature nasal chondrocyte-derived cartilage with a 3D-printed strontium-hardystonite-gahnite trabecular bone scaffold, which was tested in an osteochondral defect model in sheep. Nasal chondrocytes were encapsulated in a hyaluronan transglutaminase-alginate hydrogel generating hyaline-like cartilage with physiologically relevant compressive properties (1.0 +/- 0.2 MPa) after 6 weeks of in vitro maturation. MicroCT scans of the osteochondral unit were used to design biomimetic trabecular bone scaffolds. Controlled infiltration of the hydrogel into the trabecular pores and subsequent cartilage maturation created a mechanical interlock between cartilage and bone layer, reaching an interfacial shear strength of 201 +/- 42 kPa. The translational potential of this approach was evaluated in a proof-of-concept ovine study. The engineered cartilage remained attached to the bone scaffold for three months following implantation, but osteochondral repair was limited by implant sinking, likely caused by inadequate implant fixation in the defect, resulting in micromotion, synovial fluid infiltration, osteolysis and subsequent bone cyst formation. Together, this work demonstrates the feasibility of engineering mechanically mature autologous osteochondral grafts while identifying subchondral bone integration as the primary bottleneck limiting successful osteochondral regeneration and future clinical translation.
affiliations: IBEC (corresponding author)

papers.title: Functional dynamics of the eukaryotic RNA exosome upon complex formation
papers.abstract: Rather than being static, proteins adopt multiple conformations and undergo dynamics on a wide range of timescales. Such conformational changes can be routinely probed by solution state NMR for protein sizes below 40 kDa and can be extended to large protein complexes with selective methyl-labeling strategies. Here, we expand the limit of methyl-NMR dynamics experiments to asymmetric protein complexes bigger than 300 kDa by investigating the inert core of the eukaryotic RNA exosome, Exo9. We demonstrate that isolated subunits are highly dynamic on the ms-s dynamics, which facilitates assembly. While ring subunits lose dynamics upon complex-formation, cap subunits and functional loops retain a large degree of flexibility as demonstrated by relaxation dispersion and chemical exchange saturation transfer experiments in the fully asymmetric Exo9 complex. Employing EPR spectroscopy we additionally revealed changes in the conformational ensemble and nanosecond dynamics of a spin-labeled functional loop region in the presence of the catalytic subunit Rrp44 and in response to substrate RNA binding. We thus demonstrate that an integrated NMR-EPR approach facilitates the characterization of functional dynamics that occur on a wide range of timescales in very large protein complexes.
affiliations: University of Regensburg (corresponding author)

papers.title: Arsenic Impairs Critical Cellular Events of Human Cardiac Development Across Differentiation and Metabolic Maturation
papers.abstract: Arsenic (As) is a widespread environmental contaminant, with exposure occurring primarily through contaminated food and water or cigarette smoke. Maternal exposure to As represents a significant risk factor for congenital heart disease in offspring. However, the mechanisms underlying As induced developmental cardiotoxicity remain poorly defined. Pluripotent stem cells provide an excellent platform for studying mechanisms of developmental toxicity. Embryoid bodies (EBs) derived from stem cells, can recapitulate many key events of early embryogenesis including germ layers specification. Human cardiomyocytes are derived from mesodermal progenitors. NKX2.5 governs cardiac specification and morphogenesis, and its mutation produces atrial and ventricular defects in humans. Using an NKX2.5 reporter stem cell line, we modeled mesoderm differentiation in EBs and cardiac induction in a 2D cardiomyocyte differentiation system. In an 8 day differentiation protocol, As (0.05 M; 3.75 ppb) significantly suppressed cardiomyocyte differentiation and cardiac induction. However, As increased mesodermal markers (HAND1, SNAI2, HOPX) gene expression. In contrast, cardiac specific genes, including NKX2.5, GATA4, Troponin T, and alpha actinin, were markedly downregulated in the presence of As. As also reduced expression of genes related to cardiac induction, fibroblast function, and vascular markers in the cardiac organoid model. As impaired cardiomyocyte maturation related gene expressions at concentrations without affecting cardiomyocyte proliferation. In a zebrafish model of early heart development, As increased heart rate and disrupted ion channel gene expression. In conclusion, As inhibits ESC differentiation into cardiomyocytes and disrupts cardiomyocyte maturation. Combining stem cell derived models with zebrafish exposure, this study illuminates adverse outcome pathways for As induced congenital heart defect.
affiliations: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Brody School of Medicine, East Carolina University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Engineered regulatory states resolve context-dependent genetics in macular degeneration
papers.abstract: The effects of many genes and disease-associated variants remain hidden in standard cellular models, limiting functional interpretation. Here we engineer regulatory states via CRISPR activation of transcription factors (TFs) in human RPE-1 cells, a model for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Multiome Perturb-seq profiling of single-TF perturbations identified regulators that selectively opened chromatin at AMD GWAS variants inaccessible in resting RPE-1. Priming of partner motifs in chromatin made accessible by single-TF perturbations predicted TF pairs generating emergent transcriptional states in combinatorial Perturb-seq, providing a design principle for selecting informative interactions. Distinct TF pairs also showed variable convergence between polygenic AMD signals and Mendelian retinal disease genes, supporting an omnigenic model shaped by regulatory states. Finally, Mosaic, a chromatin-informed model of TF interaction phenotypes, nominated out-of-sample regulators, including a higher-order combination with experimentally validated emergent effects on AMD-associated programs. Engineered regulatory states thus bring hidden disease biology within experimental reach.
affiliations: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Application of Bayesian-Derived Gene Interaction Network and Subnetwork for Classification of Idiopathic Parkinson Disease with Biomarkers
papers.abstract: Given the expenses associated with Parkinson Disease (PD), it is imperative to develop a method for accurate diagnosis before emergence of motor symptoms. While there are tests that can measure early onset of PD, these tests still rely on subjective input from patients and can thus be biased. Factors influencing their accuracy include environmental agents such as education and culture. Thus, blood-based transcriptomic signatures are a promising direction for biomarkers in PD that are minimally invasive and more objective than clinical evaluation. In this paper, we analyzed gene expression from the PPMI cohort. Using a Bayesian framework, a gene interaction network was constructed to enhance differential expressed genes (DEG) analysis through signal diffusion. In tandem with clinical traits, 13 genes were selected for optimal discrimination using a random forest model. Within the holdout test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.972, outperforming contemporary models. The model performance demonstrates the potential of using blood-based transcriptomics to enhance clinical diagnosis of PD. Other genes recovered by network diffusion but missed by traditional DEG analysis are already validated as potential biomarkers in contemporary PD research. By combining transcriptomic signatures with clinical evaluation, accurate diagnosis of PD can happen before the major destruction of dopaminergic neurons, which is critical for effective intervention and treatment.
affiliations: University of Texas Health, San Antonio (corresponding author)

papers.title: Identification of the Col4a3-/- mouse as a model of chronic kidney disease-associated cachexia
papers.abstract: Background: Cachexia is a frequent complication of advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD), i.e. renal cachexia, particularly in patients undergoing hemodialysis in whom it represents one of the strongest predictors of morbidity and mortality. Yet, our understanding of the molecular mechanisms leading to body wasting in CKD and management of cachectic patients are still poorly defined. To date, a preclinical mouse model of robust and reproducible CKD-associated cachexia is missing. Here, we assessed in a systematic manner the cachectic phenotype of the genetic Col4a3-/- mouse model of CKD. Methods: 129/SvJ Col4a3-/- male and female animals were monitored longitudinally until they developed kidney failure. Measured glomerular filtration rate (mGFR), body composition and grip strength were recorded at baseline (6 weeks of age, before onset of kidney dysfunction) and at endpoint (CKD with weight loss or 12 weeks of age). The severity of CKD was confirmed by biochemical and histological analyses. Muscle atrophy was assessed via fiber cross-sectional area analysis, atrogene expression and transcriptomics. Adipose tissue wasting was assessed by measuring adipocyte area and proteins involved in lipid synthesis and breakdown. Liver acute phase response and systemic inflammation were evaluated by measuring circulating levels of key factors using ELISA. Results: Col4a3-/- animals developed CKD (decrease in mGFR: -85%, P<0.0001) and cachexia within 8-12 weeks of age. Cachexia was characterized by a progressive loss of body weight (-17.8% +/- 1.0, P<0.0001), lean (-8.2% +/- 2.0, P<0.0001) and fat mass (-66.5% +/- 4.7, P<0.0001) associated with reduced grip strength (-24.3% +/- 0.0, P=0.0002). At the tissue level, cachexia led to muscle atrophy and induction of atrogenes. Muscle transcriptomics further validated the cachectic phenotype of the Col4a3-/-, with 47% of genes altered in a similar manner with the well-established colon-C26 mouse model of cancer cachexia. It also revealed signatures that appeared more specific to renal cachexia. Adipose tissue wasting was characterized by a depletion in fat stores, consecutive to an imbalance between proteins involved in lipogenesis and lipolysis. Cachexia in this model was also associated with the induction of acute phase response in liver, elevated circulating levels of serum amyloid A and systemic inflammation, with the induction of established cachexia mediators (IL-6, GDF-15 P<0.0001). Both male and female mice developed cachexia. Conclusions: Our data highlight the potential of using the Col4a3-/- mouse model of CKD for the future study of renal cachexia, offering a more robust alternative to classically used models of partial nephrectomy or adenine-rich diet.

papers.title: Development of a nanomedicine approach to improve the therapeutic index of bexarotene.
papers.abstract: Bexarotene (BEX), a retinoid X receptor (RXR) agonist, has demonstrated therapeutic potential in oncology, neurodegenerative diseases and inflammatory conditions, including multiple sclerosis (MS). However, its broader clinical application is limited by poor aqueous solubility, low bioavailability, and dose-limiting adverse effects, most notably hypertriglyceridaemia. In this study, we investigated whether conjugation of BEX to dextrin, a biodegradable polysaccharide, could improve its physicochemical properties and therapeutic index. A dextrin-BEX conjugate was synthesised using succinoylated dextrin (30 mol%) and characterised by gel permeation chromatography (GPC), Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance (1H-NMR) and dynamic light scattering (DLS). The effects of conjugation on solubility, aggregation behaviour and biological activity were evaluated using in vitro cytotoxicity assays in leukaemia, liver and fibroblast cell lines, alongside measurements of intracellular triglyceride levels. The impact on lipid metabolism and toxicity was further assessed in an in vivo murine model of hyperlipidaemia. Dextrin conjugation significantly increased the aqueous solubility of BEX (from <0.004 mg/mL to 9.88 mg/mL) and led to the formation of nanoscale aggregates in solution. This was associated with a marked increase in in vitro potency, with IC50 values reduced by up to 14-fold across multiple cell lines. However, the increased cytotoxicity was not selective for cancer cells and was also observed in normal fibroblast and hepatic cell models. The dextrin-BEX conjugate did not induce intracellular triglyceride accumulation in vitro. In vivo, dextrin conjugation did not mitigate BEX-associated lipid dysregulation, while serum triglyceride levels and markers of liver injury remained unchanged. However, although free BEX led to a significant increase in liver weight after 14 days, the dextrin-BEX conjugate did not produce a statistically significant effect. In conclusion, dextrin conjugation markedly improves the solubility and in vitro potency of BEX but does not enhance its selectivity or reduce its metabolic toxicity in vivo. These findings suggest that while polymer conjugation is an effective strategy for addressing physicochemical limitations, it is insufficient to overcome the inherent dyslipidaemia associated with systemic RXR activation. Future strategies should focus on integrating targeting and controlled release mechanisms, alongside approaches that address the underlying pharmacological drivers of lipid dysregulation.

papers.title: T-bet marks contact-capable regulatory T cells embedded within Th1-dendritic cell networks in skin-draining lymph nodes
papers.abstract: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) adapt to inflammatory environments while preserving Foxp3-dependent suppressive identity. In type 1 inflammation, Tregs can upregulate T-bet, but whether T-bet Tregs represent a stable regulatory subset or exhibit plasticity toward an effector-like state remains incompletely understood. To probe the positioning and interactions of T-bet Tregs during type 1 inflammation, we performed live lymph node section microscopy in T-bet-ZsGreen Foxp3-RFP dual-reporter mice during a subcutaneous complete Freunds adjuvant (CFA) challenge. T-bet Tregs accumulated rapidly in the draining lymph nodes within 24 hours, coincident with the appearance of T-bet dendritic cells (DCs) and Th1-like CD4 T cells. Analysis of lymph node sections revealed that T-bet Tregs were incorporated into Th1-DC contact networks, displaying increased contact frequency and contact volume compared with T-bet- Tregs. In parallel, flow cytometric analysis of the immune response showed that T-bet Tregs maintained a stable regulatory profile distinct from T-bet effector T cells, with retained high expression of Foxp3 and regulatory-associated surface molecules including FR4, CD25, Nrp-1, CD39, and GARP. They also expressed elevated adhesion and activation-associated molecules, including LFA-1, ICOS, PD-1, CD44, and CD103 compared with T-bet- Tregs, and were enriched for CD103 cells across the inflammatory time course. Adoptive transfer studies further showed that pre-existing T-bet expression enhanced recovery of antigen-specific Tregs from CFA-draining lymph nodes in a context-dependent manner, whereas T-bet expression did not confer a unique advantage in canonical in vitro suppression of Th1 proliferation. Together, these findings identify T-bet Tregs as a contact-capable regulatory subset embedded within early Th1-DC networks during the priming phase of type 1 inflammation rather than a destabilized or effector-converted Treg population.
