A health-system-scale, episode-resolved multimodal atlas of cancer cachexia
papers.abstract: Using longitudinal data from 52,236 patients with cancer, this study created a multimodal atlas of cancer cachexia, demonstrating that weight loss episodes are linked to systemic serologic signatures and specific tumor genotypes and can be predicted using integrated clinical and molecular data, enabling earlier identification.

papers.title: Zbtb44-mediated transcriptional repression critically regulates colonic inflammation
papers.abstract: Poojary and colleagues show that the transcription factor Zbtb44 suppresses colonic inflammation and epithelial cell damage by deregulated T cells.

papers.title: An RNA mark for pluripotency
papers.abstract: A chemical modification of 7SK RNA links RNA modification to chromatin remodeling during human cell reprogramming. PUS7 installs this modification, enabling reprogramming without exogenous OCT4 and providing an alternative route to induced pluripotency.

papers.title: PUS7 pseudouridylation of 7SK orchestrates human somatic cell reprogramming into iPS cells
papers.abstract: Reprogramming human somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells) provides huge potential for regenerative medicine but its molecular regulation remains incompletely understood. In this study, we identify PUS7 as an RNA modification checkpoint that promotes acquisition of pluripotency. PUS7 loss markedly impairs reprogramming, whereas its overexpression accelerates reprogramming efficiency and kinetics. Mechanistically, PUS7 pseudouridylates U250 of the chromatin-associated noncoding RNA 7SK, enhancing its interaction with the BRG/BRM-associated factor (BAF) complex. Loss of this modification disrupts 7SK–BAF association, reduces BAF chromatin occupancy and decreases global chromatin accessibility. We further establish PSKM (PUS7, SOX2, KLF4, MYC) reprogramming, which generates iPS cells with faithful imprinting, robust lineage potential and improved developmental fidelity. PSKM-iPS cells differentiate efficiently toward neural and hematopoietic lineages and undergo gastrulation-like morphogenesis. These findings link 7SK pseudouridylation to chromatin remodeling and establish PSKM as a framework for generating high-quality human iPS cells for modeling and regenerative medicine.

papers.title: Skin-resident CXCR6+ memory CD4+ T cells and dendritic cells form dermal perivascular hubs that drive relapse in allergic dermatitis
papers.abstract: Tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells are heterogeneous, but how pathogenic subsets drive relapse in allergic dermatitis remains unclear. Asahina et al. identify a pathogenic CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM subset sustained through CXCL16-dependent clustering with CD301b+ cDC2s, revealing the TRM-DC niche as a potential therapeutic target for allergic dermatitis.

papers.title: Microbial cues for a stem-like lymphoid niche
Hitting KRAS G12D without the gut punch: Can immunotherapy make it last?
Toward the next generation of CAR T cell therapies for cancer
papers.abstract: CAR T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of blood cancers but faces persistent challenges in solid tumors. In this review, Usta and Mackall synthesize clinical lessons, next-generation engineering strategies, and emerging in vivo manufacturing approaches to define opportunities for broader, safer, and more effective CAR T cell therapies.

papers.title: A CK2-β-TrCP kinase-E3 ubiquitin ligase cascade is a metabolic sensor regulating tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase stability
papers.abstract: How metabolic enzyme levels are regulated is poorly understood. Studying the tryptophan (Trp)-metabolizing enzyme TDO2, Thielen et al. discover a CK2 kinase-β-TrCP E3 ligase pathway that regulates stability in response to substrate availability. Trp occupation of an exosite restricts degron accessibility, whereas low Trp releases the degron for phosphorylation-ubiquitylation-mediated degradation.

papers.title: PHYHD1-mediated translational control regulates renal cell carcinoma progression
papers.abstract: Liang et al. identify phytanoyl-CoA dioxygenase domain containing 1 (PHYHD1) as a tumor suppressor that regulates protein production in kidney cancer. Loss of PHYHD1 promotes disease progression by increasing ceramide transporter 1 (CERT1) production, uncovering a regulatory pathway that may help predict patient outcomes and provide a therapeutic opportunity for PHYHD1-deficient tumors.

papers.title: Rotational settings quantize nucleosome movement by chromatin regulators
papers.abstract: Chromatin regulators are thought to override intrinsic DNA sequence preferences. La et al. show regulators move nucleosomes in quantized 10 bp steps to take advantage of the shallow energy potential created by DNA sequence, preserving rotational setting and the DNA face contacting histones.

papers.title: Meningeal inflammation and arachnoid barrier breakdown in a mouse model of neonatal bacterial meningitis
papers.abstract: Kim et al. show the neonatal arachnoid barrier is compromised after GBS infection, causing increased permeability and proinflammatory signaling in most meningeal cell types including meningeal fibroblasts. A systemic injection of TNF-α alone is sufficient to break down the arachnoid barrier, suggesting its potential contribution in in vivo meningitis model.

papers.title: Aberrant recursive splicing in a human disease locus
papers.abstract: Boone et al. delete a recursive exon in CADM2 to understand the role of recursive splicing (RS) and explain these deletions’ association with ADHD. RS loss alters intronic RNA abundance, impacts transcript usage, decreases CADM2 expression, reduces exon usage downstream of the missing recursive exon, and perturbs neuronal gene programs.

papers.title: Disease-causing helix-8 mutations reprogram parathyroid hormone receptor-1 effector selectivity
papers.abstract: Höppner et al. show that disease-associated substitutions in PTH1R helix-8 selectively rewire receptor coupling to G proteins and βarrestin. Distinct mutations bias PTH1R engagement toward either Gαq or βarrestin pathways and impair Gαs activation. These findings reveal mutation-driven shifts in effector selectivity as a previously unrecognized mechanism in PTH1R-associated disease.

papers.title: Orally delivered metabolically reprogrammed probiotics for cascade-activated antitumor immunity in colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Wang et al. develop an oral metabolically engineered bacterial platform (EcN-HlpA-CGL [EHC]) for colorectal cancer immunotherapy, which triggers ferroptosis in colorectal cancer cells to boost immunogenicity, while the bacterial adjuvanticity reshapes the immunosuppressive microenvironment. This approach activates both systemic and gut mucosal immunity, effectively suppressing orthotopic tumor growth and metastasis.

papers.title: Gene regulation at the early human maternal–fetal interface
papers.abstract: Human placentation establishes a dynamic maternal–fetal interface in which fetal trophoblast cells coordinate tissue remodelling, immune adaptation and resource exchange to support pregnancy. In this Review, the authors discuss how single-cell, spatial and functional omics are uncovering gene regulatory mechanisms underlying trophoblast differentiation and maternal interactions and how these insights are advancing understanding of healthy placentation and pregnancy disorders.

papers.title: Filling the massive AI drug discovery data gap
Human-specific CCG-repeat insertion in the RBFOX1 promoter implicated in autism and speech enhances EGR1-responsive activity
papers.abstract: Human-specific promoter innovations have been predicted to shape human-specific traits. Here, we investigated the RBFOX1 splice regulator gene, which is specifically upregulated in human and songbird speech/song brain areas. We found that the human RBFOX1 promoter associated with autism and language impairment harbors a human-specific CCG trinucleotide insertion creating a functional CCG-repeat motif. Comparative single-nucleus transcriptome analyses of primate brains indicate that the human promoter drives differential expression in cortical excitatory neurons. Reporter assays show that the human CCG-repeat motif, relative to the chimpanzee allele, increases promoter activity with the EGR1 transcription factor. Genome-wide, the CCG-repeat motif marks core promoters of 104 genes, related to postsynaptic function and autism. In PTCHD1, a clinical duplication in autism patients creates another CCG-repeat motif that similarly increases EGR1-responsive promoter activity. Our findings suggest that small CCG-repeat variants in regulatory regions can exert large effects on gene regulation and apparent associated traits.
affiliations: The Rockefeller University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A StayGold-based calcium ion indicator
papers.abstract: Genetically encoded calcium ion (Ca2+) indicators (GECIs) enable visualization of Ca2+ dynamics in living systems but often suffer from limited photostability during prolonged imaging. The recent discovery of StayGold, a green fluorescent protein (FP) with exceptional brightness and photostability, opened the possibility of addressing this longstanding challenge. Here, we sought to establish whether a monomeric variant of StayGold (mStayGold) could be converted into a single FP-based GECI. Through extensive protein engineering, we generated a functional mStayGold-based GECI, HiCaRI (Highly intensiometric Ca2+ Responsive Indicator) by fusing Calmodulin (CaM) and the ckkap binding peptide from K-GECO1 into mStayGold(J). HiCaRI exhibits a large Ca2+-dependent inverse fluorescence response ({triangleup}F/Fmin = -15) while retaining high brightness and improved photostability relative to previously reported GFP-based GECIs. Although the current variant represents a first-generation prototype with shortcomings in terms of Ca2+ affinity and photostability (relative to StayGold and mStayGold(J)), this work demonstrates the feasibility of constructing single FP-based GECIs from a highly photostable fluorescent protein.
affiliations: The University of Tokyo (corresponding author)

papers.title: The essential role of connective-tissue cells during axolotl limb regeneration
papers.abstract: Axolotls (Ambystoma mexicanum) are known for their remarkable limb-regeneration abilities, which involve the formation of the blastema, a specialized structure consisting of progenitor cells contributed by all major tissues of the limb. Lateral plate mesoderm (LPM)-derived connective tissue (CT) cells dedifferentiate and play a critical role in blastema formation and subsequent limb regeneration. However, the complexity of the blastema cellular composition and the extent of CT participation and necessity have not been rigorously explored. To address this gap, we conducted spatial transcriptomics using a select array of probes, revealing that CT cells constitute up to 75% of the blastema cells. Genetic ablation of CT cells significantly delays or truncates limb regeneration, underscoring their necessity during this process. Analysis of the molecular profile during blastema formation identifies a temporally ordered gene expression pattern reflecting sequential phases of CT cell dedifferentiation, proliferation, and redifferentiation. Finally, a cell-cell communication inference identifies a CT-cell-autonomous FGFR1/AKT1 signaling axis as a cell-intrinsic molecular requirement for limb regeneration. Together, our work reaffirms the central role of CT cells in axolotl limb regeneration and lays the foundation for identifying molecular mechanisms that govern blastema formation during the initial phases of limb regeneration.
affiliations: Mount Desert Island Biological Laboratory (corresponding author)

papers.title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.
affiliations: University of Denver (corresponding author)

papers.title: Non-canonical cleavage expands prime editing in 5' direction
papers.abstract: Cleavage-dependent CRISPR-Cas gene editing relies on RNA-guided DNA cleavage that drives cellular machinery to incorporate intended edits. Beyond canonical cleavage, CRISPR nucleases can also execute non-canonical cleavage on the displaced DNA strand. Here, we report a modified design principle for prime editing that leverages the non-canonical cleavage activity, enabling editing in the 5' direction of a classic nick site. We elucidate the non-canonical-cleavage-driven reverse transcription pathway that initiates upstream of the classic nick site. We identify competition between the canonical and non-canonical routes, which can be modulated by rationally designing RNA templates carrying the intended edits. We demonstrate that cellular physiology enhances editing efficiency from individual reverse-transcription product yet exerts limited influence on pathway competitions. Our findings revise the design principle of prime editing and establish a new dimension for engineering CRISPR-Cas systems by harnessing its intrinsic, non-host-specific, non-canonical cleavage activity.
affiliations: Shandong University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Identifiability of metabolic resilience from sparse longitudinal metabolomics
papers.abstract: Sparse and irregular longitudinal metabolomic measurements can make dynamical quantities numerically estimable without making them scientifically identifiable. We formulate effective-landscape inference as an observation-timescale inverse problem and evaluate its operating characteristics using stochastic systems with known ground truth and longitudinal stool metabolomics from the Integrative Human Microbiome Project. Across simulation ensembles, recovery of a known double-well topology declined sharply as observations became sparse, whereas the tested monostable controls did not generate spurious secondary minima. Findings establish an identifiability hierarchy: global topology requires sufficient within-subject state-space coverage, whereas local return descriptors remain vulnerable to bias from the observation process. The framework therefore shifts the emphasis from assigning stability labels to determining what a sampling design can support. It provides a basis for designing denser longitudinal experiments and for validating clinical and machine-learning studies in which sparse observations might otherwise be overinterpreted as evidence about underlying dynamics.
affiliations: UC Berkeley (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chromid transforms opportunistic pathogen into beneficial symbiont to raise coral's thermal tipping point
papers.abstract: Resilient turbid coral reefs, found 1{degrees} north of the equator, experience fewer and less intense bleaching events despite being situated within the world's busiest shipping port in highly urbanised Singapore. We hypothesised that bacteria within the coral holobiont play a role in maintaining coral health by conferring traits that enhance thermal tolerance. Eleven Pseudovibrio isolates were obtained from the scleractinian coral Pachyseris speciosa, and their genomes differed by only four single nucleotide polymorphisms. A ~490 kbp chromid, pCJH, was present in 7 of the 11 isolates. A Pseudovibrio isolate without pCJH is an opportunistic pathogen of P. speciosa, accelerating bleaching disease. In contrast, the chromid reduces Pseudovibrio's fecundity, enhances its host colonisation and consequently increases P. speciosa's thermal tolerance by 1 {degrees}C. Interaction analyses in experimentally heat-stressed corals revealed a negative interaction between Pseudovibrio and Vibrio ASVs. The Pseudovibrio genomes and chromid encode several diffusible antibiotic biosynthetic gene clusters and two type six secretion systems (T6SS) for contact-dependent inhibition, with both types of inhibitory activity shown against opportunistic coral pathogens from local (i.e. isolated from the same coral host) and type-strain Vibrio spp. Together, these findings support the Coral Probiotic Hypothesis that bacteria enhance coral resilience, and identify a chromid responsible for Pseudovibrio's climatically driven Jekyll-and-Hyde lifestyle from opportunistic pathogen to beneficial symbiont.
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (corresponding author)

papers.title: Spatiotemporal distribution of Delta-like protein 1 during mouse pituitary ontogeny and its relationship with differentiating endocrine cell populations
papers.abstract: Delta-like protein 1 (DLK1) is a transmembrane protein involved in the regulation of cellular differentiation and stem cell maintenance in several tissues, including the pituitary gland. Although DLK1 expression has been reported in the adult pituitary, its spatiotemporal distribution during mouse pituitary development remains incompletely characterized. The aim of this study was to analyse the distribution of DLK1 during embryonic and postnatal development of the mouse pituitary gland and to characterize its relationship with hormone-producing cell populations. Immunohistochemistry was performed in Swiss albino mice from embryonic day 9.5 (e9.5) to postnatal day 15 (p15). Double immunofluorescence was used at e18.5 and p15 to examine the association of DLK1 immunoreactivity with ACTH-, TSH-, GH-, FSH- and PRL-producing cells. DLK1 immunoreactivity was detected from the earliest stages of pituitary development in Rathke`s pouch and the ventral diencephalon. During embryonic development, DLK1-ir cells were widely distributed throughout adenohypophyseal and neurohypophyseal primordia. As development progressed, DLK1 immunoreactivity became progressively regionalized within the anterior, intermediate and tuberal lobes, as well as in the median eminence of the hypothalamus and the posterior pituitary lobe. Colocalization of DLK1 with each of the hormone-producing cell populations analysed was observed at e18.5 and p15. Semiquantitative analysis at p15 indicated that approximately 32% of adenohypophyseal cells were DLK1-immunoreactive. These findings provide a detailed description of the spatiotemporal distribution of DLK1 during mouse pituitary ontogeny and suggest that DLK1 immunoreactivity is associated with differentiating endocrine cell populations throughout pituitary development.
affiliations: Universidad de La Laguna (corresponding author)

papers.title: Coordinated Enhancement of Molecular and Spatial Fidelity for Biological Inference in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Understanding tissue organization requires accurate molecular quantification and faithful spatial localization. Spatial omics, particularly spatial transcriptomics (ST), face measurement trade-offs that limit simultaneous achievement of molecular and spatial fidelity across spatial resolution, detection sensitivity, molecular-tissue alignment and cell-level fidelity. Existing computational methods typically target individual aspects and optimize them in isolation, despite their interdependence. Here we present FOCUS, a multimodal generative foundation model for coordinated ST enhancement. FOCUS integrates native ST with histology images, cell masks, scRNA-seq references and spatial co-expression priors through task-specific modules, with cross-task coordination enabling joint correction of co-occurring limitations. FOCUS improved the performance of individual enhancement tasks and provided additional gains with coordinated mitigation of coupled limitations. Across immunology, tissue development and oncology, FOCUS recovered biologically consistent patterns obscured in native ST or isolated enhancement, enabling clearer inference of neutrophil-tumor interactions, spatial osteocyte differentiation and primary-metastatic HNSCC programs. Together, FOCUS establishes coordinated enhancement of molecular and spatial fidelity as a strategy for downstream biological inference from ST.
affiliations: Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Cambridge, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Inherent limitations of zero-shot mutation prediction in protein engineering
papers.abstract: Predicting mutation effects is critical for protein engineering. A commonly pursued strategy is zero-shot prediction with deep-learning models, whose performance is typically evaluated using aggregate benchmark scores that obscure multidimensional biological tradeoffs. Here, we evaluate sequence, structure, and hybrid foundation models across curated datasets to expose the practical limitations of zero-shot predictions. We demonstrate that model performance is highly variable and heavily influenced by experimental noise and competing phenotypic goals. Notably, predictions from competing models often correlate more strongly with one another than with experimental outcomes. While current models effectively filter deleterious mutations and enrich high-scoring variants for natural functions, they struggle to identify precise optimal mutations and consistently fail to predict mutations that drive new-to-nature functions. These models learn from evolutionary constraints that tend to oppose the extreme biophysical optimizations required in targeted engineering. Consequently, zero-shot scoring serves as a valuable initial filter but cannot substitute for task-specific prediction.
affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin (corresponding author)

papers.title: A critical evaluation of Gene Ontology priors in biologically-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: Biologically-informed neural networks (BINNs) embed prior knowledge such as the Gene Ontology (GO) into their architecture to produce interpretable representations, yet whether and how this prior improves performance or interpretation remains unclear. We introduce GONNECT, a BINN incorporating GO into an autoencoder. We evaluate GO constraints in the encoder, decoder, or both on RNA-seq tumour samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), comparing against published BINNs (OntoVAE, VEGA), an unconstrained baseline, randomized priors, and untrained networks. Across various performance metrics, GO structure adds little to reconstruction or latent-space organization, frequently matched by randomized or unconstrained models. Node activations agree with a gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)-derived reference, but this agreement largely arises from the architectural constraint: it is lost when GO connections are randomized, present even before training in the encoder, and learned in the decoder. Regularized soft links outside GO (GONNECT-SL) are unstable across runs and concentrate where the ontology is sparse, compensating for the prior's constraints rather than revealing new biology. Within this setting, we find no evidence that node activations capture biological information beyond that encoded by the predefined gene sets, suggesting that their apparent interpretability largely reflects the prior imposed by the architecture.
affiliations: Delft University of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Histology-aware Inference of Cell-cell Communication in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Cell-cell communication (CCC) is fundamental to tissue organization and function, yet inferring communication from spatial transcriptomics (ST) remains challenging because molecular and spatial information does not fully capture the anatomical context of signaling. Paired hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained images provide complementary insights into tissue architecture and cellular morphology, which remain underutilized as the explicit contextual constraint of CCC inference. Here we present HARMONIC, a histology-aware graph learning framework for anatomically contextualized CCC inference from ST and H&E images. HARMONIC uses conditional mutual information to model dependencies among tissue architecture, ligand-receptor-mediated signaling, gene expression and morphology, and integrates these representations through self-supervised graph learning. Across synthetic and biological datasets spanning platforms, species and tissues, HARMONIC suppresses less anatomically plausible interactions while recovering context-supported signaling across tumor-immune interfaces, necrotic transitions, anatomical compartments and microvascular structures. These findings establish tissue architecture as the explicit contextual constraint of spatial CCC inference.
affiliations: Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Cambridge, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cell Painting and machine learning for mechanistic profiling of hepatotoxic botanicals and their constituents
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Botanicals are widely consumed as herbal remedies and plant-derived products, but their complex and variable chemical composition presents major challenges for safety assessment. Although hepatotoxicity has been reported for several botanicals, the constituent compounds responsible and the underlying mechanisms often remain poorly characterised. OBJECTIVES We aimed to determine whether Cell Painting could identify candidate constituent drivers of botanical bioactivity and generate hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action in primary human hepatocytes. METHODS We profiled 13 botanical extracts and 85 known constituents across multiple concentrations using Cell Painting alongside assays of metabolic activity and membrane integrity. To interpret morphological phenotypes, we trained machine-learning models using a Cell Painting reference atlas of >1,000 chemicals linked to ToxCast/Tox21 molecular and cellular bioactivity annotations. RESULTS Cell Painting detected bioactivity in 11/13 botanical extracts and 46/85 constituents, compared with 9/13 extracts and 40/85 constituents in the cell-health assays, and generally detected activity at lower concentrations. For 9/13 extracts, at least one constituent was active at a lower concentration than the corresponding botanical extract, supporting the contribution of a subset of potent constituents to mixture-level responses. Aristolochia and goldenseal were the most potent extracts across Cell Painting and cell-health assays and contained highly active constituents. Reference-atlas models generated specific mechanistic hypotheses, including cytotoxicity-, endocrine-, and genotoxicity-associated responses for several botanicals and constituents. CONCLUSION These results support Cell Painting combined with machine learning as a sensitive approach for characterising cellular responses to botanicals, prioritising candidate constituent drivers of hepatotoxicity-associated phenotypes, and generating testable hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action.
affiliations: European Bioinformatics Institute, European Molecular Biology Laboratory, Hinxton, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Targeting Lysosomal MCOLN1/TRPML1 Ion Channels to Alleviate Diabetes Mellitus via a Ca2+- CaMKKβ-AMPK pathway
papers.abstract: Type 2 Diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a metabolic syndrome characterized by hyperglycemia and various complications. Current drugs are limited by side effects and resistance, necessitating novel targets and therapies. Previous studies have shown that MK-83, a synthetic agonist of transient receptor potential mucolipin 1 (TRPML1/ MCOLN1), a lysosomal Ca2+ channel, activates adenosine 5'-monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a key therapeutic target in diabetes. However, whether targeting TRPML1 can treat T2DM remains unclear. In this study, we found that transgenic overexpression or pharmacological activation of TRPML1 regulates AMPK phosphorylation via a Ca2+-CaMKK{beta}-dependent mechanism. This activation promotes glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4) translocation and increases intracellular glucose uptake. Conversely, genetic inactivation or pharmacologically inhibition of TRPML1 blocks both AMPK activation and glucose uptake. More importantly, pharmacological activation of TRPML1 in vivo alleviates hyperglycemia in db/db mice (a T2DM model), as evidenced by random blood glucose levels, fasting blood glucose levels and HbA1c levels. Furthermore, other hallmark features of db/db mice- including impaired oral glucose tolerance, reduced insulin tolerance, and elevated ALT and AST levels- were all ameliorated upon TRPML1 activation. Hence, targeting lysosomal TRPML1 channel represents a promising therapeutic strategy for T2DM, with highly specific TRPML1 agonists as potential anti-diabetic agents.
affiliations: Zhejiang University of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mesodermal-niche interactions direct specification and differentiation of pancreatic endocrine cells in human multilineage organoids
authors: Martinez Garcia de la Torre, R. A.
papers.abstract: Tissues develop and function within complex microenvironments, where diverse cell types interact through tightly regulated spatial and temporal cues. These interactions shape cell identity, differentiation, and spatial organisation, ultimately establishing functional tissue architecture. Understanding and modelling these processes in humans therefore require multicellular systems that capture the cellular diversity and interactions of developing tissues. Here, we combine spatial transcriptomics of the human foetal pancreas with an induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based multilineage model that recapitulates key features of human endocrine pancreatic development and incorporates a mesoderm-derived cellular niche. We comprehensively characterise the multilineage organoid transcriptomes across differentiation stages and benchmark their fidelity against single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiles of human foetal pancreas. We demonstrate that iPSC-derived pancreatic mesenchymal cells promote endocrine commitment by restricting off-target cell fates and enhancing {beta}-cell differentiation. Together, these findings establish a framework for investigating the cellular mechanisms underlying human endocrine development and disease.
affiliations: King's College London (corresponding author)

papers.title: simSOMA: a cell-lineage based simulator of the somatic VAF spectrum in plants
papers.abstract: Plants accumulate somatic mutations during growth, some of which spread into branches, organs, or reproductive tissues. These variants are of growing interest because they underlie bud-sport traits in perennial crops, contribute to within-organism selection, and are a source of heritable genetic variation. Recent genomic sequencing of bulk or layer-enriched plant tissues has revealed complex variant allele-frequency (VAF) spectra. Interpreting these spectra requires modelling how somatic mutations are filtered or amplified by shoot growth, branching, and organ formation, a problem that is difficult to derive analytically. Here, we present simSOMA, a modular simulator linking plant topologies to shoot apical meristem cell-lineage dynamics. simSOMA models mutation accumulation during stem-cell self-renewal, clonal expansion to the meristem periphery, branch founding, and organ formation. We demonstrate how simSOMA isolates developmental processes that shape organ-level VAF spectra and among-organ variant sharing, and transforms spectra for bulk or layer-enriched sampling, phased or unphased readouts, and read-level sequencing noise. SAM layers can be simulated as independent cell lineages and combined into bulk tissue samples. simSOMA can be used to explore developmental hypotheses about the origin of somatic variation, and to design somatic sequencing experiments and variant-detection strategies. simSOMA is available at https://github.com/jlab-code/simSOMA.
affiliations: Technical University of Munich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Microbial Invasion and Immunosuppression Drives Adenoma Progression in Early Colorectal Cancer Development
papers.abstract: Several inherited predispositions to colorectal cancer exist, most notably familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), which typically involves a germline loss-of-function mutation in one APC allele. A second hit in APC or related loci leads to aberrant Wnt signalling, triggering adenoma formation with near-complete penetrance. Yet, substantial variability in disease onset and severity, even among siblings with identical APC germline mutations, implicates environmental modifiers. Emerging evidence points to the gut microbiome as a critical regulator of adenoma initiation and progression, particularly in early-onset CRC. Here, we show that bacterial invasion is associated with neutrophil immunosuppression, T-cell exclusion and adenoma progression in a porcine model of FAP. Longitudinal mapping of progressing and regressing polyps using single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics and integrated microbiome profiling resolved the cellular and microbial architecture underlying these divergent lesion states. Single-cell RNA-seq identified 35 cell subpopulations and showed that regressing polyps are enriched for central-memory CD4+ T cells, cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and inflammatory neutrophils, whereas progressing polyps contain immunosuppressive/PD-L1-associated neutrophils, regulatory and dysfunctional T cells. Spatial transcriptomics with a custom host panel and targeted bacterial probes linked bacterial-high adenomatous regions to immunosuppressive neutrophil niches and T cell exclusion, while regressing lesions showed predominantly lumen-adjacent bacterial localization and spatially organized immune surveillance. These results provide a spatially resolved map of cellular and microbial organisation in early colorectal polyp progression and regression and reveal a microbiome-driven, neutrophil-mediated mechanism of early tumour progression with implications for CRC interception.
affiliations: Technical University of Munich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Phosphorylation of β-arrestins impacts recruitment to Parathyroid Hormone Receptor 1 (PTH1R) at the cell surface and endosomes
papers.abstract: {beta}-arrestins 1 and 2 are intracellular adaptor proteins that regulate the subcellular localisation and signalling of GPCRs including Parathyroid Hormone Receptor 1 (PTH1R), which produces {beta}-arrestin-dependent signalling that may selectively stimulate bone anabolism. {beta}-arrestins can themselves be regulated by post-translational modifications including phosphorylation, which dictates the translocation and signalling of the few GPCRs studied in this context to date. We aimed to investigate whether phosphorylation of {beta}-arrestins modulates their subcellular translocation in response to PTH1R activation. Translocation of {beta}-arrestins to the plasma membrane and early endosomes was quantified using BRET biosensors and immunocytochemistry with high content analysis. Phosphoknockout or phosphomimetic mutations were introduced to previously demonstrated phosphorylation sites in {beta}-arrestins 1 and 2, initially in bulk to assess overall effects. Plasma membrane translocation was altered only subtly, whereas early endosome translocation was markedly reduced for both mutations but to a greater degree for the phosphomimetic. Contributions of individual or paired sites were assessed by restoration to wildtype from the bulk phosphomimetic mutants. Dual restoration of S13 and T275 in {beta}-arrestin 1, or the analogous sites in {beta}-arrestin 2, restored the greatest degrees of early endosomal translocation, with complete restoration for {beta}-arrestin 1 and partial for {beta}-arrestin 2. Restoration of other sites had minimal or no effect. Dephosphorylation therefore appears to be required for PTH1R-stimulated {beta}-arrestin early endosomal translocation, with different phosphorylation sites implicated than some other GPCRs. These findings raise the possibility of differential {beta}-arrestin regulation by distinct stimuli which may have implications in therapeutic targeting of {beta}-arrestin-dependent pathways.
affiliations: University of Auckland (corresponding author)

papers.title: Spatial isotope tracing maps compartmentalized nutrient use across the adult fruit fly
papers.abstract: Drosophila melanogaster is a powerful model for studying systemic metabolism. Although metabolism is compartmentalized across tissues, prior work in adult Drosophila has mostly measured it in dissected tissues rather than in situ, limiting the spatial information that can be gained. Here, we combine whole-fly mass-spectrometry imaging with stable-isotope tracing and flux modeling to quantify metabolic activities across the adult fruit fly in a spatially resolved manner. Across 68 tracer-fed Oregon-R female flies and 187,709 pixels, we map 81 metabolites onto eight annotated regions, including muscle, fat body, gut, and nervous system. Glucose labeling and fitted relative fluxes indicate higher glycolytic and tricarboxylic acid cycle turnover in thoracic muscle than in abdominal fat body; proline labels the nervous system and eye; glutamine the abdominal reproductive system and gut. Alanine carries glucose-derived carbon through the hemolymph and transfers nitrogen into glutamate. In flies bearing yorkie-driven gut tumors, alanine contribution to malate rises in gut and abdomen, and reducing gut alanine uptake lowers tumor burden. Together, this work establishes a framework for quantitative spatial metabolic analysis, showing compartmentalized nutrient use across the adult fruit fly.
affiliations: Harvard Medical School (corresponding author)

papers.title: Beyond the Final Layer: Evaluating Single-Cell Foundation Model Representations for Molecular Prediction
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) are commonly benchmarked using final-layer embeddings, although useful depth may depend on the task. We evaluate Geneformer, scBERT, scGPT, and scFoundation as frozen feature extractors for cell-type and perturbation-response prediction using layer-wise probes, leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) selection, readout controls, representation diagnostics, centered kernel alignment (CKA), and retrieval/collapse analyses. Intermediate layers significantly improve cell-type accuracy for scGPT and scBERT in several settings, while Geneformer and scFoundation generally show performance comparable to their final layers. For perturbation prediction, LODO identifies layer 1 as an earliest-on-par candidate across all four models, without establishing universal superiority. Paired scGPT CLS and mean-pooling analyses show that readout affects preferred depth. CKA and representation metrics reveal model- and task-dependent geometric changes, while retrieval and collapse checks support the robustness of perturbation findings. We recommend reporting extraction depth, readout, selection protocol, and task-specific diagnostics. A validated non-final layer may also reduce computation, although efficiency was not directly benchmarked.
affiliations: Department of Computational Medicine and Bioinformatics, University of Michigan (corresponding author)

papers.title: SP2 impedes the pluripotent-to-totipotent state transition in an RA-dependent manner
papers.abstract: The pluripotency-to-totipotency transition represents a transient developmental reversal that remains not fully understood. Although chemical approaches can induce a 2-cell (2C)-like state in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), how cells choose between totipotency acquisition and alternative developmental fates remains unclear. Here, we established a chemical induction system that efficiently drives mESCs toward the 2C-like state. We found that mESCs under induction treatment followed distinct trajectories, with a subset activating developmental programs rather than acquiring 2C-like features. SP2 was preferentially expressed along this developmental trajectory and progressively reduced during successful 2C-like induction. Loss of SP2 enhanced 2C-like cell formation, whereas SP2 overexpression impaired the transition. Transcriptomic analysis of SP2-deficient cells showed reduced expression of developmental genes, including Hox family genes, accompanied by increased expression of 2C-associated genes. Consistent with this finding, SP2 occupied the promoters of Hox family genes in the reprogrammed cells. Notably, the effect of SP2 loss was particularly evident upon activation of retinoic acid (RA) signaling, linking SP2-dependent developmental gene activation to the RA-responsive branch of the transition. Altogether, our findings identify SP2 function as a barrier that limits acquisition of the 2C-like state by promoting a competing developmental program, highlighting the importance of coordinated extracellular signaling and transcriptional regulation in directing cell fate transitions.
affiliations: Guangzhou National Laboratory, Guangzhou, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: ETSAM: effectively segmenting cell membranes in cryo-electron tomograms
Anticipatory regulation of stem cell-based technologies: a UK case study
papers.abstract: Biotechnological advances are prompting governments to fear falling behind and missing out on growth and investment. Yet science often moves faster and less predictably than legislation. Using the United Kingdom’s stem cell regulation as a case study, we examine anticipatory regulation, sandboxes, and other agile governance tools for managing both over-regulation and regulatory gaps.

papers.title: A tetracycline-inducible promoter for gene expression in Gram-negative bacteria including Acinetobacter baumannii
papers.abstract: Carbohydrate inducible promoters on expression plasmids are widely used for biotechnology and basic science research. However, using carbohydrates for inducers has drawbacks including influencing bacterial metabolism, the inducer being used as a carbon source by the bacteria, high background expression, and only a subset of cells experiencing promoter activation. Furthermore, some bacteria including the pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii currently lack good carbohydrate-inducible promoters. To address this issue, a tetracycline-inducible promoter, PtetB, isolated from A. baumannii was cloned and evaluated in a number of important bacteria: Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Pseudomonas fluorescens, and Serratia marcescens. A highly sensitive luxCDABE reporter was used to evaluate promoter activity. S. marcescens strains with elevated and reduced cyclic-AMP levels were used to evaluate the impact of cAMP on PtetB function. The PtetB promoter was induced over 800-fold in A. baumannii and 10-750-fold inducible in the other tested species. Background expression was lower from PtetB in the pseudomonads than previously described carbohydrate inducible promoters. Data indicated that the PtetB promoter system may be a useful tool for future basic science research with the tested bacteria.
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh (corresponding author)

papers.title: EF-P-resolved ribosome stalling and collision trigger Rae1-mediated mRNA decay
papers.abstract: Ribosome stalling compromises proteome integrity and cellular fitness, and requires efficient mechanisms to eliminate problematic mRNAs and rescue blocked ribosomes. We previously identified Rae1 as an endoribonuclease that cleaves mRNAs at the tail end of stalled ribosomes to promote mRNA degradation in Bacillus subtilis. Here, we show that Rae1 has a broader role in the quality control of mRNAs that encounter translation problems. Global 5-end sequencing identified 31 previously unknown Rae1 cleavage sites, many of them associated with ribosome pausing at polyproline motifs in the absence of elongation factor P (EF-P). We also demonstrate that Rae1 cleaves mRNAs with ribosomes stalled on truncated transcripts lacking a stop-codon (non-stop mRNAs), provided that the transcript is sufficiently long to accommodate multiple collided ribosomes. Rae1 cleavage depends on a cytosine-poor context at the cut site, showing that both ribosome collisions and RNA sequence at the cleavage site govern the ability of Rae1 to promote the removal of stalled ribosomes from mRNA.
affiliations: CNRS UNIVERSITE PARIS CITE (corresponding author)

papers.title: Asymmetric bloom lengthening drives high-latitude ocean chlorophyll accumulation imbalance
papers.abstract: This study shows that unequal changes in bloom duration between hemispheres contribute to contrasting high-latitude ocean chlorophyll trends, linking asymmetric phytoplankton phenology to marine ecosystem changes under climate warming.

papers.title: In situ reduction-driven formation of sub-nanometer alternating heterostructures
papers.abstract: Sub-nanometer heterostructures offer opportunities to tune interfacial reactivity, but their precise construction remains challenging. Here, the authors report alternating Ni/NiMoO₄ heterostructures that promote hydrogen evolution and sustain durable high-current electrolysis.

papers.title: A method quantifying soil melanin to understand fungal impacts on soil carbon stability
papers.abstract: Fungal necromass, particularly dead microbial cells rich in melanin, is an important contributor to long-term soil carbon stabilization. Progress in understanding the role of soil melanin is limited by the lack of validated analytical methods. DNA-based approaches estimate only the genetic potential for melanin production and therefore provide indirect evidence of melanin occurrence. To directly assess soil melanin, we evaluated spectroscopic and spectrophotometric assays; however, both approaches proved insufficiently specific due to interference from chemically related compounds. Here, we introduce a liquid chromatography method that enables quantification of major fungal melanin types in soils. By enabling direct quantification of fungal melanin in soil, this framework allows longstanding hypotheses regarding melanized fungal necromass and soil carbon stabilization to be tested mechanistically. Here, we show with the proposed method that soil melanin concentrations are strongly correlated with total soil carbon, supporting a central role for fungal melanin in long-term soil carbon stabilization.

papers.title: A supergene and genomic mosaicism are associated with phenotypic evolution in Galápagos tree finches
papers.abstract: Adaptive radiations provide powerful models to study the origins of phenotypic novelty and species diversity. Darwin’s finches constitute a classic example of adaptive radiation, in which beak morphology is a key trait related to fitness. Here, we focus on Camarhynchus tree finches by analyzing whole genomes in combination with morphological data to revisit long-standing questions regarding their origins raised before genetic evidence became available. Camarhynchus diversified over the last 100,000 years, yielding some striking morphological differences despite shallow genetic divergence. We identify several highly differentiated loci, including G03 , a supergene affecting beak and body size. We reveal a striking example of genomic mosaicism, in which autosomal differentiation between two sympatric species is restricted primarily to a single locus -( G03 )- that approaches fixation, shifting them from one phenotypic optimum to another. Contextualized in a broader phylogenetic framework, we also reveal an unexpected diversity of G03 haplotypes and show that the small and large G03 alleles diverged early in the radiation, suggesting a key genetic innovation enabling ecological expansion among species of Darwin’s finches. Our results further establish Camarhynchus as a model example of speciation with gene flow, underscoring the broader role of hybridization in generating biodiversity.

papers.title: HCV incidence and prevalence trends among people who use drugs in France 2004 to 2023
papers.abstract: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) remains a key public health challenge, particularly among people who use and inject drugs (PWUD, PWID). While direct-acting antivirals (DAA) have revolutionized HCV treatment, meeting the WHO’s 2030 elimination target requires accurate estimation of incidence and prevalence to guide prevention and care. We analyze cross-sectional surveys conducted in France in 2004, 2013, and 2023, recruiting PWUD at harm reduction services and collecting behavioral and biological data. We estimate age-and time-dependent prevalence of HCV antibodies and HCV RNA using multivariate regression models while incidence was estimated from two-state transmission models. The demographic profile of PWUD has aged over time (mean age 35 years in 2004 vs. 44 in 2023) while injection prevalence remained stable (61.7% in 2023). Between 2013 and 2023, HCV burden declined substantially: HCV RNA prevalence fell from 19.4% (95% CI 16.3–23.0) to 9.5% (7.2–12.3) among all PWUD, and from 29.6% to 14.5% among PWID. Incidence among PWID decreased from 6.5 (4.1–8.0) to 2.4 (1.4–4.2) per 100 person-years. These reductions likely reflect the combined impact of DAA scale-up and harm reduction policies, marking substantial progress toward elimination targets. However, ongoing transmission highlights persistent barriers requiring targeted public health actions.

papers.title: Time-lapse RESOLFT nanoscopy empowered by deep learning
papers.abstract: Capturing the dynamic interplay of proteins and organelles within cells requires microscopy methods with high spatial and temporal resolution. Reversible Saturable OpticaL Fluorescent Transition (RESOLFT) demonstrated great potential for live cell nanoscopy by using patterned light and reversibly switching fluorescent probes. Despite the latest improvement in both switching probes and optical schemes, the duration and frame rate of the time-lapse are still limited by photobleaching and spatial sampling steps. Here, we present two distinct strategies based on deep learning to restore low signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) or under-sampled images pushing the experimental boundaries of RESOLFT. We demonstrate the capability of Hierarchical DivNoising (HDN) to restore low-SNR RESOLFT data while maintaining full spatial resolution, both in supervised and unsupervised settings. This allows a 10-fold reduction of light dose per frame, and up to 5 times longer imaging. Then, we present Fast-MoNaLISA, a method that reduces the acquisition time of any point-scanning systems. This allows a 4-fold increase in frame rate, and a reduction of scanning artefacts. Overall, our methods open up possibilities for dynamic data acquisition at the sub-organelle level, such as vesicles budding in and out from intact mitochondria, or the actin meshwork formation and dissociation.

papers.title: Intensification of near-inertial currents in the Atlantic Ocean over the past two decades
papers.abstract: Ocean drifter observations reveal that Atlantic near-inertial currents intensified by almost 4% per decade during 2003–2022. This intensification is primarily driven by changes in wind forcing associated with mesoscale weather systems.

papers.title: An automated operon refactoring workflow for heterologous expression of non-ribosomal peptide biosynthetic gene clusters
papers.abstract: Existing approaches for biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) discovery are labor-intensive, depend on de novo DNA synthesis and are difficult to scale. Here we show that an automated platform for one-step assembly and refactoring of BGCs facilitates facile novel product discovery.

papers.title: Intrinsically flexible inorganic piezoelectric subnanowire enables wireless wearable bioelectronics for non-invasive multimodal human-machine interfacing
H3K27M cooperates with ASCL1 to maintain progenitor states and drive gliomagenesis
papers.abstract: Histone 3 lysine 27-to-methionine substitutions (H3K27M) drive aggressive diffuse midline gliomas by blocking differentiation of radial glial progenitor cells committed to oligodendrogenesis. We establish prolonged differentiation as a powerful tool to uncover regulators of glioma cell states and demonstrate that the pioneer transcription factor (TF) ASCL1 is a key mediator of H3K27M-driven plasticity and tumorigenesis. H3K27M prevents Polycomb silencing of ASCL1 , co-opting this TF to maintain oligodendroglial progenitor states. Consistently, ASCL1 loss drastically impairs tumor formation in vivo. Mechanistically, ASCL1 synergizes with H3K27M to redistribute the chromatin remodeler BRG1 to regulatory elements co-enriched for ASCL1 and SOX motifs, promoting expression of stem and neural progenitor genes at the expense of mesenchymal genes in DMGs. ASCL1 loss acts as a “fire exit”, enabling alternative differentiation despite H3K27M, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeting stalled differentiation and tumor plasticity in histone-mutant gliomas and cancers with a stem cell hierarchy.

papers.title: Fruit-eating adaptations in a Late Cretaceous oviraptorosaur (Theropoda)
papers.abstract: The diversification of herbivorous dinosaurs and the rise of angiosperms in the Late Cretaceous are each well established, but the link between them is debated. Broad-scale diversity patterns in the two groups appear not to closely align, and there is no direct evidence of dinosaur adaptation to angiosperm-based diets. Here we describe Infernogallus jamesi gen. et. sp. nov., a diminutive caenagnathid oviraptorosaur, and show that these theropods were specialised herbivores that originated alongside the rise of fleshy angiosperm fruits. The nearly complete, articulated skull of Infernogallus jamesi —the first for the clade—reveals drastic changes to the adductor musculature organisation, unique in non-avian theropods but converged upon by extant frugivorous parrots. These modifications enabled extensive oral processing of soft food using anteroposterior movement of the mandible and occlusion of ridges and grooves on opposed elements. Altogether, this attests to a highly specialised herbivorous diet in caenagnathids, which likely consisted in large part of fleshy angiosperm fruits, which increased in size and diversity in concert with the radiation of oviraptorosaurs. Caenagnathids thus provide one of the strongest candidates for angiosperm-based diet adaptations in dinosaurs, but their role in the Late Cretaceous proliferation of fruit—which shaped early Cenozoic flora—remains unclear.

papers.title: Large-scale identical-location electron microscopy enables quantifying nanoparticulate electrocatalyst degradation
papers.abstract: Fuel cells convert chemical energy into electricity, and their performance relies on electrocatalysts whose durability during operation remains poorly understood. Deep mechanistic insight into electrocatalyst stability is essential to design durable, resource-efficient fuel cells. Nanoparticulate electrocatalysts degrade via diverse nanoscale processes, yet particle-to-particle heterogeneity in structure, support interaction, and local microenvironment make true particle-level quantification and understanding impossible with classical approaches. Here we scale up identical-location scanning transmission electron microscopy, which repeatedly images the very same nanoparticles, to track the structural evolution of hundreds of carbon-supported platinum-cobalt nanoparticles, a prototypical oxygen reduction reaction electrocatalyst. We present a three-step image analysis workflow comprising segmentation, tracking, and degradation-event classification with progressive automation, including machine-learning-assisted detection of overlapping particles. By pairing nanoscale resolution and local history with population-level statistics, the pipeline enables unbiased identification and quantification of degradation pathways across statistically meaningful particle sets. We reveal particle size- and shape-dependent effects, showing that smaller and irregular nanoparticles are more prone to detachment, and provide a data-driven framework for probing electrocatalyst degradation at scale.

papers.title: Quantum-sensing-based super-resolution live cell microenvironment imaging
A dual-attribution framework reveals how foreign investment and trade redistribute cobalt availability
PRPF19 drives hepatic stellate cell activation and liver fibrosis via PKM2-mediated glycolytic reprogramming
Corpus Callosum Dysgenesis is concomitant with reduced metacognitive efficiency and sensitivity across multiple cohorts and modalities
A self-limiting mechanotransduction feedback loop ensures robust organ formation
Extensive genomic diversity in Desulfovibrio reveals species-specific functional traits associated with disease
papers.abstract: Desulfovibrio spp. are associated with inflammatory diseases and human health, yet limited representative genomes and isolates hinder our understanding of their role in disease. Here, we assembled a comprehensive database of 2658 Desulfovibrio genomes across 90 diseases and 32 countries, including 24 human isolates. Genomic analyses showed extensive species diversity and revealed disease-associated functional traits, including flagellin and adaptation-associated genes (i.e., ureases). Flagellin-mediated Toll-like receptor 5 activation was species-specific and D. desulfuricans flagellin downregulated TGF-beta signalling in murine small intestinal organoids, suggesting impaired immune tolerance. Additionally, we investigated genomic capacity for hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) production, a main Desulfovibrio metabolite. While health- and disease-associated Desulfovibrio spp. mainly encoded dissimilatory sulfate reduction, tetrathionate metabolism-encoding bacteria were exclusively detected in inflammatory bowel diseases, including Proteus mirabilis and Morganella morganii . Overall, our study provides a comprehensive genomic Desulfovibrio resource and identifies new links associating strain variation, functional traits and H 2 S-production with inflammatory diseases.

papers.title: Disability related disparities in diagnosis and survival of digestive system cancers in Northern Italy
papers.abstract: Individuals with disabilities may experience disparities in cancer diagnosis, but population-based evidence remains limited. We conduct a population-based cohort study using linked cancer registry and administrative healthcare data for digestive system cancers diagnosed between 2018 and 2021 in Northern Italy, examining diagnostic routes and one-year survival according to pre-existing impairments. Individuals with impairments are more likely to be diagnosed following emergency presentation compared with those without impairments (51.8% compared with 37.9%; adjusted odds ratio 1.41, 95% confidence interval 1.23–1.61), particularly those with impairments of mental and neuromusculoskeletal functions. They also have higher one-year mortality (hazard ratio 1.36, 95% confidence interval 1.26–1.46), independent of socio-demographic and clinical factors. Here, we show that disability-related disparities in emergency cancer diagnosis and survival persist across multiple impairment categories, providing population-based evidence from a European setting on differences in diagnostic pathways across heterogeneous disability groups.

papers.title: Transposable element-mediated structural variations shape gene expression and agronomic trait diversity in Brassica napus
Long-term nitrous acid evolution modulates ozone and secondary aerosol variations in global megacities
Giant step-boundary-triggered nonlocal modulation of magnetization reversal in multi-stepped van der Waals ferromagnet Fe3GaTe2
Fluorescence-illuminated diffraction tomography using explicit neural fields
papers.abstract: Multimodal fluorescence and phase imaging provides complementary information about biological samples. However, existing simultaneous fluorescence-phase techniques primarily operate in transmission mode and are limited to thin specimens, restricting their use in thick tissues and in vivo applications. Although multiphoton microscopy enables deep-tissue fluorescence imaging, combining it with three-dimensional refractive-index (RI) imaging remains challenging because few methods can reconstruct the RI of bulky, label-free tissues in reflection mode at subcellular resolution. Here, we introduce fluorescence-illuminated diffraction tomography (FDT), which reconstructs the 3D RI of label-free and fluorescence-labeled objects from diffracted fluorescence images acquired in reflection mode under two-photon excitation. FDT uses the transport of intensity equation and a self-supervised neural network based on explicit neural fields. Compared with state-of-the-art implicit neural fields, this approach improves computational speed, reconstruction accuracy, and interpretability. We demonstrate FDT in two experimental regimes: reconstructing the 3D RI of label-free tissues up to 300 μ m thick placed on a fluorescent substrate, and reconstructing the 3D RI of fluorescence-labeled, 3D-cultured cells without transmission-side access using fluorescence emitted by the cells themselves. FDT establishes a foundation for accessible reflection-mode multimodal fluorescence-phase imaging in complex biological systems.

papers.title: Structural basis of ammonium transport and coordinated regulation of AMT1;1 in Arabidopsis thaliana
papers.abstract: Efficient ammonium uptake is essential for plant growth and nitrogen-use efficiency, yet the structural basis of ammonium transport and regulation in plant AMTs remains unclear. Here, we determined multiple cryo-electron microscopy structures of the Arabidopsis thaliana ammonium transporter AMT1;1 in apo, ammonium-bound, methylammonium-bound, low-pH and phosphomimetic states. These structures reveal a conserved ammonium conduction pathway comprising an aromatic recruitment vestibule, a Phe-gate/Twin-His-containing pore, and a polar intracellular exit region. We further identified a conserved extracellular N-terminal disulfide bond required for oligomer stability and transport activity, suggesting potential redox-dependent regulation. On the cytoplasmic side, phosphorylation modulates C-terminal interactions with intracellular loops, revealing an allosteric regulatory mechanism. Comparison with the bacterial ammonium-sensing protein Sd -Amt1 uncovers a conserved ammonium-recognition region in At AMT1;1 that contributes to transport activity but lacks the signaling module and ligand-dependent conformational switching observed in Sd -Amt1. Together, these findings provide structural insight into ammonium transport and coordinated regulation in plant AMT transporters.

papers.title: Somatosensory cortex shapes perceptual decision bias via the superior colliculus
papers.abstract: Sensory inputs reach cortical and subcortical areas in parallel, but how they coordinate to guide decisions remains unknown. We examined the roles of the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and the superior colliculus (SC) in mice performing whisker-mediated tactile detection. While inactivating S1 contralateral to the stimulus increased detection threshold, inactivating ipsilateral S1 decreased it. These opposing effects reflected shifts in choice bias rather than sensitivity. Unilateral SC inactivation produced similar directional effects, whereas bilateral inactivation of either S1 or SC neutralized bias. Furthermore, SC lesions impaired detection performance, and combined S1 inactivation caused no further impairment, indicating that S1-mediated shifts in bias were SC-dependent. S1 inactivation also decreased sensory-evoked neural activity in SC, and choice decoding revealed that behavioral impairment was more closely associated with changes in SC population activity than with loss of sensory encoding in S1. Thus, S1 shapes perceptual bias by modulating SC-dependent circuits that transform sensory evidence into perceptual decisions.

papers.title: Preserved higher-order mentalising during strategic interactions after medial prefrontal cortex damage
papers.abstract: Mentalising, the ability to infer the beliefs and intentions of others, is essential for successful social interaction. Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear. Here we show that people with focal damage to the medial prefrontal cortex retain the ability to engage in higher-order mentalising during a strategic social game. We compare their performance with patients with brain damage in other regions and lesion-free participants. Individuals with medial prefrontal cortex damage achieve similar rewards and use comparable mentalising strategies, but they are slower when making strategic decisions. Computational modelling indicates that this slowing reflects a greater tendency to require evidence before committing to a choice. Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping identifies medial prefrontal regions linked to altered decision processes rather than mentalising. These findings suggest that the medial prefrontal cortex supports strategic decisions while higher-order mentalising remains intact.

papers.title: CREST functions as a molecular bridge between neuron-specific enhancers and epigenetic regulators in mature motor neurons
papers.abstract: Motor neuron development requires precise transcriptional regulation mediated in part by BAF (BRG1/BRM-associated factor) chromatin remodeling complexes. The neuron-specific BAF subunit CREST is critical for neuronal function and is mutated in some cases of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), yet its underlying genomic mechanisms remain unclear. Using mouse embryonic stem cell differentiation, we show that CREST is essential for motor neuron maturation by activating mature neuronal genes and repressing progenitor genes. Mechanistically, CREST interacts with the neuronal transcription factors ONECUT1 and NGN2, and the BRM ATPase to target pre-existing accessible enhancers of neuronal genes. CREST deletion selectively prevents CBP histone acetyltransferase recruitment, reducing histone H3K27 acetylation at these enhancers and downregulating target gene expression, without disrupting BRM binding, enhancer accessibility, or long-range chromatin architecture. Overall, our findings identify CREST as a crucial epigenetic mediator bridging lineage-specific transcription factors, BAF complexes, and CBP to activate enhancers and promote proper motor neuron development.

papers.title: AMMPER-2: A spatially explicit agent-based model of microbial radiobiology with redox dye simulation
papers.abstract: To reduce health risks for human space exploration, it is important to model the effects of deep-space radiation on biological systems. The budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a common model organism in space radiobiology, but little is known about how radiation damage to individual cells translates into the population-level effects that experiments measure. The Agent-Based Model for Microbial Populations Exposed to Radiation (AMMPER) is a spatially explicit agent-based model that simulates the effects of ionizing radiation on S. cerevisiae cells and produces population-level results. Its goal is to improve experiment design and data interpretation. AMMPER-1 demonstrated that agent-based simulations can qualitatively reproduce the effects of proton radiation on the growth rate of wild-type and DNA-repair mutant yeast. Here, we present AMMPER-2, which addresses limitations of the first model and expands its capabilities. AMMPER-2 incorporates the dynamics of the redox dye alamarBlue, a data type commonly generated in spaceflight microbiology experiments, and models the fate of reactive oxygen species in more detail. It also adds an improved graphical interface and runs faster. AMMPER-2 remains easy to execute in Python on a standard personal laptop, providing space biologists a tool to explore experimental conditions, generate hypotheses, and interpret data from microbial space radiation experiments.
affiliations: NASA Ames Research Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Twisted superconducting quantum diodes for high fidelity anharmonic qubits
papers.abstract: In superconducting circuits, bidirectional signal propagation can cause back-reflections and back-action that couple environmental noise back to coherent elements, degrading fidelity. Nonreciprocal superconducting diodes provide an intrinsic route to suppress such back-scattering at the circuit level. However, their diode efficiency and quantum integration remain limited. Here, we realize a quantum diode in twisted NbSe2 under in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields. A mere 1∘ twist yields an efficiency enhancement over pristine devices, reaching 27.6%. Quantum simulations reveal that this intermediate efficiency, well below 100% ideal, is both experimentally practical and optimal for preserving qubit anharmonicity and stabilizing two-level systems. These findings show that maximal rectification is not always beneficial for quantum information, establishing a new principle for designing the fundamental properties of twisted superconductors towards low-power, high-fidelity quantum circuits. Superconducting diodes can provide nonreciprocal elements for superconducting and quantum circuits, but the role of diode efficiency in quantum-device performance remains unclear. Here, the authors demonstrate an enhanced superconducting diode effect in twisted NbSe2 and show that even a moderate degree of nonreciprocity is sufficient to stabilize anharmonic qubit circuits.

papers.title: Dopamine-induced mitochondrial dysfunction activates cGAS-sTING to drive IL-6 secretion in macrophages
papers.abstract: Daniali et al. demonstrate that dopamine exposure disrupts mitochondrial function in human macrophages, mediating the release of the inflammatory cytokine IL-6. Rapid mitochondrial dysregulation shifts cellular respiration toward glycolysis and induces the release of mitochondrial DNA into the cytoplasm, activating a biased cGAS-STING- NF-κB pathway.

papers.title: The ENL-USP7 complex regulates HIV latency through BRD4 protein stabilization
papers.abstract: Ahmed et al. identify ENL-USP7-BRD4 as a host pathway that maintains HIV latency. Targeted degradation of ENL or USP7 reactivates latent HIV in resting CD4+ T cells and brain microglia from individuals receiving antiretroviral therapy. Mechanistically, ENL recruits USP7 to stabilize BRD4 and maintain viral latency.

papers.title: Genomic insights into millennia of genetic continuity and trans-regional admixture in the middle-lower Yellow River basin
papers.abstract: Qin et al. reveal long-term genetic continuity in the middle-lower Yellow River basin over four millennia, punctuated by limited Silk Road-related admixture during the Tang-Song period and declining archaic hominin ancestry, highlighting the interplay of agricultural expansion, state-level transformations, and transcontinental connectivity in East Asia.

Reversible Sn 4+ /Sn 0 anode for high-energy-density flow batteries
papers.abstract: Aqueous batteries offer a relatively safe, energy-dense means to store electrochemical energy. Tin is a promising anode material, due to its potential four-electron redox-active states and lack of dendrite formation. However, the irreversible electrochemical behaviour of the Sn4+/Sn2+ couple have limited high-capacity anode development. Here we achieve the reversible Sn4+/Sn2+ conversion, enabling a Sn4+/Sn0 anode for high-energy-density flow batteries. We accomplish this by adding iodide to highly soluble SnCl4 solutions at ratios that form SnCl62− and SnI62− intermediate complexes. SnI62− reduces reorganization energy during the electrochemical reaction of Sn4+/Sn2+, ensuring reversibility. SnCl62− imparts anolyte solubility. The redox peak potential difference decreased from 978 mV (Cl−) to 97 mV (I−), with a substantial decrease to the electron transfer impedance decrease. Coupled with Br−/Br2, the assembled full battery showed 89% energy efficiency at 40 mA cm−2, 227 Ah l−1 anolyte capacity and 205 Wh l−1 anolyte energy density. Based on these studies, we developed a kilowatt-scale stack that can operate stably for over 1,000 h. Tin-based aqueous flow batteries offer high-capacity anodes due to the potential four-electron redox reactions, but irreversible Sn4+/Sn2+ electrochemistry has hindered battery development. Now it has been shown that iodide-mediated intermediate complexes enable reversible Sn4+/Sn2+ conversion and four-electron Sn4+/Sn0 chemistry, yielding a high anolyte energy density and stable long-term operation.

papers.title: A modular platform for in cellulo target engagement profiling of chromatin reader inhibitors
papers.abstract: Chromatin reader inhibitors require robust cellular assays for target-engagement profiling. Recchia et al. develop modular Acyl-eCR reporters that enable scalable live-cell measurement of bromodomain inhibitor specificity and PROTAC activity, providing a versatile platform for chromatin-targeted drug discovery.

papers.title: Microbiota-regulated TCDCA associates with Parkinson’s disease severity and promotes BBB dysfunction through VSMC TGR5 signaling in mice
papers.abstract: Zhao et al. show that circulating TCDCA associates with Parkinson’s disease severity and that TCDCA administration worsens neurovascular and motor outcomes in mice. VSMC TGR5 deletion and BSH-active L. reuteri interventions implicate a microbiota-regulated TCDCA-BBB pathway while defining its translational limitations.

papers.title: Anti-HDGFL2 cryptic protein antibodies provide a sensitive readout of TDP-43 pathology and clinical disease features
papers.abstract: Citrano, Maheswari Jawahar et al. develop sensitive immunoassays using second-generation polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies against HDGFL2-CE proteins and show that their levels in brain tissue associate with pTDP-43 pathology, earlier symptom onset, and shorter survival in patients with FTLD-TDP and FTLD-TDP/MND.

papers.title: AI-integrated RNA therapeutics in precision oncology
papers.abstract: Symmans et al. review how artificial intelligence supports RNA therapeutic development in precision oncology, spanning multi-omics target prioritization and RNA design to delivery, patient stratification, manufacturing, and clinical translation. They distinguish clinically supported applications from preclinical and speculative approaches, outlining validation, governance, and regulatory requirements.

papers.title: Breastfeeding and maternal microbial reservoirs are associated with infant gut phageome development during the first year of life
papers.abstract: Cabello-Yeves et al. use longitudinal metagenomic analysis of mother-infant dyads to show that infant gut phageomes diversify during the first year of life and are associated with feeding-related variables and maternal microbial reservoirs. Persistent bifidophages dominate early communities, highlighting the potential relevance of phages in microbiome-targeted early-life interventions.

papers.title: Spatially tuned localization of interleukins and OX40 agonists enhances synergistic anti-tumor immunity
papers.abstract: Klich et al. use a hydrogel to deliver immunotherapy combinations intratumorally and peritumorally. Rational selection of the site of administration drives tumor clearance and long-term survivors.

papers.title: Metastasizing cancer cells leave an immunogenic trail
LAG3 checkpoint function and its mechanism of action in therapeutic targeting
papers.abstract: Lymphocyte activation gene 3 (LAG3) protein is a key immune inhibitory checkpoint receptor that suppresses T cell activation, proliferation and effector functions to maintain immune homeostasis and tolerance. In persistent pathological settings, chronic T cell receptor (TCR) signalling, together with sustained LAG3 signalling and other inhibitory receptor signalling, drives T cell dysfunction, highlighting LAG3 as a promising therapeutic target. However, more than 30 years after its discovery, the fundamental mechanisms governing LAG3 signalling and function remain incompletely defined. Elucidating LAG3 downstream signalling pathways and the mechanisms of action of LAG3-blocking antibodies is essential for identifying optimal clinical indications, developing predictive biomarkers, designing more effective LAG3-targeted therapeutics and maximizing clinical efficacy. Recent advances have revealed key molecular mechanisms, including constitutive tonic signalling, ligand-induced ubiquitination-dependent signalling switches and LAG3–TCR proximity-mediated suppression. In this Review, we comprehensively examine LAG3 signalling mechanisms, synthesize current understanding of its functional effect on T cells, discuss emerging therapeutics and their mechanisms of action, and evaluate biomarker strategies for patient selection. We conclude by highlighting key challenges and outlining future directions for LAG3-targeted immunotherapy in oncology and autoimmune disease. This Review explores how the immune checkpoint receptor lymphocyte activation gene 3 (LAG3) suppresses T cell activity through newly defined signalling mechanisms, including tonic and ligand-induced pathways. The Review highlights therapeutic advances, biomarker strategies and emerging opportunities to target LAG3 in cancer and autoimmune disease.
