papers.title: Neurotechnology governance: the operational turn
papers.abstract: Neurotechnology governance is entering an operational turn, driven by the need to move beyond the articulation of ethical principles and to translate them into heterogeneous real-world settings through institutional capacity-building, regulatory fit, and coordination. This shift also concerns the conditions under which beneficial neurotechnology applications can emerge and scale responsibly.

papers.title: Manipulating rRNA levels with CRISPR
Disrupting BRD4-BD1-p62 engagement restores protective autophagy
papers.abstract: Autophagy is impaired in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Zhang et al. identify a BRD4-BD1-selective inhibitor that disrupts BRD4-BD1–p62 engagement, restores protective autophagy, and attenuates pulmonary fibrosis, revealing a druggable mechanism linking epigenetic regulation to autophagy.

papers.title: Lipid-engineered antibody-based therapeutics target inflamed joints and lymph nodes to enhance rheumatoid arthritis treatment
papers.abstract: Zhao et al. attach multiple lipid motifs to antibody-based biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (bDMARDs), enabling them to engage multiple albumin molecules in vivo and enhancing their accumulation in inflamed joints and lymph nodes. This generalizable strategy can target therapeutics larger than albumin to inflammatory sites for improved rheumatoid arthritis treatment.

papers.title: Prognostic value of cfDNA methylation in locally advanced esophageal squamous cell cancer treated with neoadjuvant immunochemoradiotherapy
papers.abstract: Chen et al. track cfDNA methylation during neoadjuvant immunochemoradiotherapy for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Methylation signals decline with treatment and are associated with pathological response and disease-free survival. The decline is reproduced in a separate 30-patient cohort, supporting further evaluation of cfDNA methylation for noninvasive monitoring.

papers.title: A spatiotemporal atlas of radiation-induced brain injury reveals dysfunction of the blood-CSF barrier
papers.abstract: Quan et al. construct a spatiotemporal transcriptomic atlas of radiation-induced brain injury and show that loss of radiosensitive Tmsb4x+ choroid plexus epithelial cells triggers blood-CSF barrier dysfunction and macrophage infiltration that sustains interferon-responsive microglial activation. These findings position the blood-CSF barrier as a potential target for mitigating post-irradiation neuroinflammation.

papers.title: Reviving low-affinity glycan-targeting CAR with combinatorial design
papers.abstract: Forcados et al. develop and test a combinatorial CAR strategy against B cell lymphoma, in which they combine CD75s and CD19 targeting. This combinatorial approach overcomes the limited efficiency of CD75s mono-targeting and lowers the risk of CAR-related toxicity seen with CD19 single targeting.

papers.title: Human genetic evidence challenges NCOA1 as a monogenic obesity gene
papers.abstract: Delplanque et al. combine large-scale human genetics with functional analyses to reassess the role of NCOA1 in obesity. Despite its biological plausibility within the melanocortin pathway, pathogenic NCOA1 variants were not associated with adiposity, questioning their relevance for precision obesity therapies targeting this pathway.

papers.title: Microbiota-mediated naringenin release limits postoperative acute gastrointestinal injury by suppressing ferroptosis
papers.abstract: Deng et al. show that reduced preoperative fecal naringenin and β-glucuronidase activity associate with postoperative acute gastrointestinal injury after cardiopulmonary bypass. Mechanistically, microbial β-glucuronidase promotes naringenin release and limits epithelial ferroptosis, highlighting candidate noninvasive biomarkers and a potential microbiota-based intervention axis.

papers.title: Engineering synthetic thermogels
Engineering synthetic thermogels
papers.abstract: Thermogels are temperature-responsive polymer systems that undergo reversible sol–gel transitions under physiologically relevant conditions, driven by temperature-induced changes in polymer hydration, hydrophilic–hydrophobic balance and molecular association. The study of thermogels encompasses a spectrum of design strategies that couple polymer chemistry and tunable molecular architecture with physicochemical characterization, gelation mapping and application-specific testing. This Primer focuses on synthetic thermogels, with poly(ethylene glycol)–polyester-based, polyurethane-based and polypeptide-based thermogels serving as three principal methodological paradigms for detailed discussion. Other synthetic thermogels, including poloxamers, poly(organophosphazene) and lower critical solution temperature-type polymers, are discussed where relevant to provide broader context, whereas thermogelling systems based primarily on naturally derived polymers, such as chitosan-based formulations, fall outside the principal scope of this Primer. We outline experimental methods used to design, synthesize and characterize thermogels, including approaches for mapping gelation behaviour, resolving microstructure, quantifying mechanical and transport properties and assessing stability and biodegradation. Emphasis is placed on how experimental choices influence gelation windows, mechanical readouts and performance across different use scenarios. Application-oriented workflows are summarized for drug delivery, tissue engineering and medical devices. We further discuss factors affecting reproducibility, propose minimum reporting standards and outline strategies for data deposition to enable cross-study comparison. Finally, we discuss how standardized high-throughput workflows and data-driven formulation mapping may support more systematic and predictive thermogel development. Together, these approaches provide a framework for improving the reproducibility, comparability and application-specific development of thermogels. Thermogels are polymeric materials that transition between sol and gel states in response to temperature changes. In this Primer, Wang et al. outline the design, synthesis and characterization of synthetic thermogels.

papers.title: Context-dependent roles of ketone metabolism in intestinal inflammation
papers.abstract: Ketone metabolism is traditionally viewed as an alternative metabolic pathway providing energy during carbohydrate deprivation through the production and utilization of ketone bodies. Ketone bodies also function as signaling molecules regulating immune and metabolic processes. Accumulating evidence shows that ketone metabolism influences diverse diseases and immune responses, including inflammation, autoimmunity, and infection. Recently, ketone metabolism has been associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a chronic inflammatory disorder of the intestine, although reported effects are heterogeneous and context-dependent. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on ketone metabolism in IBD and intestinal inflammation, highlighting its roles in barrier integrity, immune regulation, and microbiota interactions. We also discuss potential mechanisms underlying divergent outcomes and outline key questions for future research.

papers.title: Innovations and applications in synthetic biology: a PhD researcher’s perspective
papers.abstract: Prof. Tamir Tuller, cofounder and chair of the Israeli Society for Synthetic Biology (ISSB), and Dr Ilana Kolodkin-Gal, cofounder of the ISSB, speak with early-career researchers about their breakthrough studies. The conversations explore diverse engineering frontiers: reprogramming bacteria for synthetic autotrophy to tackle climate challenges, designing human cells with RNA-based parallel computation for autonomous diagnostics, utilizing machine learning to ensure the long-term evolutionary stability of genetic circuits, and engineering de novo proteins to overcome bacterial defense systems for advanced phage therapies.

papers.title: Retention and biosynthesis of diverse nitroarenes in Escherichia coli after combinatorial nitroreductase gene deletions
papers.abstract: The instability of nitroaromatic compounds or nitroarenes in the presence of microbial cells has hindered the ability to biomanufacture these industrially and pharmaceutically relevant chemicals. Although nitroreductase (NTR) gene deletions have been linked to nitroarene stability, the extent of this effect is unclear. Here we perform a comprehensive analysis of bacterial NTR activity in cells by engineering strains of Escherichia coli that contain up to 15 knockouts of known and candidate NTR genes. We evaluate the stability of over 20 exogenously supplemented nitroaromatic compounds to wild-type and engineered strains. For several chemistries, such as di-nitro compounds and nitro-aldehydes, our engineered nitroaromatic reductase knockout strains enable retention of compounds. We leverage these tools and insights to improve or enable nitroaromatic compound biosynthesis, including the biocatalytic transformation of an amine precursor to a nitro compound, the biosynthesis of nitrobenzaldehydes and the combined semi-synthesis and site-specific incorporation of nitrophenylalanines from supplemented nitrobenzaldehydes. This work advances access to nitro functional group chemistry in cell-based biocatalysis, metabolic engineering and synthetic biology. Nitroarenes are unstable in microbial cultures, limiting the biomanufacturing of these industrially and pharmaceutically important chemicals. Genome engineering of nitroreductase-deficient E. coli strains has now been shown to improve nitroarene retention during fermentation, expanding access to nitro functional group chemistry in whole-cell biocatalysis, metabolic engineering and synthetic biology.

papers.title: Orthogonal nucleophile-ordered assembly for modular access to enantiopure 1,2-amino alcohols
papers.abstract: The programmed assembly of multiple common chemicals with minimal reactivity differences into complex chiral architectures with high selectivity is a long-standing challenge in synthetic chemistry. Here we report a palladium-catalysed orthogonal multicomponent strategy that enables the sequential incorporation of two native N–H/O–H nucleophiles with similar reactivity into propargylic carbonates through a nucleophile-ordered assembly. Leveraging the tandem reactivity of the propargyl–palladium complex, this system functions as a sorting mechanism: stronger nucleophiles undergo outer-sphere addition to the propargyl–palladium intermediate, while weaker nucleophiles, guided by superior coordinating affinity, selectively attack the resulting allyl–palladium species through an inner-sphere mechanism. This strategy enables the precise recognition and ordered incorporation of diverse native nucleophile pairs, providing a platform and modular access to valuable chiral 1,2-amino alcohols and 1,2-diols with exceptional regio-, chemo-, Z- and enantiocontrol. This work demonstrates how subtle reactivity differences can be systematically harnessed for programmable complex synthesis from fundamental feedstocks. The selective assembly of multiple chemicals into complex chiral architectures in a single operation is a long-standing challenge. Now a palladium-catalysed orthogonal strategy has been shown to sort and incorporate two native N–H/O–H nucleophiles with similar reactivity, delivering enantioenriched 1,2-amino alcohols and 1,2-diols with high selectivity.

papers.title: Evolution of dipole–dipole dynamics in cold ammonia collisions
authors: Sebastiaan Y. T. van de Meerakker
papers.abstract: Cold polar molecules offer fascinating prospects for ultracold chemistry and quantum physics. However, their inherent collision properties remain largely unknown, as it seems fundamentally impossible to reach sufficiently low energies by merging two beams of molecules with substantial dipole moments. Here we report measurements of state-to-state cross-sections for collisions between ammonia isotopologues at energies between 0.3 and 100 cm−1 using an advanced beam-merging protocol. We experimentally observed a local maximum in the cross-sections, which indicates that the dipole moments can switch off at low collision energies. Scattering calculations reproduced this maximum in good agreement and explained the observed scaling with the molecule’s parity splitting energies. Measurements of the correlated energy transfer in both collision partners yielded direct evidence of the suppression of the dipole–dipole interaction at low energies. Our results demonstrate how collisions between an important class of polar molecules evolve from high temperatures towards the ultracold regime in a counterintuitive way, and offer distinctive opportunities to control cold molecular collisions with external fields. Interactions between polar molecules are expected to become increasingly strong at low collision energies through dipole–dipole forces. Now it has been shown that ammonia molecules instead exhibit suppressed dipolar interactions in the cold regime as the dipole moment effectively switches off, as shown by local maxima in the collision cross-sections.

papers.title: A triple carbonylation cascade converts aldehydes into threofuranoses
Controlling reactions via nucleophile sorting
Histone lactylation scarring transmits metabolic and epigenetic memory across the gut-liver axis
papers.abstract: Dong et al. show that ulcerative colitis remission leaves persistent LCN2+ macrophages with heightened glycolysis and H3K9la memory. Upon high-fat diet challenge, these cells contribute to gut-to-liver inflammatory transmission and increased susceptibility to steatotic liver disease through a chromatin-remodeling program, thus providing a mechanistic rationale for prior clinical observations.

papers.title: UBT251, a novel triple GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptor agonist, in adults with overweight or obesity: A multicenter, randomized phase 2 trial
papers.abstract: Zhou et al. report a phase 2 trial of UBT251, a novel triple GLP-1/GIP/GCG receptor agonist, in adults with overweight or obesity. UBT251 produced substantial weight loss and cardiometabolic improvements with an acceptable safety profile, supporting phase 3 evaluation.

papers.title: Targeting ZDHHC15-mediated S-acylation of CD155 reactivates anti-tumor immunity
papers.abstract: Reversible protein S-acylation regulates immune checkpoint function. Zhang et al. demonstrate that ZDHHC15-mediated S-acylation stabilizes CD155, whereas genetic or pharmacological disruption promotes CD155 degradation, enhances anti-tumor immunity, and suppresses tumor growth.

papers.title: Fusion-loop-engineered Zika mRNA vaccine elicits convergent B cell immunodominance to uncouple protection from ADE in macaques
papers.abstract: Yang et al. demonstrate, in primates, that a fusion-loop-engineered Zika mRNA vaccine confers full protection with negligible dengue ADE. The response is dominated by convergent B cells orthologous to human IGHV5-10-1 whose antibodies target a distinct viral hotspot, with DENV envelope N67-linked glycan preventing cross-reactivity for safer flavivirus vaccines.

papers.title: Oral microbial nitrate metabolism is associated with lower prevalence of prediabetes
papers.abstract: Zhao et al. investigate the role of the tongue microbiome in prediabetes and glycemic dysregulation. Rothia mucilaginosa and microbial nitrate metabolism are associated with lower prediabetes prevalence and improve the prediction of prediabetes progression, highlighting oral nitrate metabolism as a potential modifiable link between the oral microbiome and metabolic health.

papers.title: A translational pipeline for classification of variants of uncertain significance to support gene therapy clinical trial in OTOF-related deafness
papers.abstract: Chen et al. establish a translational functional pipeline to reclassify OTOF variants of uncertain significance. This pipeline enables definitive molecular diagnosis and eligibility for gene therapy trials; it further reveals that K1992R drives pathogenicity in the E1700Q haplotype via disrupting otoferlin localization.

papers.title: A standardized patient-derived glioblastoma organoid platform for evaluating radiotherapy efficacy and overcoming resistance
papers.abstract: Wang et al. develop a standardized reaggregated glioblastoma organoid (rGBO) platform that enables scalable evaluation of patient-specific treatment responses. The platform links organoid radiosensitivity with patient survival, identifies response-related transcriptomic signatures, and reveals BET inhibition as a strategy to enhance radiotherapy efficacy in organoid and xenograft models.

papers.title: Regional brain aging signatures predict mortality through neurovascular immune mechanisms
papers.abstract: Lee et al. integrate structural brain MRI with plasma proteomics to identify a three-region brain age model that predicts mortality more accurately than global measures and reveals shared immune and vascular mechanisms. These findings support regional brain aging as a scalable biomarker for precision geromedicine.

papers.title: A guide to B cell metabolism
papers.abstract: The metabolism of immune cells must adapt dynamically to support their diverse functions. B cells, which are the key cellular mediators of humoral immunity, undergo extensive metabolic changes throughout their development and function, starting from their commitment to the B cell lineage in the bone marrow. In the periphery, further rounds of metabolic adaptation in B cells are driven by temporally regulated changes in signalling cues, energetic demands and nutrient availability within specialized tissue niches. Although they have historically been less well studied than other immune cell types, emerging evidence shows that B cells deploy mechanistically distinct metabolic strategies that are tightly linked to their effector identity. Recognizing B cell metabolism as its own biological entity is, therefore, crucial to the study of humoral immune responses. In this Review, we examine the metabolic pathways that regulate B cell homeostasis, their integration with cell signalling networks, and their adaptation to the metabolic environment across spatial and temporal scales. We further discuss how aberrations in these pathways can contribute to B cell-driven malignancies, autoimmunity, inborn errors of immunity, and B cell-tropic infections. We position B cell metabolism as a rapidly expanding frontier within immunometabolism in both health and disease. Metabolic control is an integral component of B cell physiology, shaping fate decisions and effector functions, while also driving maladaptive programmes that contribute to diverse pathologies. This Review provides an overview of the current understanding of B cell metabolism in health and disease.

papers.title: Neuronal regulation of intestinal stem cells dictates immune homeostasis
papers.abstract: The intestinal epithelium undergoes continuous regeneration driven by intestinal stem cells (ISCs) residing within the crypt niche. Traditionally, this niche has been viewed as a stromal signaling compartment governed by gradients of Wnt, bone morphogenetic protein, and Notch activity. However, recent advances have revealed regulation via far more complex multicellular networks integrating stromal, immune, vascular, neuronal, and glial signals. In this review, we discuss emerging evidence positioning the enteric nervous system as a regulator of epithelial differentiation, regeneration, and mucosal immunity. Collectively, these findings support a revised model in which the ISC niche functions as an extended neuroglial-immune sensory unit. Understanding this integrated regulatory architecture may provide new therapeutic opportunities for inflammatory bowel disease, infection, impaired regeneration, and neuroimmune disorders of the gut.

papers.title: Engineering anaerobic fungal–bacterial consortia for direct conversion of lignocellulosic biomass into medium-chain fatty acids
papers.abstract: This study engineers an anaerobic fungal–bacterial consortium that converts untreated plant biomass directly into medium-chain fatty acids. Lactate cross-feeding assigns biomass breakdown and product formation to distinct microbial partners, making carbon flow easier to understand and engineer. The study defines design principles and performance targets for scalable lignocellulose biorefineries.

papers.title: Glycosylated RNAs travel with extracellular vesicles and shape intercellular communication
Oleic acid might induce necroptosis of CD4+ T cells, in addition to its induction of pyroptosis
papers.abstract: A recent study published in Cell Metabolism by Kumar et al. found that both oleic acid (OAc) and palmitic acid (PA) induce the mRNA expression of pyroptosis-associated genes (such as NLRP3, caspase-1, GSDMD, IL-1β, and IL-18) in CD4+ T cells and do so in a dose-dependent manner.1 The authors further showed that treatment with OAc (10 μg/mL, 6 h) increases the protein levels of NLRP3, pro-IL-1β, caspase-1, and GSDMD and also of cleaved caspase-1 and GSDMD-NT (Gasdermin D N-terminal domain). Additionally, the same treatment was found to induce the release of IL-1β and IL-18 proteins (and also cleaved caspase-1 protein) from CD4+ T cells, a finding that directly points to the OAc-induced pyroptosis of CD4+ T cells.

papers.title: Pyroptosis, not necroptosis, drives lipid-induced CD4+ T cell death
papers.abstract: We thank Dr. Berkel for the insightful comments regarding our recent study on lipid-induced CD4+ T cell death. The question of whether fatty acids such as oleic acid (OAc) may induce necroptosis in addition to pyroptosis is highly relevant and provides an opportunity to further refine the mechanistic framework of lipid-induced T cell injury.

papers.title: Metabolic advantages of a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet in in patients with metabolically unhealthy obesity
Diet-microbiome interactions enhance cancer immunotherapy in obesity
Glutamine metabolism keeps pathogenic hepatic CD4+ T cells in check
You are what you eat and translate: Feeding the code to fight cancer and viruses
Trajectories in immunometabolism
papers.abstract: Immunometabolism has rapidly evolved from an emerging area within immunology into a topic that not only impregnates most aspects of immune research but also reveals itself as a defining feature of the immune response. At the European Immunometabolism Conference celebrated in June, we asked some of the speakers to share their personal journey as researchers in this field and what questions they are currently working on.

papers.title: Non-enzymatic protein modifications at the interface of metabolism and immunity
papers.abstract: In this review, Walker et al. discuss how reactive metabolites can non-enzymatically modify proteins to shape immune cell function. They discuss mechanisms governing modification selectivity and regulation, emerging chemical biology tools to study these modifications, and how these modifications connect immunometabolism with inflammation, disease, and therapeutic opportunities.

papers.title: Disruption of the Nav1.8/Ankyrin-3 interaction in nociceptors reduces pathological pain-like behaviors in mice
papers.abstract: Chronic pain is a complex neurobiological problem whose solution is elusive. Powell et al. describe an approach to reduce chronic neuropathic pain in rodent models using a short lipidated peptide designed to inhibit the interaction between Nav1.8 and Ankyrin-3.

papers.title: Tunable underwater curcumin release through a three-layered film system to mitigate oxidative stress in corals
papers.abstract: A biobased multilayered film system for controlled curcumin release has been designed to mitigate oxidative stress in corals. Without direct contact, the system preserves chlorophyll content and Symbiodiniaceae density in corals exposed to rising temperatures, providing a sustainable strategy to enhance coral resilience under thermal stress events.

papers.title: The radical-radical cross-coupling of alkyl carboxylic acids and organoborons
papers.abstract: Carbon–carbon bond-forming reactions are fundamental in organic synthesis. Radical–radical cross-coupling stands out as a key strategy for carbon–carbon bond formation, especially for C(sp3)–C(sp3) bonds, to construct complex, three-dimensional, value-added molecules. Existing approaches for direct radical–radical cross-coupling involve a persistent radical and a transient radical to leverage the persistent radical effect. Kolbe electrolysis is one of the few methods that directly cross-couples two transient radicals via electro-oxidative activation of carboxylic acids. However, the direct cross-coupling of transient radicals from two distinct radical precursors, such as carboxylic acids and boronic acids, remains challenging. Here we integrate redox-matched alternating-polarity electrolysis with controlled activation of redox-active species to enable the cross-coupling of alkyl carboxylic acids with alkyl boronic acids. In addition, we demonstrate the synthetic utility and versatility of this transformation by showcasing homocoupling reactions and net carboxylic acid–alkene cross-coupling via in situ alkene hydroboration, as well as tandem processes with Suzuki coupling and Buchwald–Hartwig amination. Carboxylic acids and boronic acids are abundant feedstocks, yet their direct radical cross-coupling remains challenging due to uncontrolled radical reactivity. Now it has been shown that redox-matched alternating-polarity electrolysis enables their coupling, providing a general platform for C(sp3)–C(sp3) bond formation through synchronized radical generation and controlled radical recombination.

papers.title: A precursor-degassing approach for accessing boron allotropes
Arginine methylation in immunoregulation: Mechanisms and therapeutic targeting
papers.abstract: Han et al. review how protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs) coordinate chromatin regulation, RNA metabolism, and immune signaling. They discuss emerging roles of PRMTs in tumor immunity and inflammaging and discuss catalytic and non-catalytic strategies for therapeutically targeting PRMT-dependent immune regulation.

papers.title: Bridging innate and adaptive immunity: A bispecific SIRPαD1-αPCSK9 fusion protein reprograms macrophages for durable tumor clearance
papers.abstract: Xu et al. show that blocking the CD47-SIRPα phagocytic checkpoint paradoxically elevates tumor-derived PCSK9, which degrades MHC-I on macrophages and impairs antigen cross-presentation to CD8+ T cells. A bispecific fusion protein co-targeting CD47 and PCSK9 overcomes this resistance, restoring T cell priming and achieving tumor control with improved safety.

papers.title: Sympathetic nerve activity primes susceptibility to autoimmune hair loss
Engineering synthetic proteins to toggle function in response to kinase signals
Chaperone-mediated autophagy in physiological homeostasis, disease and ageing
papers.abstract: Chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), the first-described selective lysosomal degradation pathway, is distinguished from other degradative pathways by the unique mechanism by which substrates reach the lysosomal lumen: CMA relies on a cytosolic targeting chaperone and a lysosomal membrane receptor that doubles as a translocation complex. In this Review, we highlight recent discoveries of additional molecular components involved in CMA and describe how genetic and pharmacological modulation of CMA in vivo, along with the identification of the subproteome degraded by CMA in different organs, has revealed an expanding range of physiological functions regulated by CMA in an organ-specific manner. CMA not only degrades damaged proteins but also targets fully functional proteins to terminate their physiological roles. Consequently, CMA dysfunction, as observed in ageing and age-related diseases, leads to cellular alterations beyond the mere accumulation of damaged proteins. We summarize recent findings linking CMA to common diseases and discuss efforts to therapeutically target CMA in these conditions. Chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) is a selective lysosomal degradation pathway. Recent insights into its regulation, substrate repertoire and therapeutic modulation have revealed organ-specific functions and highlighted CMA as a therapeutic target in ageing and disease.

papers.title: Towards a systematic understanding of the diverse subtypes, biogenesis and functions of large extracellular vesicles
papers.abstract: Large extracellular vesicles (lEVs) are heterogeneous structures with sizes that exceed 200 nm. Unlike small extracellular vesicles, which originate from either the endosomal system or the plasma membrane, most lEVs stem directly from the plasma membrane, although the various lEV subtypes have distinct biogenesis pathways. Emerging findings have helped to update lEV classification and have provided insights into lEV biogenesis, cargo, physiological functions and relevance in disease. Classical lEVs include apoptotic bodies, microvesicles and large oncosomes, whereas detached migrasomes, exophers, mitophers, blebbisomes, large ageing neutrophil-derived vesicles were only identified later. The study of these diverse lEV subtypes has been challenging, but emerging technologies, including tools that enable multidimensional characterization, loss-of-function studies and mechanistic analyses, are likely to advance the field further, especially if they are appropriately integrated to ensure rigour and reproducibility. Large extracellular vesicle (lEV) subtypes have diverse biogenesis, cargo, functions and roles in disease. This Review article provides an overview of lEV characteristics, highlights open questions in the field and indicates how a systematic approach towards lEV characterization assisted by emerging technologies will ensure reproducibility, advancing lEV research.

papers.title: Translational benchmarking of 3D in vitro models of traumatic brain injury
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a major cause of neurological disability, yet effective therapies are limited. Advances in 3D in vitro neural models, including organoids, scaffold-based constructs, and brain-on-a-chip systems, have provided new opportunities to study neurotrauma under controlled conditions. This review evaluates recent in vitro tissue platforms through a dual framework of mechanical fidelity and biological response, benchmarking applied injury conditions against human biomechanical reconstructions and assessing the coverage of downstream responses relative to TBI pathology. Many 3D models apply clinically relevant mechanical loading regimes and reproduce select phenotypes, but remain limited by inconsistent mechanical reporting, incomplete cellular complexity, and sparse modeling of chronic and repetitive injury. Addressing these challenges will improve the translational utility of next-generation platforms.

papers.title: Single-molecule chromatin tracing reveals a diversity of megabase heterochromatin domains
papers.abstract: Chromosomes fold into distinct domains that regulate transcription, replication and repair. In addition to well-characterized topologically associating domains (TADs) and compartments, the diversity of heterochromatin domains remains poorly defined at the sequence level. Here, using single-molecule tracing of nascent heterochromatin in Caenorhabditis elegans, we identify three classes of megabase-scale domains: (1) sharp-boundary, condensin I-dependent TAD-like domains (TADLs), which arise before zygotic genome activation; (2) similarly sized, but condensin-independent, elegans condensin-independent domains (elCIDs), one of which encompasses the 5S-spliced leader repeat locus; and (3) decompacted, diffuse structures that are abundant in the population but probably missed by crosslinking assays. Condensin I sits at the border of the TADL domain, whereas DNA-binding proteins, active histone marks and maternally active genes flank the elCID domains, suggesting that boundaries are established by distinct mechanisms for different types of domains. Our results uncover previously unrecognized heterochromatin architectures and implicate maternal transcriptional activity in shaping domain boundaries in early embryos in C. elegans. Single-molecule imaging reveals diverse, megabase-scale heterochromatin domains in C. elegans. Some resemble TADs and depend on condensin I; others are independent of condensin and histone H3K9me, including one domain that encloses the 5S rDNA locus.

papers.title: Fungus Rhizopus arrhizus promotes MASLD-associated hepatocellular carcinoma through generating kynurenic acid
papers.abstract: Zhou et al. uncover the pro-tumorigenic role of gut fungus Rhizopus arrhizus in MASLD-HCC. R. arrhizus produces kynurenic acid, which directly binds to tumor cells and activates oncogenic MAPK signaling to promote MASLD-HCC. Zhou et al. also provide therapeutic insights by showing that blocking this host-fungus interaction inhibits MASLD-HCC development.

papers.title: FLIGHTED: Inferring fitness landscapes from noisy high-throughput experimental data
papers.abstract: Sundar et al. present FLIGHTED, a Bayesian method of accounting for uncertainty in protein fitness measurements by generating probabilistic fitness landscapes from noisy high-throughput experiments. FLIGHTED is applied to selection assays and to a high-throughput base-editing assay, and it improves performance of protein fitness models.

papers.title: Systematic transcriptomic evaluation of blastoid models of early human development
papers.abstract: Long et al. integrate single-cell transcriptomes across human embryo development to construct a reference and apply complementary metrics to evaluate four blastoid protocols. The analysis reveals differences in cell identity, developmental timing, and lineage structure, providing a systematic basis for comparing and refining blastoid models.

papers.title: ESCAPE enables receptor-specific chemogenetic dissection of GPCR signaling
papers.abstract: Pharmacological studies of GPCRs are often complicated by off-target effects. Matsuoka et al. develop ESCAPE, a chemogenetic platform that preserves endogenous ligand responsiveness while eliminating antagonist sensitivity, enabling receptor-specific interrogation of GPCR signaling in cells and physiological models.

papers.title: From patient cells to patient therapy: Twenty years of iPSC-based translation in neurodegenerative disease
papers.abstract: Cha and Kim review two decades of iPSC-based translation in neurodegenerative disease, highlighting disease-specific therapeutic logic and the emerging importance of transplantation biology. They propose a phase-resolved framework for the post-transplant “biological black box” linking graft survival, maturation, host interactions, and long-term therapeutic outcome.

papers.title: Multi-omics-driven personalized management of advanced HCC
papers.abstract: Sheng et al. integrate spatial multi-omics, functional models, and clinical validation to show that fibrotic stroma suppresses epithelial cGAS-STING signaling and T cell recruitment in HCC. Their GCSS model links tumor architecture to response prediction for TACE plus immune checkpoint blockade.

papers.title: Neutrality as the null hypothesis of biological evolution
Engineering phage therapeutics with intrinsic biocontainment
papers.abstract: Engineered bacteriophages (phages) are emerging as a promising next generation of antibacterial phage therapeutics, facilitated by advances in synthetic biology, genome engineering, and computational design. Engineered phage therapeutics offer standardised genome designs, expanded functionality, and improved manufacturability, which could potentially help to overcome regulatory barriers. However, genetically engineered phages raise additional biosafety and environmental concerns, making the development of effective biocontainment strategies important for clinical use. Here, we review current approaches for phage genome engineering, alongside the evolving regulatory frameworks for engineered phages. We evaluate emerging biocontainment strategies for therapeutic phages and propose a framework for assessing trade-offs between biocontainment stringency, evolutionary robustness against escape mutants, therapeutic efficacy, and translational feasibility.

papers.title: Silencing the mutant allele without compromising gene dosage
Right size, right time: The Hippo-IGF2 axis calibrates liver growth and regeneration
Activins and BMPs: The yin and yang of diffuse midline gliomas
Flipping the fetal switch across β-hemoglobinopathies
papers.abstract: Liu et al. extend the application of transformer base editing of HBG1/2 promoters from transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia alone to one patient with sickle cell disease and three patients with geographically diverse β-thalassemia genotypes. The responses are meaningful, but scale, genomic surveillance, burden of cure, and access now define the translational test.

papers.title: Editing cells in place: Targeted in vivo gene editing of hematopoietic stem cells
The accessory makes the drug: ASO-delivered siRNA enters the human CNS for ALS
Hepatic FoxO1 loss leads to pancreatic β cell deficiency via liver-derived C18/22/24 ceramides
papers.abstract: Hepatic FoxO1 is a promising therapeutic target for hyperglycemia. Gong et al. show that hepatic FoxO1 loss derepresses Cers2/4 transcription, increasing liver-derived C18/22/24 ceramides that promote pancreatic β cell apoptosis. These findings reveal an inter-organ signaling pathway with implications for FoxO1-targeting antihyperglycemic therapies.

papers.title: Enhanced liver regeneration via targeted mRNA delivery for partial in vivo reprogramming
papers.abstract: Jo et al. show that transient OSKM induction generates two distinct liver progenitor-like cell populations with limited immune activation. Liver-targeted OSKM mRNA-LNPs induce hepatocyte dedifferentiation and enhance regeneration after acetaminophen-induced liver injury, supporting transient hepatic reprogramming as a strategy for inducing regenerative plasticity with therapeutic potential for acute injury.

papers.title: HoT self-blinking probes for chromatin imaging
Selective gas adsorption in microporous materials
Selective gas adsorption in microporous materials
papers.abstract: Adsorptive separation using porous materials is an efficient and energy-saving separation technology, especially for structurally similar gases, owing to the finely tunable micropore structure of such materials. Deeper insight into the control of pore size, pore shape, pore chemistry and pore flexibility enables the design of micropores that are tailored for target molecules, realizing order of magnitude improvements in separation performance for previously infeasible gas separations. This Primer focuses on micropore design principles driven by different separation mechanisms and highlights how they can guide microporous material design for key industrial gas separation applications. The key metrics (including selectivity, capacity, kinetics and desorption) for evaluating the separation performance of microporous materials in different scenarios are discussed, and their corresponding characterization by experiment or simulation are included. We also discuss the limitations and optimizations of the current development of microporous materials, as well as the existing challenges in translating them into industrial utilization. The Primer ends with a perspective on future directions for this field that can be now enabled by advances in our fundamental understanding of separation science and the development of artificial intelligence. This Primer highlights micropore design principles governed by distinct separation mechanisms to resolve key performance trade-offs in industrial gas separations. It outlines the experimental workflow, discusses current material limitations and industrial challenges, and offers a perspective on emerging opportunities.

papers.title: Biotechnology as a platform for hair cosmetic science
papers.abstract: Hair cosmetics are undergoing a transition from conventional formulations based on passive surface deposition toward biotechnology-driven systems designed to interact with hair and scalp at the molecular level. Recent advances in proteins, peptides, biobased polymers, and responsive delivery platforms are enabling targeted repair of keratin damage, controlled reshaping, durable protection, and modulation of follicular activity. These technologies exploit biological specificity, renewable feedstocks, and programmable material properties to address limitations associated with traditional petrochemical ingredients. In this review, we examine how biotechnology is emerging as a unifying platform for hair cosmetic science, integrating biomolecular engineering, smart materials, computational design, and artificial intelligence to create more effective, sustainable, and biologically inspired hair-care solutions.

papers.title: Mapping functional signaling landscapes across the human phosphoproteome
A phosphoproteome atlas of human cell lines reveals the landscape of kinase activity
papers.abstract: Protein phosphorylation orchestrates cellular signaling and controls most biological processes, with its dysregulation driving diseases, notably cancer. Comprehensive, high-throughput phosphoproteomics remains limited by detection sensitivity, data completeness and computational bottlenecks, especially in low-input settings. Here we present a comprehensive empirical human phosphoproteome resource, regrouping over 200,000 class I phosphosites across 33 diverse human cell lines. We demonstrate that this spectral library dramatically improves single-shot phosphoproteomics with 30-fold faster data processing compared with library-free approaches and enhances confidence in phosphosite localization even from minimal sample input. Integrating proteome and phosphoproteome data, we develop a combined kinase activity score (Cscore), revealing cell line- and cancer-specific signaling vulnerabilities, many correlating with drug sensitivity. This resource accelerates deep and reproducible phosphoproteomics, enables the systematic mapping of cellular signaling networks and may empower precision oncology by highlighting actionable kinase targets in diverse cell states. Koenig et al. present a phosphoproteome atlas of 33 human cell lines covering >200,000 phosphosites, advancing cellular kinase activity scoring and drug sensitivity prediction, providing a resource for cell signaling insights and precision oncology.

papers.title: Vitamin C attenuates primate bone marrow aging at the molecular and progenitor level
Rational design of protease-resistant lipopeptides for combating antibiotic-resistant bacteria
papers.abstract: Proteolysis limits the therapeutic use of peptide antibiotics. Wang et al. develop C12RP7, a fatty-acid-modified Arg-Pro lipopeptide that resists proteases, kills antibiotic-resistant bacteria, shows low toxicity and resistance propensity, and provides oral efficacy through bacterial membrane disruption and host metabolic modulation.

papers.title: In vivo-edited CCR7+IL-7+ DCs reverse T cell exhaustion by promoting T memory stem cell differentiation
papers.abstract: Fu and Ma et al. develop DVH to edit DCs into CCR7+IL-7+ DCs, which target the T-zone within TDLNs and secrete IL-7 to promote Tscm differentiation. The Tscms can self-renew and generate effector T cells under antigen stimulation continuously, thereby killing tumor cells and reducing T cell exhaustion at the source.

papers.title: EZH2-dependent phenotypic plasticity reveals TTP-associated and mTORC1 therapeutic vulnerabilities in lethal prostate cancer
papers.abstract: German et al. use integrated multi-omics analysis to identify EZH2 as a central regulator of prostate cancer phenotypic plasticity. The study reveals TTP-associated pathways and adaptive PI3K/mTORC1 as mediators of response to EZH2 inhibition and demonstrates that co-targeting EZH2 and PI3K/mTORC1 is an effective strategy in aggressive prostate cancer models.

papers.title: Technological prominence alone does not justify leadership in SynCell governance
Malaria durably disrupts macrophage-to-macrophage crosstalk in the spleen
Beyond T cells: B cells in immune checkpoint blockade
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade is usually framed as a T cell-directed therapy. Recent studies challenge this view by showing that B cells, plasma cells, and tumor-reactive antibodies are reshaped by programmed cell death protein-1 and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein-4 blockade and can contribute to efficacy. Humoral immunity should therefore be integrated into models of checkpoint efficacy.

papers.title: Toward adaptive cyborg tissues
papers.abstract: Organoids and engineered tissues have emerged as powerful models of human biology, yet their development and function are often characterized through endpoint measurements that provide only static snapshots of dynamic biological processes. Recent advances in stretchable mesh electronics, developmental biointegration, and organoid engineering have enabled the creation of cyborg tissues with embedded sensing, stimulation, and computational capabilities. This review highlights recent progress in developmental bioelectronic integration, multifunctional tissue mapping, biological state reconstruction, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled cyborg systems. We discuss how embedded bioelectronics can be combined with molecular and spatial profiling technologies to characterize tissue function, developmental trajectories, and biological states. These advances establish cyborg tissues as biologically integrated platforms for regenerative medicine, disease modeling, drug discovery, and adaptive biotechnology.

papers.title: Synonymous sequence design controls the folding, processing, and activity of the therapeutic protein ADAMTS13
papers.abstract: Jankowska, Katneni, Lin and colleagues demonstrate that synonymous recoding of therapeutic protein a disintegrin and metalloprotease with thrombospondin type 1 repeats, member 13 is not functionally neutral as it reshapes proteostasis, glycosylation, and catalytic activity in expression system-dependent ways, revealing that gene sequence design and manufacturing platform form an integrated determinant of therapeutic protein quality.

papers.title: Mechanical regulation of cell memory
papers.abstract: Cell memory describes the capacity of a cell to retain induced biological changes following withdrawal of initiating signals. Accumulating evidence reveals that mechanical stimuli in the microenvironment not only drive immediate structural reorganization in cells and extracellular matrix (ECM), but also can induce long-term changes in cell phenotype and identity. These effects underlie critical biological phenomena, including cell migration, differentiation and reprogramming. In this Review, we present an integrative framework for understanding how mechanical signals modulate cellular structure, identity and function in the context of cell memory. We examine how external forces and the mechanical properties of the ECM reconfigure the structural memory of mechanosensitive molecules, spatial distribution of transcription factors and ECM organization. We offer insights on the mechanical regulation of epigenetic memory, highlighting both mechano-chemical pathways and direct mechanical influences on nuclear architecture. In this Review, Wu, Rashid et al. discuss how mechanical signals regulate the ability of cells to facilitate and maintain changes in cell memory. They exemplify these effects in cellular structure remodeling and epigenetic regulation.

papers.title: Microbial aldehyde-alcohol dehydrogenase degrades metformin to limit therapeutic response in type 2 diabetes
papers.abstract: Zhao et al. show that gut microbial aldehyde-alcohol dehydrogenase (AdhE) degrades metformin, reducing drug exposure and glycemic control in individuals with type 2 diabetes. A clinical trial further demonstrates that the dietary phytochemical daidzein inhibits microbial AdhE and improves metformin efficacy.

papers.title: Post-translational modifications in bacteria: From identification to function
papers.abstract: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) generate protein structure and function diversity. Advances in mass spectrometry have revealed numerous bacterial PTMs, increasing the need to understand their functional purpose. Dale et al. review these modifications and examine their evolving roles in bacterial physiology and pathogenesis.

papers.title: Reversal of the neutrophil barrier for potentiating immune-engineered bacteria therapy in pancreatic cancer
papers.abstract: Guan et al. develop an IAA-assisted engineered bacterial therapy for pancreatic cancer. IAA suppresses neutrophil recruitment and synergizes with gemcitabine to eliminate neutrophils, boosting bacterial colonization and antitumor immune efficacy.

papers.title: A multi-omics analysis of advanced triple-negative breast cancer identifies predictors to chemo-immunotherapy and on-treatment dynamics
papers.abstract: Van Renne, Agostinetto, et al. perform a multi-omics characterization of advanced TNBC to identify response predictors and treatment-induced dynamics during chemo-ICI. Poor outcomes are associated with fibrovascular and myeloid remodeling, highlighting coordinated resistance mechanisms, actionable therapeutic targets, and the value of microenvironment-based stratification for future ICI-based trials.

papers.title: The effects of IFNγ on tissue physiology through structural cells
papers.abstract: Interferon-γ (IFNγ) is classically defined by its potent ability to enhance the antimicrobial and tumour-killing activities of innate and adaptive immune cells, establishing it as an archetypal pro-inflammatory type 1 cytokine. However, as the most conserved of the interferons throughout evolution, it is possible that IFNγ may have a more fundamental physiological role beyond these immune functions. A rapidly growing body of literature now indicates that IFNγ acts extensively on non-haematopoietic, structural cells to regulate organ function, tissue homeostasis and context-dependent immune adaptation. These findings position IFNγ as a primary coordinator of diverse defence strategies, including host resistance, disease tolerance and trained immunity. In this Perspective, we examine how IFNγ signalling in non-haematopoietic cells complements or alters its canonical immune functions and argue that defining the context-specific and cell-specific actions of IFNγ is essential to inform therapeutic approaches targeting IFNγ that enhance immunity while preserving tissue function. In this Perspective, the authors use examples from evolution, animal models of disease and clinical results to explore how IFNγ, a quintessential antipathogen cytokine, also has a fundamental role in tissue homeostasis and organ function through its effects on non-haematopoietic structural cells.

papers.title: Unnatural amino acids program thermoresponsive protein–polymer diblocks into shape-shifting nanostructures
papers.abstract: Incorporating unnatural amino acids (uAAs) programs protein polymers to undergo multistep shape shifting between distinct nanostructures. uAA chemistry and position determine nanostructure morphology and temperature-dependent morphological transitions, while photoswitchable uAAs enable reversible light-driven shape shifting that alters cargo encapsulation and enzymatic activity, opening new possibilities for designing adaptive protein materials.

papers.title: Metabolic engineering of Saccharomyces cerevisiae for the biosynthesis of indole-derived compounds
papers.abstract: Sun et al. engineer Saccharomyces cerevisiae to convert glucose into indole-3-acetonitrile and multiple downstream tryptophan-derived indole compounds. By combining cytochrome P450 engineering with cofactor, endoplasmic reticulum, and precursor-supply and enzyme-mining strategies, they establish an artificial route toward 3,3′-diindolylmethane production and demonstrate the IAN as a branch point for expanding yeast biosynthesis.

papers.title: Cotranslational membrane protein biogenesis by an EMC-bound translocon
papers.abstract: Secretory and membrane protein biogenesis occurs at ribosome-bound translocons in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. Translocons consist of the Sec61 protein-conducting channel and various maturation factors including chaperones, modification enzymes and membrane insertases, which assemble dynamically in response to the biogenesis needs of a nascent polypeptide. In human cells, nascent multipass membrane proteins utilize the ER membrane protein complex (EMC) and the multipass translocon (MPT), but how these factors are deployed during biogenesis is unknown. Here we combine selective ribosome profiling, cryo-electron tomography and site-specific photocrosslinking to reveal the substrate range, timing and mechanism of EMC recruitment. We show that multipass proteins initially engage the MPT for insertion and chaperoning, with EMC being recruited when substrates begin to exceed the cytosolic or intramembrane capacity of MPT. Substrate-engaged EMC is observed at the interface between the MPT’s protected membrane cavity and the bulk ER membrane, where it is poised for insertion, chaperoning and assembly. These results show how EMC and MPT cooperate at the ribosome-bound translocon to facilitate multipass membrane protein biogenesis. The authors use selective ribosome profiling, cryo-ET and site-specific photocrosslinking to show how the ER membrane protein complex (EMC) cooperates with ribosome-bound translocons to facilitate multipass membrane protein biogenesis in human cells.

papers.title: Curved adhesions resist disruption by high-affinity αv-integrin inhibitors
papers.abstract: Integrin inhibitors are drugs designed to block cell adhesion, but they have repeatedly failed in clinical trials. Lee et al. show that these drugs cannot inhibit a newly discovered adhesion structure, curved adhesions, and therefore fail to block cancer cell invasion in 3D, potentially explaining some previous clinical failures.

papers.title: Potently neutralizing and protective human monoclonal antibodies against the measles fusion protein trimer
papers.abstract: Handal et al. isolate a panel of naturally occurring human monoclonal antibodies against the measles fusion protein that potently neutralize in vitro and inhibit viral replication in vivo, demonstrating strong clinical potential. Two antibodies bind distinct portions of the F protein simultaneously with epitopes spanning across multiple F protomers.

papers.title: Structural basis for broad orthopoxvirus neutralization by two antibodies targeting distinct L1R epitopes
papers.abstract: Chen et al. identify two neutralizing antibodies, G4 and B9, targeting distinct epitopes on the mpox virus M1R protein (an L1R homolog). Despite targeting a conventional epitope, G4 overcomes Asp35-associated neutralization escape. Both antibodies protect against multiple orthopoxviruses in vitro and in vivo, supporting their potential as broad-spectrum antiviral candidates.

papers.title: Drugging the immune system: principles of immunopharmacology
‘Trained’ sensory neurons drive allergic sensitization
What the ‘negative space’ tells us about the immunology of multiple sclerosis
p53 keeps a transcription–replication balance that prevents chromothripsis
Coupling and uncoupling cell cycle and metabolism in CD8+ T cells
papers.abstract: CD8+ T cells eliminate infected and malignant cells through coordinated proliferation and effector differentiation, processes supported by metabolic reprogramming that together form an interconnected, cross-regulated network. Emerging evidence indicates, however, that cell cycle progression and effector programming can be transiently uncoupled, with implications for T cell function and fate. Short-term modulation of cell cycle dynamics creates a window for metabolic rewiring, reshaping nutrient utilization, cytokine responsiveness, and bioenergetic capacity. This uncoupling can enhance T cell expansion, effector function, and antitumor activity. Collectively, these findings indicate that the cell cycle functions as an instructive checkpoint integrating metabolic and differentiation programs, not merely supporting proliferation. Understanding this interplay provides a conceptual framework to optimize T cell-based immunotherapies and rationally design chemoimmunotherapy combinations.

papers.title: Advancing mRNA therapeutics from design to delivery
papers.abstract: mRNA therapeutics have emerged as a transformative platform for vaccines and protein replacement therapies, yet their broader clinical and commercial translation remains constrained by challenges in product stability, safety, potency, and delivery efficiency. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of mRNA therapeutic development across the entire product lifecycle, spanning RNA design, manufacturing process optimization and characterization, scale-up and continuous manufacturing, lipid nanoparticle design, formulation, and delivery. Unlike prior reviews that focus on individual stages, we present an end-to-end perspective linking drug substance and drug product development, with emphasis on technological advances over the past 5 years. By integrating these advances, this review offers a practical roadmap for overcoming key bottlenecks and accelerating next-generation mRNA therapeutics.

papers.title: Potentiating immunotherapy in “immune-cold” solid tumors through orchestrating T cell immunity via tumor-specific genetic engineering
Human iPSC models of myocardial infarction: From injury to repair and therapeutic discovery
papers.abstract: Johnson et al. review how human induced pluripotent stem cells can model key stages of myocardial infarction, focusing on cell types involved across acute injury, repair, and remodeling. They examine current model strengths and limitations and discuss emerging applications in therapeutic discovery, patient-specific modeling, and regenerative cardiac repair.

papers.title: Punicalin targets RSV glycoprotein and fusion protein at non-overlapping sites to prevent viral escape
papers.abstract: Xiong et al. identify that punicalin broadly inhibits respiratory syncytial virus subtypes and clinical isolates by targeting the viral G and F proteins at sites outside known resistance hotspots. It retains potent activity against drug-resistant virus and, when delivered by nebulization, reduces pulmonary viral burden and inflammation in infected mice.

papers.title: Multipronged enhancement of CART cell activity against ROR1 neoantigen by inhibition of H3K27 methyltransferase EZH2
papers.abstract: Wang et al. report that inhibition of EZH2 and, to lesser degree, other epigenetic modifiers promotes expression of ROR1 neoantigen on malignant cells. CART cells targeting ROR1 are able to detect the neoantigen at very low concentration and, in combination with EZH2 inhibition, highly effectively eliminate the ROR1-expressing cells.

papers.title: iPSC-derived retinal organoids: Biological insights and progress toward photoreceptor replacement therapy
papers.abstract: Mandai et al. review iPSC-derived photoreceptor replacement therapy, contrasting cone precursor and retinal organoid transplantations. They highlight host-dependent cone integration, gene-edited organoids for enhanced integration, and synaptic rewiring in the adult primate retina, providing a framework to restore vision in patients with untreatable retinal degenerations.

papers.title: T follicular regulatory cell differentiation and functional states
papers.abstract: Follicular regulatory T (Tfr) cells enter the B-cell follicle and germinal center, where they control the magnitude, specificity, and duration of the antibody response. However, the temporal and spatial determinants of Tfr differentiation are incompletely understood. Recent advances in fate-mapping, single-cell transcriptomics, and human tissue analyses have revealed that Tfr cells differentiate progressively through distinct differentiation states, a process directed by follicular helper T cells. Tfr differentiation states have unique transcriptional identities, functional roles, and stabilities revealing intricate feedback loops controlling humoral immunity. Here, we review recent findings on the origins and functions of Tfr cells in mice and humans, how these subsets are intrinsically and extrinsically controlled, and how targeting these pathways may treat human disease.

papers.title: Immunoids: Building immunocompetent organoids from human pluripotent stem cells
papers.abstract: O’Hern et al. review advances in modeling immunity and tissue function using self-organizing hPSC-derived immunocompetent organoids, termed “immunoids.” They outline priorities for advancing the field, including standardization and biologically informed design principles to improve the physiological fidelity and translational value of next-generation models.

papers.title: Systemic delivery of phagocytosis-shielded retroviral vectors enables in vivo HSC gene therapy for sickle cell disease
papers.abstract: Klatt et al. show that phagocytosis-shielded, BaEVRLess-pseudotyped retroviral vectors transduce human hematopoietic stem cells directly in vivo in mobilized humanized mice. Chemoselection enriches gene-marked cells, and erythroid-specific knockdown of BCL11A and ZNF410 derepresses fetal globin to therapeutically relevant levels for sickle cell disease.

papers.title: Functional O-specific polysaccharide-specific antibody responses in young children following Shigella infection in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: Bernshtein et al. show that functional antibodies correlate with milder shigellosis at any age, yet only individuals over 5 years of age mount lasting responses to the surface O-specific polysaccharide that drives Shigella uptake by phagocytes and triggers IL-1β and IL-18 release.

papers.title: Genome-wide cell-free DNA methylation profiling via TAPS for moyamoya disease diagnosis and postoperative collateral formation prediction
papers.abstract: Chen et al. apply multimodal cell-free DNA (cfDNA) profiling via TET-assisted pyridine borane sequencing to moyamoya disease. They identify cfDNA methylation signatures that distinguish moyamoya disease from atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease and predict postoperative collateral formation, supporting minimally invasive diagnosis and preoperative assessment of moyamoya disease.

papers.title: Combining pro-resolving therapy with cyclosporine A restores immune homeostasis and reduces toxicity in autoimmune bone marrow failure
papers.abstract: Grazda et al. show that defective inflammation resolution persists in autoimmune bone marrow failure, despite standard-of-care cyclosporine A therapy. Combining resolvin E1 with cyclosporine A restores immune homeostasis while reducing toxicity.

papers.title: Polyoxometalates for redox chemistry
Polyoxometalates for redox chemistry
papers.abstract: Molecular metal oxides, commonly referred to as polyoxometalates (POMs), are anionic metal–oxo clusters of early, high-valent transition metals that combine atomically defined active sites with reversible multi-electron redox activity. Over the past decade, redox-active POMs have emerged as molecular analogues of solid-state metal oxides and as key components in sustainable energy and catalysis technologies. Their applications span from photocatalysis and electrocatalysis to electrochemical energy storage, redox-mediated electrosynthesis and thermal catalysis. In this Primer, we outline how redox-active POMs are selected, synthesized, characterized and integrated into functional systems. We describe best practices for correlating cluster composition and structure with target functionality, for combining complementary experimental and theoretical approaches to elucidate electronic structure and reactivity, and for assessing cluster speciation and stability under operating conditions. Emphasis is placed on distinguishing genuine molecular reactivity from decomposition-derived but still reactive metal-oxide phases. We further discuss reproducibility, data deposition and the experimental controls needed for rigorous mechanistic interpretation. Finally, we identify the principal limitations of current methods and highlight that atomic-level structural understanding, operando insights and theoretical property predictions are the central drivers towards rational design of POM-based systems for next-generation energy and catalysis technologies. Polyoxometalates (POMs) are anionic molecular metal oxide clusters composed of high-valent early transition metals. In this Primer, Anjass et al. describe how redox-active POMs are selected, synthesized, characterized and integrated into functional systems.
